↑ Extracellular [K⁺] reduces the K⁺ concentration gradient across the membrane → depolarizes the resting membrane potential (more positive).
This inactivates fast Na⁺ channels, decreasing myocardial excitability and conduction velocity.

cards.q: What is the effect of severe hypokalemia on the ventricular action potential?
cards.a:
Hypokalemia decreases conductance of delayed rectifier K⁺ channels → slows Phase 3 repolarization → prolonged action potential duration (APD).
ECG manifestations: QT prolongation and prominent U waves.

cards.q: What is the structural basis of electrical syncytium formation in myocardial tissue?
cards.a:
Myocytes are connected at intercalated discs, which contain:
  • Desmosomes (macula adherens) — mechanical coupling
  • Gap junctions (connexins) — electrical coupling, allowing low-resistance ion flow and synchronized contraction

cards.q: How does intracellular acidosis (e.g., during ischemia) affect myocardial gap junctions?
cards.a:
Intracellular acidosis triggers conformational changes that close gap junctions, electrically uncoupling ischemic cells from healthy tissue.
Consequence: Slows conduction but limits arrhythmia propagation from the necrotic zone.

cards.q: Explain the absolute requirement of extracellular Calcium for cardiac vs. skeletal muscle contraction.
cards.a:
Skeletal muscle: Uses mechanical coupling between DHPR and RyR1 — does NOT need extracellular Ca²⁺.
Cardiac muscle: Requires Calcium-Induced Calcium Release (CICR):
  • Extracellular Ca²⁺ enters via sarcolemmal L-type Ca²⁺ channels during Phase 2
  • This triggers RyR2 on the SR to release stored Ca²⁺
  • Extracellular Ca²⁺ is obligatory for contraction

cards.q: What specific troponin subunit binds calcium to initiate myofilament cross-bridge cycling?
cards.a: Cytosolic Ca²⁺ binds to Troponin C, causing a conformational change in Troponin I and Troponin T, which moves tropomyosin out of the myosin-binding groove on actin filaments, enabling cross-bridge cycling.

cards.q: Explain the dual mechanism by which the cardiac cell clears cytosolic calcium to induce relaxation (lusitropy).
cards.a:
1. SERCA2a (SR Ca²⁺-ATPase): Pumps ~70% of cytosolic Ca²⁺ back into SR lumen (ATP-dependent)
  2. NCX (Na⁺/Ca²⁺ Exchanger): Extrudes ~28% across the sarcolemma, trading 1 Ca²⁺ out for 3 Na⁺ in

cards.q: What is Phospholamban (PLN), and how does its regulatory state change during sympathetic stimulation?
cards.a:
Phospholamban: A protein that, when unphosphorylated, inhibits SERCA2a activity.
During sympathetic activation: PKA phosphorylates PLN → lifts inhibition of SERCA2a → accelerates Ca²⁺ reuptake into SR → faster relaxation (positive lusitropy).

cards.q: What structural protein anchors calcium inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum near RyR2 clusters?
cards.a:
Calsequestrin — a high-capacity, low-affinity Ca²⁺-binding protein in the SR lumen.
Lowers free SR [Ca²⁺] to help SERCA2a pump against a smaller gradient.

cards.q: What is the molecular mechanism behind the positive inotropic effect of Digoxin?
cards.a:
1. Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump
  2. → ↑ intracellular [Na⁺]
  3. → Reduces Na⁺ gradient driving NCX
  4. → Less Ca²⁺ extruded from the cell
  5. → ↑ baseline cytosolic [Ca²⁺]
  6. → SERCA2a loads SR with more Ca²⁺ → larger calcium transients
  7. → Stronger contractions

cards.q: How does an increase in heart rate acutely increase contractility via the Bowditch effect (Treppe phenomenon)?
cards.a:
At high heart rates, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase cannot keep pace with repeated sodium influx from frequent depolarizations.
→ ↑ Intracellular [Na⁺] → slows NCX-mediated Ca²⁺ extrusion → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ loading → enhanced contractility over successive beats.

cards.q: How does PKA (Protein Kinase A) activation increase cardiac contractility and lusitropy simultaneously?
cards.a:
Inotropy (contractility):
  • Phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↑ ICa,L
  • Phosphorylates RyR2 → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ release probability
Lusitropy (relaxation):
  • Phosphorylates Phospholamban → lifts SERCA2a inhibition → faster Ca²⁺ reuptake
  • Phosphorylates Troponin I → reduces Ca²⁺ affinity → faster Ca²⁺ dissociation from thin filaments

cards.q: Why can cardiac muscle NOT undergo tetanic contraction, whereas skeletal muscle can?
cards.a:
Cardiac muscle's action potential duration nearly equals the mechanical twitch duration due to the Phase 2 plateau.
The absolute refractory period overlaps with contraction — a second stimulus cannot be initiated before relaxation begins, preventing tetany.

cards.q: What is the functional consequence of RyR2 mutations linked to Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (CPVT)?
cards.a:
CPVT mutations make RyR2 channels 'leaky' during sympathetic stress.
PKA phosphorylation causes diastolic SR Ca²⁺ leak → activates NCX in forward mode (Ca²⁺ out, 3 Na⁺ in) → inward depolarizing current → Delayed Afterdepolarizations (DADs) → polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

cards.q: Map the four distinct corners of a left ventricular Pressure-Volume (PV) loop to valvular actions.
cards.a:
• Point 1 (Bottom Right): Mitral valve closes → End-Diastolic Volume (EDV); onset of isovolumetric contraction
  • Point 2 (Top Right): Aortic valve opens → onset of ventricular ejection
  • Point 3 (Top Left): Aortic valve closes → End-Systolic Volume (ESV); onset of isovolumetric relaxation
  • Point 4 (Bottom Left): Mitral valve opens → onset of ventricular filling

cards.q: How does an isolated increase in Preload change the morphology of a ventricular PV loop?
cards.a:
Right wall shifts right (↑ EDV) due to more venous return.
Frank-Starling law causes more forceful contraction → ejection reaches same baseline ESV.

Net result:
  • ↑ End-Diastolic Volume (EDV)
  • ↑ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • Constant End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
  • Loop widens horizontally

cards.q: How does an isolated increase in Afterload change the morphology of a ventricular PV loop?
cards.a:
Higher resistance to ejection → ventricle must generate greater pressure, and empties less completely.

Net result:
  • ↑ Peak LV systolic pressure (loop grows taller)
  • ↑ End-Systolic Volume (ESV) — left wall shifts right
  • ↓ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • Constant End-Diastolic Volume (EDV)

cards.q: How does an acute increase in Contractility (Inotropy) shift the End-Systolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (ESPVR)?
cards.a:
Increased inotropy shifts the ESPVR slope upward and to the left.
The ventricle contracts more forcefully and empties more completely.

Net result:
  • ↓ End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
  • ↑ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • ↑ Ejection Fraction (EF)
  • Constant EDV

cards.q: How does an isolated decrease in LV compliance change the ventricular PV loop (diastolic dysfunction)?
cards.a:
The End-Diastolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (EDPVR) curves upward more steeply.
For any given filling volume, diastolic pressure rises faster.

Net result:
  • Elevated end-diastolic pressure with reduced or normal EDV
  • Classic finding in diastolic (HFpEF) heart failure

cards.q: How does the PV loop change in chronic, compensated Aortic Stenosis?
cards.a:
• Loop grows significantly taller — LV generates extreme pressures (>200 mmHg) to overcome stenotic valve
  • Concentric LV hypertrophy helps maintain contractility
  • Left wall shifts right (↑ ESV); right wall shifts right (↑ EDV) due to fluid retention
  • Stroke volume is preserved early via Frank-Starling compensation

cards.q: How does the PV loop change in severe Mitral Regurgitation?
cards.a:
• No true isovolumetric phases — blood leaks backward into LA during 'isovolumetric contraction'
  • Chronic volume overload → right wall shifts far right (↑↑ EDV)
  • Low-resistance atrial pathway → left wall shifts inward (↓ ESV)
  • Net result: Wider loop, blunted vertical borders; ↑ total SV but ↓ forward SV

cards.q: How does the PV loop change in pure Aortic Regurgitation?
cards.a:
• No true isovolumetric relaxation — blood flows back from aorta into LV during diastole
  • Chronic diastolic filling shifts right wall far right (↑↑ EDV)
  • ↑ LV ejection pressure; ↓ aortic diastolic pressure
  • Net result: Giant, wide loop with absent isovolumetric relaxation line

cards.q: What causes the 'a', 'c', and 'v' waves on a central Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) waveform?
cards.a:
• a wave: Right Atrial contraction (after P-wave on ECG). Absent in atrial fibrillation.
  • c wave: Right ventricular isovolumetric Contraction — tricuspid valve bulges backward into RA.
  • v wave: Passive Venous filling of RA against closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole. Giant in tricuspid regurgitation.

cards.q: What event generates the JVP 'x' descent?
cards.a:
The 'x' descent is caused by:
  • Atrial relaxation after atrial systole
  • Downward displacement of the tricuspid annulus as the ventricle contracts and shortens during ejection

cards.q: What event generates the JVP 'y' descent, and how is it altered in Cardiac Tamponade vs. Constrictive Pericarditis?
cards.a:
Cause: Tricuspid valve opens → rapid blood flow from RA into RV.
  • Cardiac Tamponade: 'y' descent is blunted or absent — high external pressure restricts rapid ventricular filling.
  • Constrictive Pericarditis: 'y' descent is prominent and steep (Friedreich's sign) — rapid early filling stops abruptly at the non-compliant pericardial limit.

cards.q: What mechanical event accounts for physiological splitting of S2 during deep inspiration?
cards.a:
Inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure:
  • ↑ Venous return to RV → ↑ RV stroke volume → prolonged RV ejection → delayed P₂ (pulmonic valve closure)
  • Blood pools in expanded pulmonary vasculature → ↓ LV filling → ↓ LV stroke volume → earlier A₂ (aortic valve closure)
Net result: Wider A₂–P₂ separation heard during inspiration.

cards.q: What pathophysiological state causes a fixed, wide splitting of S2?
cards.a:
Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).
The left-to-right shunt keeps RV volume elevated regardless of the respiratory cycle → chronically prolonged RV ejection → P₂ is persistently delayed → respiratory variation is eliminated.

cards.q: What causes a Paradoxical Split of S2, and when does the split widen?
cards.a:
Cause: Conditions that delay LV ejection (e.g., Aortic Stenosis, Left Bundle Branch Block) → A₂ occurs after P₂.
  • Expiration: P₂ moves earlier → split widens
  • Inspiration: P₂ delays → split narrows (paradoxical)

cards.q: What physiological event causes S3, and when is it considered abnormal?
cards.a:
Cause: Rapid deceleration of blood entering a highly compliant ventricle during early passive filling (E wave).
  • Normal: Children, young adults, pregnancy
  • Pathologic in adults: Volume overload from systolic heart failure or severe regurgitation

cards.q: What physiological event causes S4, and what does it indicate?
cards.a:
Cause: Blood vibrating against a stiff, non-compliant ventricular wall during atrial contraction in late diastole.
S4 is always pathologic — indicates diastolic dysfunction from concentric hypertrophy (e.g., chronic hypertension, aortic stenosis).

cards.q: Define the Incisura (Dicrotic Notch) on an aortic pressure tracing.
cards.a:
The incisura is a transient dip in aortic pressure followed by a small rebound pressure rise, caused by the closure of the aortic valve.
The brief backward rebound of blood against the closed leaflets transiently raises pressure at the start of diastole.

cards.q: State the formula for Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) derived from Ohm's Law.
cards.a:
$$TPR = \frac{MAP - RAP}{CO}$$
Where MAP = Mean Arterial Pressure, RAP = Right Atrial Pressure (≈0 clinically), CO = Cardiac Output.

Clinical approximation: $$TPR \approx \frac{MAP}{CO}$$

cards.q: State the Fick Principle formula for measuring Cardiac Output from oxygen consumption.
cards.a:
$$CO = \frac{\dot{V}O_2}{C_aO_2 - C_vO_2}$$
  • $\dot{V}O_2$ = whole-body O₂ consumption rate
  • CaO₂ = arterial oxygen content
  • CvO₂ = mixed venous oxygen content (sampled from pulmonary artery catheter)

cards.q: State the formula for Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) and explain its 1/3 and 2/3 weighting.
cards.a:
$$MAP = DBP + \frac{1}{3}(SBP - DBP) = \frac{2 \cdot DBP + SBP}{3}$$
Reason for weighting: At normal resting heart rates, the heart spends approximately two-thirds of the cardiac cycle in diastole.

cards.q: State the formula for Pulse Pressure (PP) and its two primary physiological determinants.
cards.a:
$$PP = SBP - DBP$$
Primary determinants:
  • Stroke Volume — direct relationship: ↑ SV → ↑ PP
  • Arterial Compliance — inverse relationship: ↓ compliance (arterial stiffening) → ↑ PP (as seen in isolated systolic hypertension of aging)

cards.q: Provide the formula for Ejection Fraction (EF) using ventricular volumes.
cards.a:
$$EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} = \frac{EDV - ESV}{EDV}$$
Normal range: 55–70%

cards.q: According to Poiseuille's Law, how does a 2-fold reduction in vessel radius alter vascular resistance?
cards.a:
$$R = \frac{8\eta L}{\pi r^4}$$
Resistance is inversely proportional to the 4th power of radius.
Halving the radius → resistance increases by $2^4 = $ 16-fold.

cards.q: Write the formula relating blood flow velocity to volumetric flow rate and cross-sectional area. Why is velocity lowest in capillaries?
cards.a:
$$v = \frac{Q}{A}$$
Why slowest in capillaries: Although individual capillaries are tiny, the total integrated cross-sectional area of the collective capillary network is massive — far exceeding that of the aorta — causing velocity to drop to a crawl, maximizing diffusion time.

cards.q: Differentiate Laminar vs. Turbulent blood flow using the Reynolds Number (Re). Give the formula.
cards.a:
$$Re = \frac{\rho v d}{\eta}$$
  • $\rho$ = blood density, $v$ = velocity, $d$ = vessel diameter, $\eta$ = viscosity
  • Re > 2000–3000: Turbulent flow → produces bruits and murmurs
  • Severe anemia reduces viscosity (η), ↑ velocity, promoting turbulence → functional murmurs

cards.q: Write the Starling equation for net fluid filtration across microvascular beds.
cards.a:
$$J_v = K_f\left[(P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)\right]$$
  • $K_f$ = filtration coefficient
  • $P_c$ / $P_i$ = capillary / interstitial hydrostatic pressure
  • $\pi_c$ / $\pi_i$ = capillary / interstitial oncotic pressure
  • $\sigma$ = reflection coefficient for protein permeability

cards.q: How does severe nephrotic syndrome alter Starling forces to cause systemic edema?
cards.a:
1. Massive renal protein loss → ↓ plasma albumin
  2. → ↓ capillary oncotic pressure (πc)
  3. → Loss of the osmotic force reabsorbing fluid from interstitium back into vessels
  4. → ↑ Net filtration (Jv) → interstitial fluid accumulation → edema

cards.q: What is the physiological definition of Mean Systemic Filling Pressure (P<sub>msf</sub>), and what alters it?
cards.a:
Pmsf = equilibrium pressure throughout the cardiovascular system if active cardiac pumping were to stop instantly. It is the x-axis intercept of the vascular function curve.

Shifts right (↑ Pmsf): Fluid infusion, venoconstriction (α₁ stimulation).
Shifts left (↓ Pmsf): Hemorrhage, venodilation.

cards.q: How do alterations in Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) affect the slope of the Venous Return Curve?
cards.a:
• ↑ TPR: Flattens the slope of the venous return curve (blood returns more slowly against higher resistance) — pivots around the fixed Pmsf intercept.
  • ↓ TPR (e.g., arteriovenous fistula): Steepens the slope — blood returns to RA more readily, ↑ cardiac output.

cards.q: Predict where the CO-venous return intersection moves during compensated chronic heart failure.
cards.a:
• Contractility curve shifts down and right (↓ EF)
  • Renal fluid retention → ↑ blood volume → venous return curve shifts right (↑ Pmsf)
  • New equilibrium: elevated Right Atrial Pressure (RAP), borderline-normal cardiac output via Frank-Starling compensation

cards.q: Compare the anatomical location and afferent nerve pathways of the high-pressure arterial baroreceptors.
cards.a:
• Carotid Sinus: Bifurcation of common carotid artery → afferent signals via CN IX (Glossopharyngeal nerve)
  • Aortic Arch: Aortic arch wall → afferent signals via CN X (Vagus nerve)
Both project to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

cards.q: Outline the reflex cascade triggered by an acute orthostatic drop in blood pressure.
cards.a:
1. Standing → venous pooling in lower extremities → ↓ venous return → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ MAP
  2. ↓ Stretch at carotid sinus → ↓ afferent firing via CN IX → ↓ NTS inhibition of sympathetic centers
  3. Sympathetic discharge → ↑ HR, ↑ inotropy, α₁-mediated arteriolar and venous constriction
  4. ↓ Cardiovagal parasympathetic output → further ↑ HR
Net effect: Restored MAP within seconds.

cards.q: Explain the physiological mechanism behind Carotid Sinus Massage.
cards.a:
External pressure on the carotid sinus mimics a sudden massive surge in arterial blood pressure.
→ ↑ Afferent firing via CN IX → Brainstem NTS → ↑ Vagal efferent discharge to SA and AV nodes.
Clinical use: Slows heart rate, stalls AV nodal conduction → breaks re-entrant supraventricular arrhythmias.

cards.q: Contrast Peripheral vs. Central Chemoreceptors in cardiorespiratory control.
cards.a:
• Peripheral Chemoreceptors (Carotid/Aortic bodies):
    • Respond to: Hypoxemia (pO₂ < 60 mmHg), hypercapnia, metabolic acidosis
    • Primary stimulus: Low O₂
  • Central Chemoreceptors (Medulla):
    • Respond to: Changes in CSF pH from CO₂ diffusing across the blood-brain barrier
    • Insensitive to direct pO₂ changes

cards.q: What defines the classic Cushing Reflex triad, and what triggers it?
cards.a:
Trigger: Critically elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP) compresses cerebral microvessels → brainstem ischemia + local hypercapnia → massive sympathetic discharge.

Triad:
  1. Severe systemic hypertension
  2. Reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response to high BP)
  3. Irregular/altered breathing (medullary respiratory center compression)

cards.q: Define Active Hyperemia and list the key local vasodilator metabolites in exercising skeletal muscle.
cards.a:
Active hyperemia: ↑ local blood flow driven by elevated metabolic demand, overcoming systemic sympathetic vasoconstriction via metabolic autoregulation.

Local vasodilators in skeletal muscle:
  • Adenosine
  • K⁺ (intracellular efflux)
  • Lactate
  • CO₂
  • H⁺ (local acidosis)

cards.q: What cellular pathway mediates nitric oxide (NO)-induced vascular smooth muscle relaxation?
cards.a:
1. eNOS converts L-arginine → NO in endothelial cells
  2. NO diffuses into adjacent vascular smooth muscle
  3. Activates soluble guanylyl cyclase → GTP → cGMP
  4. cGMP activates Protein Kinase G (PKG)
  5. PKG → ↓ cytosolic Ca²⁺ + activates myosin light chain phosphatase → dephosphorylates myosin → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation

cards.q: What unique autoregulatory mechanism dominates the pulmonary circulation, and what is its physiological purpose?
cards.a:
Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction (HPV):
Unlike systemic vessels (which dilate with hypoxia), pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar pO₂ drops.
Purpose: Shunts blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward well-oxygenated segments → optimizes ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) matching.

cards.q: Why is myocardial O₂ extraction unique, and how does the heart meet extra oxygen demands during exercise?
cards.a:
Resting O₂ extraction: ~75–80% — already near maximum at rest.
Consequence: The heart cannot significantly increase O₂ extraction during exercise (unlike skeletal muscle).
Solution: Must meet ↑ O₂ demand solely by increasing coronary blood flow, achieved via metabolic vasodilation (adenosine, NO, CO₂, K⁺).

cards.q: Summarize the key cardiovascular metric changes during sustained aerobic exercise.
cards.a:
• Cardiac Output (CO): ↑ sharply (5-fold in trained athletes)
  • Heart Rate (HR): ↑ via sympathetic drive
  • Stroke Volume (SV): ↑ via Frank-Starling and ↑ inotropy
  • Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR): ↓ significantly (metabolic vasodilation in active muscle)
  • Pulse Pressure (PP): ↑ (higher SV + stable/lower DBP)
  • MAP: Mildly ↑ (SBP rises more than DBP falls)

cards.q: Contrast Hypovolemic, Cardiogenic, and Septic (Distributive) shock using CO, SVR, and PCWP.
cards.a:
TypeCOSVRPCWP
Hypovolemic↓↑↓
Cardiogenic↓↑↑
Septic (Distributive)↑↓↓↓/Normal

Key distinction: Cardiogenic shock is the only type with elevated PCWP (pulmonary congestion from LV failure).

cards.q: What ionic currents dominate Phase 0 through Phase 4 of a working ventricular myocyte action potential?
cards.a:
Phase 0 (Upstroke): Voltage-gated fast Na⁺ channels open → massive inward INa.
Phase 1 (Early Repolarization): Na⁺ channels inactivate; transient outward K⁺ current (Ito) activates.
Phase 2 (Plateau): Balanced inward Ca²⁺ via L-type channels (ICa,L) and outward delayed rectifier K⁺ (IK).
Phase 3 (Rapid Repolarization): L-type Ca²⁺ channels inactivate; IKr, IKs, and IK1 dominate outward K⁺ efflux.
Phase 4 (Resting Potential): Maintained near −90 mV by background K⁺ conductance via IK1 channels.

cards.q: What is the primary role of the inward rectifier potassium channel (I<sub>K1</sub>) during Phase 4 of ventricular myocytes?
cards.a:
IK1 maintains high background K⁺ permeability at rest, keeping the resting membrane potential near the K⁺ equilibrium potential (EK ≈ −96 mV).
This prevents spontaneous depolarization in working myocardium.

cards.q: Why do pacemaker cells (SA and AV nodes) lack a Phase 1 and Phase 2 plateau?
cards.a:
Pacemaker cells do not express fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (INa) or high-density inward rectifier K⁺ channels (IK1) found in working myocytes.
Their electrical cycle is driven by slower Ca²⁺ and K⁺ fluxes.

cards.q: What ionic current is responsible for the Phase 0 upstroke in the sinoatrial (SA) node?
cards.a:
Phase 0 in nodal tissue is mediated entirely by inward Ca²⁺ current through voltage-gated L-type Ca²⁺ channels (ICa,L).
This explains the significantly slower conduction velocity of nodal tissue compared to Purkinje fibers.

cards.q: What is the molecular mechanism of Phase 4 spontaneous diastolic depolarization in the SA node?
cards.a: Driven primarily by the funny current (If) — an inward mixed Na⁺/K⁺ current through Hyperpolarization-activated Cyclic Nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels that open as the membrane repolarizes below −50 mV.

cards.q: How does sympathetic β₁-adrenergic stimulation modulate the slope of Phase 4 depolarization in the SA node?
cards.a:
1. β₁ receptors → Gαs → ↑ Adenylyl Cyclase → ↑ cAMP
  2. cAMP binds directly to HCN channels, shifting activation curve more positive → ↑ If
  3. PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↑ ICa,L
Net effect: Steeper Phase 4 slope → reaches threshold faster → ↑ heart rate.

cards.q: How does parasympathetic muscarinic (M₂) stimulation reduce heart rate at the cellular level?
cards.a:
1. M₂ receptors → Gαi → ↓ cAMP → ↓ If and ↓ ICa,L
  2. Gβγ subunits open GIRK (KACh) channels → outward K⁺ current → hyperpolarizes Phase 4
Net effect: Flatter Phase 4 slope + more negative baseline → slower heart rate.

cards.q: What defines the Effective Refractory Period (ERP) of working cardiac myocytes, and what is its main function?
cards.a:
The ERP is the period during which fast Na⁺ channels are locked in their voltage-dependent inactivated state, preventing a second action potential.
Function: Prevents tetanic contraction, ensuring alternating cycles of contraction and filling (diastole).

cards.q: What distinguishes the Relative Refractory Period (RRP) from the Effective Refractory Period (ERP)?
cards.a:
During the RRP, a fraction of fast Na⁺ channels have recovered from inactivation.
A suprathreshold stimulus can trigger an action potential, but it will display:
  • Slower Phase 0 upstroke velocity
  • Lower amplitude
  • Slower tissue conduction

cards.q: Rank the components of the cardiac conduction system from fastest to slowest conduction velocity.
cards.a:
1. Purkinje fibers: ~4 m/s (fastest)
  2. Atria/Ventricles: ~1 m/s
  3. AV Node: ~0.05 m/s (slowest)

cards.q: What structural and functional properties allow Purkinje fibers to conduct action potentials so rapidly?
cards.a:
• Large cell diameter → low internal resistance
  • High density of fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (INa)
  • Abundant high-conductance gap junctions (connexins)

cards.q: What physiological mechanism delays conduction through the AV node, and what purpose does this serve?
cards.a:
Cause:
  • Small cell diameter, tortuous fiber orientation
  • Fewer gap junctions
  • Slow L-type Ca²⁺ channels for Phase 0
Purpose: Ensures atrial systole finishes emptying blood into ventricles before ventricular contraction.

cards.q: How does an increase in extracellular potassium (Hyperkalemia) affect the resting membrane potential of a cardiac myocyte?
cards.a:
↑ Extracellular [K⁺] reduces the K⁺ concentration gradient → depolarizes the resting membrane potential (more positive).
This inactivates fast Na⁺ channels → ↓ excitability and conduction velocity.

cards.q: What is the effect of severe hypokalemia on the ventricular action potential profile?
cards.a:
Hypokalemia ↓ delayed rectifier K⁺ channel conductance → slows Phase 3 repolarization → prolonged action potential duration (APD).
ECG: QT prolongation and prominent U waves.

cards.q: How does Class I antiarrhythmic drug binding alter the ventricular action potential profile?
cards.a:
Class I agents block fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → reduce slope and amplitude of Phase 0 (↓ Vmax).
  • ↓ Tissue conduction velocity
  • Shifts threshold to a more positive potential

cards.q: By what mechanism do Class III antiarrhythmic drugs extend the QT interval on a surface ECG?
cards.a: Class III agents inhibit delayed rectifier K⁺ channels (primarily IKr) → ↓ outward K⁺ efflux → prolongs Phase 3 → expanded overall action potential duration → widened QT interval.

cards.q: What cellular condition triggers Early Afterdepolarizations (EADs) and what arrhythmia can they initiate?
cards.a:
Trigger: Prolonged APD → reactivation of L-type Ca²⁺ channels during Phase 2–3.
Arrhythmia: Torsades de Pointes.

cards.q: What cellular condition triggers Delayed Afterdepolarizations (DADs) and what clinical poisoning causes them?
cards.a:
Trigger: Intracellular Ca²⁺ overload during Phase 4 → activates transient inward current (Iti) via NCX.
Classic cause: Digoxin toxicity or high catecholaminergic states.

cards.q: What is the structural basis of electrical syncytium formation in myocardial tissue?
cards.a:
Myocytes are connected at intercalated discs:
  • Desmosomes (macula adherens) — mechanical coupling
  • Gap junctions (connexins) — electrical coupling, low-resistance ion flow

cards.q: How does intracellular acidosis affect myocardial gap junction conductance?
cards.a:
Acidosis (e.g., during ischemia) triggers conformational changes that close gap junctions, electrically uncoupling ischemic cells from healthy tissue.
Net effect: Slows conduction but limits arrhythmia propagation from the necrotic zone.

cards.q: Describe the process of Calcium-Induced Calcium Release (CICR) in cardiac myocytes.
cards.a:
1. Phase 2: Small inward Ca²⁺ via sarcolemmal L-type Ca²⁺ channels (Dihydropyridine receptors)
  2. This localized influx binds to and activates Ryanodine Receptors (RyR2) on the SR
  3. Triggers massive Ca²⁺ release from SR into cytosol

cards.q: What specific troponin subunit binds calcium to initiate myofilament cross-bridge cycling?
cards.a: Ca²⁺ binds to Troponin C → conformational shift in Troponin I and T → tropomyosin moves out of the myosin-binding groove on actin → cross-bridge cycling begins.

cards.q: Explain the dual mechanism by which the cardiac cell clears cytosolic calcium to induce relaxation (lusitropy).
cards.a:
1. SERCA2a (SR Ca²⁺-ATPase): Pumps ~70% of Ca²⁺ back into SR lumen (ATP-dependent)
  2. NCX (Na⁺/Ca²⁺ Exchanger): Extrudes ~28% across sarcolemma — trades 1 Ca²⁺ out for 3 Na⁺ in

cards.q: What is Phospholamban (PLN), and how does its regulatory state change during sympathetic stimulation?
cards.a:
Phospholamban: When unphosphorylated, inhibits SERCA2a.
During sympathetic activation: PKA phosphorylates PLN → lifts SERCA2a inhibition → faster Ca²⁺ reuptake into SR → positive lusitropy.

cards.q: What structural protein anchors calcium inside the SR lumen near the RyR2 cluster?
cards.a:
Calsequestrin — a high-capacity, low-affinity Ca²⁺-binding protein in the SR lumen.
Buffers free SR [Ca²⁺] to reduce the gradient SERCA2a must work against.

cards.q: What is the molecular mechanism behind the positive inotropic effect of Digoxin (Cardiac Glycosides)?
cards.a:
1. Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump
  2. → ↑ intracellular [Na⁺]
  3. → Reduces Na⁺ gradient driving NCX
  4. → Less Ca²⁺ extruded per cycle
  5. → ↑ baseline cytosolic [Ca²⁺]
  6. → SERCA2a loads SR with more Ca²⁺ → larger calcium transients → stronger contractions

cards.q: How does an increase in heart rate acutely increase contractility via the Bowditch effect (Treppe phenomenon)?
cards.a:
At high heart rates, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase cannot keep pace with repeated sodium influx from frequent depolarizations.
→ ↑ Intracellular [Na⁺] → ↓ NCX-mediated Ca²⁺ extrusion → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ loading → enhanced contractility over successive beats.

cards.q: How does Protein Kinase A (PKA) activation increase cardiac contractility (inotropy)?
cards.a:
• Phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↑ ICa,L
  • Phosphorylates RyR2 → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ release probability
  • Phosphorylates Troponin I → ↓ Ca²⁺ affinity → faster relaxation (lusitropy)

cards.q: Why can cardiac muscle not undergo tetanic contraction, whereas skeletal muscle can?
cards.a:
In cardiac muscle, the action potential duration nearly equals the mechanical twitch duration due to the Phase 2 plateau.
The absolute refractory period overlaps with contraction — a new stimulus cannot fire before relaxation begins.

cards.q: What is the functional consequence of RyR2 mutations linked to Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (CPVT)?
cards.a:
CPVT mutations make RyR2 channels 'leaky' during sympathetic stress.
PKA phosphorylation → diastolic SR Ca²⁺ leak → activates NCX forward mode (Ca²⁺ out, 3 Na⁺ in) → depolarizing current → Delayed Afterdepolarizations (DADs) → polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

cards.q: Map the four distinct points of a left ventricular Pressure-Volume (PV) loop to specific valvular actions.
cards.a:
• Point 1 (Bottom Right): Mitral valve closes → End-Diastolic Volume (EDV); onset of isovolumetric contraction
  • Point 2 (Top Right): Aortic valve opens → onset of ventricular ejection
  • Point 3 (Top Left): Aortic valve closes → End-Systolic Volume (ESV); onset of isovolumetric relaxation
  • Point 4 (Bottom Left): Mitral valve opens → onset of ventricular filling

cards.q: Describe the morphological adjustments of a ventricular PV loop when Preload is selectively increased.
cards.a:
Right wall shifts right (↑ EDV).
Frank-Starling law → ↑ contractile force → ejection reaches same baseline ESV.
  • ↑ EDV
  • ↑ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • Constant ESV
  • Loop widens horizontally

cards.q: Describe the morphological adjustments of a ventricular PV loop when Afterload is selectively increased.
cards.a:
Higher resistance to ejection: Ventricle generates greater pressure but empties less completely.
  • ↑ Peak LV systolic pressure (loop grows taller)
  • ↑ End-Systolic Volume (ESV) — left wall shifts right
  • ↓ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • Constant EDV

cards.q: Describe the morphological adjustments of a ventricular PV loop when Contractility (Inotropy) is selectively increased.
cards.a:
ESPVR slope steepens upward and to the left → ventricle empties more completely.
  • ↓ End-Systolic Volume (ESV)
  • ↑ Stroke Volume (SV)
  • ↑ Ejection Fraction (EF)
  • Constant EDV

cards.q: How does an isolated decrease in Left Ventricular Compliance change the ventricular PV loop?
cards.a:
EDPVR curves upward more steeply → for any filling volume, diastolic pressure rises faster.
  • ↑ End-diastolic pressure with stable or ↓ EDV
  • Classic finding in diastolic (HFpEF) heart failure

cards.q: How does the left ventricular PV loop change in chronic, compensated Aortic Stenosis?
cards.a:
• Loop grows significantly taller — LV generates pressures >200 mmHg to overcome stenotic valve
  • Left wall shifts right (↑ ESV); right wall shifts right (↑ EDV) via fluid retention
  • Concentric hypertrophy helps maintain stroke volume via Frank-Starling

cards.q: Describe the changes on a left ventricular PV loop in severe Mitral Regurgitation.
cards.a:
• No true isovolumetric phases — blood leaks into LA during 'isovolumetric' contraction
  • Chronic volume overload → right wall shifts far right (↑↑ EDV)
  • Low-resistance atrial pathway → left wall shifts inward (↓ ESV)
  • Net effect: Wider loop, blunted vertical borders; ↑ total SV but ↓ forward SV

cards.q: Describe the changes on a left ventricular PV loop in pure Aortic Regurgitation.
cards.a:
• No true isovolumetric relaxation — aortic blood flows back into LV during diastole
  • Chronic diastolic filling → right wall far right (↑↑ EDV)
  • ↑ LV ejection pressure; ↓ aortic diastolic pressure
  • Net effect: Giant, wide loop with absent isovolumetric relaxation line

cards.q: What causes the 'a' wave on a central JVP tracer, and in what common arrhythmia is it completely absent?
cards.a:
The 'a' wave is caused by Right Atrial Contraction at the end of diastole.
Completely absent in Atrial Fibrillation — coordinated atrial contraction is lost.

cards.q: What mechanical event generates the 'c' wave on a Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) tracer?
cards.a: The 'c' wave is caused by Right Ventricular Isovolumetric Contraction forcing the tricuspid valve to bulge backward into the right atrium, acutely raising intra-atrial pressure.

cards.q: What event generates the JVP 'v' wave, and what pathology produces a giant 'v' wave (Lancisi sign)?
cards.a:
'v' wave = passive venous filling of the RA against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole.
Giant 'v' wave: Pathognomonic for Tricuspid Regurgitation — ventricular blood leaks backward into the atrium.

cards.q: What mechanical event is responsible for the 'x' descent on a JVP tracer?
cards.a: The 'x' descent = atrial relaxation + downward displacement of the tricuspid annulus by the contracting ventricle during ventricular ejection.

cards.q: What event is responsible for the 'y' descent on a JVP tracer, and how is it altered in Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a:
'y' descent = tricuspid valve opens → rapid blood flow from RA into RV.
Cardiac Tamponade: 'y' descent is blunted or absent — high external pericardial pressure restricts rapid ventricular filling.

cards.q: How does the 'y' descent change in Constrictive Pericarditis compared to Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a:
Constrictive Pericarditis: 'y' descent is prominent and steep (Friedreich's sign).
The rigid pericardium permits rapid early filling that then stops abruptly when the non-compliant pericardial limit is reached.

cards.q: Explain the physiological splitting of S2 heard during deep inspiration.
cards.a:
Inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure:
  • ↑ RV venous return → ↑ RV ejection time → delayed P₂
  • Pulmonary vasculature pools blood → ↓ LV return → ↓ LV SV → earlier A₂
Net: Wider A₂–P₂ separation during inspiration.

cards.q: What pathophysiological state causes a fixed, wide splitting of S2?
cards.a:
Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).
Left-to-right shunt keeps RV volume elevated regardless of respiration → RV ejection chronically prolonged → P₂ persistently delayed → respiratory variation eliminated.

cards.q: What causes a Paradoxical Split of S2, where splitting occurs during expiration instead of inspiration?
cards.a:
Conditions that delay left ventricular ejection:
  • Aortic Stenosis
  • Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)
A₂ occurs after P₂.
  • Expiration: P₂ moves earlier → split widens
  • Inspiration: P₂ delays → split narrows (paradoxical)

cards.q: What physiological event causes S3, and when is it considered abnormal?
cards.a:
Cause: Sudden deceleration of blood entering a highly compliant ventricle during early rapid passive filling.
  • Normal: Children, young adults, pregnancy
  • Pathologic in adults: Volume overload from systolic heart failure or severe regurgitation

cards.q: What physiological event causes S4, and what does it indicate?
cards.a:
Cause: Blood vibrating against a stiff, non-compliant ventricular wall during atrial contraction in late diastole.
Always pathologic → indicates diastolic dysfunction from concentric hypertrophy (e.g., chronic HTN, aortic stenosis).

cards.q: Define the Incisura (Dicrotic Notch) seen on an aortic pressure tracing.
cards.a:
A transient dip in aortic pressure followed by a small rebound, caused by aortic valve closure.
The backward rebound of blood against the closed leaflets briefly raises pressure at the onset of diastole.

cards.q: Write the equation for Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) based on MAP and Right Atrial Pressure (RAP).
cards.a:
Derived from Ohm's Law (ΔP = Q × R):
$$TPR = \frac{MAP - RAP}{CO}$$
In clinical practice, RAP ≈ 0 mmHg, simplifying to:
$$TPR \approx \frac{MAP}{CO}$$

cards.q: Write the Fick Principle formula used to determine Cardiac Output from total oxygen consumption.
cards.a:
$$CO = \frac{\dot{V}O_2}{C_aO_2 - C_vO_2}$$
  • $\dot{V}O_2$ = O₂ consumption rate
  • CaO₂ = arterial oxygen content
  • CvO₂ = mixed venous oxygen content (sampled from pulmonary artery)

cards.q: Write the equation for MAP based on resting SBP and DBP, and explain its weighting.
cards.a:
$$MAP = DBP + \frac{1}{3}(SBP - DBP) = \frac{2 \cdot DBP + SBP}{3}$$
Reason: At normal resting heart rates, the heart spends ~two-thirds of the cardiac cycle in diastole.

cards.q: Write the equation for Pulse Pressure (PP) and list its two primary cardiodynamic determinants.
cards.a:
$$PP = SBP - DBP$$
Primary determinants:
  • Stroke Volume — direct: ↑ SV → ↑ PP
  • Arterial Compliance — inverse: ↓ compliance (arterial stiffening) → ↑ PP

cards.q: Provide the formula for Ejection Fraction (EF) using ventricular volumes.
cards.a:
$$EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} = \frac{EDV - ESV}{EDV}$$
Normal range: 55–70%

cards.q: Write Poiseuille's Law for vascular resistance and state how resistance changes if vessel radius decreases by half.
cards.a:
$$R = \frac{8\eta L}{\pi r^4}$$
Resistance is inversely proportional to r⁴.
Halving the radius → resistance increases by $2^4$ = 16-fold.

cards.q: Write the formula relating blood flow velocity (v), volumetric flow rate (Q), and cross-sectional area (A). Why is velocity lowest in capillaries?
cards.a:
$$v = \frac{Q}{A}$$
Though individual capillaries are tiny, the total integrated cross-sectional area of all capillary beds is enormous → velocity drops to a crawl → maximizes time for nutrient and gas diffusion.

cards.q: State the Reynolds Number (Re) equation and the significance of a value exceeding 3000.
cards.a:
$$Re = \frac{\rho v d}{\eta}$$
  • ρ = blood density, v = velocity, d = diameter, η = viscosity
  • Re > 3000: Turbulent flow → noise heard clinically as murmurs or bruits

cards.q: How does a drop in hematocrit (Anemia) alter the Reynolds number and change flow characteristics?
cards.a:
Anemia ↓ blood viscosity (η) → ↓ denominator of the Reynolds equation → ↑ Reynolds Number.
Predisposes to turbulent blood flow → manifests as a functional systolic hemic murmur.

cards.q: Write out the Starling equation for fluid filtration across a capillary bed.
cards.a:
$$J_v = K_f\left[(P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)\right]$$
  • Kf = filtration coefficient
  • Pc/Pi = capillary/interstitial hydrostatic pressure
  • πc/πi = capillary/interstitial oncotic pressure
  • σ = reflection coefficient for protein permeability

cards.q: Explain why severe Liver Failure causes widespread peripheral pitting edema using the Starling equation.
cards.a:
1. Liver failure impairs albumin synthesis
  2. → ↓ plasma albumin → ↓ capillary oncotic pressure (πc)
  3. → ↓ osmotic reabsorption force
  4. → ↑ net fluid filtration (Jv)
  5. → Interstitial fluid accumulation → pitting edema and ascites

cards.q: How does filariasis or surgical lymph node dissection cause localized edema according to Starling principles?
cards.a:
Damage/blockage of lymphatic drainage prevents return of interstitial fluid and filtered proteins to the systemic circulation.
→ ↑ Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi) → drives more fluid out of capillaries → lymphedema.

cards.q: Write the compliance equation for a blood vessel and compare compliance between the arterial and venous systems.
cards.a:
$$C = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}$$
Venous compliance is ~20× greater than arterial compliance.
  • Veins: Capacitance vessels — hold large volumes at low pressure
  • Arteries: Stiff, high-pressure conduit vessels

cards.q: How does venomotor tone alter venous compliance and venous return?
cards.a:
Sympathetic α₁ stimulation contracts venous smooth muscle → ↓ venous compliance.
→ ↑ Intravenous pressure → shifts blood from venous reservoir → ↑ venous return to RA.

cards.q: Define the term 'Critical Closing Pressure' of a blood vessel.
cards.a:
The minimum internal hydrostatic pressure required to keep a blood vessel open.
If intravascular pressure falls below this value, inward forces from vascular smooth muscle and tissue elastic fibers collapse the vessel, stopping flow.

cards.q: Write the equation for Wall Stress based on Laplace's Law for a spherical cardiac ventricle.
cards.a:
$$\sigma = \frac{P \times r}{2h}$$
  • P = intraventricular pressure
  • r = internal ventricular radius
  • h = wall thickness
Clinical implication: The heart ↑ wall thickness (h) via hypertrophy to normalize wall stress when pressure (P) rises.

cards.q: What type of ventricular remodeling occurs in response to chronic Pressure Overload (e.g., HTN, Aortic Stenosis) according to Laplace's Law?
cards.a:
Concentric Hypertrophy — sarcomeres added in parallel.
↑ Wall thickness (h) → normalizes wall stress (σ) caused by high systolic pressure (P).

cards.q: What type of ventricular remodeling occurs in response to chronic Volume Overload (e.g., Aortic or Mitral Regurgitation)?
cards.a:
Eccentric Hypertrophy — sarcomeres added in series.
↑ Ventricular radius (r) → dilated chamber accommodates larger volumes.

cards.q: Define vascular conductance and state its mathematical relationship to resistance.
cards.a:
Conductance = measure of blood flow for a given pressure gradient:
$$Conductance = \frac{1}{Resistance}$$
Directly proportional to r⁴ (fourth power of radius) per Poiseuille's Law.

cards.q: How does the parallel arrangement of organs in the systemic circulation affect total vascular resistance?
cards.a:
$$\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_n}$$
Net effect: Total resistance is less than any single organ's resistance → allows independent flow regulation to each organ + reduces LV workload.

cards.q: What is Mean Systemic Filling Pressure (P<sub>msf</sub>) and where is it represented on a vascular function curve?
cards.a:
Pmsf = equilibrium pressure throughout the cardiovascular system if active pumping stopped.
Represented by the X-axis intercept of the venous return curve (~7 mmHg normally).

cards.q: What physiological changes shift the P<sub>msf</sub> intercept to the right?
cards.a:
• ↑ Total blood volume (e.g., IV fluid resuscitation)
  • ↑ Venous tone via α₁ sympathetic venoconstriction

cards.q: What physiological changes shift the P<sub>msf</sub> intercept to the left?
cards.a:
• ↓ Total blood volume (e.g., acute hemorrhage)
  • ↓ Venous tone via venodilators or spinal anesthesia

cards.q: How do alterations in Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) change the slope of the Venous Return curve?
cards.a:
• ↑ TPR: Flattens slope downward — blood returns more slowly against higher resistance (pivots around fixed Pmsf)
  • ↓ TPR (e.g., anaphylaxis, AV fistula): Steepens slope upward — ↑ venous return to RA

cards.q: Where do the Cardiac Output and Venous Return curves intersect under normal resting conditions?
cards.a:
They intersect at the steady-state equilibrium point:
  • Right Atrial Pressure (RAP) ≈ 2 mmHg
  • Cardiac Output ≈ 5 L/min

cards.q: How do the cardiac output and venous return curves shift during acute myocardial infarction?
cards.a:
• CO curve shifts down and right (↓ contractility)
  • Venous return curve initially unchanged
  • New intersection: ↓ Cardiac Output + ↑ Right Atrial Pressure

cards.q: How does the body compensate for chronic heart failure on cardiac output and venous return curves?
cards.a:
• Kidneys retain fluid → ↑ blood volume → venous return curve shifts right (↑ Pmsf)
  • New equilibrium: near-normal CO at the cost of chronically elevated RAP and venous pressures

cards.q: How do the curves shift during an acute, large fluid infusion?
cards.a:
• Venous return curve shifts right (↑ Pmsf)
  • CO curve remains stable
  • New intersection: ↑ Cardiac Output + ↑ Right Atrial Pressure

cards.q: How do cardiac output and venous return curves change in an individual with a large Arteriovenous (AV) Fistula?
cards.a:
• AV fistula bypasses arteriolar resistance → ↓↓ TPR
  • Venous return curve steepens upward
  • Sympathetic compensation shifts CO curve upward
  • Result: High-output cardiac state

cards.q: How does an isolated, moderate increase in myocardial contractility affect the integration curves?
cards.a:
• CO curve shifts upward and to the left
  • Venous return curve remains stable
  • New intersection: ↑ Cardiac Output + ↓ Right Atrial Pressure

cards.q: Contrast the anatomical locations, afferent pathways, and primary triggers of the high-pressure arterial baroreceptors.
cards.a:
• Carotid Sinus: Bifurcation of common carotid artery → CN IX (Glossopharyngeal) → senses both ↑ and ↓ BP
  • Aortic Arch: Aortic arch wall → CN X (Vagus) → responds primarily to ↑ BP
Both project to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

cards.q: Where do baroreceptor afferent fibers synapse in the brainstem, and what autonomic pathways do they activate?
cards.a:
Synapse in the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS).
  • NTS activates parasympathetic neurons (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus)
  • NTS inhibits sympathetic outflow from the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM)

cards.q: Outline the baroreceptor reflex cascade triggered immediately upon standing (Orthostasis).
cards.a:
1. Standing → venous pooling → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP
  2. ↓ Stretch at carotid sinus → ↓ afferent CN IX firing to NTS
  3. NTS removes inhibition on sympathetic centers
  4. ↑ Sympathetic / ↓ Parasympathetic drive
  5. → ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, α₁ arteriolar and venous constriction → BP restored

cards.q: Explain the physiological reflex triggered by Carotid Sinus Massage.
cards.a:
External pressure mimics a sudden surge in arterial blood pressure.
→ ↑ CN IX afferent firing to NTS → ↑ vagal parasympathetic output → slows SA node + delays AV conduction.
Clinical use: Terminates re-entrant supraventricular tachycardias.

cards.q: What occurs during a bilateral carotid artery occlusion experiment, and how does the nervous system respond?
cards.a: Occlusion ↓ pressure within carotid sinuses → baroreceptors interpret this as systemic hypotension → ↓ afferent firing → removes NTS inhibition of sympathetic centers → massive sympathetic discharge → marked ↑ in systemic BP and HR.

cards.q: Where are peripheral chemoreceptors located, what nerve pathways do they use, and what triggers activate them?
cards.a:
• Carotid Bodies → CN IX
  • Aortic Bodies → CN X
Triggers:
  • Hypoxemia (pO₂ < 60 mmHg) — primary stimulus
  • ↑ pCO₂ (hypercapnia)
  • ↓ pH (metabolic acidosis)

cards.q: What triggers the central chemoreceptors in the medulla, and why are they insensitive to direct changes in arterial pO₂?
cards.a:
Central chemoreceptors respond to changes in interstitial pH (H⁺) within brain tissue.
CO₂ crosses the blood-brain barrier into CSF → converted to H⁺ by carbonic anhydrase → stimulates receptors.
O₂ does not readily alter CSF pH → central receptors are insensitive to hypoxemia.

cards.q: Detail the steps and clinical triad of the Cushing Reflex secondary to elevated ICP.
cards.a:
Trigger: Elevated ICP → compresses cerebral microvessels → brainstem ischemia + local CO₂ accumulation → massive RVLM sympathetic discharge.

Triad:
  1. Severe systemic hypertension
  2. Reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response to high BP)
  3. Irregular respirations (medullary respiratory center compression)

cards.q: What is the Bainbridge (Atrial) Reflex, and how does it interact with the baroreceptor reflex during volume expansion?
cards.a:
Bainbridge Reflex: Stretch receptors in the RA sensing ↑ venous return → vagal afferents → medulla → ↑ heart rate to clear the volume.
Interaction: Counteracts baroreceptor reflex during hypervolemia — allows HR to rise despite ↑ pressure.

cards.q: Describe the Bezold-Jarisch Reflex, including its triggers and clinical presentation.
cards.a:
Triggers: Cardiopulmonary receptors in LV wall responding to ischemia, noxious chemicals, or severe hypovolemia → unmyelinated vagal afferents.
Triad:
  • Bradycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Vasodilation
Protects the underfilled, vulnerable heart.

cards.q: Differentiate between the Myogenic Hypothesis and the Metabolic Hypothesis of blood flow autoregulation.
cards.a:
• Myogenic: Vascular smooth muscle contracts when stretched by ↑ intravascular pressure → stretch-activated Ca²⁺ channels → maintains constant flow
  • Metabolic: Accumulation of vasodilator metabolic byproducts of local activity triggers vasodilation to flush them out

cards.q: Define 'Active Hyperemia' and 'Reactive Hyperemia' and distinguish them.
cards.a:
• Active Hyperemia: ↑ local blood flow driven by ↑ metabolic activity (e.g., exercising skeletal muscle)
  • Reactive Hyperemia: Transient surge in blood flow immediately after release of a temporary arterial occlusion — due to accumulated vasodilator metabolites

cards.q: List five primary local metabolic vasodilator factors in working skeletal muscle.
cards.a:
1. Adenosine (from ATP consumption)
  2. K⁺ (from repeated action potentials)
  3. Lactic acid / H⁺ (from anaerobic glycolysis)
  4. CO₂
  5. ↑ Interstitial osmolarity

cards.q: Detail the intracellular signaling pathway of Nitric Oxide (NO) inside vascular smooth muscle cells.
cards.a:
1. Shear stress → endothelial eNOS → NO from L-arginine
  2. NO diffuses into adjacent smooth muscle
  3. Activates soluble guanylyl cyclase → GTP → cGMP
  4. cGMP activates Protein Kinase G (PKG)
  5. PKG → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ + activates myosin light chain phosphatase → relaxation → vasodilation

cards.q: What metabolic vasodilator factor is the primary regulator of coronary blood flow during increased myocardial workload?
cards.a:
Adenosine (along with Nitric Oxide).
↑ O₂ demand → ATP hydrolysis outpaces rephosphorylation → ↑ adenosine → diffuses to vascular smooth muscle → coronary vasodilation.

cards.q: What local factor principally regulates cerebral blood flow, and how does hyperventilation modify cerebral perfusion?
cards.a:
Arterial pCO₂ (H⁺ ions) is the primary regulator.
Hyperventilation → ↓ pCO₂ → respiratory alkalosis → cerebral vasoconstriction → ↓ cerebral blood flow → lightheadedness/syncope.

cards.q: What unique autoregulatory mechanism dominates the pulmonary circulation, and what is its purpose?
cards.a:
Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction (HPV): Pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar pO₂ drops (opposite of systemic response).
Purpose: Shunts blood away from poorly ventilated segments → optimizes V/Q matching.

cards.q: How does the cutaneous circulation regulate heat dissipation during core hyperthermia?
cards.a:
Hyperthermia:
  • Inhibits sympathetic adrenergic vasoconstrictor tone
  • Activates sympathetic cholinergic fibers
→ Widespread cutaneous vasodilation → heat radiation from skin surface.

cards.q: What vasoactive peptide is synthesized by endothelial cells as a potent local vasoconstrictor?
cards.a:
Endothelin-1 (ET-1) — released in response to endothelial injury or low shear stress.
Binds ETA receptors on vascular smooth muscle → Gαq–PLC–IP₃ pathway → profound local vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Explain the 'Autoregulatory Range' in the context of renal perfusion.
cards.a:
The renal vascular bed maintains near-constant blood flow and GFR across an arterial pressure range of 80 to 180 mmHg, regulated by:
  • Myogenic responses of afferent arterioles
  • Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF)

cards.q: Why is the left ventricular myocardium susceptible to ischemic injury during tachycardia?
cards.a:
The LV compresses its own coronary vessels during systole → effective coronary perfusion is limited to diastole.
Tachycardia shortens diastole disproportionately more than systole → ↓ coronary perfusion time → subendocardial ischemia.

cards.q: What is the baseline oxygen extraction efficiency within the coronary circulation at rest?
cards.a:
The heart extracts 75–80% of delivered O₂ at rest — already near-maximal.
Consequence: Cannot significantly ↑ extraction during exercise → must meet ↑ O₂ demand solely by ↑ coronary blood flow via vasodilation.

cards.q: Contrast the vascular filtration properties of glomerular capillaries vs. liver sinusoids.
cards.a:
• Glomerular Capillaries: Fenestrated + negatively charged basement membrane → highly permeable to water/small solutes but restrictive to plasma proteins (σ ≈ 1)
  • Liver Sinusoids: Discontinuous with large intercellular gaps → completely permeable to plasma proteins (σ ≈ 0)

cards.q: What anatomical structure protects the brain from focal ischemia if a single carotid artery is occluded?
cards.a:
The Circle of Willis — an arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain linking:
  • Anterior (carotid) circulation
  • Posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation
Allows collateral blood flow across hemispheres.

cards.q: How does the skeletal muscle vascular bed respond to sympathetic activation at rest versus during active exercise?
cards.a:
• At Rest: Sympathetic α₁ → vasoconstriction → maintains systemic BP
  • During Exercise: Local metabolic vasodilators override sympathetic input (functional sympatholysis) → vasodilation → maximizes muscle blood flow

cards.q: Explain the role of the vasa vasorum and name a pathology that targets them.
cards.a:
Vasa vasorum: Microvascular network supplying O₂ and nutrients to the outer layers of large arterial walls.
Tertiary Syphilis: Causes endarteritis obliterans of vasa vasorum → ischemia and weakening of aortic wall → aortic root aneurysm.

cards.q: What unique capillary structural adaptation forms the physical basis of the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB)?
cards.a:
Continuous endothelial cells joined by high-resistance tight junctions (claudins/occludins) + continuous basement membrane + astrocyte foot processes.
Together, these restrict paracellular diffusion of polar molecules into the CNS.

cards.q: How does high altitude affect pulmonary arterial pressures and right ventricular workload?
cards.a: Low ambient pO₂ → generalized hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) across all lung segments → ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance → pulmonary hypertension → ↑ RV afterload → can lead to cor pulmonale.

cards.q: What mechanism prevents fluid from accumulating in the alveoli under normal conditions?
cards.a:
Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure is kept low (~10 mmHg), well below plasma oncotic pressure (~25 mmHg).
This Starling gradient continuously favors fluid reabsorption, keeping alveoli dry for optimal gas exchange.

cards.q: What specialized vascular structure allows fetal blood to bypass the high-resistance pulmonary circulation?
cards.a: The Ductus Arteriosus — a vascular shunt connecting the pulmonary artery to the proximal descending aorta, diverting RV output away from the non-functional fetal lungs.

cards.q: Define tidal volume (TV). Normal value?
cards.a:
Tidal Volume (TV): Volume of air moved into or out of the lungs during a normal quiet breath.
Normal: ~500 mL (in adults)

cards.q: What is Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)? Normal value?
cards.a:
IRV: Extra volume that can be inspired above tidal volume.
Normal: ~3000 mL

cards.q: What is Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)? Normal value?
cards.a:
ERV: Extra volume that can be expired after normal tidal expiration.
Normal: ~1100 mL

cards.q: Define Residual Volume (RV). Normal value?
cards.a:
Residual Volume (RV): Volume of air remaining in lungs after maximal expiration.
Normal: ~1200 mL
Note: Cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

cards.q: What is Vital Capacity (VC)? Formula and normal value?
cards.a:
VC = TV + IRV + ERV
Normal: ~4600 mL (male), ~3500 mL (female)
Maximum volume that can be moved in or out of the lungs.

cards.q: What is Total Lung Capacity (TLC)? Formula?
cards.a:
TLC = VC + RV
Normal: ~5800 mL (male), ~4400 mL (female)

cards.q: What is Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)? Formula and significance?
cards.a:
FRC = ERV + RV
Volume remaining in lungs after normal expiration.
Significance: Acts as a buffer against sudden changes in alveolar gas composition.

cards.q: What is Inspiratory Capacity (IC)?
cards.a:
IC = TV + IRV
Maximum volume that can be inspired from the resting expiratory level.

cards.q: Which lung volumes/capacities cannot be measured by spirometry?
cards.a:
RV, FRC, and TLC cannot be measured by spirometry.
Require:
  • Helium dilution
  • Nitrogen washout
  • Body plethysmography

cards.q: What is minute ventilation? Formula?
cards.a:
Minute Ventilation (V̇E) = TV × Respiratory Rate
Normal resting: ~6–8 L/min

cards.q: Define alveolar ventilation. Formula?
cards.a:
Alveolar Ventilation (V̇A) = (TV – Dead Space) × RR
Normal at rest: ~4.2 L/min
Most important parameter for gas exchange.

cards.q: What is anatomic dead space? Normal value?
cards.a:
Volume of conducting airways that does not participate in gas exchange.
Normal: ~150 mL (≈ 2 mL/kg ideal body weight)

cards.q: What is physiologic dead space?
cards.a:
Physiologic dead space = Anatomic dead space + Alveolar dead space (ventilated but not perfused alveoli).
Formula (Bohr equation):
VD/VT = (PaCO₂ – PECO₂) / PaCO₂

cards.q: What is the normal V/Q ratio?
cards.a: Overall V/Q ≈ 0.8 (ventilation is slightly less than perfusion at rest)

cards.q: What happens in V/Q = 0 (shunt)?
cards.a:
Perfusion without ventilation → blood passes through lungs without oxygenation.
Examples: Atelectasis, pneumonia, ARDS

cards.q: What happens in V/Q = ∞ (dead space)?
cards.a:
Ventilation without perfusion → no gas exchange occurs.
Example: Pulmonary embolism

cards.q: Where is V/Q highest and lowest in the upright lung?
cards.a:
• Apex (highest V/Q): More ventilation relative to perfusion
  • Base (lowest V/Q): More perfusion, less relative ventilation

cards.q: What is the primary drive for breathing under normal conditions?
cards.a: CO₂ (hypercapnia) is the primary drive → sensed by central chemoreceptors via changes in CSF pH.

cards.q: Where are central chemoreceptors located?
cards.a:
Ventral surface of the medulla.
Respond to changes in CSF pH (indirectly reflects PaCO₂).

cards.q: Where are peripheral chemoreceptors located?
cards.a:
• Carotid bodies (main) → CN IX
  • Aortic bodies → CN X
Respond to:
  • ↓ PaO₂ (<60 mmHg) — primary stimulus
  • ↑ PaCO₂
  • ↓ pH

cards.q: What is the effect of chronic hypercapnia on respiratory drive?
cards.a:
Chronic hypercapnia blunts central CO₂ sensitivity → patients rely on hypoxic drive (peripheral chemoreceptors).
Clinical implication: Giving high-flow O₂ can suppress ventilation in COPD patients.

cards.q: What is compliance of the lung? Formula?
cards.a:
$$C = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}$$
Change in volume per unit change in pressure.
Normal lung compliance: ~0.2 L/cmH₂O

cards.q: What is surfactant and its main function?
cards.a:
Produced by: Type II pneumocytes.
Function:
  • Reduces alveolar surface tension
  • Prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis)
  • Increases lung compliance
  • Stabilizes small alveoli via Laplace's Law

cards.q: What is Laplace's Law for alveoli?
cards.a:
$$P = \frac{2T}{r}$$
Pressure is inversely proportional to radius.
Surfactant reduces surface tension (T) more in smaller alveoli → prevents them from collapsing into larger ones.

cards.q: What disease is caused by surfactant deficiency?
cards.a:
Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (NRDS)
Seen in premature infants (<28–32 weeks gestation).

cards.q: What is the most important muscle of inspiration?
cards.a:
Diaphragm
Innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

cards.q: What muscles are used in forced expiration?
cards.a:
• Internal intercostals
  • Abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, obliques, transversus abdominis)

cards.q: What is FEV1/FVC ratio in normal lungs?
cards.a:
≥ 80%
FEV1 = Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second

cards.q: What is the spirometry pattern in Obstructive lung disease (COPD, Asthma)?
cards.a:
• ↓ FEV1
  • Normal or ↑ FVC
  • ↓ FEV1/FVC (<70%)
  • Concave scooped appearance on flow-volume loop

cards.q: What is the spirometry pattern in Restrictive lung disease (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis)?
cards.a:
• ↓ FEV1
  • ↓ FVC (proportionally)
  • Normal or ↑ FEV1/FVC
  • ↓ TLC

cards.q: What is the diffusion capacity of the lung (DLCO)?
cards.a:
Measure of gas transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane.
  • Decreased in: Emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, anemia, pulmonary hypertension
  • Increased in: Pulmonary hemorrhage, polycythemia, asthma (mild)

cards.q: What is the partial pressure of O₂ in inspired air (PiO₂) at sea level?
cards.a: $$PiO_2 = FiO_2 \times (P_B - P_{H_2O}) = 0.21 \times (760 - 47) \approx 150\text{ mmHg}$$

cards.q: What is the normal alveolar PO₂ (PAO₂)?
cards.a: ≈ 104 mmHg (calculated using the alveolar gas equation)

cards.q: State the Alveolar Gas Equation.
cards.a:
$$P_AO_2 = PiO_2 - \frac{PaCO_2}{R}$$
Where R (respiratory quotient) ≈ 0.8

cards.q: What are the normal arterial blood gas values?
cards.a:
• pH: 7.35–7.45
  • PaCO₂: 35–45 mmHg
  • PaO₂: 75–100 mmHg
  • HCO₃⁻: 22–26 mEq/L

cards.q: What are the 5 causes of hypoxemia?
cards.a:
1. Hypoventilation
  2. V/Q mismatch
  3. Right-to-left shunt
  4. Diffusion impairment
  5. Low inspired O₂ (high altitude)

cards.q: Which cause of hypoxemia does NOT improve with supplemental O₂?
cards.a:
Right-to-left shunt
Supplemental O₂ cannot oxygenate blood that bypasses ventilated alveoli.

cards.q: What is the Haldane effect?
cards.a:
Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds CO₂ more readily than oxygenated Hb.
Facilitates CO₂ loading in peripheral tissues.

cards.q: What is the Bohr effect?
cards.a:
↑ CO₂ and ↑ H⁺ → ↓ Hb affinity for O₂ → right shift of the O₂-Hb dissociation curve.
Effect: Facilitates O₂ unloading in metabolically active tissues.

cards.q: What factors shift the O₂-Hb dissociation curve to the RIGHT?
cards.a:
CADET:
  • CO₂ ↑
  • Acid (↓ pH)
  • DPG (2,3-DPG ↑)
  • Exercise
  • Temperature ↑
Right shift = ↓ O₂ affinity = enhanced O₂ delivery to tissues.

cards.q: What carries most CO₂ in blood?
cards.a:
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) — ~70–90%
Formed via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs:
CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

cards.q: What is the chloride shift?
cards.a: HCO₃⁻ exits RBCs in exchange for Cl⁻ via the Band 3 anion exchanger, maintaining electroneutrality within RBCs.

cards.q: What stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors most strongly?
cards.a:
Severe hypoxia (PaO₂ < 60 mmHg)
Also stimulated by ↑ PaCO₂ and ↓ pH.

cards.q: What is Cheyne-Stokes respiration?
cards.a:
Crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern with periods of apnea.
Seen in: Heart failure, brain injury, high altitude.

cards.q: What is Kussmaul breathing?
cards.a:
Deep, rapid breathing seen in metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA).
Compensatory mechanism to blow off CO₂.

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of CO₂ transport in blood?
cards.a:
• ~70–90% as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)
  • ~5–7% dissolved CO₂
  • ~5–7% carbamino compounds (CO₂ bound to Hb)

cards.q: At what lung volume is pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) lowest?
cards.a:
Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)
Both alveolar and extra-alveolar vessels are at optimal balance.

cards.q: What is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction?
cards.a: Low alveolar PO₂ → constriction of pulmonary arterioles → diverts blood away from poorly ventilated areas toward better-ventilated regions → optimizes V/Q matching.

cards.q: What is the normal pulmonary artery pressure?
cards.a:
25/8 mmHg (mean ≈ 15 mmHg)
Pulmonary hypertension defined as mean PAP > 20 mmHg at rest.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pulmonary hypertension in the US?
cards.a: Left heart disease (Group 2 PH)

cards.q: What is the formula for A-a gradient?
cards.a:
A-a gradient = PAO₂ − PaO₂
Normal: <10–15 mmHg (increases with age)

cards.q: What does an increased A-a gradient suggest?
cards.a:
Indicates:
  • V/Q mismatch
  • Intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt
  • Diffusion defect
Note: NOT elevated in simple hypoventilation or low FiO₂.

cards.q: What is the effect of emphysema on lung compliance?
cards.a: ↑ Compliance due to destruction of elastic recoil fibers → 'floppy' lungs.

cards.q: What is the effect of pulmonary fibrosis on lung compliance?
cards.a: ↓ Compliance due to stiff, scarred lung parenchyma.

cards.q: What is closing capacity?
cards.a:
Volume at which small airways begin to collapse during expiration.
Normally < FRC.
Increases with age and in obstructive disease → contributes to air trapping.

cards.q: What is the primary site of airway resistance?
cards.a:
Medium-sized bronchi (airway generations 2–5).
Not the smallest bronchioles due to parallel arrangement increasing total area.

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on airways?
cards.a: Bronchoconstriction via M₃ muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle.

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on airways?
cards.a: Bronchodilation via β₂ adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle.

cards.q: What is the role of Type I pneumocytes?
cards.a:
• Primary cell for gas exchange
  • Thin squamous cells covering 95% of alveolar surface

cards.q: What is the role of Type II pneumocytes?
cards.a:
• Produce surfactant
  • Act as progenitor/stem cells for alveolar regeneration
  • Can regenerate Type I cells after injury

cards.q: What is the blood-air barrier composed of?
cards.a:
3 layers:
  1. Type I pneumocyte (alveolar side)
  2. Fused basement membranes
  3. Capillary endothelium (blood side)

cards.q: What is the embryologic origin of the respiratory tract?
cards.a:
Foregut endoderm
The respiratory diverticulum buds off the foregut around week 4.

cards.q: When does surfactant production begin in the fetus?
cards.a: ~24–28 weeks gestation; levels peak near term (~35 weeks).

cards.q: What is the most common site of inhaled foreign body aspiration?
cards.a:
Right main bronchus — wider, shorter, and more vertical than left.
Most commonly lodges in right lower lobe.

cards.q: What is the normal respiratory quotient (R)?
cards.a:
R = 0.8 (CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed)
Varies by substrate: Fat = 0.7, Carbohydrate = 1.0

cards.q: What conditions increase the respiratory quotient?
cards.a:
• Carbohydrate-only metabolism (R = 1.0)
  • Hyperventilation (excess CO₂ blown off)
  • Lipogenesis from glucose (R >1.0)

cards.q: Define physiologic shunt.
cards.a:
Portion of cardiac output that does not participate in gas exchange.
Normal physiologic shunt: ~2–5% (from bronchial and thebesian veins).

cards.q: What is West Zone 1 of the lung?
cards.a:
PA > Pa > Pv
Alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure → alveolar dead space.
Normally minimal in an upright lung; increases in hypotension or PEEP.

cards.q: What is West Zone 3?
cards.a:
Pa > Pv > PA
Both arterial and venous pressures exceed alveolar pressure → continuous perfusion.
Dominant at the lung base.

cards.q: What stimulates J receptors (juxtacapillary receptors)?
cards.a: Engorgement of pulmonary capillaries (e.g., pulmonary edema, PE) → triggers rapid, shallow breathing via vagal reflex.

cards.q: What is the Hering-Breuer reflex?
cards.a:
Pulmonary stretch receptors activated by lung inflation → send afferent signals via vagus → inhibit further inspiration.
Function: Protective against overinflation.

cards.q: What is the diving reflex?
cards.a: Facial immersion in cold water → bradycardia + apnea mediated by trigeminal nerve → conserves O₂.

cards.q: What acid-base disorder results from acute hyperventilation?
cards.a:
Respiratory Alkalosis
↓ PaCO₂ → ↑ pH
Symptoms: Lightheadedness, perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm.

cards.q: What is the renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis?
cards.a:
↑ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption and generation in the kidney → ↑ serum HCO₃⁻
Partially normalizes pH.

cards.q: What is the most sensitive indicator of adequate ventilation?
cards.a:
PaCO₂
Normal: 35–45 mmHg

cards.q: What is the normal mixed venous PO₂?
cards.a: ~40 mmHg (normal O₂ extraction by tissues)

cards.q: What is the normal arterial-venous O₂ content difference?
cards.a: ~5 mL O₂/dL blood

cards.q: What is the effect of anemia on oxygen content?
cards.a:
↓ Hemoglobin → ↓ CaO₂ despite normal PaO₂ and SaO₂.
Tissue hypoxia occurs despite normal arterial O₂ tension.

cards.q: What is the oxygen content equation?
cards.a:
$$CaO_2 = (1.34 \times Hb \times SaO_2) + (0.003 \times PaO_2)$$
Units: mL O₂/dL blood

cards.q: What is the primary determinant of oxygen delivery (DO₂) to tissues?
cards.a:
$$DO_2 = CO \times CaO_2$$
Cardiac Output × Arterial Oxygen Content

cards.q: What is methemoglobinemia?
cards.a:
Hb iron oxidized to Fe³⁺ → cannot bind O₂.
Causes: Dapsone, nitrites, benzocaine.
Treatment: Methylene blue (reduces Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺).

cards.q: What is the effect of carbon monoxide poisoning on the O₂-Hb curve?
cards.a:
• Left shift of O₂-Hb curve (↑ O₂ affinity → impairs tissue unloading)
  • ↓ Total O₂-carrying capacity (CO occupies Hb binding sites)
  • Normal PaO₂ and SpO₂ pulse oximetry — deceptively normal

cards.q: What is the treatment for CO poisoning?
cards.a:
• 100% O₂ via non-rebreather mask (first-line)
  • Hyperbaric oxygen for severe cases (neurologic symptoms, loss of consciousness, pregnancy)

cards.q: Define dyspnea.
cards.a: Subjective sensation of uncomfortable breathing or breathlessness.

cards.q: What is orthopnea?
cards.a:
Dyspnea when lying flat (supine).
Classic symptom of congestive heart failure (pulmonary congestion worsens when supine).

cards.q: What is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)?
cards.a:
Sudden awakening at night with severe dyspnea.
Classic symptom of CHF (fluid redistribution from lower extremities to pulmonary circulation when supine).

cards.q: What is platypnea?
cards.a:
Dyspnea that worsens when upright and improves when supine.
Associated with hepatopulmonary syndrome or intracardiac shunts.

cards.q: What causes digital clubbing?
cards.a:
Chronic hypoxemia → release of PDGF and VEGF → periosteal hyperplasia.
Associated with: Lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cyanotic heart disease, IBD, cirrhosis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of central cyanosis?
cards.a:
Right-to-left shunt
Cyanosis affects mucous membranes and tongue.

cards.q: What is peripheral cyanosis due to?
cards.a:
Low blood flow / increased O₂ extraction at the periphery.
Causes: Cold, shock, Raynaud's phenomenon.

cards.q: What is the normal dead space to tidal volume ratio (VD/VT)?
cards.a: ~0.3 (30%) — one-third of each breath is dead space.

cards.q: What increases physiologic dead space?
cards.a:
• Pulmonary embolism
  • Hypotension (↓ pulmonary perfusion)
  • Positive pressure ventilation
  • Emphysema (destroyed capillaries)

cards.q: What is the main stimulus for erythropoietin release?
cards.a: Hypoxia sensed by peritubular fibroblasts in the renal cortex (via HIF-1α pathway).

cards.q: What is the effect of acute high altitude exposure on ventilation?
cards.a: ↓ Atmospheric O₂ → ↓ PaO₂ → peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: What is acclimatization to high altitude?
cards.a:
• ↑ Ventilation (sustained hyperventilation)
  • ↑ 2,3-DPG (right shifts O₂-Hb curve)
  • Renal compensation: ↓ HCO₃⁻ (normalizes pH)
  • ↑ Erythropoietin → polycythemia over weeks

cards.q: What is acute mountain sickness?
cards.a:
Symptoms: Headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness.
Cause: Hypoxia and hypocapnia-induced cerebral vasodilation.
Treatment: Descent, acetazolamide, dexamethasone.

cards.q: What is high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE)?
cards.a: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema due to uneven hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → high-pressure, high-flow areas leak fluid.

cards.q: What is the treatment for HAPE?
cards.a:
• Immediate descent
  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Nifedipine (pulmonary vasodilator)
  • Dexamethasone
  • Portable hyperbaric chamber if available

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypoxemic respiratory failure?
cards.a: V/Q mismatch

cards.q: What is the hallmark of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
cards.a: PaCO₂ > 50 mmHg with respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35).

cards.q: What is the primary treatment for hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD?
cards.a:
Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP)
Improves ventilation without intubation; reduces work of breathing.

cards.q: What is the Berlin definition of ARDS?
cards.a:
• Acute onset (<1 week)
  • Bilateral opacities on CXR/CT not fully explained by effusions or collapse
  • Not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
  • PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 300 mmHg with PEEP ≥ 5

cards.q: What is the most important ventilatory strategy in ARDS?
cards.a: Lung-protective ventilation: Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury (barotrauma/volutrauma).

cards.q: What is the role of PEEP in ARDS management?
cards.a:
• Prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration
  • Improves oxygenation by recruiting collapsed alveoli
  • Reduces FiO₂ requirements

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of theophylline?
cards.a:
Phosphodiesterase inhibitor → ↑ cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation.
Also mild anti-inflammatory effects.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of montelukast?
cards.a:
Leukotriene receptor antagonist (CysLT₁ blocker)
Prevents bronchoconstriction and inflammation from leukotrienes.
Used in: Asthma, allergic rhinitis.

cards.q: What class of drugs is first-line for acute asthma exacerbation?
cards.a:
• Short-acting β₂ agonists (SABAs) — e.g., albuterol (reliever)
  • Systemic corticosteroids — reduce inflammation
  • Supplemental oxygen

cards.q: What is the most common trigger of asthma in children?
cards.a: Viral respiratory infections

cards.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
cards.a:
Exaggerated drop in systolic BP (>10 mmHg) during inspiration.
Seen in: Severe asthma, cardiac tamponade, large pleural effusion, tension pneumothorax.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae

cards.q: What is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia?
cards.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

cards.q: What CXR finding is classic for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)?
cards.a:
Bilateral interstitial infiltrates with 'ground glass' appearance.
Seen in HIV patients with CD4 <200.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other Gram-negative rods; also MRSA.

cards.q: What is the definition of chronic bronchitis?
cards.a:
Productive cough for ≥3 months in ≥2 consecutive years.
A clinical diagnosis.

cards.q: What is the pathological definition of emphysema?
cards.a: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls — without significant fibrosis.

cards.q: What is the most important risk factor for COPD?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking (responsible for ~85–90% of cases).

cards.q: Differentiate centrilobular from panacinar emphysema.
cards.a:
• Centrilobular: Associated with smoking; upper lobe predominant; affects respiratory bronchioles
  • Panacinar: Associated with α₁-antitrypsin deficiency; lower lobe predominant; entire acinus involved

cards.q: What genetic deficiency causes early-onset emphysema?
cards.a:
α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency
Leads to unchecked neutrophil elastase activity → alveolar wall destruction.

cards.q: What is the treatment for α₁-antitrypsin deficiency-related emphysema?
cards.a:
IV α₁-antitrypsin augmentation therapy (weekly infusions)
+ Standard COPD management, smoking cessation, lung transplant in severe cases.

cards.q: What is cor pulmonale?
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy and/or failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pulmonary hypertension worldwide?
cards.a:
Schistosomiasis (in endemic regions)
In the US: Left heart disease (Group 2).

cards.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a: Right heart catheterization (mean PAP >20 mmHg at rest).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (Group 1)?
cards.a:
• Endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, macitentan)
  • PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil)
  • Prostacyclin analogs (epoprostenol)
  • Lung transplant for refractory cases

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome with small cell lung cancer?
cards.a:
• SIADH (hyponatremia)
  • Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH)
  • Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome

cards.q: What is the most common primary lung cancer in non-smokers?
cards.a:
Adenocarcinoma
Most common lung cancer overall (in both smokers and non-smokers).

cards.q: What lung cancer is most strongly associated with smoking?
cards.a:
Small cell lung cancer (~99% associated with smoking).
Also squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: What is Pancoast tumor?
cards.a:
Apical lung tumor causing:
  • Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
  • Shoulder and arm pain
  • Brachial plexus involvement (C8–T2)

cards.q: What is superior vena cava syndrome most commonly caused by?
cards.a:
Lung cancer (especially small cell)
Presents with facial/arm swelling, JVD, dilated superficial veins.

cards.q: What is the most common benign lung tumor?
cards.a:
Hamartoma
Classic CXR: 'popcorn calcification'; coin lesion.

cards.q: What is the most common site of lung cancer metastasis?
cards.a: Brain, bone, adrenal glands, liver

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hemoptysis worldwide?
cards.a: Tuberculosis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of massive hemoptysis in the US?
cards.a: Bronchiectasis or cavitary TB.

cards.q: What is the classic CXR finding in sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) — often with or without pulmonary infiltrates.

cards.q: What is the most common interstitial lung disease?
cards.a: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)

cards.q: What is the characteristic PFT pattern in IPF?
cards.a:
Restrictive pattern:
  • ↓ TLC, ↓ FVC, ↓ FEV1
  • Normal or ↑ FEV1/FVC
  • ↓ DLCO

cards.q: What is honeycombing on HRCT?
cards.a:
Subpleural cystic spaces with thick walls arranged in clusters.
Classic pattern of Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) — associated with IPF.

cards.q: What is the treatment for IPF?
cards.a:
• Antifibrotics: Nintedanib or pirfenidone (slow progression)
  • No steroids (worsens outcomes)
  • Lung transplant in suitable candidates

cards.q: What causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
cards.a:
Repeated inhalation of organic antigens → immune-mediated lung inflammation.
Examples: Farmer's lung (thermophilic actinomycetes), Bird fancier's lung (avian proteins).

cards.q: What is Goodpasture syndrome?
cards.a:
