Anti-GBM (anti-glomerular basement membrane) antibodies → simultaneous:
  • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
  • Pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis)

cards.q: What is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's)?
cards.a:
• c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) positive
  • Upper + lower respiratory tract + kidney involvement
  • Saddle nose deformity, sinusitis, hemoptysis, hematuria

cards.q: What is Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss)?
cards.a:
• p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA) positive
  • Asthma + eosinophilia + vasculitis
  • Peripheral neuropathy, skin nodules

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) — usually from iliofemoral veins.

cards.q: What is the most common ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
cards.a:
Sinus tachycardia (most common).
Classic (but rare): S1Q3T3 pattern.

cards.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing PE?
cards.a: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)

cards.q: What is the treatment for massive PE with hemodynamic instability?
cards.a:
• Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) — first-line if no contraindications
  • Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy if thrombolysis fails/contraindicated

cards.q: What is the most common symptom of pneumothorax?
cards.a: Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea.

cards.q: What is tension pneumothorax?
cards.a:
Life-threatening — air enters pleural space but cannot escape (one-way valve mechanism).
Signs: Tracheal deviation away from affected side, hypotension, JVD, absent breath sounds.

cards.q: What is the immediate treatment of tension pneumothorax?
cards.a:
1. Needle decompression — 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
  2. Followed by chest tube insertion

cards.q: What is spontaneous pneumothorax most associated with?
cards.a:
• Primary: Tall, thin young males — rupture of apical bleb
  • Secondary: Underlying lung disease (COPD, CF, PCP)

cards.q: What is the most common organism in cystic fibrosis-related pneumonia?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (especially mucoid strains in older CF patients).

cards.q: What is the treatment for cystic fibrosis?
cards.a:
• CFTR modulators: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) — most effective
  • Mucolytics (dornase alfa, hypertonic saline)
  • Antibiotics for exacerbations
  • Chest physiotherapy / airway clearance

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in infants?
cards.a: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)

cards.q: What is croup?
cards.a:
Cause: Parainfluenza virus (type 1 most common).
Presentation: Barking cough, inspiratory stridor, steeple sign on AP CXR.
Treatment: Racemic epinephrine, dexamethasone.

cards.q: What is epiglottitis?
cards.a:
Cause: Haemophilus influenzae type B (rare now due to vaccination).
Presentation: High fever, drooling, dysphagia, thumbprint sign on lateral CXR.
Medical emergency — secure airway immediately.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of stridor in children?
cards.a: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis)

cards.q: What is the most common site of aspiration pneumonia?
cards.a: Right lower lobe (when upright) or right upper lobe posterior segment (when supine).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of lung abscess?
cards.a:
Anaerobic oral flora (due to aspiration).
Seen in patients with impaired consciousness, poor oral hygiene.

cards.q: What CXR finding suggests lung abscess?
cards.a: Cavitary lesion with air-fluid level.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of a solitary pulmonary nodule?
cards.a:
Granuloma (healed infection — TB, histoplasmosis).
Most SPNs are benign.

cards.q: What size solitary pulmonary nodule is most concerning for malignancy?
cards.a: >8 mm (risk increases with size, patient age, and smoking history).

cards.q: What is the next step for a suspicious solitary pulmonary nodule?
cards.a:
• <6 mm: Routine follow-up CT
  • 6–8 mm: Follow-up CT at 3–6 months
  • >8 mm: PET-CT or CT-guided biopsy

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pleural effusion overall?
cards.a: Congestive heart failure (transudative)

cards.q: State Light's criteria for exudative pleural effusion.
cards.a:
Effusion is exudative if ANY one criterion is met:
  • Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5
  • Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6
  • Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH

cards.q: What is the most common cause of exudative pleural effusion?
cards.a:
Parapneumonic effusion (most common overall)
Malignancy (second most common)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bloody pleural effusion?
cards.a: Malignancy

cards.q: What is chylothorax?
cards.a:
Milky white pleural fluid with high triglycerides.
Cause: Thoracic duct injury or lymphoma.
Diagnosis: Pleural TG >110 mg/dL.

cards.q: What is the treatment for malignant pleural effusion?
cards.a:
• Thoracentesis (for symptom relief)
  • Pleurodesis (talc — prevents recurrence)
  • Indwelling pleural catheter (tunneled)

cards.q: What malignancy is most strongly associated with asbestos exposure?
cards.a:
Mesothelioma (30–80× increased risk)
Also ↑ risk of lung cancer (synergistic with smoking).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of asbestosis?
cards.a:
• Progressive dyspnea
  • Bibasilar crackles (Velcro-like)
  • Pleural plaques on CXR (calcified)
  • Restrictive PFT pattern with ↓ DLCO

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome in squamous cell lung cancer?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia — due to PTHrP secretion.

cards.q: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
cards.a:
Associated with small cell lung cancer.
Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ acetylcholine release.
Classic: Proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated activity.

cards.q: What is the recommended screening test for lung cancer in high-risk patients?
cards.a:
Annual low-dose CT chest (LDCT)
USPSTF criteria: Ages 50–80, ≥20 pack-year history, current smoker or quit within 15 years.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer?
cards.a:
Surgical resection (lobectomy)
± adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II–IIIA.

cards.q: What is the treatment for limited-stage small cell lung cancer?
cards.a:
Concurrent chemoradiation (etoposide + platinum-based agent)
+ Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) if complete response.

cards.q: What is the most common molecular mutation in lung adenocarcinoma in non-smokers?
cards.a:
EGFR mutation
Targetable with osimertinib (especially T790M resistance mutation).

cards.q: What is the treatment for ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma?
cards.a:
Alectinib (first-line) or crizotinib.
ALK rearrangement = ~3–7% of lung adenocarcinomas.

cards.q: What is Horner syndrome triad?
cards.a:
1. Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
  2. Miosis (constricted pupil)
  3. Anhidrosis (loss of sweating on ipsilateral face)
Due to disruption of sympathetic chain — classic in Pancoast tumor.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bronchiectasis worldwide?
cards.a: Post-infectious (TB, severe pneumonia, measles)

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Kartagener syndrome?
cards.a:
1. Bronchiectasis
  2. Sinusitis
  3. Situs inversus
Cause: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (immotile cilia — dynein arm defect).

cards.q: What is the treatment for bronchiectasis exacerbations?
cards.a:
• Airway clearance (chest physiotherapy, nebulized hypertonic saline)
  • Antibiotics targeting common organisms (Pseudomonas, H. influenzae)
  • Macrolides for maintenance (azithromycin — anti-inflammatory)

cards.q: What is the initial management of massive hemoptysis?
cards.a:
1. Secure airway (intubate if necessary)
  2. Position bleeding side down
  3. Bronchoscopy (localize and tamponade bleeding)
  4. Bronchial artery embolization or surgery

cards.q: What is the CURB-65 score used for?
cards.a:
Pneumonia severity assessment and inpatient vs outpatient triage:
  • C — Confusion
  • U — Urea >7 mmol/L (or BUN >20)
  • R — Respiratory rate ≥30
  • B — BP <90/60 mmHg
  • 65 — Age ≥65
Score ≥2 → consider hospitalization.

cards.q: What is the treatment for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
cards.a:
Voriconazole (first-line antifungal).
Alternative: Isavuconazole.

cards.q: What is mucormycosis?
cards.a:
Aggressive fungal infection (Mucor, Rhizopus) in diabetics or immunocompromised.
Classic: Black eschar of nose/palate; rapidly invasive.
Treatment: Surgical debridement + amphotericin B.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy?
cards.a: Sarcoidosis

cards.q: What is Löfgren syndrome?
cards.a:
Acute sarcoidosis triad:
  • Erythema nodosum
  • Bilateral hilar adenopathy
  • Arthritis
Good prognosis — often self-limiting.

cards.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Tissue biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas (after excluding other causes).

cards.q: What is silicosis?
cards.a:
Nodular pulmonary fibrosis from silica dust inhalation.
  • Upper lobe predominant
  • 'Eggshell' calcification of hilar lymph nodes on CXR
  • ↑ Risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis)

cards.q: What is the most serious complication of silicosis?
cards.a: Silicotuberculosis — silica impairs macrophage function → susceptibility to TB.

cards.q: What is coal worker's pneumoconiosis?
cards.a:
• Simple: Macules and nodules, minimal symptoms
  • Complicated (PMF): Progressive Massive Fibrosis — large conglomerate masses

cards.q: What is Caplan syndrome?
cards.a: Rheumatoid arthritis + coal worker's pneumoconiosis → large pulmonary nodules (distinct from PMF).

cards.q: What is the latency period for asbestos-related diseases?
cards.a:
20–40 years for asbestosis/lung cancer.
30–40 years for mesothelioma.

cards.q: What is the most common benign primary lung tumor?
cards.a:
Hamartoma — 'popcorn calcification' on CXR.
Hamartoma of the lung contains cartilage, fat, and epithelium.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of fat embolism syndrome?
cards.a:
1. Respiratory distress (hypoxemia)
  2. Neurologic abnormalities (confusion, seizures)
  3. Petechial rash (non-palpable, on trunk/axillae)
Cause: Long bone fractures (femur, tibia).

cards.q: What is catamenial pneumothorax?
cards.a:
Recurrent pneumothorax associated with menstruation.
Cause: Pleural/diaphragmatic endometriosis.
Treatment: VATS + hormonal suppression.

cards.q: What is the treatment for recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax?
cards.a: Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) with pleurodesis or bleb resection.

cards.q: What is berylliosis?
cards.a:
Chronic beryllium disease — clinically mimics sarcoidosis (non-caseating granulomas).
Occupation: Aerospace, electronics, nuclear industry workers.

cards.q: What is byssinosis?
cards.a:
Brown lung disease — caused by cotton, flax, or hemp dust inhalation.
Classic: 'Monday morning fever' (symptoms worst at start of work week).

cards.q: What is the prognosis of malignant mesothelioma?
cards.a: Poor — median survival ~12 months despite treatment.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in the elderly?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in lung cancer patients?
cards.a: Metastatic disease

cards.q: What is the overall 5-year survival for all lung cancers?
cards.a: ~25% (due to late-stage diagnosis in most patients).

cards.q: What is amniotic fluid embolism?
cards.a:
Sudden onset of hypoxia, hypotension, and DIC during labor or immediately postpartum.
Mortality: ~20–40%.
Treatment: Supportive (ICU care, blood products).

cards.q: What are the essential amino acids?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: PVT TIM HaLL
Phenylalanine, Valine, Tryptophan, Threonine, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Leucine, Lysine.
Arginine is conditionally essential (required during growth/stress).

cards.q: Which amino acids are glucogenic only?
cards.a:
Most amino acids are glucogenic.
Key ones: Alanine, Glycine, Serine, Threonine, Cysteine, Methionine, Valine, Histidine, Arginine, Glutamate, Glutamine, Proline, Aspartate, Asparagine.
They can enter gluconeogenesis via pyruvate or TCA intermediates.

cards.q: Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?
cards.a:
Only Leucine and Lysine are purely ketogenic — they cannot be converted to glucose.
Mnemonic: LL = Lipo Lovers (Leucine & Lysine).

cards.q: Which amino acids are both glucogenic AND ketogenic?
cards.a:
Isoleucine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, Tyrosine, Threonine.
Mnemonic: I PhyTT (I fight).

cards.q: What is the pKa significance of amino acid side chains for USMLE?
cards.a:
• Histidine (pKa ~6): Only AA with pKa near physiological pH → key buffer and active site catalyst
  • Cysteine (pKa ~8): Thiol group forms disulfide bonds
  • Aspartate/Glutamate: Acidic (negative charge at pH 7)
  • Lysine/Arginine: Basic (positive charge at pH 7)

cards.q: What are the charged amino acids and their one-letter codes?
cards.a:
Acidic (−): Asp (D), Glu (E)
Basic (+): Lys (K), Arg (R), His (H)
Histidine is unique: Imidazole ring; acts as proton shuttle in enzyme active sites (e.g., chymotrypsin catalytic triad).

cards.q: What are the aromatic amino acids and their key derivatives?
cards.a:
Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, Tryptophan (Histidine sometimes included).
  • All absorb UV light at ~280 nm → basis for protein quantification
  • Tryptophan: precursor to serotonin and niacin (B3)
  • Tyrosine: precursor to dopamine, NE, epinephrine, T3/T4, melanin

cards.q: Phenylketonuria (PKU): enzyme defect, accumulation, clinical features?
cards.a:
Defect: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (or BH4 cofactor deficiency).
Accumulation: Phenylalanine → phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate).
Clinical:
  • Intellectual disability, seizures
  • Fair skin/hair (↓ melanin)
  • Mousy/musty odor
  • Eczema
Treatment: Phenylalanine-restricted diet + tyrosine supplementation.

cards.q: Alkaptonuria: defect, accumulation, clinical features?
cards.a:
Defect: Homogentisate oxidase (in tyrosine degradation pathway).
Accumulation: Homogentisic acid.
Clinical:
  • Dark urine on standing
  • Ochronosis — blue-black pigment in connective tissue
  • Arthritis (degenerative)
Relatively benign.

cards.q: What is Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)?
cards.a:
Defect: Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (B1/thiamine-dependent).
Accumulates: Isoleucine, Leucine, Valine (branched-chain AAs) and their ketoacids.
Clinical:
  • Sweet maple-syrup odor of urine/cerumen
  • Encephalopathy, feeding problems, vomiting
  • Early death if untreated
Treatment: Restrict branched-chain AAs; high-dose thiamine in responsive cases.

cards.q: Homocystinuria: causes and clinical features?
cards.a:
Causes:
  1. Cystathionine synthase deficiency (B6-dependent)
  2. Methionine synthase deficiency (B12/folate-dependent)
  3. MTHFR mutation
Clinical:
  • Marfanoid habitus
  • Downward lens dislocation (vs. Marfan: upward)
  • Intellectual disability, thromboembolism
  • Premature atherosclerosis

cards.q: Cystinuria: mechanism and clinical features?
cards.a:
Defect: Defective PCT/intestinal transporter for COLA amino acids:
Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine.
Clinical: Recurrent cystine kidney stones (hexagonal crystals on UA).
Treatment:
  • High fluid intake
  • Alkalinize urine (sodium bicarbonate)
  • D-penicillamine (chelates cystine)

cards.q: Hartnup disease: mechanism and features?
cards.a:
Defect: Neutral amino acid transporter → fails to absorb tryptophan in intestine/PCT.
Result: ↓ Tryptophan → ↓ niacin → pellagra-like symptoms.
Clinical: 3 Ds (Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia) + cerebellar ataxia (with poor diet).
Treatment: High-protein diet + nicotinamide supplementation.

cards.q: What stabilizes each level of protein structure?
cards.a:
• Primary: Peptide bonds (covalent)
  • Secondary: Hydrogen bonds (α-helix, β-sheet)
  • Tertiary: Hydrophobic interactions, H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds
  • Quaternary: Same forces as tertiary, between subunits

cards.q: What is the difference between α-helix and β-sheet secondary structures?
cards.a:
α-helix:
  • Right-handed coil
  • H-bonds between every 4th residue (n → n+4)
  • ~3.6 residues/turn
β-sheet:
  • Parallel: Same direction, weaker H-bonds
  • Antiparallel: Opposite direction, stronger H-bonds
Collagen: Left-handed triple helix (unique — not a standard α-helix).

cards.q: What is protein denaturation vs. renaturation?
cards.a:
Denaturation: Disruption of 2°/3°/4° structure (NOT primary peptide bonds) by heat, extreme pH, organic solvents, reducing agents.
Renaturation: Proteins can refold spontaneously if primary structure is intact; aided by chaperones in vivo.

cards.q: What are molecular chaperones? Give examples.
cards.a:
Proteins that assist in proper folding and prevent inappropriate aggregation.
  • Hsp70 (BiP): Binds unfolded chains co-translationally in cytoplasm/ER
  • Hsp90: Stabilizes steroid hormone receptors
  • GroEL/GroES (Hsp60): Barrel-shaped; encloses misfolded protein for refolding
Ubiquitin tags misfolded proteins for proteasomal degradation.

cards.q: What are amyloid diseases? Give examples.
cards.a:
Diseases caused by misfolded proteins that aggregate into insoluble β-pleated sheet fibrils (amyloid).
  • AL amyloid: Light chains — multiple myeloma
  • AA amyloid: Serum amyloid A — chronic inflammation
  • Aβ: APP cleavage → Alzheimer's disease plaques
  • TTR (Transthyretin): Senile cardiac amyloidosis

cards.q: What is collagen structure, synthesis, and key associated diseases?
cards.a:
Structure: Triple helix of 3 α-chains; Gly-X-Y repeats (X = Pro, Y = Hydroxyproline).
Synthesis: Fibroblasts → procollagen → cleaved → tropocollagen → cross-linked fibrils.
Diseases:
  • Scurvy: Vit C deficiency → impaired hydroxylation of Pro/Lys → weak collagen
  • Osteogenesis Imperfecta: Type I collagen mutation → brittle bones, blue sclerae
  • Ehlers-Danlos: Collagen synthesis/processing defect → hyperextensible skin, joint laxity

cards.q: Define Km and Vmax. What does a high Km indicate?
cards.a:
• Km: Substrate concentration at which V = ½ Vmax; reflects enzyme-substrate affinity
  • Vmax: Maximum reaction velocity; proportional to enzyme concentration
  • High Km = low affinity (needs more substrate to reach half-maximal rate)
  • Low Km = high affinity

cards.q: What does a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot show?
cards.a:
Plots 1/V vs. 1/[S] → straight line.
  • X-intercept = −1/Km
  • Y-intercept = 1/Vmax
  • Slope = Km/Vmax
Used to distinguish inhibitor types by how they shift the intercepts.

cards.q: Compare Competitive, Non-competitive, and Uncompetitive inhibition effects on Km and Vmax.
cards.a:
TypeKmVmax
Competitive↑No change
Non-competitiveNo change↓
Uncompetitive↓↓

Competitive inhibition is overcome by ↑ substrate; non-competitive is NOT.

cards.q: What is allosteric regulation of enzymes?
cards.a:
Binding of a molecule to a non-active site (allosteric site) changes enzyme conformation and activity.
  • Positive allosteric activator: ↑ enzyme activity (e.g., AMP activates PFK-1)
  • Negative allosteric inhibitor: ↓ enzyme activity (e.g., ATP/citrate inhibit PFK-1)
Kinetics: Sigmoidal V vs. [S] curve (cooperative binding).

cards.q: What is feedback inhibition? Give a metabolic example.
cards.a:
The end product of a pathway inhibits an early enzyme (usually the first committed/rate-limiting step).
  • UTP inhibits CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis
  • Cholesterol inhibits HMG-CoA reductase
  • ATP/citrate inhibit PFK-1 in glycolysis
Prevents overproduction; highly efficient regulatory strategy.

cards.q: What is a zymogen (proenzyme)? Give clinical examples.
cards.a:
An inactive enzyme precursor activated by proteolytic cleavage.
  • Pepsinogen → Pepsin (stomach acid)
  • Trypsinogen → Trypsin (enteropeptidase)
  • Prothrombin → Thrombin (coagulation)
  • Chymotrypsinogen → Chymotrypsin
Protects the synthesizing cell from self-digestion.

cards.q: Fat-soluble vitamins (ADEK): functions, deficiency, toxicity?
cards.a:
• A (Retinol): Vision (rhodopsin), epithelial integrity. Def: Night blindness, xerophthalmia. Tox: Teratogenic, pseudotumor cerebri
  • D (Calcitriol): Ca/PO₄ absorption. Def: Rickets/osteomalacia. Tox: Hypercalcemia
  • E (Tocopherol): Antioxidant. Def: Hemolytic anemia, spinocerebellar ataxia
  • K: Clotting factors II, VII, IX, X; Protein C/S. Def: Bleeding (↑PT/PTT)

cards.q: B1 (Thiamine): function, deficiency syndromes, cofactor role?
cards.a:
Active form: TPP (Thiamine Pyrophosphate).
Key enzyme cofactor for:
  • Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH)
  • α-KG dehydrogenase
  • Transketolase (HMP shunt)
  • Branched-chain AA dehydrogenase (MSUD)
Deficiency:
  • Wet Beriberi: High-output heart failure, edema
  • Dry Beriberi: Peripheral neuropathy
  • Wernicke-Korsakoff (alcoholism): Confusion, ataxia, nystagmus → amnesia, confabulation

cards.q: B2 (Riboflavin): function and deficiency?
cards.a:
Function: Precursor of FAD and FMN — electron carriers in redox reactions (ETC, TCA cycle, fatty acid oxidation).
Deficiency (the 3 Cs):
  • Cheilosis (lip fissures)
  • Corneal vascularization
  • Angular Cheilitis/stomatitis
Also: Photophobia, glossitis.

cards.q: B3 (Niacin): function, deficiency (Pellagra), and pharmacologic use?
cards.a:
Function: Precursor of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ — electron carriers in >200 redox reactions.
Synthesis: From Tryptophan (requires B2, B6).
Deficiency → Pellagra:
  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis (photosensitive rash)
  • Dementia
  • Death (if untreated)
Drug use: High-dose niacin → ↑ HDL, ↓ LDL/VLDL/TG. Side effect: Flushing (prostaglandin-mediated; blocked by aspirin).

cards.q: B5 (Pantothenic acid): function and deficiency?
cards.a:
Function: Component of Coenzyme A (CoA) and Acyl Carrier Protein (ACP).
Essential for:
  • Fatty acid synthesis/oxidation
  • TCA cycle (acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA)
  • Steroid and heme synthesis
Deficiency: Rare; 'Burning feet' syndrome, dermatitis, enteritis, alopecia.

cards.q: B6 (Pyridoxine): function, deficiency, and drug interactions?
cards.a:
Active form: Pyridoxal Phosphate (PLP).
Functions:
  • Transamination (ALT, AST)
  • Decarboxylation (neurotransmitters: serotonin, GABA, dopamine)
  • Heme synthesis (ALA synthase)
  • Glycogenolysis (glycogen phosphorylase)
Deficiency: Sideroblastic anemia, peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, seizures (↓ GABA).
Drug interaction: Isoniazid (INH) depletes B6 → supplement B6 with INH therapy.

cards.q: B7 (Biotin): function, deficiency, and avidin connection?
cards.a:
Function: Cofactor for carboxylase enzymes (CO₂ transfer):
  • Pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → OAA)
  • Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA)
  • Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Deficiency: Dermatitis, alopecia, enteritis.
Cause: Raw egg white consumption — avidin binds biotin → prevents absorption.

cards.q: B9 (Folate): function, deficiency, and neural tube defects?
cards.a:
Active form: THF (Tetrahydrofolate).
Function: 1-carbon transfer reactions; purine and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.
Deficiency:
  • Megaloblastic anemia (↑ MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils)
  • Glossitis
  • Neural Tube Defects (NTDs) — spina bifida, anencephaly
Drug blocks: Methotrexate, Trimethoprim, Pyrimethamine inhibit DHFR → ↓ THF.

cards.q: B12 (Cobalamin): function, deficiency, and absorption pathway?
cards.a:
Functions (2):
  1. Methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine; requires THF recycling)
  2. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA)
Deficiency:
  • Megaloblastic anemia
  • Subacute combined degeneration (posterior + lateral spinal columns)
  • Peripheral neuropathy
Absorption: Requires Intrinsic Factor (IF) from gastric parietal cells → terminal ileum.
Causes: Pernicious anemia (anti-IF Ab), Crohn's (terminal ileum), strict veganism, gastrectomy.

cards.q: Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid): functions and deficiency (Scurvy)?
cards.a:
Functions:
  1. Hydroxylation of Pro/Lys in collagen synthesis
  2. Antioxidant
  3. Enhances iron absorption (Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺)
  4. Dopamine β-hydroxylase cofactor (NE synthesis)
Scurvy:
  • Perifollicular hemorrhage
  • Gingival bleeding
  • Poor wound healing
  • 'Corkscrew' hair
  • Splinter hemorrhages

cards.q: Outline the key steps and regulation of glycolysis.
cards.a:
Location: Cytoplasm.
Regulated enzymes:
  1. Hexokinase/Glucokinase — step 1 (glucose → G-6-P)
  2. PFK-1 (rate-limiting): ↑ by AMP, F-2,6-BP; ↓ by ATP, citrate
  3. Pyruvate kinase: ↑ by F-1,6-BP; ↓ by ATP, alanine
Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 Pyruvate.

cards.q: Hexokinase vs. Glucokinase: key differences?
cards.a:
PropertyHexokinaseGlucokinase
LocationAll tissuesLiver, β-cells
KmLow (high affinity)High (low affinity)
VmaxLowHigh
Inhibited by G-6-P?YesNo
Induced by insulin?NoYes

Glucokinase acts as a glucose sensor in β-cells and liver.

cards.q: What is the Warburg effect?
cards.a:
Cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis — converting glucose → lactate even in the presence of O₂.
Why: Provides biosynthetic precursors for rapidly dividing cells; generates NADPH via HMP shunt.
Clinical use: Basis for ¹⁸F-FDG PET scans — tumors take up more glucose and light up on imaging.

cards.q: What is the Cori cycle?
cards.a:
Metabolic cycle between muscle/RBCs and liver:
  1. Exercising muscle: glucose → lactate (anaerobic glycolysis)
  2. Lactate travels to liver via blood
  3. Liver: lactate → pyruvate → glucose (gluconeogenesis)
  4. Glucose returns to muscle
Purpose: Regenerates glucose; prevents lactic acidosis.
Net: Transfers the energy burden (6 ATP cost) to the liver.

cards.q: What is the Glucose-Alanine (Cahill) Cycle?
cards.a:
Analogous to the Cori cycle but uses alanine as the carrier:
  1. Muscle: Pyruvate + glutamate → alanine (via ALT) + α-KG
  2. Alanine travels to liver
  3. Liver: Alanine → pyruvate + glutamate → glucose + urea
Purpose: Transfers amino groups from muscle to liver for urea synthesis; glucose precursor for muscle.

cards.q: What enzyme deficiency causes hemolytic anemia in glycolysis? Mechanism?
cards.a:
Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency — most common glycolytic enzyme deficiency causing hemolytic anemia.
  • RBCs rely entirely on glycolysis for ATP
  • ↓ PK → ↓ ATP → membrane pump failure → hemolysis
  • ↑ 2,3-BPG (substrate accumulates) → right-shifted O₂ curve — protective
Labs: ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin.

cards.q: List the TCA cycle key steps, cofactors, and products per turn.
cards.a:
Location: Mitochondrial matrix.
Key enzymes:
  • Citrate synthase: OAA + Acetyl-CoA → Citrate
  • Isocitrate dehydrogenase: → α-KG + CO₂ + NADH (regulated: ↑ ADP; ↓ ATP, NADH)
  • α-KG dehydrogenase: → Succinyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH (requires B1, B2, B3, B5, lipoic acid)
  • Succinate dehydrogenase: → Fumarate + FADH₂ (only TCA enzyme in inner mitochondrial membrane = Complex II)
  • Malate dehydrogenase: → OAA + NADH
Per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂.

cards.q: What is the net ATP yield per glucose molecule (aerobic respiration)?
cards.a:
• Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH (cytoplasmic)
  • PDH: 2 NADH (mitochondrial)
  • TCA (×2): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 GTP
  • ETC: NADH → ~2.5 ATP; FADH₂ → ~1.5 ATP
Modern estimate: ~30–32 ATP total per glucose.
Classic textbook value: 36–38 ATP (older calculation).

cards.q: What is the PDH complex? What inhibits and activates it?
cards.a:
Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH): Converts pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA (irreversible); links glycolysis to TCA.
Cofactors (Tender Loving Care For Nancy): B1 (TPP), B2 (FAD), B3 (NAD), B5 (CoA), Lipoic acid.
Inhibited by: Acetyl-CoA, NADH, ATP (products); PDH kinase.
Activated by: CoA, NAD⁺, pyruvate (substrates); Insulin, Ca²⁺, ADP.

cards.q: PDH deficiency: presentation and treatment?
cards.a:
Defect: PDH complex deficiency (most common: E1 subunit — thiamine-dependent).
Result: Cannot make acetyl-CoA; pyruvate → lactate + alanine.
Clinical:
  • Lactic acidosis
  • Neurological defects (brain needs acetyl-CoA for energy)
  • Elevated pyruvate
Treatment: High-fat, low-carbohydrate diet (ketone bodies as CNS fuel); thiamine supplementation.

cards.q: What are the substrates and unique enzymes of gluconeogenesis?
cards.a:
Location: Liver (mainly), renal cortex.
Substrates (GLAP): Glycerol, Lactate, Amino acids (glucogenic), Propionate.
Unique enzymes (not in glycolysis):
  1. Pyruvate carboxylase (mito): Pyruvate → OAA (requires biotin; activated by acetyl-CoA)
  2. PEPCK: OAA → PEP (requires GTP)
  3. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: F-1,6-BP → F-6-P
  4. Glucose-6-phosphatase (ER): G-6-P → Glucose (only liver/kidney)

cards.q: What inhibits and activates gluconeogenesis?
cards.a:
Activated by:
  • Glucagon, cortisol, epinephrine (fasting hormones)
  • NADH, acetyl-CoA (activate pyruvate carboxylase)
Inhibited by:
  • Insulin
  • AMP (activates AMPK → inhibits GNG)
  • Alcohol (↑ NADH depletes OAA and pyruvate substrates)
Key concept: Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are reciprocally regulated.

cards.q: Why can't fatty acids (even-chain) be converted to glucose in humans?
cards.a:
• Fatty acid β-oxidation generates Acetyl-CoA
  • Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to pyruvate or OAA (PDH reaction is irreversible)
  • Therefore even-chain fatty acids provide no net glucose
Exceptions:
  • Odd-chain FA: → Propionyl-CoA → Succinyl-CoA → TCA → OAA → glucose
  • Glycerol (from TG backbone) → glucose via DHAP

cards.q: Glycogen synthesis: key enzymes and steps?
cards.a:
Location: Liver (glucose buffer) and muscle (energy reserve).
Steps:
  1. G-6-P → G-1-P (Phosphoglucomutase)
  2. G-1-P + UTP → UDP-Glucose (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase)
  3. UDP-Glucose added by Glycogen synthase (α-1,4 links)
  4. Branching enzyme adds α-1,6 branches
Primer: Glycogenin (self-glucosylating).
Regulation: Insulin activates; glucagon/epinephrine inhibit via PKA.

cards.q: Glycogen degradation: key enzymes?
cards.a:
Steps:
  1. Glycogen phosphorylase (requires B6/PLP): Cleaves α-1,4 bonds → G-1-P
  2. Debranching enzyme: Cleaves α-1,6 branches → free glucose
  3. G-1-P → G-6-P (Phosphoglucomutase)
  4. G-6-P → Glucose via Glucose-6-phosphatase (only in liver/kidney — muscle lacks this)
Regulation: Glucagon/Epi → PKA → phosphorylation → activates phosphorylase; Insulin → inactivates.

cards.q: Glycogen storage diseases: types, enzyme defects, and features?
cards.a:
DiseaseEnzymeKey Feature
Von Gierke (I)G-6-PaseHypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, ↑ uric acid/lipids
Pompe (II)α-1,4-glucosidase (lysosomal)Cardiomegaly, hypotonia — 'Pompe destroys the Pump'
Cori (III)Debranching enzymeMilder Von Gierke variant
McArdle (V)Muscle phosphorylasePainful cramps, myoglobinuria with exercise

cards.q: What is the HMP shunt (Pentose Phosphate Pathway)? Purpose and location?
cards.a:
Location: Cytoplasm.
Active tissues: Liver, RBCs, adrenal cortex, testes, mammary glands.
Products (no ATP generated):
  • NADPH — reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense
  • Ribose-5-phosphate — nucleotide synthesis
Rate-limiting enzyme: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD).

cards.q: G6PD deficiency: pathophysiology, triggers, and presentation?
cards.a:
Inheritance: X-linked recessive.
Pathophysiology: ↓ NADPH → ↓ Glutathione (GSH) → oxidative stress → Heinz body formation → hemolytic anemia.
Triggers: Primaquine, Dapsone, Sulfonamides, Nitrofurantoin, Fava beans, infection.
Labs: Bite cells, Heinz bodies, ↑ indirect bilirubin.
Note: Most common enzyme deficiency worldwide; protective against malaria.

cards.q: What is NADPH used for in the body?
cards.a:
• Fatty acid synthesis (FAS enzyme)
  • Cholesterol synthesis
  • Glutathione reduction (GSH — antioxidant defense in RBCs)
  • Respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase in neutrophils → superoxide)
  • Cytochrome P450 reactions (drug metabolism)
  • Nitric oxide synthesis (NOS)
CGD = NADPH oxidase defect → no respiratory burst → recurrent catalase+ infections.

cards.q: Fatty acid synthesis: location, rate-limiting enzyme, and cofactors?
cards.a:
Location: Cytoplasm (liver, mammary gland, adipose).
Rate-limiting enzyme: Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase (ACC) — requires biotin.
  • Activated by: Insulin, citrate
  • Inhibited by: Glucagon, epinephrine, palmitate, AMPK
Process: Acetyl-CoA + CO₂ → Malonyl-CoA → fatty acid chain elongation by FAS using NADPH.

cards.q: How does Acetyl-CoA exit the mitochondria for fatty acid synthesis (Citrate Shuttle)?
cards.a:
1. Acetyl-CoA + OAA → Citrate (inside mitochondria)
  2. Citrate exits to cytoplasm via citrate transporter
  3. ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate → Acetyl-CoA + OAA (cytoplasm)
  4. OAA → malate → pyruvate, generating NADPH for fatty acid synthesis

cards.q: β-Oxidation of fatty acids: steps, location, and yield?
cards.a:
Location: Mitochondrial matrix (carnitine shuttle required for entry).
Steps per cycle:
  1. Oxidation (FAD → FADH₂)
  2. Hydration
  3. Oxidation (NAD⁺ → NADH)
  4. Thiolysis → Acetyl-CoA released, chain shortened by 2C
Example — Palmitate (16C): 7 cycles → 8 Acetyl-CoA → ~106 ATP total.

cards.q: Carnitine shuttle: function and deficiency?
cards.a:
Function: Transports long-chain fatty acids from cytoplasm into mitochondria for β-oxidation.
Steps: Fatty acyl-CoA + Carnitine → Acylcarnitine (via CPT-I) → crosses inner membrane → CoA reattaches (CPT-II).
CPT-I inhibited by Malonyl-CoA (prevents FA oxidation when synthesis is active).
Carnitine deficiency: Weakness, hypoglycemia, hypoketosis, cardiomyopathy.

cards.q: Ketone body synthesis (ketogenesis): when, where, and products?
cards.a:
When: Fasting, starvation, DKA, prolonged exercise.
Where: Liver mitochondria (only; liver cannot use its own ketones — lacks thiophorase).
Substrate: Acetyl-CoA (from β-oxidation).
Products:
  • Acetoacetate
  • β-Hydroxybutyrate (major ketone in blood)
  • Acetone (volatile; fruity breath)
Ketolysis: Brain/heart/muscle use succinyl-CoA + thiophorase → Acetyl-CoA → TCA.

cards.q: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): biochemical mechanism?
cards.a:
Trigger: Absolute insulin deficiency (Type 1 DM).
  1. ↓ Insulin → ↑ Glucagon → ↑ Lipolysis → ↑ Free fatty acids to liver
  2. ↑ β-oxidation → ↑ Acetyl-CoA overwhelms TCA → ↑ Ketogenesis
  3. ↓ Malonyl-CoA → CPT-I active → more FA into mitochondria
Result: Anion gap metabolic acidosis, hyperglycemia, ketonemia, dehydration.

cards.q: What is MCAD deficiency?
cards.a:
Defect: Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase — cannot oxidize C6–C12 fatty acids.
Clinical:
  • Hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting
  • Vomiting, lethargy → coma
  • Sudden death in infancy
Diagnosis: Newborn screen (tandem MS) — elevated C8 acylcarnitine (octanoylcarnitine).
Treatment: Avoid fasting; carnitine supplementation.

cards.q: Lipoproteins: composition, function, and density order?
cards.a:
LipoproteinMain LipidApolipoproteinFunction
ChylomicronTG (dietary)B-48, C-II, EGut → periphery
VLDLTG (hepatic)B-100, C-II, ELiver → periphery
LDLCholesterolB-100Delivers Chol to tissues
HDLProteinA-IReverse cholesterol transport

cards.q: Key apolipoproteins and their functions?
cards.a:
• Apo A-I: Activates LCAT (cholesterol esterification); HDL structural protein
  • Apo B-48: Chylomicron (made in intestine)
  • Apo B-100: VLDL, IDL, LDL; LDL receptor ligand
  • Apo C-II: Activates LPL (lipoprotein lipase — cleaves TG from lipoproteins)
  • Apo E: Remnant clearance (IDL, chylomicron remnants)

cards.q: Familial hypercholesterolemia: mutation, lipid profile, clinical features?
cards.a:
Defect: LDL receptor mutation (autosomal dominant).
Lipid profile: Markedly ↑ LDL, normal TG.
Clinical:
  • Tendon xanthomas, xanthelasmas, corneal arcus
  • Premature atherosclerosis/CAD
  • Heterozygous: LDL ~500 mg/dL
  • Homozygous: LDL >1000 mg/dL (childhood MI)
Treatment: High-dose statins, PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab).

cards.q: Cholesterol synthesis: rate-limiting step and inhibitors?
cards.a:
Rate-limiting enzyme: HMG-CoA reductase (located in ER).
Inhibited by:
  • Statins (competitive inhibitors)
  • Cholesterol (feedback)
  • Glucagon, cortisol (fasting)
Activated by: Insulin, thyroxine.
Mevalonate pathway also produces: Isoprenoids, Dolichol, Ubiquinone (CoQ10).

cards.q: De novo purine synthesis: key facts and drug targets?
cards.a:
Purines (A, G): Two-ring structure.
Substrate: Ribose-5-phosphate (from HMP shunt).
Rate-limiting enzyme: PRPP amidotransferase (inhibited by AMP, GMP).
Drug targets:
  • Methotrexate (inhibits DHFR → ↓ THF → ↓ purines)
  • 6-MP (purine analog → inhibits de novo synthesis)

cards.q: De novo pyrimidine synthesis and Orotic Aciduria?
cards.a:
Pyrimidines (C, T, U): Single-ring structure.
Rate-limiting enzyme: CPS II (inhibited by UTP; activated by PRPP).
Orotic Aciduria:
  • Deficiency of UMP synthase → orotic acid accumulates
  • Megaloblastic anemia NOT corrected by B12/folate
  • Treatment: Uridine supplementation

cards.q: Purine salvage pathway: HGPRT and Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome?
cards.a:
HGPRT: Salvages hypoxanthine and guanine → IMP, GMP using PRPP.
Deficiency → Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome (X-linked recessive):
  • Hyperuricemia (gout), renal stones
  • Intellectual disability, choreoathetosis
  • Self-mutilation (biting lips/fingers — pathognomonic)
Treatment: Allopurinol (XO inhibitor) for hyperuricemia.

cards.q: What is Gout? Biochemistry and treatment targets?
cards.a:
Mechanism: Hyperuricemia → monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints.
Uric acid: End product of purine degradation via Xanthine Oxidase.
Treatments:
  • Allopurinol/Febuxostat: Inhibit Xanthine Oxidase → ↓ uric acid production
  • Probenecid: Blocks urate reabsorption in PCT → ↑ excretion
  • Colchicine: Inhibits microtubule polymerization → ↓ neutrophil migration (acute attack)
  • NSAIDs/Glucocorticoids: Anti-inflammatory for acute attacks

cards.q: Key enzymes of DNA replication and their functions?
cards.a:
• Helicase: Unwinds double helix (breaks H bonds)
  • Primase: Synthesizes RNA primer (5'→3')
  • DNA Pol III (prokaryote) / δ, ε (eukaryote): Elongates 5'→3'
  • DNA Pol I: Removes RNA primer, replaces with DNA
  • DNA Ligase: Seals nicks between Okazaki fragments
  • Topoisomerase I: Cuts 1 strand (relieves tension)
  • Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase): Cuts both strands; target of fluoroquinolones

cards.q: What is the 'Leading vs. Lagging Strand' in DNA replication?
cards.a:
• Leading strand: Synthesized continuously 5'→3' in direction of fork movement
  • Lagging strand: Synthesized discontinuously 5'→3' away from fork → Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase
Both strands require an RNA primer.
DNA polymerase can only add to an existing 3'-OH group — cannot start de novo.

cards.q: What is telomerase? Clinical significance?
cards.a:
Telomerase: Reverse transcriptase that adds repetitive TTAGGG sequences to chromosome ends, preventing shortening with each division.
  • Active in: Germ cells, stem cells, most cancer cells
  • Inactive in: Most somatic cells → progressive shortening → senescence/apoptosis
Clinical: Upregulated in cancer → immortality; potential drug target.

cards.q: What are the main DNA repair mechanisms?
cards.a:
MechanismDamage TypeKey Gene/Enzyme
BEROxidized/deaminated basesDNA glycosylases, AP endonuclease
NERBulky adducts, thymine dimersXPA-XPG genes
MMRReplication mismatchesMSH2, MLH1
HRDSB (high fidelity)BRCA1/2, RAD51
NHEJDSB (error-prone)Ku proteins, DNA-PK

cards.q: Xeroderma Pigmentosum: defect and clinical features?
cards.a:
Defect: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) deficiency → cannot repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
Inheritance: Autosomal recessive.
Clinical:
  • Extreme photosensitivity
  • Early-onset skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma)
  • Ocular abnormalities, progressive neurodegeneration
  • ~1000× increased skin cancer risk

cards.q: Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC): defect and cancer risk?
cards.a:
Defect: Mismatch Repair (MMR) gene mutation (MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, PMS2) → microsatellite instability (MSI-H).
Inheritance: Autosomal dominant.
Cancers: Colorectal (most common), endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract.
Treatment: Colonoscopy q1-2yr; checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab) respond well to MMR-deficient tumors.

cards.q: BRCA1/2 mutations: function and cancer predisposition?
cards.a:
Function: Tumor suppressor genes involved in Homologous Recombination (HR) for double-strand break repair.
  • BRCA1: ↑ breast, ovarian, fallopian tube, pancreatic cancer
  • BRCA2: ↑ breast (M&F), ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, melanoma
Treatment: PARP inhibitors (olaparib) — exploit HR deficiency (synthetic lethality).

cards.q: RNA Polymerases in eukaryotes: types and functions?
cards.a:
• RNA Pol I: rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S) — in nucleolus
  • RNA Pol II: mRNA and most snRNA/miRNA; target of α-amanitin
  • RNA Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, small RNAs
Mnemonic: '1, 2, 3 = r, m, t-RNA'.
Prokaryotes: Single RNA Pol; target of Rifampin (TB/meningococcal prophylaxis).

cards.q: mRNA processing in eukaryotes: what modifications are made?
cards.a:
1. 5' 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap: Required for ribosome binding, mRNA stability, export, and translation initiation
  2. 3' Poly-A tail: ~200 adenine residues added by poly-A polymerase; enhances stability and export
  3. Splicing: Introns removed by spliceosome (snRNPs); exons joined via lariat intermediate
Alternative splicing → one gene → multiple protein isoforms.

cards.q: What is alternative splicing? Give an example.
cards.a:
Definition: Different combinations of exons included/excluded → multiple protein isoforms from one gene.
Example: Calcitonin gene:
  • Thyroid C-cells → calcitonin mRNA
  • Neurons → CGRP mRNA
Significance: ~95% of multi-exon human genes undergo alternative splicing → proteome diversity far exceeds genome size.

cards.q: Steps of translation and antibiotic targets?
cards.a:
Ribosome sites: A (aminoacyl) → P (peptidyl) → E (exit)
Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA
Antibiotic targets:
TargetDrugMechanism
30SAminoglycosidesBlock initiation/misreading
30STetracyclinesBlock A site
50SChloramphenicolInhibits peptidyl transferase
50SMacrolides/LinezolidBlock translocation

cards.q: What are the properties of the genetic code?
cards.a:
1. Triplet: Each codon = 3 nucleotides
  2. Non-overlapping
  3. Degenerate/redundant: Multiple codons → same AA (wobble at 3rd base)
  4. Unambiguous: Each codon specifies only 1 AA
  5. Universal: Same across virtually all organisms
Start codon: AUG (Met in eukaryotes; fMet in prokaryotes).
Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.

cards.q: What is tRNA structure and aminoacylation?
cards.a:
Structure: Cloverleaf (2D), L-shaped (3D); 73–93 nt.
Key sites:
  • Anticodon loop: recognizes mRNA codon (antiparallel 3'→5')
  • 3' CCA end: amino acid attachment site (3'-OH)
Charging (aminoacylation): Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase attaches correct AA to correct tRNA using ATP.
Wobble hypothesis: 3rd codon position is flexible → one tRNA can recognize multiple codons.

cards.q: Posttranslational modifications: types and significance?
cards.a:
• Glycosylation: N-linked (ER), O-linked (Golgi); protein folding, targeting, immune recognition
  • Phosphorylation: Ser/Thr/Tyr by kinases; regulates enzyme activity
  • Ubiquitination: Tags protein for proteasomal degradation
  • Acetylation: Histone acetylation → open chromatin → gene activation
  • Hydroxylation: Collagen Pro/Lys — requires Vitamin C
  • Carboxylation: Clotting factors II, VII, IX, X — requires Vitamin K

cards.q: Epigenetics: DNA methylation and histone modification?
cards.a:
DNA Methylation: Methylation of CpG islands → gene silencing (heritable).
Promoter methylation → transcriptional repression (tumor suppressors often silenced in cancer).

Histone Modifications:
  • Acetylation (HAT): Opens chromatin → transcription ON
  • Deacetylation (HDAC): Closes chromatin → transcription OFF
  • H3K4me3: Active transcription marker
  • H3K27me3: Repressive marker

cards.q: What is X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis)?
cards.a:
• One X chromosome in each female somatic cell is inactivated → condensed Barr body
  • Random: Either maternal or paternal X inactivated
  • Irreversible: All daughter cells maintain same inactivation pattern
  • Mediated by XIST gene coating the inactive X
Clinical:
  • Turner (45,X): 0 Barr bodies
  • Klinefelter (47,XXY): 1 Barr body

cards.q: What is genomic imprinting? Compare Prader-Willi vs. Angelman syndrome.
cards.a:
Imprinting: Epigenetic silencing of one parental allele (methylation); expression depends on parent of origin.
Chromosome 15q11-13:
  • Prader-Willi (deletion of paternal 15 OR maternal UPD): Hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism
  • Angelman (deletion of maternal 15 OR paternal UPD): 'Happy puppet' — severe ID, seizures, inappropriate laughter, absent speech

cards.q: Types of point mutations and their effects?
cards.a:
• Silent (synonymous): Changed codon → same AA (wobble)
  • Missense: Changed codon → different AA (e.g., HbS: Glu→Val)
  • Nonsense: Changed codon → stop codon → truncated protein (severe)
  • Frameshift: Insertion/deletion → shift in reading frame → altered protein
  • Splice site: Altered splice site → intron retention or exon skipping

cards.q: What is the difference between gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutations?
cards.a:
Loss-of-function: ↓ or absent protein activity; usually recessive.
  • CF (CFTR), PKU (PAH), enzyme deficiencies
Gain-of-function: New or enhanced protein activity; usually dominant.
  • Achondroplasia (FGFR3 constitutively active)
  • Huntington's (toxic polyglutamine repeat)
Dominant negative: Mutant protein inhibits wild-type → dominant (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta).

cards.q: Trinucleotide repeat diseases: examples and anticipation?
cards.a:
Anticipation: Worsening severity/earlier onset in successive generations due to expanding repeats.
  • Huntington's (CAG): AD; caudate atrophy; chorea, dementia; onset 30–50s
  • Myotonic Dystrophy (CTG): AD; myotonia, cataracts, hypogonadism
  • Fragile X (CGG): XL; most common inherited intellectual disability; macro-orchidism, autism
  • Friedreich's Ataxia (GAA): AR; spinocerebellar ataxia, cardiomyopathy

cards.q: Cell cycle phases and key checkpoints?
cards.a:
Phases: G1 → S (DNA synthesis) → G2 → M (mitosis) → G1.
Checkpoints:
  • G1/S (Restriction Point): Rb phosphorylated by CDK4/6-CyclinD → releases E2F → S phase entry; p53 arrests here after DNA damage
  • G2/M: CDK1-CyclinB (MPF) activation; p53/CHEK2 arrest if DNA damaged
  • Spindle Assembly (M): Ensures all chromosomes attached to spindle before anaphase

cards.q: Proto-oncogenes vs. tumor suppressor genes: examples and mechanism?
cards.a:
Proto-oncogenes → Oncogenes (gain-of-function, usually dominant):
  • RAS (~30% of cancers), MYC, HER2/neu, BCR-ABL
Tumor Suppressors (loss-of-function, usually recessive — both alleles lost):
  • Rb (retinoblastoma), p53 (most commonly mutated in cancer), BRCA1/2, APC (FAP), VHL

cards.q: What is the p53 pathway? How does it respond to DNA damage?
cards.a:
p53 (TP53): Transcription factor; induced by DNA damage, hypoxia, oncogene activation.
Actions:
  1. Activates p21 (CDK inhibitor) → G1 arrest → time for repair
  2. Activates GADD45 → DNA repair
  3. If irreparable → activates BAX, PUMA → apoptosis
MDM2: Ubiquitinates p53 → proteasomal degradation (negative feedback).
Li-Fraumeni syndrome: Germline TP53 mutation → multiple early cancers.

cards.q: What is apoptosis? Compare intrinsic vs. extrinsic pathways.
cards.a:
Apoptosis: Programmed cell death; caspase-mediated; no inflammation (vs. necrosis).
Intrinsic (mitochondrial): DNA damage → BAX → cytochrome c release → APAF-1 → caspase-9 → caspases 3/6/7.
Extrinsic (death receptor): FasL/Fas (CD95) or TNF/TNFR → FADD → caspase-8 → caspases 3/6/7.
BCL-2: Anti-apoptotic; overexpressed in follicular lymphoma (t(14;18)).

cards.q: GPCR signaling: Gs, Gi, and Gq pathways — ligands and effects?
cards.a:
Gs (stimulatory): ↑ Adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP → ↑ PKA.
Ligands: Glucagon, Epinephrine (β), ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, PTH, ADH (V2), Calcitonin.

Gi (inhibitory): ↓ Adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP.
Ligands: Somatostatin, α₂-adrenergic, M₂/M₄ muscarinic.

Gq: ↑ PLC → IP₃ (→ Ca²⁺ release) + DAG (→ PKC).
Ligands: α₁-adrenergic, M₁/M₃ muscarinic, H₁ histamine, V₁ vasopressin.

cards.q: What are the two types of nephrons and their key differences?
cards.a:
• Cortical Nephrons (85%): Short loops of Henle, glomeruli in outer 2/3 of cortex, peritubular capillaries.
  • Juxtamedullary Nephrons (15%): Long loops of Henle extending deep into medulla, vasa recta, crucial for urine concentration.

cards.q: State normal values for RBF, RPF, GFR, and Filtration Fraction.
cards.a:
• RBF: 1.1 L/min (20–25% of cardiac output)
  • RPF: ~625 mL/min
  • GFR: 120–125 mL/min
  • Filtration Fraction (FF): GFR/RPF ≈ 0.20 (20%)

cards.q: What is the formula for GFR using Starling forces?
cards.a:
$$\text{GFR} = K_f \times [(P_{gc} - P_{bs}) - (\pi_{gc} - \pi_{bs})]$$
  • Kf = filtration coefficient
  • Pgc = glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (~55 mmHg)
  • Pbs = Bowman’s space hydrostatic pressure (~15 mmHg)
  • πgc = glomerular oncotic pressure (~28 mmHg)

cards.q: How is GFR clinically measured? What is the gold standard?
cards.a:
• Gold standard: Inulin clearance (freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted).
  • Clinical approximation: Creatinine clearance (slightly overestimates due to tubular secretion).

cards.q: What is autoregulation of GFR and RBF? What is the range?
cards.a:
Intrinsic ability of kidney to maintain constant RBF and GFR despite changes in mean arterial pressure.
Range: 80–180 mmHg (mainly 60–160 mmHg).
Mechanisms: Myogenic + Tubuloglomerular feedback.

cards.q: Explain Tubuloglomerular Feedback.
cards.a:
Macula densa senses ↑ NaCl delivery → releases adenosine/ATP → afferent arteriole constriction → ↓ GFR.
Purpose: Protects glomerulus from hypertension and maintains distal delivery.

cards.q: What is the effect of Angiotensin II on glomerular arterioles?
cards.a: Preferentially constricts efferent arteriole > afferent → ↑ glomerular hydrostatic pressure → maintains GFR when renal perfusion is low.

cards.q: Trace the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
cards.a: ↓ Renal perfusion / ↓ Na⁺ / ↑ sympathetic → Juxtaglomerular cells release Renin → Angiotensinogen → Ang I → (ACE) Ang II → vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, thirst, ADH.

cards.q: Where is aldosterone produced and what are its main actions?
cards.a:
Produced in Zona Glomerulosa of adrenal cortex.
Actions (Principal cells of CD): ↑ ENaC and Na/K-ATPase → Na⁺ reabsorption, K⁺ & H⁺ secretion.

cards.q: What is the countercurrent multiplier system?
cards.a:
Mechanism in loop of Henle that creates hyperosmotic medullary interstitium.
  • Descending limb: water permeable
  • Thick ascending limb: actively pumps NaCl (impermeable to water)

cards.q: What is the role of vasa recta in the kidney?
cards.a: Countercurrent exchanger that preserves the medullary osmotic gradient by removing excess solute and water without dissipating the gradient.

cards.q: Compare the permeability of different parts of the nephron to water and solutes.
cards.a:
• PCT: Highly permeable to water and solutes
  • Descending LoH: Water permeable, solute impermeable
  • Ascending LoH: Water impermeable, solute permeable (active transport)
  • CD: ADH-dependent water permeability (aquaporins)

cards.q: What percentage of filtered load is reabsorbed in each segment?
cards.a:
• PCT: 65–67%
  • Loop of Henle: 25%
  • DCT: 5–10%
  • Collecting Duct: Variable (ADH & Aldosterone dependent)

cards.q: What is the effect of ADH (Vasopressin) on the kidney?
cards.a: Binds V2 receptors → insertion of Aquaporin-2 channels in collecting duct → ↑ water reabsorption → concentrated urine.

cards.q: What is the action of Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP)?
cards.a:
Released in response to atrial stretch.
Effects: ↑ GFR, ↓ renin, ↓ aldosterone, ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → natriuresis and diuresis.

cards.q: List the major classes of diuretics and their sites of action.
cards.a:
• Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Proximal tubule
  • Loop diuretics: Thick ascending limb
  • Thiazides: Distal convoluted tubule
  • K⁺-sparing: Collecting duct

cards.q: What is the most common cause of metabolic alkalosis from diuretics?
cards.a: Loop and Thiazide diuretics cause volume contraction → secondary hyperaldosteronism → increased H⁺ and K⁺ secretion → contraction alkalosis.

cards.q: What is Fanconi Syndrome?
cards.a: Generalized dysfunction of proximal tubule → glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting (Type 2 RTA).

cards.q: Compare the 4 types of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA).
cards.a:
• Type 1 (Distal): Cannot excrete H⁺ → hypokalemia, urine pH >5.5
  • Type 2 (Proximal): Cannot reabsorb HCO₃⁻
  • Type 3: Rare (mixed)
  • Type 4 (Hypoaldosteronism): Hyperkalemia, mild acidosis

cards.q: What is the clearance formula?
cards.a:
$$C_x = \frac{U_x \times V}{P_x}$$
Where Ux = urine concentration, V = urine flow rate, Px = plasma concentration.

cards.q: What substances have clearance equal to GFR, RPF, and > GFR?
cards.a:
• GFR: Inulin
  • RPF: PAH (Para-aminohippuric acid)
  • > GFR: Substances that are secreted (e.g., creatinine slightly)

cards.q: What is effective circulating volume (ECV)?
cards.a: Volume sensed by baroreceptors and kidneys (not the same as total body volume). Determines renin release.

cards.q: What happens in SIADH?
cards.a: Inappropriate ADH secretion → water retention → hyponatremia with low plasma osmolality and high urine osmolality.

cards.q: What is Diabetes Insipidus? Differentiate central vs nephrogenic.
cards.a:
Central: ↓ ADH production
Nephrogenic: Kidneys do not respond to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin defect).
Both cause polyuria and polydipsia with dilute urine.

cards.q: How does the kidney handle potassium?
cards.a:
Almost all filtered K⁺ is reabsorbed in PCT and LoH.
Regulation occurs in collecting duct: Aldosterone → ↑ K⁺ secretion.

cards.q: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus composed of?
cards.a:
1. Juxtaglomerular cells (renin)
  2. Macula densa
  3. Extraglomerular mesangial cells

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on the kidney?
cards.a: Constricts afferent arterioles → ↓ RBF and GFR, ↑ renin release.

cards.q: Name the segments of the nephron where Na⁺ is reabsorbed and the transporters.
cards.a:
• PCT: NHE3, Na-glucose, Na-amino acid cotransporters
  • Thick Asc. LoH: NKCC2
  • DCT: NCC
  • CD: ENaC

cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for blood pH?
cards.a: $$\text{pH} = 6.1 + \log\left(\frac{[\text{HCO}_3^-]}{0.03 \times P\text{CO}_2}\right)$$

cards.q: How does the kidney compensate for chronic respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: Increased HCO₃− reabsorption and generation (via glutamine metabolism → NH₄⁺ excretion).

cards.q: What is the role of PTH in the kidney?
cards.a: ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT), ↓ PO₄ reabsorption (PCT), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase activity.

cards.q: What is the role of Vitamin D in the kidney?
cards.a: Active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) increases Ca²⁺ and PO₄ reabsorption.

cards.q: Define osmotic diuresis and give an example.
cards.a: Increased urine output due to non-reabsorbable solute in tubule (e.g., glucose in uncontrolled diabetes).

cards.q: What is the filtration barrier of the glomerulus?
cards.a:
1. Fenestrated endothelium
  2. Glomerular basement membrane
  3. Podocyte slit diaphragm (nephrin)

cards.q: What is minimal change disease?
cards.a: Loss of podocyte foot processes → selective proteinuria (mostly albumin), normal light microscopy.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
cards.a: Minimal change disease.

cards.q: What is the Starling force that favors filtration in glomerulus?
cards.a: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pgc).

cards.q: What is the main determinant of renal oxygen consumption?
cards.a: Sodium reabsorption (especially in PCT and thick ascending limb).

cards.q: What is the effect of NSAIDs on the kidney?
cards.a: Inhibit prostaglandins → unopposed afferent constriction (by Ang II) → ↓ RBF and GFR (especially in volume-depleted states).

cards.q: What is ACE inhibitor effect on GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
cards.a: Dramatic drop in GFR (efferent arteriole dilation removes compensatory mechanism).

cards.q: Define free water clearance.
cards.a: Volume of water cleared from plasma per unit time beyond isotonic urine.

cards.q: What is the urine to plasma osmolality ratio in central DI?
cards.a: Very low (<1.0) even after water deprivation.

cards.q: What hormone increases urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct?
cards.a: ADH (Vasopressin).

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of the macula densa?
cards.a: Senses NaCl delivery and modulates renin release and afferent arteriole tone.

cards.q: What is the primary site of action of acetazolamide?
cards.a: Proximal convoluted tubule (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor).

cards.q: What is the most potent diuretic class?
cards.a: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide).

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is common with loop and thiazide diuretics?
cards.a: Hypokalemia.

cards.q: What is the effect of spironolactone on acid-base balance?
cards.a: Can cause hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis (Type 4 RTA-like).

cards.q: What is the primary site of bicarbonate reabsorption in the kidney?
cards.a: Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) — 80–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed here via carbonic anhydrase and Na/H exchanger.

cards.q: How does the kidney generate new bicarbonate?
cards.a: Via glutamine metabolism in proximal tubule cells → NH₄⁺ excretion + new HCO₃⁻ generation (ammoniagenesis). Also via titratable acids (H₂PO₄⁻).

cards.q: What is the main buffer in urine for acid excretion?
cards.a: Phosphate (HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻) and Ammonia (NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺).

cards.q: Differentiate the 4 types of Renal Tubular Acidosis (full comparison).
cards.a:
Type 1 (Distal): Defective H⁺ secretion, hypokalemia, urine pH >5.5
Type 2 (Proximal): Defective HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, hypokalemia
Type 4: Aldosterone deficiency/resistance, hyperkalemia, mild acidosis

cards.q: What is the effect of hyperkalemia on renal acid-base handling?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia inhibits ammoniagenesis → reduced new HCO₃⁻ generation → metabolic acidosis (Type 4 RTA mechanism).

cards.q: How does aldosterone affect acid-base balance?
cards.a: Promotes H⁺ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells (via H⁺-ATPase) and K⁺ secretion. Aldosterone deficiency → hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the anion gap in Type 4 RTA?
cards.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (hyperchloremic).

cards.q: What is the urine anion gap used for?
cards.a:
To differentiate GI vs renal cause of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Negative UAG: GI loss (diarrhea)
Positive UAG: Renal cause (RTA)

cards.q: What hormones regulate calcium reabsorption in the kidney?
cards.a:
PTH: ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT
Vitamin D: ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption
Calcitonin: Minor inhibitory effect

cards.q: Where is phosphate primarily reabsorbed?
cards.a: Proximal tubule (80–90%) via Na⁺-Pi cotransporter. Regulated by PTH (↓ reabsorption).

cards.q: What is the effect of PTH on phosphate handling?
cards.a: Inhibits phosphate reabsorption in proximal tubule → phosphaturia (increases serum Ca²⁺ by reducing Ca-PO₄ precipitation).

cards.q: What is the role of FGF-23 in phosphate regulation?
cards.a: Fibroblast Growth Factor 23: ↓ phosphate reabsorption in PCT and ↓ 1α-hydroxylase activity.

cards.q: What is the clearance of a substance that is completely reabsorbed?
cards.a: Zero clearance (e.g., glucose under normal conditions).

cards.q: What is the clearance of a substance that is completely secreted?
cards.a: Equals Renal Plasma Flow (e.g., PAH at low concentrations).

cards.q: Define filtration fraction and its normal value.
cards.a: GFR / RPF. Normal value ≈ 0.20 (20%).

cards.q: What happens to filtration fraction in dehydration?
cards.a: Increases due to preferential efferent constriction by Angiotensin II → maintains GFR.

cards.q: What is the effect of high protein diet on GFR?
cards.a: Increases GFR (amino acids → afferent arteriolar dilation via tubuloglomerular feedback changes).

cards.q: What drugs cause afferent arteriole constriction?
cards.a: NSAIDs (↓ prostaglandins), cyclosporine, high-dose norepinephrine.

cards.q: What is prerenal azotemia?
cards.a: Decreased renal perfusion → ↑ BUN:Creatinine ratio (>20:1), low urine Na⁺ (<20 mEq/L), high urine osmolality.

cards.q: Differentiate ATN vs prerenal azotemia by urine indices.
cards.a:
Prerenal: FENa <1%, Uosm >500, Urine Na <20
ATN: FENa >2%, Uosm <350, Urine Na >40, muddy brown casts.

cards.q: What is the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) formula?
cards.a: $$\text{FE}_{\text{Na}} = \frac{U_{\text{Na}} / P_{\text{Na}}}{U_{\text{Cr}} / P_{\text{Cr}}} \times 100$$

cards.q: What is Bartter Syndrome?
cards.a: Defect in thick ascending limb (NKCC2 or ROMK) → mimics chronic loop diuretic use: hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, normal blood pressure.

cards.q: What is Gitelman Syndrome?
cards.a: Defect in DCT (NCC transporter) → mimics chronic thiazide use: hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypocalciuria.

cards.q: What is Liddle Syndrome?
cards.a: Gain of function in ENaC → hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, low renin/aldosterone.

cards.q: What is pseudohypoaldosteronism Type 1?
cards.a: Resistance to aldosterone → hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the effect of pregnancy on GFR?
cards.a: GFR increases by 40–50% due to increased renal blood flow.

cards.q: What is the site of action of mannitol?
cards.a: Osmotic diuretic — works throughout the tubule, especially proximal tubule and descending loop.

cards.q: What is the major side effect of acetazolamide?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis (due to HCO₃⁻ loss) and hypokalemia.

cards.q: Why do loop diuretics cause ototoxicity?
cards.a: Inhibition of NKCC1 in the inner ear (similar transporter as NKCC2 in kidney).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of thiazide-induced hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Volume depletion → ↑ proximal Ca²⁺ reabsorption + direct effect on DCT.

cards.q: What is the primary use of potassium-sparing diuretics?
cards.a: To prevent hypokalemia when used with loop or thiazide diuretics; also in heart failure.

cards.q: What is the danger of combining ACE inhibitors with spironolactone?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia (both reduce aldosterone effect).

cards.q: What is hepatorenal syndrome?
cards.a: Functional renal failure in advanced liver disease due to intense renal vasoconstriction (low effective circulating volume).

cards.q: What is the role of the kidney in erythropoiesis?
cards.a: Peritubular interstitial cells produce Erythropoietin (EPO) in response to hypoxia.

cards.q: What is uremic frost?
cards.a: Deposition of urea crystals on skin in severe uremia.

cards.q: What is the effect of acute ureteral obstruction on GFR?
cards.a: Initial increase then sharp decrease due to back pressure.

cards.q: What is the Goldman equation used for in renal physiology?
cards.a: To calculate equilibrium potential for ions (especially in tubular cells).

cards.q: What is the main driving force for paracellular reabsorption in PCT?
cards.a: Solvent drag and electrochemical gradient created by active Na⁺ transport.

cards.q: What is the juxtamedullary nephron's main advantage?
cards.a: Ability to create and maintain a steep corticomedullary osmotic gradient for water conservation.

cards.q: What stimulates renin release from JG cells?
cards.a:
1. ↓ afferent arteriole pressure
  2. ↓ NaCl at macula densa
  3. ↑ sympathetic activity (β1 receptors)

cards.q: What inhibits renin release?
cards.a: Angiotensin II (negative feedback), high NaCl at macula densa, atrial natriuretic peptide.

cards.q: What is the effect of dopamine on renal vessels at low dose?
cards.a: Vasodilation of afferent and efferent arterioles → ↑ RBF and GFR.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of the filtration slit diaphragm?
cards.a: Prevents protein loss; mutation in nephrin causes congenital nephrotic syndrome.

cards.q: What is the normal daily urine output range?
cards.a: 0.5–2.5 L/day (average ~1–1.5 L).

cards.q: What is the maximum urine concentrating ability of human kidney?
cards.a: Approximately 1200–1400 mOsm/L.

cards.q: What is the minimum urine osmolality possible?
cards.a: Approximately 50 mOsm/L (in absence of ADH).

cards.q: What is the difference between osmolar clearance and free water clearance?
cards.a:
Osmolar clearance (Cosm): Volume of plasma cleared of osmoles per unit time.
Free water clearance (CH₂O): Volume of water cleared in excess of (or less than) isotonic urine.
Positive CH₂O = dilute urine; Negative = concentrated urine.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of FeNa in acute kidney injury?
cards.a:
FeNa <1%: Prerenal azotemia or acute glomerulonephritis
FeNa >2%: Acute tubular necrosis or post-renal obstruction

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic activation on renal blood flow during hemorrhage?
cards.a: Strong vasoconstriction of afferent arterioles → ↓ RBF and GFR to preserve blood flow to heart and brain.

cards.q: What is the pressure natriuresis mechanism?
cards.a: Increase in arterial pressure → increased Na⁺ excretion (independent of hormones) to maintain long-term blood pressure control.

cards.q: What is the role of the medullary interstitium in urine concentration?
cards.a: Hyperosmotic gradient (300–1200 mOsm/L) created by countercurrent multiplier allows water reabsorption in collecting duct under ADH influence.

cards.q: How does ADH affect urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct?
cards.a: Increases urea permeability (via UT-A1 transporters) → contributes to medullary hypertonicity.

cards.q: What is the effect of hypercalcemia on ADH action?
cards.a: Causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by downregulating aquaporin-2 channels.

cards.q: What is the primary defect in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Defect in V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 channel → kidneys cannot respond to ADH.

cards.q: What drugs can cause nephrogenic DI?
cards.a: Lithium, demeclocycline, amphotericin B, foscarnet.

cards.q: What is the treatment of central vs nephrogenic DI?
cards.a:
• Central: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
  • Nephrogenic: Thiazide diuretics + amiloride + low salt diet

cards.q: What is SIADH? List common causes.
cards.a:
Inappropriate ADH secretion → euvolemic hyponatremia.
Causes: Small cell lung cancer, CNS disorders, pulmonary disease, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine).

cards.q: How do you correct hyponatremia in SIADH?
cards.a: Fluid restriction (first line). Severe/symptomatic: hypertonic saline + loop diuretic.

cards.q: What is the danger of rapid correction of hyponatremia?
cards.a: Central Pontine Myelinolysis (Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome).

cards.q: What is the effect of aldosterone on principal cells?
cards.a: Increases number and activity of ENaC channels and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion.

cards.q: What is the effect of atrial natriuretic peptide on the kidney?
cards.a: Increases GFR, inhibits Na⁺ reabsorption in collecting duct, inhibits renin and aldosterone.

cards.q: What is the role of prostaglandins in the kidney?
cards.a: Maintain RBF and GFR during volume depletion by dilating afferent arterioles (oppose Ang II).

cards.q: Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in volume-depleted patients?
cards.a: Block prostaglandins → unopposed afferent constriction → acute drop in GFR.

cards.q: What is the site of action of SGLT2 inhibitors?
cards.a: Proximal convoluted tubule — block Na⁺-glucose cotransporter 2 → glucosuria and natriuresis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of acetazolamide in altitude sickness?
cards.a: Causes metabolic acidosis → stimulates ventilation → increases PaO₂.

cards.q: What is the effect of loop diuretics on calcium excretion?
cards.a: Increase Ca²⁺ excretion (used in hypercalcemia).

cards.q: What is the effect of thiazides on calcium excretion?
cards.a: Decrease Ca²⁺ excretion (used in calcium nephrolithiasis).

cards.q: What is pseudohyperaldosteronism?
cards.a: Conditions mimicking hyperaldosteronism but with low aldosterone (e.g., Liddle syndrome, licorice ingestion).

cards.q: What is the effect of cortisol on mineralocorticoid receptors?
cards.a: Cortisol can bind MR but is normally inactivated by 11β-HSD2 in kidney. Deficiency (apparent mineralocorticoid excess) → hypertension + hypokalemia.

cards.q: What is the transtubular potassium gradient (TTKG)?
cards.a: Used to assess aldosterone activity in hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What is the renal response to metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: Increased HCO₃⁻ excretion (bicarbonaturia) and reduced H⁺ secretion.

cards.q: What maintains metabolic alkalosis in volume-depleted patients?
cards.a: Secondary hyperaldosteronism → continued H⁺ and K⁺ loss.

cards.q: What is the renal handling of magnesium?
cards.a: Primarily reabsorbed in thick ascending limb via paracellular route (driven by NKCC2-generated potential).

cards.q: What is the effect of hypomagnesemia on potassium?
cards.a: Causes refractory hypokalemia (impairs K⁺ reabsorption and increases renal K⁺ wasting).

cards.q: What is the role of the kidney in vitamin D activation?
cards.a: 1α-hydroxylase in proximal tubule converts 25-OH vitamin D to active 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D.

cards.q: What stimulates 1α-hydroxylase activity?
cards.a: PTH, low serum Ca²⁺, low phosphate.

cards.q: What inhibits 1α-hydroxylase?
cards.a: High phosphate, FGF-23, high 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D (feedback).

cards.q: What is the effect of chronic kidney disease on vitamin D?
cards.a: Decreased 1α-hydroxylase → low active vitamin D → secondary hyperparathyroidism.

cards.q: What is renal osteodystrophy?
cards.a: Bone disease in CKD due to secondary hyperparathyroidism, low vitamin D, and phosphate retention.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of erythropoietin production?
cards.a: Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts sense hypoxia via HIF-1α → EPO synthesis.

cards.q: What is the effect of ACE inhibitors on efferent arteriole?
cards.a: Dilation of efferent arteriole → ↓ glomerular hydrostatic pressure → ↓ GFR (especially in renal artery stenosis).

cards.q: What is the advantage of ARBs over ACE inhibitors?
cards.a: Do not increase bradykinin → less cough and angioedema.

cards.q: What is the juxtaglomerular apparatus feedback loop?
cards.a: Macula densa senses low NaCl → adenosine/ATP → afferent constriction + renin release.

cards.q: What is the myogenic mechanism of autoregulation?
cards.a: Increased pressure → stretch of afferent arteriole smooth muscle → vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the filtration coefficient (Kf)?
cards.a: Product of hydraulic conductivity and surface area of glomerular capillaries.

cards.q: What decreases Kf in glomerular disease?
cards.a: Reduced glomerular surface area (e.g., glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy).

cards.q: What is the normal range of serum creatinine?
cards.a: 0.6–1.2 mg/dL (varies with muscle mass).

cards.q: What is cystatin C and why is it useful?
cards.a: Marker of GFR; less affected by muscle mass, age, and sex than creatinine.

cards.q: What is the Cockcroft-Gault equation used for?
cards.a: Estimates creatinine clearance (used for drug dosing).

cards.q: What is the MDRD/CKD-EPI equation?
cards.a: Estimates GFR based on serum creatinine, age, sex, and race.

cards.q: What is the gold standard for measuring GFR?
cards.a: Inulin clearance (research setting).

cards.q: What is the effect of high blood glucose on GFR?
cards.a: Initially increases GFR (glomerular hyperfiltration) in early diabetes.

cards.q: What is the renal response to acute respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: Increased H⁺ secretion and new HCO₃⁻ generation (via ammoniagenesis) to compensate.

cards.q: What is the renal response to chronic respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: Decreased HCO₃⁻ reabsorption and reduced ammoniagenesis → compensatory metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the difference between azotemia and uremia?
cards.a:
Azotemia: Elevated BUN and creatinine.
Uremia: Symptomatic azotemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, platelet dysfunction, etc.).

cards.q: What are the uremic toxins?
cards.a: Urea, creatinine, guanidino compounds, middle molecules, and parathyroid hormone.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Chronic Kidney Disease (due to low 1,25-vitamin D and phosphate retention).

cards.q: What is the effect of metabolic acidosis on potassium?
cards.a: Causes hyperkalemia (H⁺/K⁺ exchange across cell membranes).

cards.q: What is the effect of insulin on potassium handling?
cards.a: Drives K⁺ into cells via Na/K-ATPase stimulation.

cards.q: What is the emergency treatment of severe hyperkalemia?
cards.a:
1. Calcium gluconate (membrane stabilization)
  2. Insulin + glucose, albuterol
  3. Sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic)
  4. Kayexalate / loop diuretics / dialysis

cards.q: What is the role of the kidney in blood pressure regulation (short vs long term)?
cards.a:
Short term: Baroreceptors and sympathetic system.
Long term: Pressure natriuresis and RAAS.

cards.q: What is malignant hypertension?
cards.a: Severe hypertension with end-organ damage (papilledema, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury).

cards.q: What is the renal lesion in malignant hypertension?
cards.a: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ('onion skin' lesions) and fibrinoid necrosis.

cards.q: What is the effect of ACE inhibitors in diabetic nephropathy?
cards.a: Reduce intraglomerular pressure → slow progression of proteinuria and decline in GFR.

cards.q: What is the hallmark of diabetic nephropathy on biopsy?
cards.a: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis).

cards.q: What is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide?
cards.a: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).

cards.q: What is the presentation of Goodpasture syndrome?
cards.a: Pulmonary hemorrhage + rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (anti-GBM antibodies).

cards.q: What is the classic finding in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
cards.a: Subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, low C3.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults?
cards.a: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or membranous nephropathy.

cards.q: What is Alport syndrome?
cards.a: Hereditary nephritis with sensorineural deafness and ocular abnormalities (defect in type IV collagen).

cards.q: What is the triad of nephrotic syndrome?
cards.a: Proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema (± hyperlipidemia).

cards.q: What is the most serious complication of nephrotic syndrome?
cards.a: Hypercoagulable state (loss of antithrombin III) → renal vein thrombosis.

cards.q: What is the effect of hypoalbuminemia on GFR?
cards.a: Decreases oncotic pressure → increases GFR initially.

cards.q: What is the renal handling of uric acid?
cards.a: Filtered, reabsorbed, and secreted in proximal tubule. Underexcretion is most common cause of gout.

cards.q: What drugs increase uric acid reabsorption?
cards.a: Thiazides and loop diuretics (volume depletion → increased proximal reabsorption).

cards.q: What is the treatment of tumor lysis syndrome?
cards.a: Hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase, urinary alkalinization (controversial).

cards.q: What is the most common inherited cause of kidney stones?
cards.a: Hypercalciuria (idiopathic).

cards.q: What type of stone is associated with alkaline urine and infection?
cards.a: Struvite stones (Mg-ammonium-phosphate) — caused by urease-producing bacteria (Proteus).

cards.q: What is the most common type of kidney stone?
cards.a: Calcium oxalate.

cards.q: What is the Randall plaque?
cards.a: Subepithelial calcification in the papilla that serves as nidus for calcium oxalate stones.

cards.q: What is the treatment of uric acid stones?
cards.a: Urinary alkalinization (potassium citrate) + allopurinol.

cards.q: What is the role of citrate in stone prevention?
cards.a: Inhibits calcium stone formation by binding calcium and increasing solubility.

cards.q: What is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
cards.a: Mutation in PKD1 or PKD2 → bilateral enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts, hypertension, berry aneurysms.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Alport syndrome?
cards.a: Usually X-linked (COL4A5 mutation).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute interstitial nephritis?
cards.a: Drug-induced (NSAIDs, antibiotics — especially beta-lactams, PPIs).

cards.q: What are the classic findings in acute interstitial nephritis?
cards.a: Fever, rash, eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, sterile pyuria.

cards.q: What is analgesic nephropathy?
cards.a: Chronic interstitial nephritis + papillary necrosis due to long-term NSAID + phenacetin use.

cards.q: What is the most common organism causing pyelonephritis?
cards.a: Escherichia coli.

cards.q: What is the difference between pyelonephritis and cystitis?
cards.a: Pyelonephritis involves kidney (fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness); cystitis is bladder only (dysuria, frequency, no fever).

cards.q: What is renal papillary necrosis associated with?
cards.a: Diabetes, analgesic abuse, sickle cell disease, severe pyelonephritis.

cards.q: What is the most common renal malignancy in adults?
cards.a: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of renal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass (late finding).

cards.q: What paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with RCC?
cards.a: Erythrocytosis (EPO production), hypercalcemia (PTHrP), hypertension (renin).

cards.q: What is Wilms tumor?
cards.a: Most common renal malignancy in children; associated with WAGR syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease in the US?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: What is the second most common cause of ESRD?
cards.a: Hypertension.

cards.q: What is the leading cause of death in dialysis patients?
cards.a: Cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: What are the four layers of the GI tract wall (from lumen to outside)?
cards.a:
1. Mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae)
  2. Submucosa (contains Meissner’s plexus)
  3. Muscularis propria (inner circular + outer longitudinal muscle; Auerbach’s plexus between layers)
  4. Serosa / Adventitia

cards.q: What is the enteric nervous system?
cards.a: Intrinsic nervous system of the gut consisting of Meissner’s (submucosal) plexus (controls secretion) and Auerbach’s (myenteric) plexus (controls motility). Can function independently of CNS.

cards.q: Differentiate peristalsis from segmentation.
cards.a:
• Peristalsis: Propulsive movement — contraction behind bolus, relaxation ahead.
  • Segmentation: Rhythmic mixing contractions (mainly small intestine) that increase contact with absorptive surface.

cards.q: What is the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC)?
cards.a: Occurs during fasting every 90–120 minutes. Strong peristaltic contractions from stomach to ileum that clear residual debris and prevent bacterial overgrowth. Regulated by motilin.

cards.q: List the major GI hormones and their primary actions.
cards.a:
• Gastrin: ↑ gastric acid
  • CCK: Gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzyme secretion
  • Secretin: ↑ pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion
  • GIP: Inhibits gastric acid + stimulates insulin
  • Motilin: Initiates MMC

cards.q: What are the three phases of gastric acid secretion?
cards.a:
• Cephalic (30%): Vagus nerve (sight/smell/thought)
  • Gastric (60%): Distension and peptides → gastrin release
  • Intestinal (10%): Enterogastrones (secretin, CCK) inhibit acid secretion

cards.q: Which cells secrete HCl and Intrinsic Factor?
cards.a: Parietal cells in gastric glands (fundus and body). Stimulated by ACh, histamine (H2), and gastrin.

cards.q: What stimulates and inhibits parietal cell acid secretion?
cards.a:
• Stimulators: Histamine (H2), ACh (M3), Gastrin
  • Inhibitors: Somatostatin, prostaglandins (PGE₂), secretin, CCK, GIP

cards.q: What is the role of chief cells?
