cards.a: Secrete pepsinogen, which is activated to pepsin by low pH.

cards.q: What protects the gastric mucosa from acid?
cards.a: Mucus-bicarbonate barrier, prostaglandins (↑ mucus & blood flow), tight junctions, and adequate mucosal blood flow.

cards.q: What is the source and function of salivary amylase?
cards.a: Produced by parotid glands. Begins starch digestion in mouth and continues in stomach until inactivated by acid.

cards.q: What are the three major salivary glands?
cards.a: Parotid (serous, amylase), Submandibular (mixed), Sublingual (mucous). Daily secretion ~1–1.5 L.

cards.q: What is the composition of pancreatic juice?
cards.a: Alkaline (rich in HCO₃⁻) + digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases). Secreted in response to secretin (HCO₃⁻) and CCK (enzymes).

cards.q: What stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
cards.a: Secretin — released when acidic chyme enters duodenum.

cards.q: What stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
cards.a: CCK — released in response to fats and proteins in duodenum.

cards.q: Outline carbohydrate digestion and absorption.
cards.a: Salivary + pancreatic amylase → oligosaccharides → brush border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase) → monosaccharides. Absorbed via SGLT1 (glucose/galactose) and GLUT5 (fructose).

cards.q: Outline protein digestion and absorption.
cards.a: Stomach: pepsin. Duodenum: trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidases → amino acids, di/tripeptides. Absorbed via Na⁺-dependent transporters in proximal small intestine.

cards.q: Describe fat digestion and absorption.
cards.a: Bile salts emulsify fats → pancreatic lipase + colipase → monoglycerides + FFAs → micelles → absorbed into enterocytes → re-esterified into chylomicrons → lymphatics.

cards.q: What vitamins require bile salts for absorption?
cards.a: Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K.

cards.q: Where is Vitamin B12 absorbed?
cards.a: Terminal ileum — requires Intrinsic Factor from parietal cells.

cards.q: What is the enterohepatic circulation?
cards.a: Bile salts secreted into intestine → 95% reabsorbed in terminal ileum → returned to liver via portal vein.

cards.q: What is the function of the gallbladder?
cards.a: Stores and concentrates bile. Contracts in response to CCK.

cards.q: What is the role of the sphincter of Oddi?
cards.a: Controls flow of bile and pancreatic juice into duodenum. Relaxes in response to CCK.

cards.q: What is the law of the intestine (Bayliss-Starling law)?
cards.a: Distension of intestine causes contraction proximal to the bolus and relaxation distal to it.

cards.q: What is the role of VIP in the GI tract?
cards.a: Vasodilation and smooth muscle relaxation. Increases intestinal secretion (water and electrolytes).

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on GI function?
cards.a: Increases motility, secretion, and blood flow (via vagus and pelvic splanchnics).

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on GI function?
cards.a: Decreases motility and secretion, increases sphincter tone.

cards.q: What is the cephalic phase of digestion?
cards.a: Anticipatory response mediated by vagus nerve triggered by sight, smell, or thought of food.

cards.q: What is the ileocecal sphincter and its regulation?
cards.a: Prevents backflow from colon to ileum. Relaxes when ileum is distended; contracts when cecum is distended.

cards.q: What is the gastrocolic reflex?
cards.a: Distension of stomach → increased colonic motility (especially after meals).

cards.q: What is Hirschsprung’s disease?
cards.a: Absence of ganglion cells (Auerbach’s plexus) in distal colon → functional obstruction and megacolon.

cards.q: What is achalasia?
cards.a: Failure of LES relaxation due to loss of inhibitory neurons (nitric oxide, VIP). Bird-beak appearance on barium swallow.

cards.q: What is the role of gastrin in the stomach?
cards.a: Stimulates HCl secretion, increases gastric motility, and promotes growth of gastric mucosa.

cards.q: What inhibits gastrin release?
cards.a: Low gastric pH (somatostatin), secretin, CCK, and GIP.

cards.q: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
cards.a: Gastrinoma → excessive gastrin → hypersecretion of gastric acid → refractory peptic ulcers.

cards.q: What is the most potent stimulant of gastric acid secretion?
cards.a: Histamine (via H2 receptors on parietal cells).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)?
cards.a: Irreversible inhibition of H⁺/K⁺-ATPase on parietal cells.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of H2 receptor blockers?
cards.a: Competitive inhibition of histamine on parietal cells.

cards.q: What protects against NSAID-induced gastric ulcers?
cards.a: Misoprostol (PGE₁ analog) — increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion.

cards.q: What is the role of intrinsic factor?
cards.a: Binds Vitamin B12 in stomach → allows absorption in terminal ileum.

cards.q: What is pernicious anemia?
cards.a: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → lack of Intrinsic Factor → Vitamin B12 deficiency.

cards.q: What is the most common site of peptic ulcers?
cards.a: First part of duodenum (duodenal bulb).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease?
cards.a: Helicobacter pylori infection.

cards.q: What is dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Rapid emptying of hyperosmolar chyme into small intestine after gastric surgery → osmotic fluid shift → diarrhea, hypotension, tachycardia.

cards.q: What is the primary site of nutrient absorption in the small intestine?
cards.a: Jejunum — highest absorptive capacity due to large surface area (villi + microvilli) and rich blood supply.

cards.q: Compare the jejunum and ileum.
cards.a:
• Jejunum: Thicker wall, more vascular, longer vasa recta, fewer Peyer’s patches.
  • Ileum: Thinner wall, more Peyer’s patches, shorter vasa recta, absorbs bile salts and B12.

cards.q: What is the role of brush border enzymes?
cards.a: Final digestion of carbohydrates (maltase, sucrase, lactase) and peptides (aminopeptidases, dipeptidases) on the apical membrane of enterocytes.

cards.q: How are bile salts recycled?
cards.a: Enterohepatic circulation: 95% reabsorbed in terminal ileum via Na⁺-bile salt cotransporter → portal vein → liver.

cards.q: What happens if terminal ileum is resected?
cards.a: Bile salt malabsorption → steatorrhea + Vitamin B12 deficiency.

cards.q: What is the role of the colon?
cards.a: Absorbs water and electrolytes (mainly Na⁺ and Cl⁻), forms and stores feces, and harbors gut microbiota.

cards.q: What is the maximum water absorption capacity of the colon per day?
cards.a: Approximately 4–5 liters.

cards.q: What is the gastrocolic reflex?
cards.a: Ingestion of food → increased colonic motility and mass movements, mediated by gastrin and vagus nerve.

cards.q: What is the haustral contraction?
cards.a: Slow segmentation movements in the colon that mix contents and promote water absorption.

cards.q: What is mass movement in the colon?
cards.a: Powerful peristaltic contractions that occur 3–4 times daily, propel feces toward rectum.

cards.q: What is the rectoanal inhibitory reflex?
cards.a: Distension of rectum → relaxation of internal anal sphincter (parasympathetic mediated).

cards.q: What maintains voluntary continence?
cards.a: External anal sphincter (skeletal muscle, pudendal nerve, S2–S4).

cards.q: What is Hirschsprung’s disease?
cards.a: Congenital absence of ganglion cells in distal colon → failure of relaxation → functional obstruction and megacolon.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the foregut, midgut, and hindgut?
cards.a:
• Foregut: Celiac trunk
  • Midgut: Superior mesenteric artery
  • Hindgut: Inferior mesenteric artery

cards.q: What is the portal circulation?
cards.a: Venous blood from GI tract, spleen, and pancreas drains into portal vein → liver sinusoids → hepatic veins.

cards.q: What is the unique feature of splanchnic circulation?
cards.a: Two capillary beds in series (intestinal capillaries → hepatic sinusoids).

cards.q: What stimulates liver regeneration?
cards.a: Hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and other cytokines after partial hepatectomy.

cards.q: What are the major functions of the liver?
cards.a: Metabolism (carb, protein, lipid), detoxification, synthesis (albumin, clotting factors), bile production, storage (glycogen, vitamins).

cards.q: What is bilirubin metabolism pathway?
cards.a: Heme → unconjugated bilirubin (bound to albumin) → liver conjugation (glucuronidation) → conjugated bilirubin → bile → intestine → urobilinogen (some reabsorbed, some excreted as stercobilin).

cards.q: Differentiate conjugated vs unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
cards.a: Unconjugated: Heme → unconjugated bilirubin (bound to albumin) → liver conjugation (glucuronidation) → conjugated bilirubin → bile → intestine → urobilinogen (some reabsorbed, some excreted as stercobilin).

cards.q: What is the cause of jaundice in hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Conjugated: Biliary obstruction, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Biliary tract obstruction (e.g., gallstones, pancreatic cancer).

cards.q: What is the function of Kupffer cells?
cards.a: Macrophages in liver sinusoids that clear bacteria, toxins, and old RBCs.

cards.q: What is the space of Disse?
cards.a: Perisinusoidal space between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium — site of exchange.

cards.q: What is the significance of Zone 1 vs Zone 3 in liver acinus?
cards.a:
• Zone 1 (periportal): Oxygen-rich, resistant to hypoxia.
  • Zone 3 (centrilobular): Oxygen-poor, most susceptible to hypoxic and toxic injury.

cards.q: What is the effect of secretin on the liver?
cards.a: Increases bile flow (choleresis) by stimulating bicarbonate-rich secretion from bile ductules.

cards.q: What is the effect of CCK on the biliary system?
cards.a: Causes gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation.

cards.q: What are the primary bile acids?
cards.a: Cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid (synthesized from cholesterol in hepatocytes).

cards.q: What are secondary bile acids?
cards.a: Deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid (formed by bacterial modification in colon).

cards.q: What is the role of bile salts in fat absorption?
cards.a: Emulsification of fats and formation of micelles to transport lipid digestion products to enterocytes.

cards.q: What is cholestasis?
cards.a: Impaired bile flow — can be intrahepatic or extrahepatic.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults?
cards.a: Chronic alcohol abuse.

cards.q: What is the function of pancreatic lipase?
cards.a: Hydrolyzes triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids.

cards.q: What is the role of colipase?
cards.a: Cofactor that allows pancreatic lipase to function in the presence of bile salts.

cards.q: What activates trypsinogen?
cards.a: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on duodenal brush border.

cards.q: What is the function of pancreatic bicarbonate?
cards.a: Neutralizes acidic chyme in duodenum to provide optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity.

cards.q: What is the secretin stimulation test used for?
cards.a: Assessing pancreatic exocrine function.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas?
cards.a: Pancreas divisum.

cards.q: What hormone inhibits gastric emptying?
cards.a: CCK and secretin (enterogastrones).

cards.q: What is receptive relaxation of the stomach?
cards.a: Vagus-mediated relaxation of fundus and body to accommodate food without increasing pressure.

cards.q: What is the pacemaker of gastric motility?
cards.a: Interstitial cells of Cajal in the greater curvature.

cards.q: What is the basic electrical rhythm (BER) of the stomach?
cards.a: 3 cycles per minute slow waves.

cards.q: What is the role of motilin?
cards.a: Initiates the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) during the fasting state to clear the GI tract of residual contents.

cards.q: What is the role of VIP in the intestine?
cards.a: Causes relaxation of smooth muscle and increases intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes.

cards.q: What is the effect of somatostatin on the GI tract?
cards.a: Inhibits release of most GI hormones (including gastrin, CCK, secretin), decreases motility and secretion.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of cholera toxin?
cards.a: Activates Gs protein → ↑ cAMP → opens CFTR Cl⁻ channels → massive secretory diarrhea.

cards.q: What causes traveler’s diarrhea (ETEC)?
cards.a: Heat-labile toxin (LT) increases cAMP similar to cholera toxin; heat-stable toxin (ST) increases cGMP.

cards.q: What is the absorptive mechanism for iron?
cards.a: Ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) absorbed in duodenum via DMT1 transporter. Regulated by hepcidin.

cards.q: What is the site of calcium absorption?
cards.a: Primarily duodenum and proximal jejunum (vitamin D dependent).

cards.q: What is the consequence of lactose intolerance?
cards.a: Undigested lactose reaches colon → fermented by bacteria → osmotic diarrhea, gas, bloating.

cards.q: What is celiac disease?
cards.a: Autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten → villous atrophy in proximal small intestine → malabsorption.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic finding in celiac disease?
cards.a: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies + villous atrophy on biopsy.

cards.q: What is tropical sprue?
cards.a: Malabsorption syndrome in tropical regions, responds to antibiotics + folate.

cards.q: What is Whipple’s disease?
cards.a: Caused by Tropheryma whipplei → PAS-positive macrophages in lamina propria, malabsorption.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of steatorrhea?
cards.a: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis) or bile salt deficiency.

cards.q: What is the Schilling test used for?
cards.a: Diagnosing Vitamin B12 malabsorption (pernicious anemia vs ileal disease).

cards.q: What is dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Post-gastric surgery complication: hyperosmolar chyme rapidly enters small intestine → osmotic fluid shift and vasomotor symptoms.

cards.q: What is the role of the appendix in immunity?
cards.a: Contains abundant lymphoid tissue and may serve as a reservoir for gut microbiota.

cards.q: What is the normal daily volume of intestinal secretions?
cards.a: Approximately 7–9 liters (most is reabsorbed).

cards.q: What is the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger in the pancreas?
cards.a: On apical membrane of duct cells; allows HCO₃⁻ secretion in exchange for Cl⁻.

cards.q: What is the effect of vagotomy on gastric acid secretion?
cards.a: Reduces cephalic and gastric phases of acid secretion (used historically for peptic ulcer disease).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of proton pump inhibitors?
cards.a: Irreversible inhibition of H⁺/K⁺-ATPase on parietal cell canalicular membrane.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of sucralfate?
cards.a: Forms a protective barrier over ulcer base in acidic environment.

cards.q: What is the role of prostaglandins in gastric protection?
cards.a: Increase mucus and bicarbonate secretion, enhance mucosal blood flow.

cards.q: What is the most common location of a Meckel’s diverticulum?
cards.a: 2 feet from ileocecal valve on antimesenteric border.

cards.q: What is the rule of 2s for Meckel’s diverticulum?
cards.a: 2% of population, 2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, presents by age 2, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric/pancreatic).

cards.q: What is intussusception?
cards.a: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another — common cause of intestinal obstruction in children.

cards.q: What is volvulus?
cards.a: Twisting of bowel on its mesentery — sigmoid volvulus most common in elderly.

cards.q: What is the most common site of peptic ulcer perforation?
cards.a: Anterior wall of the first part of duodenum.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of lower GI bleeding in adults?
cards.a: Diverticulosis (usually left-sided).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Peptic ulcer disease.

cards.q: What is the role of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater)?
cards.a: Site where common bile duct and main pancreatic duct join and empty into duodenum.

cards.q: What is the sphincter of Oddi?
cards.a: Controls release of bile and pancreatic secretions into duodenum.

cards.q: What stimulates release of secretin?
cards.a: Acid in the duodenum (pH < 4.5).

cards.q: What stimulates release of CCK?
cards.a: Fats and amino acids in the duodenum.

cards.q: What is the effect of CCK on the stomach?
cards.a: Inhibits gastric emptying (enterogastrone effect).

cards.q: What is the function of GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide)?
cards.a: Inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates insulin release in response to glucose.

cards.q: What is the difference between short-chain and long-chain fatty acid absorption?
cards.a:
Short-chain: absorbed directly into portal blood.
Long-chain: re-esterified into chylomicrons → lymphatic system.

cards.q: What is the site of absorption of most water-soluble vitamins?
cards.a: Jejunum.

cards.q: What is the site of absorption of folate?
cards.a: Jejunum (as monoglutamate).

cards.q: What is the site of absorption of Vitamin B12?
cards.a: Terminal ileum (requires intrinsic factor).

cards.q: What is the consequence of bile acid malabsorption?
cards.a: Diarrhea (bile acid diarrhea) due to stimulation of colonic secretion.

cards.q: What is the function of enterochromaffin cells?
cards.a: Secrete serotonin (5-HT) → regulates motility and secretion.

cards.q: What is carcinoid syndrome?
cards.a: Tumor of enterochromaffin cells → excess serotonin → flushing, diarrhea, valvular heart disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in developed countries?
cards.a: Chronic alcohol abuse.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes (especially trypsin) inside the pancreas → autodigestion.

cards.q: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Gallstones and alcohol.

cards.q: What are Ranson’s criteria used for?
cards.a: Prognostic scoring system for severity of acute pancreatitis.

cards.q: What are the clinical signs of retroperitoneal hemorrhage in severe pancreatitis?
cards.a: Cullen’s sign (periumbilical) and Grey-Turner’s sign (flank).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: Early ERCP if cholangitis or severe obstruction is present.

cards.q: What is the function of pancreatic alpha-amylase?
cards.a: Hydrolyzes internal α-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch and glycogen.

cards.q: What activates pancreatic proenzymes?
cards.a: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) from duodenal mucosa activates trypsinogen → trypsin then activates other zymogens.

cards.q: What inhibits pancreatic enzyme secretion?
cards.a: Somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas?
cards.a: Pancreas divisum.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the pancreas?
cards.a: Branches of celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the pancreas?
cards.a: Primarily into the portal venous system.

cards.q: What hormone is secreted by delta cells of the pancreas?
cards.a: Somatostatin (inhibits insulin and glucagon).

cards.q: What is the role of glucagon in the GI tract?
cards.a: Inhibits GI motility and secretion.

cards.q: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
cards.a: Gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) → severe peptic ulcer disease and diarrhea.

cards.q: Where are gastrinomas most commonly located?
cards.a: Duodenum and pancreas (triangle of gastrinomas).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
cards.a: Fasting serum gastrin level + secretin stimulation test.

cards.q: What is the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor?
cards.a: Insulinoma.

cards.q: What is the Whipple triad for insulinoma?
cards.a:
1. Hypoglycemic symptoms
  2. Low blood glucose
  3. Relief with glucose administration.

cards.q: What is VIPoma?
cards.a: Verner-Morrison syndrome — watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome).

cards.q: What is glucagonoma syndrome?
cards.a: Necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss, anemia.

cards.q: What is somatostatinoma?
cards.a: Inhibits GI hormones → steatorrhea, diabetes, gallstones.

cards.q: What is the law of the intestine?
cards.a: Distension causes contraction above and relaxation below the bolus (peristalsis).

cards.q: What are interstitial cells of Cajal?
cards.a: Pacemaker cells of the GI tract that generate slow waves.

cards.q: What is the basic electrical rhythm (BER) frequency in stomach vs small intestine?
cards.a:
Stomach: 3/min
Small intestine: 12/min (duodenum) decreasing distally.

cards.q: What is the effect of motilin on the stomach?
cards.a: Increases gastric motility during fasting (part of MMC).

cards.q: What is the gastroileal reflex?
cards.a: Food in stomach → increased ileal motility and relaxation of ileocecal sphincter.

cards.q: What is the defecation reflex?
cards.a: Rectal distension → parasympathetic mediated relaxation of internal anal sphincter + urge to defecate.

cards.q: What maintains fecal continence?
cards.a: Internal anal sphincter (sympathetic + tonic) and external anal sphincter (voluntary, pudendal nerve).

cards.q: What is the most common site of colonic diverticula?
cards.a: Sigmoid colon.

cards.q: What is the difference between diverticulosis and diverticulitis?
cards.a:
Diverticulosis = presence of diverticula.
Diverticulitis = inflammation/infection of diverticula.

cards.q: What is Ogilvie’s syndrome?
cards.a: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (massive colonic dilation without mechanical obstruction).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial overgrowth?
cards.a: Impaired motility (scleroderma, diabetes, post-surgical blind loops).

cards.q: What breath test is used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)?
cards.a: Lactulose or glucose hydrogen breath test.

cards.q: What is the role of gut microbiota in short-chain fatty acid production?
cards.a: Fermentation of dietary fiber → butyrate, propionate, acetate (energy source for colonocytes).

cards.q: What is the function of Peyer’s patches?
cards.a: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) involved in mucosal immunity and antigen sampling.

cards.q: What cells sample antigens in the gut lumen?
cards.a: M cells (microfold cells) overlying Peyer’s patches.

cards.q: What immunoglobulin is secreted into the gut lumen?
cards.a: Secretory IgA (dimeric IgA + secretory component).

cards.q: What is the significance of the gut-brain axis?
cards.a: Bidirectional communication between enteric nervous system and central nervous system via vagus nerve and hormones.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital GI anomaly?
cards.a: Meckel’s diverticulum.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the enteric nervous system?
cards.a: Neural crest cells.

cards.q: What is the foregut-midgut junction?
cards.a: Major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater).

cards.q: What is the midgut-hindgut junction?
cards.a: Distal third of transverse colon (cannonical point).

cards.q: What is the difference between endocrine, paracrine, and autocrine signaling?
cards.a:
• Endocrine: Hormone released into blood → distant target.
  • Paracrine: Acts on nearby cells.
  • Autocrine: Acts on the same cell that secreted it.

cards.q: What are the two major chemical classes of hormones?
cards.a:
1. Peptide/Protein hormones (water-soluble, act via membrane receptors)
  2. Steroid hormones (lipid-soluble, act via intracellular receptors)
  3. Thyroid hormones behave like steroids despite being amino acid derivatives.

cards.q: What is the second messenger for peptide hormones that use G-protein coupled receptors?
cards.a: Commonly cAMP (Gs or Gi) or IP3/DAG (Gq).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of steroid hormones?
cards.a: Diffuse into cell → bind cytoplasmic or nuclear receptor → hormone-receptor complex acts as transcription factor → alters gene expression.

cards.q: What is the hypothalamic-pituitary axis?
cards.a: Hypothalamus releases releasing/inhibiting hormones → anterior pituitary releases tropic hormones → target glands.

cards.q: Which hormones are released from the posterior pituitary?
cards.a: ADH (Vasopressin) and Oxytocin (synthesized in hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary).

cards.q: Which hormones are released from the anterior pituitary?
cards.a: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, GH, Prolactin (FLAT PiG mnemonic).

cards.q: What is the function of Growth Hormone (GH)?
cards.a: Promotes linear growth, protein synthesis, lipolysis, and insulin resistance. Stimulated by GHRH, inhibited by somatostatin.

cards.q: What mediates most effects of Growth Hormone?
cards.a: IGF-1 (Somatomedin C) produced mainly in the liver.

cards.q: What is the feedback regulation of GH?
cards.a: IGF-1 and GH provide negative feedback on hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.

cards.q: What is acromegaly vs gigantism?
cards.a:
• Gigantism: GH excess before epiphyseal closure.
  • Acromegaly: GH excess after epiphyseal closure (enlarged hands, feet, jaw, visceromegaly).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acromegaly?
cards.a: Pituitary adenoma secreting GH.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for acromegaly?
cards.a: Failure of GH suppression after oral glucose load + elevated IGF-1.

cards.q: What is prolactin’s main function?
cards.a: Stimulates milk production (lactation). Inhibited by dopamine (PIH).

cards.q: What are common causes of hyperprolactinemia?
cards.a: Prolactinoma, pregnancy, dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics), hypothyroidism (↑ TRH).

cards.q: What are the clinical features of prolactinoma?
cards.a: Galactorrhea, amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, headaches/visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopia).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for prolactinoma?
cards.a: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine).

cards.q: What is the function of ACTH?
cards.a: Stimulates adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) to produce cortisol.

cards.q: What is the diurnal rhythm of cortisol?
cards.a: Highest in early morning, lowest at midnight.

cards.q: What is the primary regulator of ACTH and cortisol?
cards.a: CRH from hypothalamus → ACTH from pituitary → cortisol (negative feedback on CRH and ACTH).

cards.q: What are the major effects of cortisol (glucocorticoids)?
cards.a: ↑ gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, protein catabolism, anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, stress response.

cards.q: What is Cushing syndrome vs Cushing disease?
cards.a:
• Cushing syndrome: Any cause of excess glucocorticoids.
  • Cushing disease: Pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH.

cards.q: What is the dexamethasone suppression test used for?
cards.a: To differentiate causes of Cushing syndrome.

cards.q: What is Addison’s disease?
cards.a: Primary adrenal insufficiency → ↓ cortisol and ↓ aldosterone → hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hyperpigmentation.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: Autoimmune adrenalitis (in developed countries).

cards.q: What is a key lab finding in primary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: High ACTH (due to loss of negative feedback) + hyperpigmentation.

cards.q: What is the function of aldosterone?
cards.a: ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺/H⁺ secretion in collecting duct (principal and alpha-intercalated cells).

cards.q: What regulates aldosterone secretion?
cards.a: Mainly Angiotensin II and hyperkalemia. ACTH has minor role.

cards.q: What is Conn syndrome?
cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal adenoma) → hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the renin level in primary vs secondary hyperaldosteronism?
cards.a:
• Primary (Conn): Low renin.
  • Secondary: High renin (e.g., renal artery stenosis).

cards.q: What is the function of thyroid hormones (T₃ & T₄)?
cards.a: ↑ basal metabolic rate, ↑ protein synthesis, ↑ β-adrenergic receptors, critical for brain development.

cards.q: Which is more potent: T₃ or T₄?
cards.a: T₃ is 3–4 times more potent. Most T₄ is converted to T₃ peripherally.

cards.q: What is the regulation of thyroid hormone synthesis?
cards.a: TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (anterior pituitary) → thyroid gland. Negative feedback by T₃/T₄.

cards.q: What is the role of thyroglobulin?
cards.a: Storage and precursor for T₃ and T₄ synthesis in thyroid follicles.

cards.q: What is the Wolff-Chaikoff effect?
cards.a: High iodine levels temporarily inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis.

cards.q: What is the Jod-Basedow phenomenon?
cards.a: Hyperthyroidism induced by iodine load in patients with autonomous thyroid nodules.

cards.q: What lab pattern is seen in primary hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: ↑ T₄/T₃, ↓ TSH.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: Graves’ disease.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in Graves’ disease?
cards.a: TSH receptor stimulating antibodies (TSI).

cards.q: What are the extrathyroidal manifestations of Graves’ disease?
cards.a: Exophthalmos (proptosis), pretibial myxedema, thyroid acropachy.

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of hormone action for steroid hormones?
cards.a: Bind intracellular (nuclear) receptors → hormone-receptor complex acts as transcription factor → alters gene expression (slow onset, long duration).

cards.q: What are the two main types of cell-surface hormone receptors?
cards.a:
1. G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs)
2. Receptor tyrosine kinases (e.g., insulin receptor) or associated tyrosine kinases (JAK-STAT for GH, prolactin).

cards.q: Which hormones use cAMP as second messenger? (Mnemonic)
cards.a:
FLAT ChAMP
FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, CRH, hCG, ADH (V2), Melanocyte-stimulating hormone, PTH.

cards.q: Which hormones use IP3/DAG pathway?
cards.a: GnRH, TRH, Oxytocin, ADH (V1), Angiotensin II, α₁-adrenergic.

cards.q: Compare the half-life and storage of peptide vs. steroid hormones.
cards.a:
• Peptide/Amine (water-soluble): Stored in vesicles, short half-life, rapid action.
  • Steroid/Thyroid (lipid-soluble): Not stored, longer half-life, bound to carrier proteins in blood.

cards.q: What is the hypothalamic-pituitary axis regulation?
cards.a: Hypothalamus releases releasing/inhibiting hormones into portal system → Anterior pituitary → Tropic hormones → Target glands → Negative feedback.

cards.q: Name the anterior pituitary hormones (FLAT PiG mnemonic).
cards.a: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, Prolactin, iGH (Growth hormone).

cards.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone is under predominant inhibitory control?
cards.a: Prolactin — inhibited by dopamine (PIH) from hypothalamus.

cards.q: What is the effect of dopamine on prolactin?
cards.a: Inhibits prolactin release. Dopamine antagonists (e.g., antipsychotics) cause hyperprolactinemia.

cards.q: Trace the pathway of Growth Hormone (GH) signaling.
cards.a: GHRH → Anterior pituitary → GH release → Liver produces IGF-1 (somatomedin) → growth effects. GH also has direct effects (lipolysis, insulin resistance).

cards.q: What stimulates and inhibits GH secretion?
cards.a:
• Stimulators: GHRH, hypoglycemia, exercise, sleep, amino acids, ghrelin.
  • Inhibitors: Somatostatin, IGF-1, hyperglycemia, free fatty acids.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acromegaly?
cards.a: GH-secreting pituitary adenoma (macroadenoma).

cards.q: Clinical presentation of acromegaly vs. gigantism.
cards.a:
• Gigantism: Excess GH before epiphyseal closure (linear growth).
  • Acromegaly: After closure → acral growth, coarsening features, prognathism, visceromegaly.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for acromegaly.
cards.a: Failure of GH suppression after oral glucose load + elevated IGF-1.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for acromegaly?
cards.a: Transsphenoidal surgical resection; medical: octreotide (somatostatin analog), pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist), cabergoline.

cards.q: What is Sheehan syndrome?
cards.a: Postpartum pituitary necrosis due to hemorrhage/hypotension → panhypopituitarism.

cards.q: What is the most common pituitary adenoma?
cards.a: Prolactinoma (microadenoma in women, macroadenmac in men).

cards.q: Classic presentation of prolactinoma in women vs. men.
cards.a:
• Women: Amenorrhea-galactorrhea.
  • Men: Decreased libido, impotence, gynecomastia (later due to mass effect).

cards.q: Treatment of prolactinoma.
cards.a: Dopamine agonists: Bromocriptine or Cabergoline (first-line).

cards.q: What are the posterior pituitary hormones and their origin?
cards.a: ADH (Vasopressin) and Oxytocin — synthesized in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of hypothalamus, stored and released from posterior pituitary.

cards.q: What stimulates ADH release?
cards.a: ↑ Plasma osmolality (osmoreceptors), ↓ blood volume/pressure (baroreceptors), angiotensin II, nausea, pain, nicotine.

cards.q: What are the two main receptors for ADH?
cards.a:
• V1 (vascular): IP3/DAG → vasoconstriction.
  • V2 (renal): cAMP → insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

cards.q: What is SIADH? Key lab findings.
cards.a: Inappropriate ADH secretion → euvolemic hyponatremia, ↓ serum osmolality, ↑ urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg), high urine Na⁺.

cards.q: Most common causes of SIADH.
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer, CNS disorders (meningitis, stroke), pulmonary disease, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine).

cards.q: Treatment of SIADH.
cards.a: Fluid restriction (first-line), demeclocycline, tolvaptan (V2 antagonist), hypertonic saline (severe/symptomatic).

cards.q: What is central diabetes insipidus? Diagnostic test.
cards.a: Deficiency of ADH. Water deprivation test: urine osmolality remains low; responds to desmopressin.

cards.q: What is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Kidneys do not respond to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin defect). No response to desmopressin.

cards.q: Causes of nephrogenic DI.
cards.a: Lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, demeclocycline, congenital (V2/AQP2 mutations).

cards.q: What is the hypothalamic hormone that stimulates TSH?
cards.a: TRH (Thyrotropin-releasing hormone).

cards.q: What inhibits TSH release?
cards.a: Thyroid hormones (T₃/T₄) via negative feedback on pituitary and hypothalamus.

cards.q: Outline thyroid hormone synthesis steps.
cards.a:
1. Iodide uptake (NIS)
  2. Oxidation & organification (Thyroid peroxidase)
  3. Coupling (MIT + DIT → T₃; DIT+DIT → T₄)
  4. Storage as thyroglobulin
  5. Proteolysis & release.

cards.q: Which enzyme is inhibited by PTU and methimazole?
cards.a: Thyroid peroxidase (organification and coupling).

cards.q: Which drug also inhibits peripheral T₄ → T₃ conversion?
cards.a: PTU (Propylthiouracil) (also used in pregnancy).

cards.q: What is the most active thyroid hormone?
cards.a: T₃ (3–4× more potent than T₄). Most T₃ comes from peripheral deiodination of T₄.

cards.q: What is the effect of thyroid hormones on metabolism?
cards.a: ↑ Basal metabolic rate, ↑ O₂ consumption, ↑ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, ↑ thermogenesis, ↑ β-adrenergic sensitivity.

cards.q: What are the causes of primary hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: Graves’ disease (most common), toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Graves’ disease.
cards.a: TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies (TSI) → diffuse thyroid hyperplasia and excess hormone production.

cards.q: Classic triad of Graves’ disease.
cards.a: Hyperthyroidism + diffuse goiter + exophthalmos (proptosis) + pretibial myxedema.

cards.q: Lab findings in primary hyperthyroidism.
cards.a: ↑ T₄/T₃, ↓ TSH (suppressed).

cards.q: Treatment options for Graves’ disease.
cards.a: Antithyroid drugs (methimazole/PTU), radioactive iodine (¹³¹I), thyroidectomy, β-blockers for symptoms.

cards.q: What is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis?
cards.a: Autoimmune (anti-TPO, anti-Tg antibodies) → chronic lymphocytic infiltration → hypothyroidism.

cards.q: Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas.
cards.a: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

cards.q: Lab findings in primary hypothyroidism.
cards.a: ↓ T₄/T₃, ↑ TSH.

cards.q: What is the Wolff-Chaikoff effect?
cards.a: High iodine load inhibits thyroid peroxidase → temporary decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis.

cards.q: What is the Jod-Basedow phenomenon?
cards.a: Iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (seen in patients with autonomous nodules).

cards.q: What is the function of parathyroid hormone (PTH)?
cards.a: ↑ Serum Ca²⁺ by: bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, 1α-hydroxylase activation (↑ Vit D), ↓ renal PO₄ reabsorption.

cards.q: What is the effect of PTH on phosphate?
cards.a: Phosphaturic (increases renal excretion).

cards.q: Primary hyperparathyroidism: labs and most common cause.
cards.a: ↑ Ca²⁺, ↑ or inappropriately normal PTH, ↓ PO₄. Most common: parathyroid adenoma.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Chronic kidney disease (↓ Vit D activation + phosphate retention).

cards.q: What is the treatment of hypoparathyroidism?
cards.a: Calcium + active vitamin D (calcitriol).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of parathyroid glands?
cards.a: Superior: 4th pharyngeal pouch; Inferior: 3rd pharyngeal pouch.

cards.q: What are the zones of the adrenal cortex and their products? (Mnemonic)
cards.a:
GFR (Salt, Sugar, Sex)
Glomerulosa: Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid)
Fasciculata: Cortisol (glucocorticoid)
Reticularis: Androgens (DHEA).

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting step in steroid hormone synthesis?
cards.a: Cholesterol → Pregnenolone via Desmolase (CYP11A1) (stimulated by ACTH via StAR protein).

cards.q: What stimulates aldosterone release?
cards.a: Angiotensin II (main), hyperkalemia, ACTH (minor).

cards.q: What is Conn syndrome?
cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (aldosterone-producing adenoma) → hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin.

cards.q: What is Addison’s disease? Classic presentation.
cards.a: Primary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for Addison’s disease.
cards.a: ACTH stimulation test (low cortisol response).

cards.q: What is Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (usually in meningococcal sepsis) → acute adrenal crisis.

cards.q: What is Cushing syndrome vs. Cushing disease?
cards.a:
• Cushing syndrome: Any cause of excess glucocorticoids.
  • Cushing disease: Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (most common endogenous cause).

cards.q: Best initial screening test for Cushing syndrome.
cards.a: Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test or 24h urinary free cortisol.

cards.q: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test result in Cushing disease.
cards.a: Cortisol suppresses (pituitary origin still feedback-sensitive).

cards.q: What is the main glucocorticoid in humans and its primary metabolic effects?
cards.a:
Cortisol
  • ↑ Gluconeogenesis
  • ↑ Lipolysis
  • ↑ Protein catabolism
  • Anti-inflammatory & immunosuppressive effects.

cards.q: What is the permissive effect of cortisol on catecholamines?
cards.a: Cortisol upregulates α₁ and β-adrenergic receptors → enhances vascular and cardiac response to catecholamines.

cards.q: How does cortisol affect immune function?
cards.a: Inhibits inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), stabilizes lysosomal membranes, ↓ neutrophil migration, ↓ lymphocyte proliferation.

cards.q: What is the diurnal rhythm of cortisol?
cards.a: Highest in early morning (around 6–8 AM), lowest at midnight. Regulated by CRH-ACTH axis.

cards.q: What is the difference between primary, secondary, and tertiary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a:
• Primary (Addison’s): Adrenal gland damage → ↑ ACTH, hyperpigmentation
  • Secondary: Pituitary (↓ ACTH)
  • Tertiary: Hypothalamic (↓ CRH) — most common after steroid withdrawal.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries?
cards.a: Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison’s disease).

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormalities are seen in adrenal crisis?
cards.a: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Treatment of acute adrenal crisis.
cards.a: IV Hydrocortisone + IV fluids (normal saline with dextrose) + treat underlying cause.

cards.q: What is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation sequence?
cards.a: ↓ Renal perfusion → Renin (JG cells) → Angiotensinogen → Ang I → ACE (lungs) → Ang II → Aldosterone release + vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the effect of aldosterone on the principal cells of the collecting duct?
cards.a: ↑ ENaC channels and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → Na⁺ reabsorption + K⁺ & H⁺ secretion.

cards.q: Clinical features of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).
cards.a: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, muscle weakness, suppressed plasma renin.

cards.q: How do you screen for primary hyperaldosteronism?
cards.a: Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) — elevated aldosterone with low renin.

cards.q: What is the most common pancreatic endocrine tumor?
cards.a: Insulinoma.

cards.q: Whipple’s triad for insulinoma diagnosis.
cards.a:
1. Symptoms of hypoglycemia
  2. Low blood glucose (<45–50 mg/dL)
  3. Relief of symptoms with glucose.

cards.q: What suppresses insulin release?
cards.a: Somatostatin, α₂-adrenergic stimulation, low blood glucose.

cards.q: What are the major actions of insulin on metabolism?
cards.a: ↑ Glucose uptake (GLUT₄), ↑ glycogenesis, ↑ lipogenesis, ↑ protein synthesis, ↓ lipolysis, ↓ gluconeogenesis.

cards.q: What is the counter-regulatory hormone to insulin?
cards.a: Glucagon (also cortisol, epinephrine, GH).

cards.q: Where is glucagon produced and what stimulates its release?
cards.a: Alpha cells of pancreas. Stimulated by hypoglycemia, amino acids, epinephrine.

cards.q: Main actions of glucagon.
cards.a: ↑ Glycogenolysis, ↑ gluconeogenesis, ↑ ketogenesis, ↑ lipolysis.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
cards.a: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells → absolute insulin deficiency → hyperglycemia, ketoacidosis.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
cards.a: Insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency. Strong genetic component + obesity.

cards.q: Classic symptoms of diabetes mellitus (4 P’s + weight loss).
cards.a: Polyuria, Polydipsia, Polyphagia, Poor wound healing, and unexplained weight loss.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus.
cards.a:
• Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL
  • HbA1c ≥6.5%
  • Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms
  • OGTT 2h glucose ≥200 mg/dL.

cards.q: What is the Somogyi effect?
cards.a: Nocturnal hypoglycemia (from excess insulin) → rebound hyperglycemia in morning due to counter-regulatory hormones.

cards.q: What is the Dawn phenomenon?
cards.a: Morning hyperglycemia due to surge in GH, cortisol, and glucagon in early morning (no preceding hypoglycemia).

cards.q: What is DKA? Key metabolic derangements.
cards.a: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Hyperglycemia, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketonemia. Due to insulin deficiency → lipolysis → ketone production.

cards.q: Treatment of DKA.
cards.a: IV fluids, insulin infusion, potassium replacement (even if serum K normal), correct acidosis if severe.

cards.q: What is HHS (Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State)?
cards.a: Severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), hyperosmolarity, profound dehydration, no significant ketoacidosis. More common in Type 2 DM.

cards.q: What is the role of C-peptide in diabetes diagnosis?
cards.a: Low C-peptide in Type 1 (no endogenous insulin). Normal/high in Type 2 (insulin resistance).

cards.q: What is the effect of incretins (GLP-1 and GIP) on insulin?
cards.a: Enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, inhibit glucagon, slow gastric emptying.

cards.q: Name two GLP-1 receptor agonists used in Type 2 DM.
cards.a: Exenatide, Liraglutide (also promote weight loss).

cards.q: What is the function of amylin?
cards.a: Co-secreted with insulin; slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypocalcemia in hospitalized patients?
cards.a: Hypoalbuminemia (correct with formula) or hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: How does PTH increase serum calcium?
cards.a:
1. Bone resorption
  2. Renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption (DCT)
  3. ↑ 1α-hydroxylase → active Vit D → intestinal Ca absorption.

cards.q: What is the effect of Vitamin D on phosphate?
cards.a: Increases intestinal absorption of both Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻.

cards.q: What is the role of calcitonin?
cards.a: Lowers serum calcium (minor role in humans); secreted by parafollicular C cells of thyroid in response to hypercalcemia.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Tetany, Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, prolonged QT interval, muscle cramps.

cards.q: What is pseudohypoparathyroidism?
cards.a: End-organ resistance to PTH → hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia + elevated PTH. Associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, round face).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients vs inpatients?
cards.a:
• Outpatient: Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Inpatient: Malignancy (PTHrP or osteolytic metastases).

cards.q: What is multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) Type 1 (Wermer syndrome)?
cards.a: 3 P’s: Parathyroid, Pituitary, Pancreas (gastrinoma, insulinoma).

cards.q: What is MEN Type 2A (Sipple syndrome)?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia.

cards.q: What is MEN Type 2B?
cards.a: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, Pheochromocytoma, Mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid habitus.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of MEN syndromes?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (RET proto-oncogene in MEN 2A/2B).

cards.q: What hormone is elevated in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Calcitonin.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal medulla?
cards.a: Neural crest cells (chromaffin cells).

cards.q: What catecholamines are produced by the adrenal medulla?
cards.a: Epinephrine (mainly) and norepinephrine.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
cards.a: Tyrosine hydroxylase.

cards.q: Clinical features of pheochromocytoma (Rule of 10s).
cards.a: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant, 10% in children, 10% familial.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for pheochromocytoma.
cards.a: 24-hour urinary metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive).

cards.q: Preoperative management of pheochromocytoma.
cards.a: α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) first → then β-blockade. Never start with β-blocker alone (unopposed α → hypertensive crisis).

cards.q: What is the function of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)?
cards.a: Released in response to atrial stretch → natriuresis, diuresis, ↓ renin & aldosterone.

cards.q: What is the difference between ANP and BNP?
cards.a: ANP from atria; BNP from ventricles. Both counter-regulate RAAS and sympathetic system.

cards.q: What is the hypothalamic hormone that controls GnRH release?
cards.a: Kisspeptin (from arcuate nucleus neurons) stimulates GnRH neurons.

cards.q: What is the pattern of GnRH secretion required for normal reproductive function?
cards.a: Pulsatile secretion. Continuous GnRH leads to downregulation of GnRH receptors → suppression of FSH/LH (used in GnRH agonist therapy).

cards.q: What hormones are secreted by theca cells vs granulosa cells in the ovary?
cards.a:
• Theca cells: Androgens (androstenedione) under LH stimulation.
  • Granulosa cells: Convert androgens to estrogens via aromatase under FSH stimulation.

cards.q: What is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory of estrogen synthesis?
cards.a: LH stimulates theca cells → androgens → granulosa cells (FSH) aromatize them to estradiol.

cards.q: What is the main estrogen in non-pregnant women? In pregnancy?
cards.a:
Non-pregnant: Estradiol (E2).
Pregnancy: Estriol (E3).

cards.q: What is the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle?
cards.a: Secreted by corpus luteum after ovulation. Prepares endometrium for implantation, inhibits uterine contractions.

cards.q: What maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
cards.a: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) produced by syncytiotrophoblast.

cards.q: What is the feedback effect of estrogen on LH/FSH before vs after ovulation?
cards.a:
Low estrogen: negative feedback.
High sustained estrogen (late follicular): positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation.

cards.q: What is the LH surge trigger for ovulation?
cards.a: High estradiol levels from dominant follicle → positive feedback on pituitary.

cards.q: What happens during the luteal phase if no fertilization occurs?
cards.a: Corpus luteum regresses → ↓ progesterone/estrogen → endometrial shedding (menses).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea with absent uterus?
cards.a: Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome).

cards.q: What is Turner syndrome (45,X) endocrine presentation?
cards.a: Primary ovarian failure → streak gonads, high FSH/LH, low estrogen, amenorrhea, short stature.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea?
cards.a: Pregnancy (must be ruled out first).

cards.q: What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) pathophysiology?
cards.a: Increased LH/FSH ratio → theca cell hyperplasia → excess androgens → anovulation, polycystic ovaries, insulin resistance.

cards.q: Classic clinical features of PCOS.
cards.a: Oligo/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, infertility, increased risk of Type 2 DM.

cards.q: First-line treatment for PCOS in a patient desiring fertility.
cards.a: Clomiphene citrate (anti-estrogen → ↑ FSH).

cards.q: What is the function of inhibin in the reproductive axis?
cards.a: Inhibin B (from granulosa cells) selectively inhibits FSH secretion from pituitary.

cards.q: What hormone peaks mid-cycle and triggers ovulation?
cards.a: Luteinizing hormone (LH) surge.

cards.q: What is the role of relaxin during pregnancy?
cards.a: Relaxes pelvic ligaments and inhibits uterine contractions.

cards.q: What maintains the endometrium during the luteal phase?
cards.a: Progesterone.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of testosterone-producing cells in males?
cards.a: Leydig cells (stimulated by LH).

cards.q: What cells in the seminiferous tubules produce inhibin and support spermatogenesis?
cards.a: Sertoli cells (stimulated by FSH).

cards.q: What is the role of androgen-binding protein (ABP)?
cards.a: Produced by Sertoli cells; concentrates testosterone in seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis.

cards.q: What is the effect of testosterone on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis?
cards.a: Negative feedback on GnRH and LH secretion.

cards.q: What is 5α-reductase responsible for?
cards.a: Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) — more potent androgen responsible for prostate growth and male-pattern baldness.

cards.q: What is the most potent androgen?
cards.a: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

cards.q: What causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most common form)?
cards.a: 21-hydroxylase deficiency → ↓ cortisol & aldosterone, ↑ androgens → virilization in females, salt-wasting crisis in severe cases.

cards.q: What is the enzyme deficiency in the most common form of CAH that causes virilization without salt wasting?
cards.a: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency → ↑ deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid activity) + androgens.

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for the development of male internal genitalia?
cards.a: Testosterone (from fetal Leydig cells).

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for the development of male external genitalia?
cards.a: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

cards.q: What hormone causes regression of Müllerian ducts in males?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) from Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of male hypogonadism?
cards.a: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) — primary hypogonadism, tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes.

cards.q: What is Kallmann syndrome?
cards.a: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism + anosmia (failure of GnRH neuron migration with olfactory neurons).

cards.q: What hormone is elevated in pregnancy and used in pregnancy tests?
cards.a: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).

cards.q: What maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over hormone production?
cards.a: hCG.

cards.q: When does the placenta begin producing progesterone and estrogen independently?
cards.a: After ~8–10 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: What is the role of human placental lactogen (hPL)?
cards.a: Similar to growth hormone and prolactin; increases maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis to provide nutrients to fetus.

cards.q: What causes gestational diabetes?
cards.a: hPL-induced insulin resistance + increased placental hormones.

cards.q: What is the effect of thyroid hormones on fetal development?
cards.a: Critical for brain development. Maternal hypothyroidism in pregnancy can cause cretinism if untreated.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy?
cards.a: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis or Graves’ disease.

cards.q: Why is PTU preferred over methimazole in first trimester?
cards.a: Lower risk of teratogenicity (methimazole associated with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia).

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for milk production (lactogenesis)?
cards.a: Prolactin.

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for milk ejection (let-down reflex)?
cards.a: Oxytocin (released in response to suckling via neural reflex).

cards.q: What inhibits prolactin release during pregnancy?
cards.a: High levels of estrogen and progesterone.

cards.q: What is the effect of suckling on GnRH/LH/FSH?
cards.a: Inhibits GnRH pulsatility → lactational amenorrhea (natural contraception for ~6 months).

cards.q: What is the feedback mechanism of testosterone on the HPG axis?
cards.a: Negative feedback on hypothalamus (GnRH) and pituitary (LH).

cards.q: What is the primary regulator of spermatogenesis?
cards.a: FSH (acts on Sertoli cells) + testosterone (acts on Sertoli cells).

cards.q: What is the role of Sertoli cells in spermatogenesis?
cards.a: Nourish developing sperm, produce inhibin and ABP, form blood-testis barrier.

cards.q: What lab pattern distinguishes primary from secondary hypothyroidism?
cards.a:
• Primary: ↑ TSH, ↓ T₄
  • Secondary: ↓ or normal TSH, ↓ T₄ (pituitary issue).

cards.q: What is subclinical hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Elevated TSH with normal free T₄. Often asymptomatic but may progress to overt hypothyroidism.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of goiter worldwide?
cards.a: Iodine deficiency.

cards.q: What is Riedel’s thyroiditis?
cards.a: Rare fibrotic thyroiditis that can cause hard goiter and compressive symptoms (mimics malignancy).

cards.q: What is the effect of amiodarone on thyroid function?
cards.a: Can cause both hyperthyroidism (Type 1) and hypothyroidism (Type 2) due to high iodine content and direct toxicity.

cards.q: What is the treatment of thyroid storm?
cards.a: PTU or methimazole + β-blocker (propranolol) + iodine (after thionamide) + glucocorticoids + supportive care.

cards.q: What is myxedema coma? Key features.
cards.a: Severe hypothyroidism: altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hyponatremia, respiratory failure. High mortality.

cards.q: What is the most sensitive test for thyroid function?
cards.a: TSH (best screening test in most patients).

cards.q: How do you interpret thyroid function tests in pregnancy?
cards.a: Total T₄ and T₃ increase due to ↑ TBG; use free T₄ and TSH. TSH reference range is lower in first trimester.

cards.q: What is the role of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)?
cards.a: Major carrier protein for T₄ and T₃. Increased by estrogen, pregnancy, OCPs; decreased by androgens, liver disease.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of bisphosphonates?
cards.a: Inhibit osteoclast activity → ↓ bone resorption. Used in osteoporosis and hypercalcemia of malignancy.

cards.q: What is the difference between osteoporosis and osteomalacia?
cards.a:
• Osteoporosis: Normal bone mineralization, ↓ bone mass.
  • Osteomalacia: Defective mineralization (Vitamin D deficiency).

cards.q: What is the effect of chronic glucocorticoid excess on bone?
cards.a: Inhibits osteoblast function, ↑ osteoclast activity → osteoporosis.

cards.q: What is hungry bone syndrome?
cards.a: Profound hypocalcemia after parathyroidectomy due to rapid bone uptake of calcium.

cards.q: What malignancy is most associated with hypercalcemia via PTHrP?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma (lung, head & neck).

cards.q: What is the treatment of severe hypercalcemia?
cards.a: IV fluids (first), bisphosphonates (zoledronate), calcitonin, loop diuretics (after hydration).

cards.q: What is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)?
cards.a: Inactivating mutation in CaSR → mild hypercalcemia, low urine calcium, normal/high PTH. Benign, no treatment needed.

cards.q: What is the most common pituitary hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Growth hormone deficiency.

cards.q: What is the order of pituitary hormone loss in compressive lesions?
cards.a: GH → FSH/LH → TSH → ACTH (last: prolactin may increase due to loss of inhibition).

cards.q: What is empty sella syndrome?
cards.a: Herniation of arachnoid into sella turcica → pituitary compression. Can cause hypopituitarism.

cards.q: What is the most common functioning pituitary adenoma after prolactinoma?
cards.a: GH-secreting (acromegaly/gigantism).

cards.q: What is Nelson syndrome?
cards.a: Rapid enlargement of pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy (loss of cortisol feedback → ↑ ACTH).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin response.

cards.q: What is psychogenic polydipsia?
cards.a: Excessive water intake → dilute urine, low plasma osmolality. Distinguish from DI by water deprivation test.

cards.q: What is the effect of cortisol on vascular reactivity?
cards.a: Permissive effect: required for normal vascular response to catecholamines.

cards.q: What is the difference between Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease?
cards.a:
Cushing syndrome = any cause of glucocorticoid excess.
Cushing disease = pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome?
cards.a: Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma).

cards.q: What test distinguishes pituitary from ectopic ACTH production?
cards.a: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test or inferior petrosal sinus sampling.

cards.q: What are the zones of the adrenal cortex and their main products?
cards.a:
Glomerulosa: Aldosterone
Fasciculata: Cortisol
Reticularis: Androgens (DHEA).

cards.q: What is the precursor for all steroid hormones?
cards.a: Cholesterol.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
cards.a: Tyrosine hydroxylase (converted to DOPA).

cards.q: What is pheochromocytoma rule of 10s?
cards.a: 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% in children, 10% familial.

cards.q: What is the screening test for pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Plasma free metanephrines or 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines.

cards.q: Preoperative preparation for pheochromocytoma resection.
cards.a: α-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine) first, followed by β-blockade.

cards.q: What is the most common extra-adrenal site of pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Organ of Zuckerkandl (near aortic bifurcation).

cards.q: What is the embryologic origin of chromaffin cells?
cards.a: Neural crest.

cards.q: What is the function of ANP and BNP?
cards.a: Promote natriuresis, diuresis, vasodilation, and inhibit RAAS.

cards.q: Where is BNP primarily released from?
cards.a: Ventricular myocytes (in response to wall stretch).

cards.q: What is the clinical use of BNP/NT-proBNP?
cards.a: Diagnosis and prognosis of heart failure.

cards.q: What hormone is released in response to hypoglycemia from pancreatic alpha cells?
cards.a: Glucagon.

cards.q: What is incretin effect?
cards.a: Greater insulin release after oral glucose than IV glucose due to GLP-1 and GIP.

cards.q: Name two DPP-4 inhibitors.
cards.a: Sitagliptin, saxagliptin.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors?
cards.a: Block glucose reabsorption in proximal tubule → glucosuria, natriuresis, weight loss.

cards.q: What is the honeymoon phase in Type 1 DM?
cards.a: Temporary partial remission after starting insulin due to residual beta cell function.

cards.q: What are the microvascular complications of diabetes?
cards.a: Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in Type 1 DM patients?
cards.a: Cardiovascular disease (macrovascular complication).

cards.q: What is the target HbA1c for most diabetic patients?
cards.a: <7.0% (individualized; stricter in younger patients, less strict in elderly).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the indifferent gonad?
cards.a: Derived from genital ridge (intermediate mesoderm) + primordial germ cells (from yolk sac endoderm).

cards.q: What gene on the Y chromosome determines male gonadal differentiation?
cards.a: SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y) → testis development.

cards.q: What hormone causes regression of Müllerian ducts in males?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) secreted by Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What hormone stimulates development of Wolffian ducts (male internal genitalia)?
cards.a: Testosterone produced by fetal Leydig cells.

cards.q: What hormone is required for development of male external genitalia?
cards.a: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) (converted by 5α-reductase).

cards.q: What is the default developmental pathway of the reproductive system?
cards.a: Female (Müllerian ducts develop into uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina in absence of SRY/AMH/testosterone).

cards.q: What is the most common disorder of sexual development in genetic males with ambiguous genitalia?
cards.a: 5α-reductase deficiency (normal internal male genitalia, ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth).

cards.q: What is the karyotype and classic phenotype of Turner syndrome?
cards.a: 45,X. Short stature, streak gonads, primary amenorrhea, webbed neck, coarctation of aorta.

cards.q: What is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome? Key features?
cards.a: 47,XXY. Tall stature, gynecomastia, small firm testes, infertility, hypogonadism.

cards.q: What cells in the testis produce testosterone?
cards.a: Leydig cells (stimulated by LH).

cards.q: What cells support spermatogenesis and produce inhibin?
cards.a: Sertoli cells (stimulated by FSH).

cards.q: What is the role of androgen-binding protein (ABP)?
cards.a: Produced by Sertoli cells; concentrates testosterone within seminiferous tubules to maintain high local levels for spermatogenesis.

cards.q: What is the hypothalamic hormone that regulates the male reproductive axis?
cards.a: GnRH (pulsatile) → stimulates FSH and LH release from anterior pituitary.

cards.q: What provides negative feedback on FSH secretion in males?
cards.a: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What provides negative feedback on LH secretion in males?
cards.a: Testosterone (and DHT).

cards.q: Outline the stages of spermatogenesis.
cards.a: Spermatogonium (2n) → Primary spermatocyte (meiosis I) → Secondary spermatocyte (meiosis II) → Spermatid → Spermatozoa (spermiogenesis).

cards.q: Where does spermiogenesis occur?
cards.a: In the seminiferous tubules with support from Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What is the function of the blood-testis barrier?
cards.a: Formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells; protects developing sperm from immune attack.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of male infertility?
cards.a: Varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus, usually left side).

cards.q: What hormone is essential for initiation and maintenance of spermatogenesis?
cards.a: FSH + high intratesticular testosterone.

cards.q: What is the effect of chronic GnRH agonist administration?
cards.a: Downregulation of GnRH receptors → decreased FSH/LH → chemical castration (used in prostate cancer, endometriosis).

cards.q: What is the source of fructose in semen?
cards.a: Seminal vesicles.

cards.q: What provides the alkaline pH of semen?
cards.a: Seminal vesicles and prostate.

cards.q: What is the composition of the sperm acrosome?
cards.a: Contains hydrolytic enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase) needed for penetration of zona pellucida.

cards.q: What maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
cards.a: hCG (produced by syncytiotrophoblast).

cards.q: What is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory?
cards.a: LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens → FSH stimulates granulosa cells to aromatize androgens into estrogens.

cards.q: What hormone triggers the LH surge and ovulation?
cards.a: High sustained levels of estradiol (positive feedback on pituitary).

cards.q: What maintains the endometrium during the secretory (luteal) phase?
cards.a: Progesterone from the corpus luteum.

cards.q: What causes the ischemic phase leading to menses?
cards.a: Regression of corpus luteum → sharp drop in progesterone and estrogen.

cards.q: What is the average length of the menstrual cycle? What is the most variable phase?
cards.a: 28 days. Follicular (proliferative) phase is most variable.

cards.q: What is mittelschmerz?
cards.a: Mid-cycle pelvic pain due to ovulation (peritoneal irritation by follicular fluid).

cards.q: What is the dominant hormone in the follicular phase vs luteal phase?
cards.a:
Follicular: Estrogen.
Luteal: Progesterone.

cards.q: What is the effect of progesterone on basal body temperature?
cards.a: Increases it by ~0.5°C (used in natural family planning).

cards.q: What is the role of relaxin in pregnancy?
cards.a: Softens cervix and pelvic ligaments; inhibits uterine contractions.

cards.q: What is human placental lactogen (hPL) function?
cards.a: Causes maternal insulin resistance, promotes lipolysis, ensures glucose availability to fetus.

cards.q: When does the placenta take over progesterone production?
cards.a: Around 8–10 weeks of gestation (luteoplacental shift).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea with normal secondary sexual characteristics?
cards.a: Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome) — absent uterus/vagina.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea?
cards.a: Pregnancy (must always be ruled out first).

cards.q: What is Asherman syndrome?
cards.a: Intrauterine adhesions (usually post-D&C) causing amenorrhea and infertility.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of PCOS?
cards.a: ↑ LH/FSH ratio → theca cell androgen excess → anovulation, multiple cysts, insulin resistance.

cards.q: What are the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS diagnosis?
cards.a: Need 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound.

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for PCOS infertility?
cards.a: Clomiphene citrate (selective estrogen receptor modulator → ↑ FSH).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of clomiphene?
cards.a: Blocks estrogen receptors in hypothalamus/pituitary → removes negative feedback → ↑ GnRH → ↑ FSH/LH.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of female infertility?
cards.a: Anovulation (often due to PCOS).

cards.q: What hormone is measured to assess ovarian reserve?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) — produced by granulosa cells of preantral follicles.

cards.q: What is the effect of estrogen on the uterus (proliferative phase)?
cards.a: Endometrial proliferation and ↑ myometrial excitability.

cards.q: What is the effect of progesterone on the uterus (secretory phase)?
cards.a: Secretory changes, decidualization, decreased myometrial excitability.

cards.q: What is the proliferative phase of the endometrium driven by?
cards.a: Estrogen — causes glandular and stromal proliferation.

cards.q: What is the secretory phase of the endometrium driven by?
cards.a: Progesterone — induces glandular secretion, decidualization, and increased vascularity.

cards.q: What causes the LH surge?
cards.a: High sustained estradiol levels exerting positive feedback on the anterior pituitary.

cards.q: When does ovulation typically occur in a 28-day cycle?
cards.a: Day 14 (approximately 24–36 hours after LH surge).

cards.q: What is the corpus luteum?
cards.a: Remnant of the ruptured Graafian follicle after ovulation; secretes progesterone and estrogen.

cards.q: What maintains the corpus luteum if fertilization occurs?
cards.a: hCG from the implanted blastocyst.

cards.q: What is the lifespan of the corpus luteum if no pregnancy occurs?
cards.a: Approximately 10–14 days.

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for the mid-cycle increase in basal body temperature?
cards.a: Progesterone.

cards.q: What is the role of prostaglandins in menstruation?
cards.a: Cause uterine contractions and vasoconstriction leading to endometrial shedding.

cards.q: What is dysmenorrhea?
cards.a: Painful menstruation, primarily due to excess prostaglandin F₂α.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of combined oral contraceptives (COCs)?
cards.a: Suppress GnRH pulsatility → inhibit FSH/LH surge → prevent ovulation + thicken cervical mucus + thin endometrium.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of progestin-only pills (mini-pill)?
cards.a: Primarily thicken cervical mucus and alter endometrium; ovulation may still occur in some cycles.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of emergency contraception (levonorgestrel)?
cards.a: Delays or inhibits ovulation if taken before LH surge.

cards.q: What is the most effective form of long-acting reversible contraception (LARC)?
cards.a: Levonorgestrel IUD or copper IUD (both >99% effective).

cards.q: What is endometriosis?
cards.a: Presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus (most commonly ovaries, peritoneum). Causes dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, infertility.

cards.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosis of endometriosis?
cards.a: Laparoscopy with biopsy.

cards.q: What is adenomyosis?
cards.a: Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium → enlarged, tender uterus, heavy painful periods.

cards.q: What is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Ampulla of the fallopian tube.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Amenorrhea + abdominal pain + vaginal bleeding.

cards.q: What hormone is used to monitor viability in early pregnancy?
cards.a: β-hCG (should double every 48 hours in normal early pregnancy).

cards.q: What is the role of progesterone in early pregnancy?
cards.a: Maintains endometrium, inhibits uterine contractions, promotes decidualization.

cards.q: What causes morning sickness?
cards.a: Elevated hCG and estrogen levels.

cards.q: What cardiovascular change occurs in pregnancy due to increased blood volume?
cards.a: Increased cardiac output (↑ stroke volume + ↑ heart rate).

cards.q: What is the effect of pregnancy on respiratory physiology?
cards.a: Increased tidal volume and minute ventilation (progesterone-driven hyperventilation) → mild respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: What is supine hypotensive syndrome?
cards.a: Compression of inferior vena cava by gravid uterus when lying supine → decreased venous return and hypotension.

cards.q: What is the role of oxytocin during labor?
cards.a: Causes uterine contractions (positive feedback during labor).

cards.q: What is Ferguson’s reflex?
cards.a: Pressure on cervix → increased oxytocin release → stronger contractions.

cards.q: What hormone softens the cervix and pubic symphysis before labor?
cards.a: Relaxin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage?
cards.a: Uterine atony.

cards.q: What maintains milk production after delivery?
cards.a: Prolactin (stimulated by suckling).

cards.q: What triggers the milk ejection reflex?
cards.a: Oxytocin released in response to suckling (neural reflex).

cards.q: What is lactational amenorrhea?
cards.a: Suckling-induced inhibition of GnRH pulsatility → suppressed ovulation (natural contraception for ~6 months if exclusive breastfeeding).

cards.q: What is menopause?
cards.a: Permanent cessation of menstruation due to ovarian follicle depletion (average age 51).

cards.q: What hormonal change defines menopause?
cards.a: Marked decrease in estrogen and inhibin → elevated FSH and LH.

cards.q: What are common symptoms of menopause?
cards.a: Hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, osteoporosis risk, mood changes.

cards.q: What is the most serious long-term consequence of estrogen deficiency?
cards.a: Osteoporosis (accelerated bone loss).

cards.q: What is the definition of premature ovarian failure?
cards.a: Menopause before age 40.

cards.q: What is the most common chromosomal cause of premature ovarian failure?
cards.a: Turner syndrome (45,X).

cards.q: What is the role of estrogen in bone health?
cards.a: Inhibits osteoclast activity and promotes osteoblast function.

cards.q: What is the effect of estrogen on HDL and LDL?
cards.a: Increases HDL, decreases LDL (protective against atherosclerosis before menopause).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of tamoxifen?
cards.a: SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator) — antagonist in breast tissue, agonist in bone and endometrium.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of raloxifene?
cards.a: SERM — agonist in bone (prevents osteoporosis), antagonist in breast and endometrium.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of male hypogonadism?
cards.a: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).

cards.q: What is the presentation of androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS)?
cards.a: 46,XY karyotype, female external phenotype, absent uterus, undescended testes, no pubic/axillary hair.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ambiguous genitalia in genetic females?
cards.a: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ambiguous genitalia in genetic males?
cards.a: 5α-reductase deficiency or partial androgen insensitivity.

cards.q: What is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing primary amenorrhea?
cards.a: Turner syndrome (45,X) — streak gonads and ovarian failure.

cards.q: What is the karyotype and phenotype of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS)?
cards.a: 46,XY. Female external genitalia, blind-ending vagina, no uterus, undescended testes, scant pubic/axillary hair.

cards.q: What is the underlying defect in 5α-reductase deficiency?
cards.a: Inability to convert testosterone to DHT → ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth, but virilization at puberty.

cards.q: What is true hermaphroditism (ovotesticular DSD)?
cards.a: Presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue. Rare.

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for thelarche (breast development)?
cards.a: Estrogen.

cards.q: What hormone is responsible for pubarche (pubic/axillary hair)?
cards.a: Androgens (mainly adrenal DHEA in females).

cards.q: What is the first visible sign of puberty in girls?
cards.a: Thelarche (breast budding).

cards.q: What is the first visible sign of puberty in boys?
cards.a: Testicular enlargement.

cards.q: What is the average age of menarche in the US?
cards.a: Approximately 12.5 years.

cards.q: What is precocious puberty?
cards.a: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of central precocious puberty?
cards.a: Idiopathic (constitutional).

cards.q: What is the treatment for central precocious puberty?
cards.a: GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide) to suppress gonadotropin release.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty in boys?
cards.a: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia or Leydig cell tumor.

cards.q: What is delayed puberty?
cards.a: No secondary sexual characteristics by age 13 in girls or 14 in boys.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of delayed puberty in both sexes?
cards.a: Constitutional delay (normal variant).

cards.q: What lab finding distinguishes primary from secondary hypogonadism?
cards.a:
• Primary: ↑ FSH/LH, ↓ sex steroids.
  • Secondary: ↓ or normal FSH/LH, ↓ sex steroids.

cards.q: What is the most common genetic cause of primary hypogonadism in males?
cards.a: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).

cards.q: What is the treatment for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (e.g., Kallmann syndrome)?
cards.a: Pulsatile GnRH or exogenous FSH + LH (or hCG + FSH).

cards.q: What is the role of aromatase in females?
cards.a: Converts androgens to estrogens in granulosa cells.

cards.q: What is the effect of aromatase deficiency?
cards.a: Excess androgens → maternal virilization during pregnancy and virilization of female fetus.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility?
cards.a: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

cards.q: What lab pattern is classic in PCOS?
cards.a: ↑ LH/FSH ratio (>2:1), ↑ androgens, normal/low FSH.

cards.q: What is the long-term risk associated with unopposed estrogen in PCOS?
cards.a: Endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of metformin in PCOS?
cards.a: Improves insulin sensitivity → reduces hyperinsulinemia → decreases ovarian androgen production.

cards.q: What is the definition of menopause?
cards.a: 12 months of amenorrhea after the final menstrual period.

cards.q: What is the average age of menopause in the US?
cards.a: 51 years.

cards.q: What hormonal change is the hallmark of menopause?
cards.a: Marked decrease in estrogen and inhibin → elevated FSH (>30 IU/L) and LH.

cards.q: What is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes) of menopause?
cards.a: Systemic estrogen therapy (HRT).

cards.q: What is the major risk of long-term unopposed estrogen replacement therapy?
cards.a: Endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma.

cards.q: What is added to estrogen in HRT for women with an intact uterus?
cards.a: Progestin (to oppose estrogen effect on endometrium).

cards.q: What is the effect of estrogen on bone?
cards.a: Inhibits osteoclast activity and promotes osteoblast survival.

cards.q: What is the leading cause of death in postmenopausal women?
cards.a: Cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: What is the effect of estrogen on coagulation?
cards.a: Increases clotting factors and decreases antithrombin III → increased risk of venous thromboembolism.

cards.q: What is the most common site of breast cancer?
cards.a: Upper outer quadrant.

cards.q: What is the most common histologic type of breast cancer?
cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the role of BRCA1/BRCA2 genes?
cards.a: Tumor suppressor genes involved in DNA repair (homologous recombination). Mutations greatly increase breast and ovarian cancer risk.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
cards.a: Intraductal papilloma.

cards.q: What is the most common breast mass in women under 25?
cards.a: Fibroadenoma.

cards.q: What is the most common breast mass in postmenopausal women?
cards.a: Carcinoma (until proven otherwise).

cards.q: What is the role of oxytocin in male reproduction?
cards.a: Facilitates sperm transport during ejaculation.

cards.q: What is the blood-testis barrier composed of?
cards.a: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What is the function of the epididymis?
cards.a: Sperm maturation, acquisition of motility, and storage.

cards.q: What is the effect of chronic alcohol use on male reproduction?
cards.a: Inhibits testosterone synthesis, increases estrogen via enhanced aromatization, testicular atrophy.

cards.q: What is the effect of anabolic steroid abuse on the HPG axis?
cards.a: Exogenous androgens → negative feedback → suppression of GnRH, FSH, LH → testicular atrophy and infertility.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of infertility in women?
cards.a: Anovulation (most frequently due to PCOS).

cards.q: What is the most common treatable cause of male infertility?
cards.a: Varicocele.
