cards.q: What is the definition of primary infertility?
cards.a: Inability to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse in a couple who have never conceived.

cards.q: What is the definition of secondary infertility?
cards.a: Inability to conceive after 12 months in a couple who have previously conceived.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of tubal factor infertility?
cards.a: Pelvic inflammatory disease (especially Chlamydia trachomatis).

cards.q: What test evaluates tubal patency?
cards.a: Hysterosalpingography (HSG).

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for anovulatory infertility in PCOS?
cards.a: Clomiphene citrate.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of letrozole in ovulation induction?
cards.a: Aromatase inhibitor → ↓ estrogen → removes negative feedback → ↑ FSH.

cards.q: What are the risks of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)?
cards.a: Ovarian enlargement, ascites, pleural effusion, thromboembolism, hypovolemia.

cards.q: What is the role of progesterone in luteal phase support?
cards.a: Maintains endometrium for implantation.

cards.q: What is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Ampullary region of the fallopian tube.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for ectopic pregnancy when patient is stable?
cards.a: Transvaginal ultrasound + quantitative β-hCG.

cards.q: What is the discriminatory zone for β-hCG?
cards.a: Approximately 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL (above this level, an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal US).

cards.q: What is the treatment for unruptured ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Methotrexate (if criteria met) or laparoscopic salpingostomy/salpingectomy.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of first-trimester spontaneous abortion?
cards.a: Chromosomal abnormalities (especially trisomies).

cards.q: What is the role of progesterone in threatened abortion?
cards.a: Controversial; sometimes used in recurrent pregnancy loss with documented luteal phase defect.

cards.q: What is the definition of preeclampsia?
cards.a: New-onset hypertension (>140/90) after 20 weeks + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia?
cards.a: Delivery of the fetus and placenta.

cards.q: What is HELLP syndrome?
cards.a: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — a severe variant of preeclampsia.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of gestational diabetes?
cards.a: Human placental lactogen (hPL) and other hormones cause insulin resistance.

cards.q: What is the screening test for gestational diabetes?
cards.a: 50g oral glucose challenge test (1-hour) at 24–28 weeks.

cards.q: What is the confirmatory test for gestational diabetes?
cards.a: 100g oral glucose tolerance test (3-hour).

cards.q: What are the major fetal risks of uncontrolled gestational diabetes?
cards.a: Macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, hypoglycemia, respiratory distress syndrome.

cards.q: What is the effect of pregnancy on thyroid-binding globulin (TBG)?
cards.a: Increases due to estrogen → higher total T₄/T₃ but normal free levels.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (first trimester)?
cards.a: Propylthiouracil (PTU).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of postpartum thyroiditis?
cards.a: Autoimmune (similar to Hashimoto’s).

cards.q: What is Sheehan syndrome?
cards.a: Postpartum pituitary necrosis due to severe hemorrhage and hypotension → panhypopituitarism.

cards.q: What is the most common pituitary hormone affected in Sheehan syndrome?
cards.a: Growth hormone and gonadotropins (often presents with failure to lactate).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea in a reproductive-age woman?
cards.a: Pregnancy.

cards.q: What lab test is first performed in the workup of amenorrhea?
cards.a: Urine or serum β-hCG.

cards.q: What is the workup for primary amenorrhea with normal secondary sexual characteristics?
cards.a: Pelvic ultrasound (to check for uterus) and karyotype.

cards.q: What is the workup for primary amenorrhea with absent secondary sexual characteristics?
cards.a: FSH level + karyotype.

cards.q: What is Asherman syndrome?
cards.a: Intrauterine synechiae (adhesions) usually following D&C or endometritis → amenorrhea and infertility.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Asherman syndrome?
cards.a: Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis + estrogen therapy to regenerate endometrium.

cards.q: What is the most common ovarian tumor in young women?
cards.a: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst).

cards.q: What is the most common malignant ovarian tumor?
cards.a: Serous cystadenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in yolk sac tumor?
cards.a: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in choriocarcinoma?
cards.a: β-hCG.

cards.q: What is the most common testicular tumor in young men?
cards.a: Seminoma.

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in seminoma?
cards.a: May have mildly elevated β-hCG; normal AFP.

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in nonseminomatous germ cell tumors?
cards.a: AFP and/or β-hCG.

cards.q: What is cryptorchidism?
cards.a: Undescended testis. Increases risk of infertility and testicular cancer.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of scrotal swelling in adult males?
cards.a: Hydrocele.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in adolescents?
cards.a: Testicular torsion.

cards.q: What is the main intracellular cation? Main extracellular cation?
cards.a:
• Intracellular: K⁺
  • Extracellular: Na⁺

cards.q: What maintains the Na⁺/K⁺ gradient across the cell membrane?
cards.a: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, uses ATP).

cards.q: What is the resting membrane potential of a typical neuron?
cards.a: Approximately -70 mV (inside negative relative to outside).

cards.q: What primarily determines the resting membrane potential?
cards.a: High permeability to K⁺ via leak channels (Nernst potential for K⁺ ≈ -90 mV).

cards.q: What is the Nernst equation used for?
cards.a: Calculates equilibrium potential for a single ion: $$E = \frac{61}{z} \log\left(\frac{[\text{ion}]_{\text{out}}}{[\text{ion}]_{\text{in}}}\right)$$ at body temperature.

cards.q: What is the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation?
cards.a: Calculates resting membrane potential taking into account permeability of multiple ions (mainly K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻).

cards.q: What causes depolarization in an action potential?
cards.a: Rapid influx of Na⁺ through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.

cards.q: What causes repolarization in an action potential?
cards.a: Efflux of K⁺ through voltage-gated K⁺ channels.

cards.q: What is the absolute refractory period?
cards.a: Period during which no new action potential can be generated (Na⁺ channels inactivated).

cards.q: What is the relative refractory period?
cards.a: Period during which a stronger-than-normal stimulus can generate an action potential.

cards.q: What is saltatory conduction?
cards.a: Action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons → faster conduction.

cards.q: What is the effect of myelination on conduction velocity?
cards.a: Greatly increases speed (up to 100 m/s in large myelinated fibers).

cards.q: Compare Aα, Aβ, Aδ, and C nerve fibers.
cards.a:
Aα: Largest, fastest, motor & proprioception.
Aβ: Touch, pressure.
Aδ: Sharp pain, cold.
C: Slow pain, temperature, unmyelinated.

cards.q: What is the neuromuscular junction neurotransmitter?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors.

cards.q: What is the sequence of events at the neuromuscular junction?
cards.a: Action potential → Ca²⁺ influx → ACh release → binds nicotinic receptor → Na⁺ influx → end-plate potential → muscle AP.

cards.q: What disease is caused by autoantibodies against nicotinic ACh receptors?
cards.a: Myasthenia gravis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of botulinum toxin?
cards.a: Inhibits ACh release from presynaptic terminal → flaccid paralysis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of succinylcholine?
cards.a: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (persistent agonist at nicotinic receptors).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of curare/non-depolarizing blockers?
cards.a: Competitive antagonists at nicotinic ACh receptors.

cards.q: What are the two types of skeletal muscle fibers?
cards.a: Type I (slow oxidative) and Type II (fast glycolytic).

cards.q: What is the sliding filament theory?
cards.a: Actin thin filaments slide over myosin thick filaments during contraction, shortening sarcomere.

cards.q: What ion triggers skeletal muscle contraction?
cards.a: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → exposes myosin-binding sites on actin.

cards.q: What is the role of T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum?
cards.a: T-tubules transmit AP deep into muscle fiber; SR releases Ca²⁺ via ryanodine receptors.

cards.q: What is excitation-contraction coupling?
cards.a: Link between muscle membrane depolarization and contraction (via Ca²⁺ release).

cards.q: What is the length-tension relationship in muscle?
cards.a: Optimal overlap of actin-myosin produces maximum tension (optimal sarcomere length).

cards.q: What is tetanus in muscle physiology?
cards.a: Sustained maximal contraction due to high-frequency stimulation (no relaxation between twitches).

cards.q: What is the motor unit?
cards.a: One motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.

cards.q: What is recruitment in muscle contraction?
cards.a: Progressive activation of more motor units to increase force.

cards.q: What is the size principle of motor unit recruitment?
cards.a: Small motor units (slow, fatigue-resistant) recruited first, then larger ones.

cards.q: What is the role of troponin and tropomyosin?
cards.a: Troponin binds Ca²⁺; tropomyosin blocks myosin-binding sites on actin in relaxed state.

cards.q: What is rigor mortis?
cards.a: Postmortem muscle stiffening due to ATP depletion (cross-bridges cannot detach).

cards.q: Compare skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle contraction triggers.
cards.a:
Skeletal: ACh → voltage-gated Ca²⁺.
Cardiac: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ (plateau).
Smooth: Ca²⁺ from SR or extracellular (calmodulin pathway).

cards.q: What is the autonomic nervous system neurotransmitter for preganglionic fibers?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (nicotinic receptors) in both sympathetic and parasympathetic.

cards.q: What is the postganglionic neurotransmitter for sympathetic vs parasympathetic?
cards.a:
Sympathetic: Norepinephrine (except sweat glands: ACh).
Parasympathetic: Acetylcholine (muscarinic).

cards.q: What receptor mediates sympathetic vasoconstriction?
cards.a: α₁-adrenergic receptors.

cards.q: What receptor mediates sympathetic increase in heart rate and contractility?
cards.a: β₁-adrenergic receptors.

cards.q: What receptor mediates parasympathetic decrease in heart rate?
cards.a: M₂ muscarinic receptors.

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on bronchioles?
cards.a: Bronchodilation via β₂ receptors.

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on GI motility?
cards.a: Increases motility and secretion.

cards.q: What is the fight-or-flight response mediated by?
cards.a: Sympathetic nervous system + adrenal medulla (epinephrine).

cards.q: What is the rest-and-digest response mediated by?
cards.a: Parasympathetic nervous system.

cards.q: What is the primary neurotransmitter of the sympathetic nervous system at the effector organs (except sweat glands)?
cards.a: Norepinephrine (acting on adrenergic receptors).

cards.q: What receptor type mediates most sympathetic vasoconstriction?
cards.a: α₁-adrenergic receptors (Gq → ↑ IP3/DAG → ↑ Ca²⁺).

cards.q: What receptor mediates sympathetic cardiac stimulation?
cards.a: β₁-adrenergic receptors (Gs → ↑ cAMP → ↑ heart rate and contractility).

cards.q: What receptor mediates bronchodilation?
cards.a: β₂-adrenergic receptors.

cards.q: What is the effect of α₂-adrenergic receptor activation?
cards.a: Presynaptic inhibition of norepinephrine release (negative feedback) and decreased insulin secretion.

cards.q: What is the main second messenger for muscarinic M₁, M₃, M₅ receptors?
cards.a: IP3/DAG pathway (Gq coupled).

cards.q: What is the main second messenger for muscarinic M₂ and M₄ receptors?
cards.a: ↓ cAMP (Gi coupled).

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on the heart?
cards.a: Decreased heart rate (negative chronotropy) via M₂ receptors.

cards.q: What is the effect of parasympathetic stimulation on salivary glands?
cards.a: Increased watery secretion (via M₃ receptors).

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on sweat glands?
cards.a: Increased secretion (cholinergic sympathetic fibers, muscarinic receptors).

cards.q: What is the baroreceptor reflex?
cards.a: Increased blood pressure → baroreceptors (carotid sinus, aortic arch) → ↑ vagal tone + ↓ sympathetic → ↓ HR and vasodilation.

cards.q: What is the chemoreceptor reflex?
cards.a: Low O₂, high CO₂, or low pH stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors → increased ventilation and sympathetic activity.

cards.q: What is the difference between temporal and spatial summation?
cards.a:
Temporal: multiple signals from same synapse in rapid succession.
Spatial: simultaneous signals from multiple synapses.

cards.q: What is long-term potentiation (LTP)?
cards.a: Persistent strengthening of synapses based on recent patterns of activity (basis of learning and memory).

cards.q: What is the role of NMDA receptors in LTP?
cards.a: Voltage and ligand-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers intracellular cascades for synaptic strengthening.

cards.q: What is the all-or-none principle?
cards.a: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, the AP fires with full amplitude.

cards.q: What determines the strength of a stimulus in nerve signaling?
cards.a: Frequency of action potentials (rate coding) and number of fibers activated (recruitment).

cards.q: What is accommodation in nerve physiology?
cards.a: Gradual increase in threshold when a nerve is slowly depolarized, preventing firing.

cards.q: What is the effect of hyperkalemia on resting membrane potential?
cards.a: Depolarization (less negative RMP) → can lead to paralysis or arrhythmias.

cards.q: What is the effect of hypokalemia on resting membrane potential?
cards.a: Hyperpolarization (more negative) → muscle weakness.

cards.q: What is the role of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger in cardiac muscle?
cards.a: Removes Ca²⁺ from the cell in exchange for Na⁺ (important in relaxation).

cards.q: What is the plateau phase in cardiac action potential?
cards.a: Phase 2: Balance of Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels) and K⁺ efflux.

cards.q: What is the pacemaker potential in SA node?
cards.a: Phase 4 spontaneous depolarization due to funny current (If) and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.

cards.q: What determines heart rate in the SA node?
cards.a: Slope of phase 4 depolarization (influenced by sympathetic and parasympathetic input).

cards.q: What is the effect of norepinephrine on SA node?
cards.a: Increases slope of phase 4 → positive chronotropy.

cards.q: What is the effect of acetylcholine on SA node?
cards.a: Decreases slope of phase 4 → negative chronotropy.

cards.q: What is the conduction velocity order in the heart?
cards.a: Purkinje fibers > Atria > Ventricles > AV node (slowest).

cards.q: Why is the AV node delay important?
cards.a: Allows atrial contraction to complete before ventricular contraction begins.

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on contractility?
cards.a: Positive inotropy (increased Ca²⁺ influx via phosphorylation of L-type channels).

cards.q: What is Starling’s law of the heart?
cards.a: Increased end-diastolic volume (preload) → increased stroke volume (up to a point).

cards.q: What is the Anrep effect?
cards.a: Increased afterload → increased contractility (intrinsic myocardial response).

cards.q: What is the Bowditch effect (Treppe)?
cards.a: Increased heart rate → increased contractility (due to increased intracellular Ca²⁺).

cards.q: What is the difference between isotonic and isometric contraction?
cards.a:
Isotonic: muscle shortens against constant load.
Isometric: tension increases with no change in length.

cards.q: What is the role of dystrophin in skeletal muscle?
cards.a: Links cytoskeleton to extracellular matrix; mutation causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

cards.q: What is the difference between multi-unit and single-unit smooth muscle?
cards.a:
Multi-unit: independently innervated (e.g., iris).
Single-unit: gap junctions, contracts as a syncytium (e.g., gut, uterus).

cards.q: What is the latch state in smooth muscle?
cards.a: Sustained contraction with low energy use (cross-bridges remain attached longer).

cards.q: What is the role of calmodulin in smooth muscle contraction?
cards.a: Binds Ca²⁺ → activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) → phosphorylation of myosin.

cards.q: What is the effect of nitric oxide on smooth muscle?
cards.a: Activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → relaxation (vasodilation).

cards.q: What is the role of interstitial cells of Cajal?
cards.a: Pacemaker cells in GI tract that generate slow waves.

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of heat production in neonates?
cards.a: Non-shivering thermogenesis via brown adipose tissue (activated by norepinephrine on β₃ receptors).

cards.q: What is the role of the hypothalamus in temperature regulation?
cards.a: Thermoregulatory center (preoptic area) — anterior hypothalamus for heat dissipation, posterior for heat conservation/production.

cards.q: What physiological responses occur in response to cold exposure?
cards.a: Cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering, piloerection, increased metabolic rate.

cards.q: What physiological responses occur in response to heat exposure?
cards.a: Cutaneous vasodilation, sweating, increased respiration.

cards.q: What is the effect of fever on the hypothalamic set point?
cards.a: Pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) → ↑ PGE2 → raises hypothalamic temperature set point.

cards.q: What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke?
cards.a:
Heat exhaustion: dehydration + salt depletion, sweating intact.
Heat stroke: failure of thermoregulation, core temp >40.5°C, CNS dysfunction, often dry skin.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Genetic defect in ryanodine receptor → uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release from SR after triggering agents (halothane, succinylcholine).

cards.q: What is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Dantrolene (inhibits Ca²⁺ release from SR) + cooling + supportive care.

cards.q: What is the difference between isotonic, hypertonic, and hypotonic solutions?
cards.a:
Isotonic: no net water movement.
Hypertonic: water leaves cell.
Hypotonic: water enters cell.

cards.q: What happens to RBCs in hypotonic solution?
cards.a: Swelling and hemolysis (crenation in hypertonic).

cards.q: What is the osmolarity of normal plasma?
cards.a: Approximately 285–295 mOsm/L.

cards.q: What is effective osmole vs ineffective osmole?
cards.a:
Effective: does not freely cross cell membrane (Na⁺, glucose).
Ineffective: freely crosses (urea).

cards.q: What is the effect of hyponatremia on brain cells?
cards.a: Hypo-osmolar hyponatremia → cerebral edema.

cards.q: What is the effect of rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia?
cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome).

cards.q: What maintains cell volume in response to hyperosmolar stress?
cards.a: Accumulation of intracellular organic osmolytes (idiogenic osmoles).

cards.q: What is the Donnan effect?
cards.a: Presence of impermeable anions (proteins) inside cell causes unequal distribution of permeable ions (more cations inside).

cards.q: What is the reflection coefficient (σ)?
cards.a: Measure of membrane permeability to a solute (1 = impermeable, 0 = freely permeable).

cards.q: What is the Starling equation for fluid movement across capillaries?
cards.a: $$J_v = K_f [(P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)]$$

cards.q: What forces favor filtration at the arterial end of capillary?
cards.a: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) > plasma oncotic pressure (πc).

cards.q: What favors reabsorption at the venous end of capillary?
cards.a: Plasma oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure.

cards.q: What is edema?
cards.a: Excess fluid in interstitial space due to imbalance in Starling forces.

cards.q: What are the four main causes of edema?
cards.a: ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure, ↓ plasma oncotic pressure, ↑ capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction.

cards.q: What is the role of lymphatics in fluid balance?
cards.a: Return excess interstitial fluid and proteins to circulation.

cards.q: What is the effect of increased venous pressure on capillary filtration?
cards.a: Increases filtration → edema (e.g., right heart failure).

cards.q: What is the effect of hypoalbuminemia on fluid balance?
cards.a: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure → edema (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, liver failure).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
cards.a: Block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in inactivated state → prevent action potential propagation.

cards.q: Why are local anesthetics less effective in infected tissue?
cards.a: Acidic environment → more ionized form → less penetration into nerve.

cards.q: What is the order of nerve fiber blockade by local anesthetics?
cards.a: Small myelinated > small unmyelinated > large myelinated (pain > temperature > touch > pressure > motor).

cards.q: What is the difference between sensory and motor nerve susceptibility to local anesthetics?
cards.a: Sensory fibers (especially pain) are blocked before motor fibers.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of tetrodotoxin (TTX) and saxitoxin?
cards.a: Block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels from outside the membrane.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of batrachotoxin?
cards.a: Prevents Na⁺ channel inactivation → persistent depolarization.

cards.q: What is the role of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in maintaining resting potential?
cards.a: Electrogenic (3 Na⁺ out vs 2 K⁺ in) contributes a small hyperpolarizing effect.

cards.q: What is the effect of ouabain/digitalis on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump?
cards.a: Inhibits it → increased intracellular Na⁺ → reduced Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange → increased intracellular Ca²⁺ → positive inotropy.

cards.q: What is the Q10 effect?
cards.a: Rate of biological processes increases ~2–3 fold for every 10°C rise in temperature.

cards.q: What is the basal metabolic rate (BMR) primarily determined by?
cards.a: Thyroid hormone levels.

cards.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) for carbohydrates, fats, and proteins?
cards.a:
Carbs: 1.0
Fats: 0.7
Proteins: ~0.8

cards.q: What is the normal core body temperature?
What is the difference between conduction, convection, radiation, and evaporation?
cards.a:
Conduction: direct contact.
Convection: air movement.
Radiation: infrared emission.
Evaporation: sweat.

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism for heat loss during exercise in a hot environment?
cards.a: Evaporation of sweat (most effective when ambient humidity is low).

cards.q: What is the effect of acclimatization to heat?
cards.a: Increased sweat rate, earlier onset of sweating, lower sweat sodium concentration, and improved plasma volume.

cards.q: What is the effect of dehydration on thermoregulation?
cards.a: Impaired sweating and cutaneous vasodilation → higher core temperature.

cards.q: What is the difference between obligatory and facultative water loss?
cards.a:
Obligatory: unavoidable (urine, feces, insensible losses).
Facultative: adjustable by kidneys (mainly via ADH).

cards.q: What is the daily insensible water loss?
cards.a: Approximately 600–900 mL (skin + lungs).

cards.q: What is the minimum obligatory urine output?
cards.a: Approximately 400–500 mL/day (to excrete daily solute load).

cards.q: What is the effect of severe hypovolemia on ADH secretion?
cards.a: Massive increase (non-osmotic stimulus via baroreceptors).

cards.q: What is the effect of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) on renal function?
cards.a: Increases GFR, inhibits Na⁺ reabsorption, inhibits renin and aldosterone.

cards.q: What is the role of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in volume regulation?
cards.a: Low effective circulating volume → renin release → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na⁺ retention.

cards.q: What is the difference between isotonic contraction and volume contraction?
cards.a:
Isotonic contraction: loss of isotonic fluid (e.g., hemorrhage) → normal osmolality.
Hypertonic contraction: loss of hypotonic fluid (e.g., dehydration).

cards.q: What is the effect of aldosterone on potassium handling?
cards.a: Increases renal K⁺ excretion (principal cells of collecting duct).

cards.q: What is pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1?
cards.a: Resistance to aldosterone → salt wasting, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the role of the vasa recta in the kidney?
cards.a: Countercurrent exchange that preserves the medullary osmotic gradient.

cards.q: What is the primary buffer system in extracellular fluid?
cards.a: Bicarbonate buffer system (HCO₃⁻ / H₂CO₃).

cards.q: What is the primary intracellular buffer?
cards.a: Proteins and organic phosphates.

cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation?
cards.a: $$\text{pH} = 6.1 + \log\left(\frac{[\text{HCO}_3^-]}{0.03 	imes P\text{CO}_2}\right)$$

cards.q: What is the renal compensation for respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: Increased H⁺ secretion and new HCO₃⁻ generation (increased ammoniagenesis).

cards.q: What is the respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) to blow off CO₂.

cards.q: What is the anion gap? Normal value?
cards.a: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Normal: 8–12 mEq/L.

cards.q: What causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis? (Mnemonic)
cards.a: MUDPILES: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Paraldehyde/Phenformin, Iron/INH, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

cards.q: What causes normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: GI HCO₃⁻ loss (diarrhea), renal HCO₃⁻ loss (RTA), or addition of HCl.

cards.q: What is the urine anion gap used for?
cards.a: Differentiates GI vs renal cause of normal anion gap acidosis (negative = GI, positive = renal).

cards.q: What is the primary disturbance in respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: Decreased PCO₂ due to hyperventilation.

cards.q: What is the renal compensation for chronic respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: Decreased HCO₃⁻ reabsorption and generation.

cards.q: What is the most common acid-base disorder in critically ill patients?
cards.a: Mixed disorders (often metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis).

cards.q: What is the effect of salicylate overdose on acid-base balance?
cards.a: Mixed: respiratory alkalosis (early) + high anion gap metabolic acidosis (late).

cards.q: What is the effect of severe vomiting on acid-base balance?
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis (loss of HCl) + volume contraction.

cards.q: What maintains metabolic alkalosis in a volume-depleted patient?
cards.a: Secondary hyperaldosteronism → continued H⁺ and K⁺ loss.

cards.q: What is the chloride-responsive vs chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a:
Responsive: urine Cl⁻ low (e.g., vomiting, diuretics).
Resistant: urine Cl⁻ high (e.g., hyperaldosteronism).

cards.q: What is the role of the kidney in long-term acid-base balance?
cards.a: Excretion of H⁺ as titratable acid and ammonium + generation of new HCO₃⁻.

cards.q: What is the major urinary buffer for H⁺ excretion?
cards.a: Phosphate (HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻) and ammonia (NH₃ → NH₄⁺).

cards.q: What is the effect of hyperventilation on cerebral blood flow?
cards.a: Decreased PCO₂ → cerebral vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the effect of hypoventilation on cerebral blood flow?
cards.a: Increased PCO₂ → cerebral vasodilation.

cards.q: What is the primary regulator of cerebral blood flow under normal conditions?
cards.a: PaCO₂ (most potent).

cards.q: What is autoregulation in cerebral circulation?
cards.a: Maintenance of relatively constant blood flow over a wide range of perfusion pressures.

cards.q: What is Cushing’s triad?
cards.a: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration — sign of increased intracranial pressure.

cards.q: Define sensitivity.
cards.a:
Proportion of people with the disease who test positive.
SnOUT = Sensitive test rules OUT disease when negative.

cards.q: Define specificity.
cards.a:
Proportion of people without the disease who test negative.
SpIN = Specific test rules IN disease when positive.

cards.q: What is the formula for positive predictive value (PPV)?
cards.a: $$\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}$$. Depends on prevalence.

cards.q: What is the formula for negative predictive value (NPV)?
cards.a: $$\text{NPV} = \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FN}}$$. Depends on prevalence.

cards.q: How does increasing prevalence affect PPV and NPV?
cards.a: ↑ Prevalence → ↑ PPV, ↓ NPV.

cards.q: What is the difference between incidence and prevalence?
cards.a:
• Incidence: New cases over time (risk).
  • Prevalence: Existing cases at a point in time.

cards.q: What is the formula for odds ratio (OR)?
cards.a: $$\text{OR} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c}$$.

cards.q: When is odds ratio used?
cards.a: Case-control studies and logistic regression.

cards.q: What is relative risk (RR)?
cards.a: Risk in exposed / Risk in unexposed. Used in cohort studies.

cards.q: What does a relative risk of 2.0 mean?
cards.a: Exposed group has twice the risk of the outcome compared to unexposed.

cards.q: What is absolute risk reduction (ARR)?
cards.a: $$\text{ARR} = \text{Risk}_{\text{control}} - \text{Risk}_{\text{treatment}}$$.

cards.q: What is number needed to treat (NNT)?
cards.a: $$\text{NNT} = \frac{1}{\text{ARR}}$$. Number of patients needed to treat to prevent one adverse outcome.

cards.q: What is a Type I error (α)?
cards.a: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true (false positive).

cards.q: What is a Type II error (β)?
cards.a: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false (false negative).

cards.q: What is power of a study?
cards.a: 1 − β. Probability of correctly detecting a true effect.

cards.q: How do you increase study power?
cards.a: Increase sample size, increase effect size, decrease variability, increase α.

cards.q: What is a p-value?
cards.a: Probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed, assuming null hypothesis is true.

cards.q: What p-value is conventionally considered statistically significant?
What is a confidence interval?
cards.a: Range of values within which the true population parameter is likely to lie (usually 95%).

cards.q: If a 95% CI for RR includes 1.0, what does it mean?
cards.a: Result is not statistically significant.

cards.q: What is selection bias?
cards.a: Systematic difference in how subjects are selected or retained in a study.

cards.q: What is recall bias?
cards.a: Cases remember exposures differently than controls (common in case-control studies).

cards.q: What is information bias?
cards.a: Systematic error in measurement or classification of exposure/outcome.

cards.q: What is confounding?
cards.a: A third variable associated with both exposure and outcome, distorting the apparent relationship.

cards.q: How do you control for confounding in study design?
cards.a: Randomization, matching, restriction.

cards.q: How do you control for confounding in analysis?
cards.a: Stratification, multivariable regression.

cards.q: What is the difference between prospective and retrospective cohort studies?
cards.a:
Prospective: exposure → follow for outcome.
Retrospective: use existing data (exposure already occurred).

cards.q: What is the strongest study design for establishing causality?
cards.a: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT).

cards.q: What is intention-to-treat analysis?
cards.a: Analyzes patients in the groups they were originally randomized to, regardless of compliance.

cards.q: What is per-protocol analysis?
cards.a: Only includes patients who completed the study according to protocol.

cards.q: What is a crossover study?
cards.a: Each participant receives both treatments in sequence (washout period needed).

cards.q: What is a case-control study best for?
cards.a: Rare diseases or diseases with long latency.

cards.q: What is a cross-sectional study?
cards.a: Snapshot in time — measures prevalence, cannot establish temporality.

cards.q: What is ecological study?
cards.a: Compares groups/populations rather than individuals.

cards.q: What is a systematic review?
cards.a: Structured review of all available evidence using explicit methods.

cards.q: What is a meta-analysis?
cards.a: Statistical combination of results from multiple studies.

cards.q: What is publication bias?
cards.a: Tendency to publish positive results more than negative ones.

cards.q: What is Berkson’s bias?
cards.a: Selection bias in hospital-based studies (both exposure and disease affect hospitalization).

cards.q: What is lead-time bias?
cards.a: Early detection makes survival appear longer without changing actual course.

cards.q: What is length-time bias?
cards.a: Screening preferentially detects slower-growing (less aggressive) diseases.

cards.q: What is the Hawthorne effect?
cards.a: People change behavior because they know they are being observed.

cards.q: What is the placebo effect?
cards.a: Improvement due to expectation of benefit.

cards.q: What is blinding in clinical trials?
cards.a:
Single-blind: patient unaware.
Double-blind: patient and investigator unaware.

cards.q: What is allocation concealment?
cards.a: Prevents investigators from knowing upcoming treatment assignments.

cards.q: What is the difference between efficacy and effectiveness?
cards.a:
Efficacy: performance under ideal conditions.
Effectiveness: performance in real-world settings.

cards.q: What is a hazard ratio?
cards.a: Ratio of hazard rates in two groups over time. Used in survival analysis (e.g., Cox proportional hazards model).

cards.q: What does a hazard ratio of 0.7 mean?
cards.a: The treatment group has 30% lower risk of the event at any given time compared to control.

cards.q: What is Kaplan-Meier analysis?
cards.a: Method to estimate survival function from lifetime data, accounting for censored observations.

cards.q: What is a log-rank test used for?
cards.a: Compares survival curves between two or more groups.

cards.q: What is the difference between incidence rate and cumulative incidence?
cards.a:
Incidence rate: new cases per person-time.
Cumulative incidence: proportion of new cases over a fixed period.

cards.q: What is person-time?
cards.a: Total time all individuals in a study are at risk and observed.

cards.q: What is a cohort study?
cards.a: Follows a group (cohort) forward in time from exposure to outcome. Can be prospective or retrospective.

cards.q: What is the major advantage of RCTs over observational studies?
cards.a: Randomization minimizes confounding and selection bias.

cards.q: What is cluster randomization?
cards.a: Groups (e.g., hospitals, schools) are randomized rather than individuals.

cards.q: What is the number needed to harm (NNH)?
cards.a: $$\text{NNH} = \frac{1}{\text{ARI}}$$. Number needed to treat to cause one additional adverse event.

cards.q: What is a forest plot used for?
cards.a: Graphical display of results from multiple studies in a meta-analysis.

cards.q: What does a diamond crossing the line of no effect mean in a forest plot?
cards.a: Overall result is not statistically significant.

cards.q: What is heterogeneity in meta-analysis?
cards.a: Variation in results across studies. Assessed by I² statistic.

cards.q: What is a funnel plot used for?
cards.a: Detects publication bias (asymmetry suggests bias).

cards.q: What is the difference between correlation and causation?
cards.a: Correlation shows association; causation requires temporality, strength, consistency, biological plausibility, etc. (Hill’s criteria).

cards.q: What is Simpson’s paradox?
cards.a: Trend appears in several groups but disappears or reverses when groups are combined (due to confounding).

cards.q: What is a surrogate endpoint?
cards.a: Substitute for a clinically meaningful outcome (e.g., blood pressure instead of stroke).

cards.q: What is a composite endpoint?
cards.a: Combines multiple outcomes into one (e.g., death/MI/stroke).

cards.q: What is attrition bias?
cards.a: Systematic difference in loss to follow-up between groups.

cards.q: What is reporting bias?
cards.a: Selective reporting of outcomes (e.g., only positive results).

cards.q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
cards.a:
Accuracy: how close to true value.
Precision: how reproducible the measurements are.

cards.q: What is reliability vs validity?
cards.a:
Reliability: consistency/reproducibility.
Validity: measures what it is supposed to measure.

cards.q: What is internal validity?
cards.a: Degree to which a study accurately measures the effect within the study population.

cards.q: What is external validity (generalizability)?
cards.a: Extent to which results can be applied to other populations/settings.

cards.q: What is a likelihood ratio?
cards.a:
How much a test result changes the odds of having disease.
$$\text{LR}^+ = \frac{\text{Sensitivity}}{1 - \text{Specificity}}$$.

cards.q: How do you convert pretest probability to post-test probability?
cards.a: Use Fagan nomogram or Bayes theorem with likelihood ratios.

cards.q: What is a screening test?
cards.a: Applied to asymptomatic people to detect disease early.

cards.q: What are the criteria for a good screening test? (Wilson-Jungner)
cards.a: Important disease, effective treatment, suitable test, acceptable to population, etc.

cards.q: What is overdiagnosis bias?
cards.a: Detecting disease that would never cause symptoms or death.

cards.q: What is verification bias?
cards.a: Only patients with positive screening test undergo gold standard test.

cards.q: What is the difference between a case series and a case-control study?
cards.a:
Case series: descriptive, no controls.
Case-control: analytic, has controls.

cards.q: What is a cross-sectional study’s main limitation?
cards.a: Cannot establish temporality (which came first — exposure or outcome).

cards.q: What type of bias is healthy worker effect?
cards.a: Selection bias — workers are healthier than general population.

cards.q: What is the null hypothesis (H₀)?
cards.a: No difference or no association between groups.

cards.q: What is an alternative hypothesis (H₁)?
cards.a: There is a difference or association.

cards.q: What is a two-tailed vs one-tailed test?
cards.a:
Two-tailed: difference in either direction.
One-tailed: difference in one specific direction.

cards.q: What does a wide confidence interval indicate?
cards.a: Low precision (small sample size or high variability).

cards.q: What is the Bonferroni correction?
cards.a: Adjusts significance level when performing multiple comparisons to reduce Type I error.

cards.q: What is a post-hoc analysis?
cards.a: Analysis performed after data collection, not pre-specified.

cards.q: What is an interim analysis?
cards.a: Analysis performed before study completion (with predefined stopping rules).

cards.q: What is a non-inferiority trial?
cards.a: Designed to show new treatment is not worse than standard by more than a predefined margin.

cards.q: What is an equivalence trial?
cards.a: Designed to show two treatments are clinically similar within a margin.

cards.q: What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric tests?
cards.a:
Parametric: assumes normal distribution (e.g., t-test).
Non-parametric: no distribution assumption (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon).

cards.q: What is the difference between a t-test and ANOVA?
cards.a:
t-test: compares means between **two** groups.
ANOVA: compares means among **three or more** groups.

cards.q: What is the chi-square test used for?
cards.a: Compares categorical (proportional) data between groups.

cards.q: When is Fisher’s exact test preferred over chi-square?
cards.a: When expected frequencies in any cell are <5.

cards.q: What is McNemar’s test used for?
cards.a: Paired categorical data (e.g., before-after studies).

cards.q: What is a matched case-control study?
cards.a: Controls are matched to cases on key variables (age, sex, etc.) to reduce confounding.

cards.q: What is the purpose of stratification in analysis?
cards.a: Controls for confounding by analyzing subgroups separately.

cards.q: What is multivariate analysis?
cards.a: Statistical methods that adjust for multiple variables simultaneously (e.g., multiple regression).

cards.q: What is logistic regression used for?
cards.a: Predicts binary outcomes; output is odds ratios.

cards.q: What is linear regression used for?
cards.a: Predicts continuous outcomes.

cards.q: What is Cox proportional hazards model used for?
cards.a: Survival analysis; output is hazard ratios.

cards.q: What does 'intention-to-treat' analysis preserve?
cards.a: Randomization and real-world applicability.

cards.q: What is a per-protocol analysis?
cards.a: Only includes patients who adhered to the protocol (can introduce bias).

cards.q: What is a sensitivity analysis?
cards.a: Tests how robust results are to changes in assumptions or missing data.

cards.q: What is a subgroup analysis?
cards.a: Examining treatment effect in specific patient subgroups (often exploratory).

cards.q: What is the difference between absolute risk and relative risk?
cards.a:
Absolute risk: actual difference in event rates.
Relative risk: ratio of risks.

cards.q: What is attributable risk?
cards.a: Excess risk in exposed group attributable to the exposure.

cards.q: What is population attributable risk?
cards.a: Proportion of disease in the population due to a particular exposure.

cards.q: What is the difference between prevalence and incidence?
cards.a:
Prevalence = existing cases / population.
Incidence = new cases / population at risk over time.

cards.q: What is the formula for prevalence?
cards.a: $$\text{Prevalence} = \text{Incidence} \times \text{Duration}$$.

cards.q: What study design is best for calculating incidence?
cards.a: Prospective cohort study.

cards.q: What study design is best for rare diseases?
cards.a: Case-control study.

cards.q: What study design is best for establishing causality?
cards.a: Randomized controlled trial (RCT).

cards.q: What is a double-blind study?
cards.a: Neither participants nor investigators know treatment assignment.

cards.q: What is allocation concealment?
cards.a: Hiding the randomization sequence from those enrolling patients.

cards.q: What is the difference between efficacy and effectiveness?
cards.a:
Efficacy: results under ideal conditions.
Effectiveness: results in real-world practice.

cards.q: What is a pragmatic trial?
cards.a: Designed to reflect real-world effectiveness rather than ideal efficacy.

cards.q: What is the NNT formula?
cards.a: $$\text{NNT} = \frac{1}{\text{ARR}}$$.

cards.q: What does a negative NNT mean?
cards.a: Harm (Number Needed to Harm).

cards.q: What is a confidence interval?
cards.a: Range likely to contain the true population parameter.

cards.q: If the 95% CI for an odds ratio includes 1.0, what does it mean?
cards.a: The result is not statistically significant.

cards.q: What is a Type I error?
cards.a: False positive — rejecting null when it is true.

cards.q: What is a Type II error?
cards.a: False negative — failing to reject null when it is false.

cards.q: How do you increase study power?
cards.a: Larger sample size, larger effect size, lower variability, higher α.

cards.q: What is a p-value?
cards.a: Probability of observing data (or more extreme) assuming null hypothesis is true.

cards.q: What does p < 0.05 mean?
cards.a: Less than 5% chance the results occurred by random variation if null is true.

cards.q: What is multiple testing problem?
cards.a: Increased chance of Type I error when performing many statistical tests.

cards.q: What is the Bonferroni correction?
cards.a: Adjusts α level downward (e.g., 0.05 / number of tests).

cards.q: What is a funnel plot used to detect?
cards.a: Publication bias.

cards.q: What is heterogeneity in meta-analysis?
cards.a: Variation in effect sizes across included studies (measured by I²).

cards.q: What is a fixed-effect vs random-effects model in meta-analysis?
cards.a:
Fixed: assumes one true effect size.
Random: accounts for variation between studies.

cards.q: What is the most important factor when interpreting a meta-analysis?
cards.a: Quality and homogeneity of included studies.

cards.q: What is a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve?
cards.a: Graph of sensitivity vs 1-specificity at different cut-off points. Area under curve (AUC) measures test accuracy.

cards.q: What does an AUC of 0.5 mean on an ROC curve?
cards.a: Test performs no better than chance.

cards.q: What is the Youden index?
cards.a: Sensitivity + Specificity - 1. Used to find optimal cut-off on ROC curve.

cards.q: What is a likelihood ratio positive (LR+)?
cards.a: $$\text{LR}^+ = \frac{\text{Sensitivity}}{1 - \text{Specificity}}$$. How much a positive test increases odds of disease.

cards.q: What is a likelihood ratio negative (LR-)?
cards.a: $$\text{LR}^- = \frac{1 - \text{Sensitivity}}{\text{Specificity}}$$. How much a negative test decreases odds of disease.

cards.q: How do you use likelihood ratios with pre-test probability?
cards.a: Convert probability to odds → multiply by LR → convert back to post-test probability.

cards.q: What is Bayes' theorem?
cards.a: Post-test odds = Pre-test odds × Likelihood Ratio.

cards.q: What is a nomogram?
cards.a: Graphical tool to calculate post-test probability using pre-test probability and likelihood ratio.

cards.q: What is the difference between a prospective and retrospective study?
cards.a:
Prospective: data collected forward in time.
Retrospective: data from past records.

cards.q: What is a historical control?
cards.a: Control group from previous data rather than concurrent patients.

cards.q: What is ecological fallacy?
cards.a: Making inferences about individuals based on group-level data.

cards.q: What is the Hawthorne effect?
cards.a: Participants change behavior because they know they are being studied.

cards.q: What is the placebo effect?
cards.a: Improvement due to belief in receiving treatment, not the treatment itself.

cards.q: What is the nocebo effect?
cards.a: Negative outcomes due to expectation of harm.

cards.q: What is regression to the mean?
cards.a: Extreme values tend to move closer to average on repeat measurement.

cards.q: What is a washout period in crossover trials?
cards.a: Time between treatments to eliminate carryover effects.

cards.q: What is a run-in period?
cards.a: Pre-randomization phase to assess compliance or exclude non-responders.

cards.q: What is a factorial design?
cards.a: Tests two or more interventions simultaneously in one study.

cards.q: What is a non-inferiority margin?
cards.a: Maximum acceptable difference where new treatment is still considered acceptable.

cards.q: What is the difference between superiority, non-inferiority, and equivalence trials?
cards.a:
Superiority: new > standard.
Non-inferiority: new not much worse.
Equivalence: new similar within margin.

cards.q: What is a cluster-randomized trial?
cards.a: Randomization at group level (schools, hospitals) rather than individuals.

cards.q: What is contamination in cluster trials?
cards.a: Intervention leaks to control group.

cards.q: What is the unit of analysis in a cluster trial?
cards.a: The cluster (not the individual).

cards.q: What is the most important strength of RCTs?
cards.a: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders.

cards.q: What is the major limitation of RCTs?
cards.a: Often expensive, time-consuming, and may have limited external validity.

cards.q: What is a pragmatic trial?
cards.a: Designed to test effectiveness in real-world conditions.

cards.q: What is an explanatory trial?
cards.a: Tests efficacy under ideal/controlled conditions.

cards.q: What is the CONSORT statement?
cards.a: Guidelines for reporting randomized controlled trials.

cards.q: What is the STROBE statement?
cards.a: Guidelines for reporting observational studies.

cards.q: What is the PRISMA statement?
cards.a: Guidelines for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

cards.q: What is the GRADE system?
cards.a: Method for rating quality of evidence in systematic reviews.

cards.q: What is a systematic error vs random error?
cards.a:
Systematic: bias (consistent direction).
Random: variability (reduced by larger sample).

cards.q: What is the most common source of bias in case-control studies?
cards.a: Recall bias and selection bias.

cards.q: What is the most common source of bias in cohort studies?
cards.a: Loss to follow-up (attrition bias).

cards.q: What is Berkson’s bias?
cards.a: Hospital-based studies distort associations because both exposure and disease affect hospitalization.

cards.q: What is collider bias?
cards.a: Conditioning on a common effect of exposure and outcome introduces bias.

cards.q: What is immortal time bias?
cards.a: Misclassification of time before treatment as exposed time in cohort studies.

cards.q: What is protopathic bias?
cards.a: Treatment given for early symptoms of disease appears to cause the disease.

cards.q: What is the healthy user bias?
cards.a: People who take preventive treatments are generally healthier.

cards.q: What is the difference between association and causation?
cards.a:
Association: statistical relationship.
Causation: one causes the other (requires Hill’s criteria).

cards.q: What is the process of gametogenesis in males called?
cards.a: Spermatogenesis — begins at puberty and continues throughout life.

cards.q: What is the process of gametogenesis in females called?
cards.a: Oogenesis — begins in fetal life; primary oocytes arrested in prophase I until puberty.

cards.q: What is the most common chromosomal abnormality in spontaneous abortions?
cards.a: Trisomy 16.

cards.q: What structure forms the female pronucleus after fertilization?
cards.a: The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II upon sperm entry.

cards.q: What is the zona pellucida?
cards.a: Glycoprotein layer surrounding the oocyte; prevents polyspermy and protects the embryo.

cards.q: What prevents polyspermy after fertilization?
cards.a: Cortical reaction (release of cortical granules) hardens the zona pellucida.

cards.q: What is the morula?
cards.a: Solid ball of 16–32 blastomeres formed after cleavage (day 3–4).

cards.q: What is the blastocyst?
cards.a: Hollow ball with inner cell mass (embryoblast) and trophoblast (day 5).

cards.q: What structure implants into the endometrium?
cards.a: Blastocyst (around day 6–7).

cards.q: Epiblast (future embryo) and Hypoblast.
cards.a: Epiblast (future embryo) and Hypoblast.

cards.q: What is gastrulation?
cards.a: Formation of the three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) from the epiblast (week 3).

cards.q: What is the primitive streak?
cards.a: Site of gastrulation; cells migrate through it to form mesoderm and endoderm.

cards.q: What is the notochord?
cards.a: Mesodermal structure that induces neural plate formation.

cards.q: What is neurulation?
cards.a: Formation of the neural tube from the neural plate (week 3–4).

cards.q:
• Anterior neuropore closes day 25
  • Posterior neuropore closes day 27
cards.a:
• Anterior neuropore closes day 25
  • Posterior neuropore closes day 27

cards.q: What defect results from failure of anterior neuropore closure?
cards.a: Anencephaly.

cards.q: What defect results from failure of posterior neuropore closure?
cards.a: Spina bifida (myelomeningocele most severe).

cards.q: What is the allantois?
cards.a: Outpouching of yolk sac; becomes urachus (median umbilical ligament).

cards.q: What is the yolk sac derivative in humans?
cards.a: Contributes to gut and primordial germ cells.

cards.q: What is the amniotic cavity?
cards.a: Space above the epiblast that becomes filled with amniotic fluid.

cards.q: What is the chorion?
cards.a: Outer membrane formed by trophoblast + extraembryonic mesoderm; becomes fetal part of placenta.

cards.q: What is the decidua basalis?
cards.a: Maternal endometrium beneath the implanted blastocyst; forms maternal part of placenta.

cards.q: What hormone maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
cards.a: hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin).

cards.q: When does the placenta take over progesterone production?
cards.a: Around 8–10 weeks (luteoplacental shift).

cards.q: Mesoderm + neural crest cells.
cards.a: Mesoderm + neural crest cells.

cards.q: What is the derivative of the 1st branchial arch?
cards.a: Mandible, maxilla, malleus, incus, muscles of mastication (Meckel’s cartilage).

cards.q: What is the derivative of the 2nd branchial arch?
cards.a: Stapes, styloid process, Reichert’s cartilage, muscles of facial expression.

cards.q: What is the derivative of the 3rd branchial arch?
cards.a: Greater horn of hyoid, stylopharyngeus muscle, inferior parathyroid, thymus.

cards.q: What is the derivative of the 4th branchial arch?
cards.a: Thyroid cartilage, cricothyroid muscle, superior parathyroid.

cards.q: What is the derivative of the 6th branchial arch?
cards.a: Cricoid cartilage, intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid).

cards.q: What is a branchial cleft cyst?
cards.a: Persistent cervical sinus (failure of 2nd–4th clefts to obliterate).

cards.q: What is a thyroglossal duct cyst?
cards.a: Persistent thyroglossal duct (midline neck mass that moves with swallowing).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the anterior pituitary?
cards.a: Rathke’s pouch (surface ectoderm).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the posterior pituitary?
cards.a: Neuroectoderm (infundibulum from diencephalon).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the thyroid gland?
cards.a: Endoderm from the floor of the primitive pharynx (foramen cecum); descends via thyroglossal duct.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the parathyroid glands?
cards.a:
• Superior parathyroids: 4th pharyngeal pouch.
  • Inferior parathyroids: 3rd pharyngeal pouch.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the thymus?
cards.a: 3rd pharyngeal pouch (ventral wings).

cards.q: What is DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: 22q11.2 deletion → failure of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch development → absent thymus and parathyroids → T-cell deficiency + hypocalcemia.

cards.q: What structures develop from the 1st pharyngeal pouch?
cards.a: Middle ear cavity and Eustachian tube.

cards.q: What structures develop from the 2nd pharyngeal pouch?
cards.a: Palatine tonsils.

cards.q: What is the aortic arch derivative of the 3rd pharyngeal arch?
cards.a: Common carotid artery and proximal internal carotid artery.

cards.q: What is the aortic arch derivative of the 4th pharyngeal arch?
cards.a:
• Right: proximal right subclavian artery.
  • Left: aortic arch.

cards.q: What is the aortic arch derivative of the 6th pharyngeal arch?
cards.a: Proximal pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus (left side).

cards.q: What is the most common aortic arch anomaly?
cards.a: Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the superior vena cava?
cards.a: Right anterior cardinal vein.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the portal vein?
cards.a: Vitelline veins.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the umbilical vein?
cards.a: Left umbilical vein (right regresses).

cards.q: What is the fate of the umbilical arteries?
cards.a: Become medial umbilical ligaments.

cards.q: What is the fate of the allantois?
cards.a: Becomes urachus → median umbilical ligament.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the kidney?
cards.a: Intermediate mesoderm.

cards.q: Pronephros → Mesonephros → Metanephros (definitive kidney).
cards.a: Pronephros → Mesonephros → Metanephros (definitive kidney).

cards.q: What induces the metanephric mesenchyme to form nephrons?
cards.a: Ureteric bud (from mesonephric duct).

cards.q: What is Potter sequence?
cards.a: Bilateral renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia, characteristic facies, limb deformities.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the gonads?
cards.a: Genital ridge (intermediate mesoderm) + primordial germ cells.

cards.q: What gene determines testicular differentiation?
cards.a: SRY gene on Y chromosome.

cards.q: What hormone causes regression of Müllerian ducts?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) from Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What hormone stimulates development of Wolffian ducts?
cards.a: Testosterone from Leydig cells.

cards.q: What is the fate of the Müllerian ducts in females?
cards.a: Uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina.

cards.q: What is the fate of the Wolffian ducts in males?
cards.a: Epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of male pseudohermaphroditism?
cards.a: 5α-reductase deficiency or androgen insensitivity syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of female pseudohermaphroditism?
cards.a: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal cortex?
cards.a: Mesoderm (intermediate mesoderm).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal medulla?
cards.a: Neural crest cells.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the spleen?
cards.a: Mesoderm (dorsal mesentery of stomach).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the liver and pancreas?
cards.a: Foregut endoderm.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the lung buds?
cards.a: Foregut endoderm.

cards.q: What is the tracheoesophageal fistula?
cards.a: Abnormal separation of respiratory diverticulum from foregut.

cards.q: What is the most common type of tracheoesophageal fistula?
cards.a: Proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF (85%).

cards.q: What is congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: Failure of pleuroperitoneal folds to close (usually left Bochdalek hernia) → pulmonary hypoplasia.

cards.q: What is omphalocele?
cards.a: Failure of abdominal wall closure at umbilicus; covered by peritoneum.

cards.q: What is gastroschisis?
cards.a: Full-thickness abdominal wall defect usually to the right of umbilicus; bowel not covered by peritoneum.

cards.q: What is the vitelline duct remnant?
cards.a: Meckel’s diverticulum (on antimesenteric border of ileum).

cards.q:

  3. 2 feet from the ileocecal valve
  4. Presents by age 2

cards.q: What is Hirschsprung’s disease?
cards.a: Absence of ganglion cells (neural crest migration failure) in distal colon → functional obstruction.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the anal canal?
cards.a:
• Upper 2/3: endoderm.
  • Lower 1/3: ectoderm (proctodeum).

cards.q: What is the most common congenital heart defect?
cards.a: Ventricular septal defect (VSD).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the atrial septum?
cards.a: Septum primum and septum secundum.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Tetralogy of Fallot.

cards.q:
• Pulmonary stenosis
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Overriding aorta
  • Ventricular septal defect (PROV)
cards.a:
• Pulmonary stenosis
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Overriding aorta
  • Ventricular septal defect (PROV)

cards.q: What is persistent truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: Failure of truncus arteriosus to divide into aorta and pulmonary trunk (often with VSD).

cards.q: What is transposition of the great arteries?
cards.a: Aorta arises from right ventricle, pulmonary trunk from left ventricle. Needs shunt for survival.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of early cyanosis in newborns?
cards.a: Transposition of the great arteries.

cards.q: What is coarctation of the aorta?
cards.a: Narrowing of aorta usually distal to left subclavian artery. Associated with Turner syndrome.

cards.q: What is patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)?
cards.a: Failure of ductus arteriosus to close after birth. Continuous 'machine-like' murmur.

cards.q: What keeps the ductus arteriosus open in fetal life?
cards.a: Low oxygen tension and high prostaglandin E₂ levels.

cards.q: What drug is used to close a PDA?
cards.a: Indomethacin (prostaglandin inhibitor).

cards.q: What drug is used to keep a PDA open?
cards.a: Prostaglandin E₁ (alprostadil).

cards.q:
• Septum transversum
  • Pleuroperitoneal folds
  • Body wall
  • Dorsal mesentery of esophagus
cards.a:
• Septum transversum
  • Pleuroperitoneal folds
  • Body wall
  • Dorsal mesentery of esophagus

cards.q: What is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: Bochdalek hernia (posterolateral, usually left side).

cards.q: What is eventration of the diaphragm?
cards.a: Incomplete muscularization leading to elevated hemidiaphragm.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the limbs?
cards.a: Limb buds (mesoderm covered by ectoderm) appear at week 4.

cards.q: What is the apical ectodermal ridge (AER)?
cards.a: Directs proximal-distal limb growth.

cards.q: What is the zone of polarizing activity (ZPA)?
cards.a: Determines anterior-posterior limb axis (via Sonic hedgehog).

cards.q: What causes phocomelia?
cards.a: Thalidomide exposure (disrupts limb bud development).

cards.q: What is the most common congenital limb defect?
cards.a: Polydactyly.

cards.q: What is syndactyly?
cards.a: Failure of apoptosis between digits.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the urinary bladder?
cards.a: Vesicourethral canal (from urogenital sinus).

cards.q: What is the urachus?
cards.a: Remnant of allantois; becomes median umbilical ligament.

cards.q: What is a patent urachus?
cards.a: Urine leaks from umbilicus.

cards.q:
• Genital tubercle
  • Urogenital folds
  • Labioscrotal swellings
cards.a:
• Genital tubercle
  • Urogenital folds
  • Labioscrotal swellings

cards.q: What hormone drives male external genitalia differentiation?
cards.a: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

cards.q: What is the indifferent stage of external genitalia?
cards.a: Until week 9–10, male and female genitalia are identical.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the penis?
cards.a: Hypospadias (urethral opening on ventral surface).

cards.q: What is epispadias associated with?
cards.a: Exstrophy of the bladder.

cards.q: What is cryptorchidism?
cards.a: Undescended testis. Increases risk of infertility and testicular cancer.

cards.q: What is the gubernaculum?
cards.a: Fibrous cord that guides testicular descent.

cards.q: What is the processus vaginalis?
cards.a: Peritoneal evagination that precedes testicular descent; failure to obliterate → indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of primordial germ cells?
cards.a: Yolk sac endoderm; migrate to genital ridge.

cards.q: What is the fate of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts in males?
cards.a: Regress due to AMH.

cards.q: What is the fate of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts in females?
cards.a: Regress.

cards.q: What is the most common uterine anomaly?
cards.a: Septate uterus (failure of septum resorption).

cards.q: What is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome?
cards.a: Müllerian agenesis — congenital absence of uterus and upper vagina with normal ovaries and secondary sexual characteristics.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital malformation of the CNS?
cards.a: Neural tube defects (especially spina bifida).

cards.q: What maternal factor is most strongly associated with neural tube defects?
cards.a: Folate deficiency.

cards.q: What is the role of folate in embryogenesis?
cards.a: Essential for neural tube closure (DNA synthesis and methylation).

cards.q: What is holoprosencephaly?
cards.a: Failure of forebrain to divide into two hemispheres. Strongly associated with trisomy 13.

cards.q: What is anencephaly?
cards.a: Absence of cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres due to failure of anterior neuropore closure.

cards.q: What is Chiari II malformation?
cards.a: Caudal displacement of cerebellar vermis and tonsils through foramen magnum; almost always associated with myelomeningocele.

cards.q: What is Dandy-Walker malformation?
cards.a: Agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of 4th ventricle.

cards.q: What is syringomyelia?
cards.a: Central canal dilation in spinal cord (often associated with Chiari I or trauma).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the adrenal cortex vs medulla?
cards.a:
• Cortex: mesoderm.
  • Medulla: neural crest.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the anterior pituitary?
cards.a: Rathke’s pouch (oral ectoderm).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the posterior pituitary?
cards.a: Neuroectoderm (hypothalamic outgrowth).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the pineal gland?
cards.a: Neuroectoderm (diencephalon).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the lens of the eye?
cards.a: Surface ectoderm.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the retina?
cards.a: Neuroectoderm (optic cup).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the cornea?
cards.a: Surface ectoderm (epithelium) + neural crest (stroma).

cards.q: What is coloboma?
cards.a: Failure of choroid fissure to close → defect in iris, retina, or optic disc.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the external ear?
cards.a: 1st and 2nd branchial arches.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the middle ear ossicles?
cards.a:
• Malleus & incus: 1st arch.
  • Stapes: 2nd arch.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the inner ear?
cards.a: Otic placode (surface ectoderm).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the teeth?
cards.a: Ectoderm (enamel) + neural crest (dentin, pulp).

cards.q:
• Endocardial cushions
  • Septum primum and septum secundum
  • Muscular septum
  • Neural crest cells (conotruncal septum)
cards.a:
• Endocardial cushions
  • Septum primum and septum secundum
  • Muscular septum
  • Neural crest cells (conotruncal septum)

cards.q: What is the most common congenital heart defect overall?
cards.a: Ventricular septal defect (VSD).

cards.q: What is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Tetralogy of Fallot.

cards.q: What is the embryonic cause of transposition of the great arteries?
cards.a: Failure of spiral septation of the truncus arteriosus.

cards.q: What is the embryonic cause of persistent truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate and form the aorticopulmonary septum.

cards.q: What is the embryonic cause of Tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Anterior displacement of the conotruncal septum.

cards.q: What maternal infection is classically associated with congenital heart defects (PDA, pulmonary stenosis)?
cards.a: Rubella.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the kidneys?
cards.a: Intermediate mesoderm (metanephros).

cards.q: What is Potter sequence?
cards.a: Bilateral renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia, characteristic facies, limb deformities.

cards.q: What is multicystic dysplastic kidney?
cards.a: Abnormal metanephric development with multiple non-communicating cysts.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the gonads?
cards.a: Genital ridge (intermediate mesoderm) + primordial germ cells from yolk sac.

cards.q: What structure guides testicular descent?
cards.a: Gubernaculum.

cards.q: What is the processus vaginalis?
cards.a: Peritoneal evagination accompanying testicular descent; patent processus → indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele.

cards.q: What is the most common site of ectopic testis?
cards.a: Inguinal canal.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the uterus and upper vagina?
cards.a: Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts.

cards.q: What is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome?
cards.a: Müllerian agenesis — congenital absence of uterus and upper vagina with normal secondary sexual characteristics and ovaries.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the lower vagina?
cards.a: Urogenital sinus.

cards.q: What is the most common uterine anomaly?
cards.a: Septate uterus (incomplete resorption of septum).

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the prostate?
cards.a: Urogenital sinus endoderm.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the seminal vesicles?
cards.a: Mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the axilla?
cards.a:
• Anterior: pectoralis major/minor
  • Posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi
  • Medial: serratus anterior
  • Lateral: bicipital groove of humerus

cards.q: What structures pass through the thoracic outlet?
cards.a: Subclavian artery, subclavian vein, brachial plexus (lower trunk), sympathetic chain.

cards.q: What is the most common site of thoracic outlet syndrome compression?
cards.a: Between anterior and middle scalene muscles (scalene triangle) or costoclavicular space.

cards.q: What nerve is most commonly injured in axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior paralysis → winged scapula).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of winged scapula?
cards.a: Long thoracic nerve injury.

cards.q: What muscles form the rotator cuff?
cards.a:
• Supraspinatus
  • Infraspinatus
  • Teres minor
  • Subscapularis
Mnemonic: SITS

cards.q: Which rotator cuff muscle is most commonly torn?
cards.a: Supraspinatus.

cards.q: What is the function of the supraspinatus?
cards.a: Initiates abduction of the arm (first 15–20°).

cards.q: What nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor?
cards.a: Axillary nerve (C5–C6).

cards.q: What is the most common nerve injured in anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.a: Axillary nerve.

cards.q: What is Erb's palsy (upper trunk brachial plexus injury)?
cards.a:
C5–C6 injury → Waiter's tip posture:
  • Arm adducted + internally rotated
  • Elbow extended
  • Wrist flexed

cards.q: What is Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk brachial plexus injury)?
cards.a:
C8–T1 injury:
  • Claw hand
  • Horner syndrome (if T1 sympathetic rami involved)

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the upper limb?
cards.a: Subclavian → Axillary → Brachial → Radial + Ulnar arteries.

cards.q: Where is the brachial artery pulse best palpated?
cards.a: Medial to the biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa.

cards.q: What is the most common site for upper extremity arterial occlusion?
cards.a: Subclavian artery (atherosclerosis).

cards.q: What vein is most commonly used for central line placement in the upper limb?
cards.a: Internal jugular or subclavian vein.

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the breast?
cards.a: Primarily to axillary lymph nodes (especially pectoral group).

cards.q: What is the order of axillary lymph node groups from lateral to medial?
cards.a: Pectoral → subscapular → humeral → central → apical.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of Virchow's node?
cards.a: Left supraclavicular node enlargement — often indicates metastatic gastric cancer.

cards.q: What is the carpal tunnel?
cards.a: Space bounded by carpal bones and flexor retinaculum containing median nerve and 9 flexor tendons.

cards.q: What is the most common entrapment neuropathy in the upper limb?
cards.a: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve).

cards.q: What are the contents of the cubital fossa?
cards.a:
• Tendon of biceps
  • Brachial artery
  • Median nerve
Mnemonic: TAN (lateral to medial)

cards.q: What is the anatomical snuffbox?
cards.a: Bounded by extensor pollicis longus and brevis; contains radial artery and scaphoid bone.

cards.q: What bone is most commonly fractured in a fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH)?
cards.a: Scaphoid (navicular).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the scaphoid?
cards.a: Retrograde from distal to proximal — prone to avascular necrosis.

cards.q: What is Colles' fracture?
cards.a: Distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (dinner fork deformity).

cards.q: What is Smith's fracture?
cards.a: Distal radius fracture with volar angulation (reverse Colles').

cards.q: What nerve is at risk in supracondylar humerus fracture?
cards.a: Median nerve and brachial artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of radial nerve injury?
cards.a: Spiral groove of humerus (mid-shaft fracture).

cards.q: What is the motor deficit in radial nerve injury?
cards.a: Wrist drop, loss of finger extension.

cards.q: What is the sensory deficit in radial nerve injury?
cards.a: Dorsal hand (first web space).

cards.q: What is the ulnar nerve motor supply in the hand?
cards.a:
• Hypothenar muscles
  • Interossei
  • Adductor pollicis
  • Medial two lumbricals

cards.q: What is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment?
cards.a: Cubital tunnel (at elbow).

cards.q: What is the claw hand deformity caused by?
cards.a: Ulnar nerve injury (hyperextension at MCP, flexion at IP joints of 4th and 5th digits).

cards.q: What is the median nerve motor supply in the hand?
cards.a:
Thenar muscles — mnemonic LOAF:
  • Lateral two lumbricals
  • Opponens pollicis
  • Abductor pollicis brevis
  • Flexor pollicis brevis

cards.q: What is ape hand deformity?
cards.a: Median nerve injury — loss of thumb opposition.

cards.q: What is the recurrent laryngeal nerve a branch of?
cards.a: Vagus nerve (CN X).

cards.q: What is the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve?
cards.a: Loops under aortic arch.

cards.q: What is the course of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve?
cards.a: Loops under right subclavian artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of femoral hernia?
cards.a: Femoral canal (medial to femoral vein, below inguinal ligament).

cards.q: What is the boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
cards.a:
• Lateral: inferior epigastric vessels
  • Medial: rectus abdominis
  • Inferior: inguinal ligament (site of direct inguinal hernia).

cards.q: Differentiate direct vs indirect inguinal hernia.
cards.a:
• Indirect: through deep inguinal ring (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels), congenital.
  • Direct: through Hesselbach's triangle (medial to inferior epigastric vessels), acquired.

cards.q: What is the most common hernia in males?
cards.a: Indirect inguinal hernia.

cards.q: What is the most common hernia in females?
cards.a: Femoral hernia.

cards.q: What nerve is at risk during inguinal hernia repair?
cards.a: Ilioinguinal nerve.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the femoral triangle?
cards.a:
• Superior: inguinal ligament
  • Lateral: sartorius
  • Medial: adductor longus.

cards.q: What are the contents of the femoral triangle (lateral to medial)?
cards.a:
• Nerve (femoral)
  • Artery (femoral)
  • Vein (femoral)
  • Empty space
  • Lymphatics
Mnemonic: NAVEL (lateral to medial)

cards.q: What is the adductor canal?
cards.a: Passes from femoral triangle to popliteal fossa; contains femoral artery, vein, and saphenous nerve.

cards.q: What is the most common site of peripheral artery disease occlusion in the lower limb?
cards.a: Superficial femoral artery (in adductor canal).

cards.q: What is the largest branch of the femoral artery?
cards.a: Profunda femoris (deep femoral artery).

cards.q: What artery supplies the anterior compartment of the leg?
cards.a: Anterior tibial artery.

cards.q: What artery supplies the posterior compartment of the leg?
cards.a: Posterior tibial artery.

cards.q: What is the dorsalis pedis artery a continuation of?
cards.a: Anterior tibial artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site for peripheral pulses in the lower limb?
cards.a: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the anterior compartment of the leg?
cards.a: Deep peroneal (fibular) nerve.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the lateral compartment of the leg?
cards.a: Superficial peroneal (fibular) nerve.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the posterior compartment of the leg?
cards.a: Tibial nerve.

cards.q: What is foot drop caused by?
cards.a: Common peroneal nerve injury (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion).

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured nerve in knee trauma?
cards.a: Common peroneal nerve.

cards.q: What is the sensory distribution of the saphenous nerve?
cards.a: Medial leg and foot (branch of femoral nerve).

cards.q: What is the sensory distribution of the sural nerve?
cards.a: Lateral foot and little toe.

cards.q: What is the largest nerve in the body?
cards.a: Sciatic nerve (L4–S3).

cards.q: What muscles does the sciatic nerve innervate?
cards.a: Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus) and all muscles below the knee.

cards.q: What is the most common site of sciatic nerve compression?
cards.a: Piriformis muscle (piriformis syndrome).

cards.q: What is Trendelenburg sign?
cards.a: Contralateral pelvic drop when standing on one leg — due to superior gluteal nerve injury → gluteus medius weakness.

cards.q: What nerve innervates gluteus maximus?
cards.a: Inferior gluteal nerve.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the hip joint?
cards.a: Medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (branches of profunda femoris) + obturator artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of avascular necrosis of the femoral head?
cards.a: Intracapsular fracture of femoral neck.

cards.q: What is the order of structures in the popliteal fossa (lateral to medial)?
cards.a:
• Common peroneal nerve (most lateral)
  • Tibial nerve
  • Popliteal vein
  • Popliteal artery (deepest)

cards.q: What is the most common knee ligament injury?
cards.a: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear.

cards.q: What is the unhappy triad of the knee?
cards.a:
• ACL tear
  • Medial meniscus tear
  • MCL tear

cards.q: What is the most commonly injured meniscus?
cards.a: Medial meniscus (more fixed).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the knee joint?
cards.a: Femoral, obturator, and sciatic nerves.

cards.q: What is the main blood supply to the anterior compartment of the thigh?
cards.a: Femoral artery.

cards.q: What is the main blood supply to the posterior compartment of the thigh?
cards.a: Perforating branches of profunda femoris.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the anterior compartment of the thigh?
cards.a: Femoral nerve.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the medial compartment of the thigh?
cards.a: Obturator nerve.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the posterior compartment of the thigh?
cards.a: Sciatic nerve (tibial portion).

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the inguinal canal?
cards.a:
• Anterior: external oblique aponeurosis
  • Posterior: transversalis fascia
  • Roof: internal oblique and transversus abdominis
  • Floor: inguinal ligament

cards.q: What passes through the superficial inguinal ring?
cards.a: Spermatic cord (in males) or round ligament (in females) + ilioinguinal nerve.

cards.q: What is the conjoint tendon?
cards.a: Fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses; reinforces posterior wall of inguinal canal.

cards.q: What is the lacunar ligament?
cards.a: Extension of inguinal ligament to pectineal line; forms medial boundary of femoral ring.

cards.q: What is the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament)?
cards.a: Strong fibrous band along superior pubic ramus; used in hernia repairs.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the anterior abdominal wall?
cards.a: Superior epigastric (from internal thoracic) and inferior epigastric (from external iliac) arteries.

cards.q: What is the nerve supply to the anterior abdominal wall?
cards.a: T7–T12 intercostal nerves + L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal).

cards.q: What is McBurney's point?
cards.a: One-third the distance from anterior superior iliac spine to umbilicus (surface marking of appendix base).

cards.q: What layers are incised in a McBurney (gridiron) incision for appendectomy?
cards.a:
1. External oblique
  2. Internal oblique
  3. Transversus abdominis
  4. Transversalis fascia
  5. Peritoneum

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the appendix?
cards.a: Appendicular artery (branch of ileocolic artery).
