cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the appendix?
cards.a: Ileocolic vein → superior mesenteric vein → portal vein.

cards.q: What is the most common position of the appendix?
cards.a: Retrocecal.

cards.q: What are the taeniae coli?
cards.a: Three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle on the colon.

cards.q: What are haustra?
cards.a: Sacculations of the colon caused by contraction of taeniae coli.

cards.q: What are epiploic appendages?
cards.a: Fat-filled peritoneal tags on the surface of the colon.

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the foregut?
cards.a: Celiac trunk.

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the midgut?
cards.a: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the hindgut?
cards.a: Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

cards.q: What is the watershed area between SMA and IMA?
cards.a: Splenic flexure (Griffith's point) — prone to ischemia.

cards.q: What is the marginal artery of Drummond?
cards.a: Anastomosis between SMA and IMA along the colon.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the gastrointestinal tract?
cards.a: Portal venous system (to liver).

cards.q: What is the portosystemic anastomosis at the esophagus?
cards.a: Left gastric vein (portal) ↔ esophageal veins (azygos/systemic) → esophageal varices in portal HTN.

cards.q: What is the portosystemic anastomosis at the umbilicus?
cards.a: Paraumbilical veins (portal) ↔ superficial epigastric veins (systemic) → caput medusae.

cards.q: What is the portosystemic anastomosis at the rectum?
cards.a: Superior rectal vein (portal) ↔ middle & inferior rectal veins (systemic) → anorectal varices.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of portal hypertension?
cards.a: Cirrhosis.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the lesser sac (omental bursa)?
cards.a:
• Anterior: lesser omentum and stomach
  • Posterior: pancreas, left kidney, aorta
  • Superior: caudate lobe of liver

cards.q: What is the epiploic foramen (of Winslow)?
cards.a: Communication between greater and lesser sacs; anterior boundary is hepatoduodenal ligament (portal triad).

cards.q: What is Pringle's maneuver?
cards.a: Clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament to control hepatic bleeding.

cards.q: What are the peritoneal reflections in the pelvis (female)?
cards.a: Rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) — most dependent part.

cards.q: What is the most common site of peritoneal fluid collection in females?
cards.a: Rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas).

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the rectum?
cards.a: Superior rectal (IMA), middle rectal (internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage above the pectinate line?
cards.a: Internal iliac nodes (portal drainage).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage below the pectinate line?
cards.a: Superficial inguinal nodes (systemic drainage).

cards.q: What is the dentate (pectinate) line?
cards.a: Junction between endoderm (above) and ectoderm (below) in the anal canal.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of the dentate line?
cards.a: Different blood supply, innervation, lymphatic drainage, and type of hemorrhoids (internal vs external).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the liver?
cards.a: Hepatic artery (25%, oxygenated) + Portal vein (75%, nutrient-rich).

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the liver?
cards.a: Hepatic veins → inferior vena cava.

cards.q: What are the functional lobes of the liver?
cards.a: Divided by Cantlie's line (from IVC to gallbladder fossa) into right and left functional lobes.

cards.q: What is the bare area of the liver?
cards.a: Area on the diaphragmatic surface not covered by peritoneum (between coronary ligaments).

cards.q: What is Calot's triangle?
cards.a: Bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of liver. Contains cystic artery.

cards.q: What is the most common variation in hepatic arterial supply?
cards.a: Replaced right hepatic artery from superior mesenteric artery.

cards.q: What is the porta hepatis?
cards.a: Hilum of the liver; contains portal vein, hepatic artery, and common hepatic duct.

cards.q: What is the ligamentum teres hepatis?
cards.a: Remnant of left umbilical vein.

cards.q: What is the ligamentum venosum?
cards.a: Remnant of ductus venosus.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the gallbladder?
cards.a: Cystic artery (usually from right hepatic artery).

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the gallbladder?
cards.a: Cystic vein → portal vein.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the gallbladder?
cards.a: Parasympathetic via vagus; sympathetic via celiac plexus.

cards.q: What is the most common site of gallstone impaction?
cards.a: Hartmann's pouch or cystic duct.

cards.q: What is the triangle of Calot clinically important for?
cards.a: Safe dissection during cholecystectomy to avoid bile duct injury.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the pancreas?
cards.a:
• Head: Superior + inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries
  • Body & tail: Splenic artery branches

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the pancreas?
cards.a: Primarily into portal vein and splenic vein.

cards.q: What is the relationship of the pancreas to the splenic vein?
cards.a: Splenic vein runs posterior to the body and tail of the pancreas.

cards.q: What is the most common site of pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: Head of pancreas.

cards.q: What is Courvoisier's sign?
cards.a: Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = suggestive of pancreatic head cancer.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the spleen?
cards.a: Mesoderm (dorsal mesogastrium).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the spleen?
cards.a: Splenic artery (branch of celiac trunk).

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the spleen?
cards.a: Splenic vein → portal vein.

cards.q: What ligaments attach the spleen?
cards.a: Gastrosplenic ligament and splenorenal ligament.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of splenic rupture?
cards.a: Blunt abdominal trauma (especially left lower ribs).

cards.q: What is Kehr's sign?
cards.a: Left shoulder pain due to diaphragmatic irritation from splenic rupture.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the duodenum?
cards.a: Superior pancreaticoduodenal (from gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (from SMA).

cards.q: What is the most common site of duodenal ulcer?
cards.a: First part of duodenum (duodenal bulb).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the jejunum and ileum?
cards.a: Superior mesenteric artery via jejunal and ileal branches.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the ascending colon and proximal 2/3 transverse colon?
cards.a: Superior mesenteric artery.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the distal 1/3 transverse colon, descending colon, and sigmoid?
cards.a: Inferior mesenteric artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of colonic ischemia?
cards.a: Splenic flexure (watershed area).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the colon?
cards.a: Follows arterial supply to SMA and IMA nodes → cisterna chyli.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage above the dentate line?
cards.a: Superior rectal vein → inferior mesenteric vein → portal system.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage below the dentate line?
cards.a: Middle and inferior rectal veins → internal iliac veins → systemic circulation.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidney?
cards.a: Horseshoe kidney (fusion at lower poles).

cards.q: What is the most common site of ectopic kidney?
cards.a: Pelvic kidney.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the kidneys?
cards.a: Renal arteries (direct branches of abdominal aorta at L1–L2).

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the kidneys?
cards.a:
• Right renal vein → IVC.
  • Left renal vein → IVC (longer, receives left gonadal and adrenal veins).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the kidneys?
cards.a: Para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes.

cards.q: What is the most common renal artery variation?
cards.a: Multiple renal arteries (especially to lower pole).

cards.q: What is the relationship of the right renal artery to the IVC?
cards.a: Passes posterior to the IVC.

cards.q: What is the relationship of the left renal vein to the aorta?
cards.a: Crosses anterior to the aorta (nutcracker syndrome risk).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the kidneys?
cards.a: Sympathetic from T10–L1 via renal plexus.

cards.q: What is the most common site of ureteric constriction?
cards.a:
1. Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ)
  2. Crossing of common iliac artery
  3. Ureterovesical junction (UVJ)

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the ureter?
cards.a: Segmental: renal, gonadal, common iliac, internal iliac, and vesical arteries.

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the ureter?
cards.a: Follows arterial supply.

cards.q: What is the most common site of ureteric injury during surgery?
cards.a: At the level where uterine artery crosses the ureter ('water under the bridge').

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the bladder?
cards.a: Superior and inferior vesical arteries (from internal iliac).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the detrusor muscle?
cards.a: Parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2–S4).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the internal urethral sphincter?
cards.a: Sympathetic (hypogastric nerves).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the external urethral sphincter?
cards.a: Pudendal nerve (S2–S4, somatic).

cards.q: What is the trigone of the bladder?
cards.a: Smooth triangular area between ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice.

cards.q: What is the embryonic origin of the trigone?
cards.a: Mesoderm (absorbed mesonephric ducts).

cards.q: What is the most common site of bladder cancer?
cards.a: Lateral walls and trigone.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the prostate?
cards.a: Inferior vesical artery and middle rectal artery.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the prostate?
cards.a: Prostatic venous plexus → internal iliac veins (Batson's plexus — route for metastasis to vertebrae).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the prostate?
cards.a: Internal iliac and sacral nodes.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the prostate?
cards.a: Parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics) for erection; sympathetic for ejaculation.

cards.q: What are the zones of the prostate?
cards.a:
• Peripheral zone — most cancers (70%)
  • Central zone
  • Transition zone — BPH

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the testes?
cards.a: Testicular arteries (direct from abdominal aorta at L2).

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the testes?
cards.a:
• Right: testicular vein → IVC.
  • Left: testicular vein → left renal vein.

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the testes?
cards.a: Para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the scrotum?
cards.a:
• Anterior: ilioinguinal nerve.
  • Posterior: perineal branch of pudendal nerve.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the penis?
cards.a: Internal pudendal artery → dorsal artery, deep artery, and artery to bulb.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the penis?
cards.a: Deep dorsal vein → prostatic plexus.

cards.q: What is the innervation of the penis (erection vs ejaculation)?
cards.a:
• Erection: Parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnics S2–S4)
  • Ejaculation: Sympathetic (hypogastric nerves)
Mnemonic: Point (parasympathetic) and Shoot (sympathetic).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the ovary?
cards.a: Ovarian artery (from aorta) + ovarian branch of uterine artery.

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the ovary?
cards.a:
• Right: ovarian vein → IVC.
  • Left: ovarian vein → left renal vein.

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the ovary?
cards.a: Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the uterus?
cards.a: Uterine artery (branch of internal iliac).

cards.q: What is the relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery?
cards.a: Ureter passes under the uterine artery ('water under the bridge').

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the uterine fundus?
cards.a: Para-aortic nodes (via ovarian vessels).

cards.q: What is the lymphatic drainage of the cervix?
cards.a: Internal and external iliac nodes.

cards.q: What is the most common site of aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Infrarenal abdominal aorta.

cards.q: What is the most common site of aortic dissection?
cards.a: Ascending aorta (just above aortic valve).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the spinal cord?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries) and posterior spinal arteries + radicular arteries (including Artery of Adamkiewicz).

cards.q: What is the Artery of Adamkiewicz?
cards.a: Major radicular artery supplying lower 2/3 of spinal cord (usually from left T9–T12).

cards.q: What is the clinical consequence of anterior spinal artery occlusion?
cards.a:
Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome:
  • Bilateral loss of motor function (corticospinal tract)
  • Bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract)
  • Preserved proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns)

cards.q: What is the venous drainage of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Anterior and posterior spinal veins → vertebral venous plexus (Batson's plexus).

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of Batson's plexus?
cards.a: Valveless communication between pelvic veins and vertebral veins → route for prostate/breast cancer metastasis to spine.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the posterior triangle of the neck?
cards.a:
• Anterior: sternocleidomastoid
  • Posterior: trapezius
  • Inferior: clavicle.

cards.q: What structures are in the posterior triangle of the neck?
cards.a:
• Accessory nerve (CN XI)
  • Brachial plexus trunks
  • Subclavian artery
  • External jugular vein

cards.q: What is the most common nerve injured in neck dissection?
cards.a: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) → trapezius paralysis.

cards.q: What is the ansa cervicalis?
cards.a: Nerve loop from C1–C3 supplying infrahyoid muscles (except thyrohyoid).

cards.q: What is the innervation of the diaphragm?
cards.a: Phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

cards.q: What is the clinical sign of unilateral phrenic nerve injury?
cards.a: Elevated hemidiaphragm on chest X-ray.

cards.q: What are the three major openings in the diaphragm and their levels?
cards.a:
• T8 — Caval opening (IVC)
  • T10 — Esophageal hiatus (esophagus + vagus nerves)
  • T12 — Aortic hiatus (aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein)
Mnemonic: I (8) ate (10) eggs (12) at the table.

cards.q: What is the most common type of diaphragmatic hernia in adults?
cards.a: Hiatal hernia (sliding type most common).

cards.q: What is Bochdalek hernia?
cards.a: Congenital posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia (usually left side).

cards.q: What is Morgagni hernia?
cards.a: Congenital anterior diaphragmatic hernia (retrosternal).

cards.q: What is the most common site of lumbar puncture?
cards.a: L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace (below termination of spinal cord).

cards.q: What are the layers traversed during lumbar puncture?
cards.a:
1. Skin
  2. Subcutaneous tissue
  3. Supraspinous ligament
  4. Interspinous ligament
  5. Ligamentum flavum
  6. Epidural space
  7. Dura mater
  8. Arachnoid mater
  9. Subarachnoid space (CSF)

cards.q: What is the termination level of the spinal cord in adults?
cards.a: L1–L2 (conus medullaris).

cards.q: What is the termination level of the dural sac?
What is the cauda equina?
cards.a: Bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below L1–L2.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the posterior 1/3 of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Posterior spinal arteries.

cards.q: What is the clinical importance of the epidural space?
cards.a: Site for epidural anesthesia.

cards.q: What is the clinical importance of the subarachnoid space?
cards.a: Contains CSF; site for lumbar puncture and spinal anesthesia.

cards.q: What are the major contents of the carotid sheath?
cards.a: Common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve (CN X).

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of the carotid body?
cards.a: Chemoreceptor sensing O₂, CO₂, and pH.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of the carotid sinus?
cards.a: Baroreceptor regulating blood pressure.

cards.q: What nerve innervates the carotid sinus and body?
cards.a: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve).

cards.q: What is the most common site of berry aneurysm?
cards.a: Anterior communicating artery.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm.

cards.q: What is the most common site of epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Middle meningeal artery (temporal bone fracture).

cards.q: What is the most common site of subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Bridging veins.

cards.q: What is the most common site of intracerebral hemorrhage in hypertensives?
cards.a: Basal ganglia (putamen).

cards.q: What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation?
cards.a:
• Rubor — redness
  • Tumor — swelling
  • Calor — heat
  • Dolor — pain
  • Functio laesa — loss of function

cards.q: What are the main components of acute inflammation?
cards.a: Vascular changes (vasodilation, increased permeability) + Cellular events (leukocyte recruitment).

cards.q: What is the first leukocyte to arrive at the site of acute inflammation?
cards.a: Neutrophils (within minutes to hours).

cards.q: What are the steps of leukocyte extravasation?
cards.a:
1. Margination
  2. Rolling (selectins)
  3. Adhesion (integrins)
  4. Transmigration / Diapedesis
  5. Chemotaxis

cards.q: What are the main opsonins?
cards.a: IgG, C3b, and mannose-binding lectin.

cards.q: What is the role of histamine in inflammation?
cards.a: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability (from mast cells and basophils).

cards.q: What are the major chemotactic factors?
cards.a: C5a, LTB4, IL-8 (CXCL8), bacterial products.

cards.q: What is the difference between transudate and exudate?
cards.a:
• Transudate: low protein, low cells (due to pressure imbalance).
  • Exudate: high protein, high cells (due to inflammation).

cards.q: What are the types of chronic inflammation?
cards.a: Granulomatous and non-granulomatous.

cards.q: What cells characterize granulomatous inflammation?
cards.a: Epithelioid macrophages ± multinucleated giant cells.

cards.q: What are the two types of granulomas?
cards.a: Caseating (e.g., TB) and Non-caseating (e.g., sarcoidosis).

cards.q: What is the difference between regeneration and repair?
cards.a:
• Regeneration: complete restoration of normal tissue.
  • Repair: fibrosis/scarring when regeneration is limited.

cards.q: What are the labile, stable, and permanent tissues?
cards.a:
• Labile: high turnover (skin, GI epithelium, bone marrow)
  • Stable: low turnover but can regenerate (liver, kidney, pancreas)
  • Permanent: cannot divide (neurons, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle)

cards.q: What is granulation tissue?
cards.a: Proliferating fibroblasts, new capillaries, and macrophages — precursor to scar.

cards.q: What is the most important growth factor in wound healing?
cards.a: TGF-β (Transforming Growth Factor Beta).

cards.q: What is primary intention wound healing?
cards.a: Clean surgical wounds with approximated edges → minimal scarring.

cards.q: What is secondary intention wound healing?
cards.a: Large wounds with significant tissue loss → granulation tissue fills defect → more scarring.

cards.q: What are the complications of wound healing?
cards.a:
• Infection
  • Dehiscence (wound reopening)
  • Keloid / Hypertrophic scar
  • Contracture

cards.q: What is a keloid?
cards.a: Excessive collagen deposition beyond original wound boundaries (more common in dark-skinned individuals).

cards.q: What is amyloidosis?
cards.a: Extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins that stain with Congo red (apple-green birefringence under polarized light).

cards.q: What is the most common type of amyloidosis?
cards.a: AL (primary) amyloidosis — from plasma cell dyscrasia (light chains).

cards.q: What is AA amyloidosis associated with?
cards.a: Chronic inflammation (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, TB).

cards.q: What is the most common organ affected in amyloidosis?
cards.a: Kidney (nephrotic syndrome).

cards.q: What are the hallmarks of reversible cell injury?
cards.a:
• Cellular swelling (hydropic change)
  • Fatty change (steatosis)
  • Plasma membrane blebbing

cards.q: What are the hallmarks of irreversible cell injury?
cards.a:
• Mitochondrial damage (flocculent densities)
  • Plasma membrane rupture
  • Nuclear changes: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis

cards.q: What is the most sensitive organelle to hypoxic injury?
cards.a: Mitochondria.

cards.q: What is liquefactive necrosis?
cards.a: Enzymatic digestion of tissue (seen in brain infarcts and abscesses).

cards.q: What is caseous necrosis?
cards.a: Cheese-like appearance (classic in TB granulomas).

cards.q: What is fat necrosis?
cards.a: Enzymatic fat digestion (seen in acute pancreatitis).

cards.q: What is fibrinoid necrosis?
cards.a: Deposition of fibrin-like material in vessel walls (seen in vasculitis).

cards.q: What is gangrenous necrosis?
cards.a: Coagulative necrosis + superimposed bacterial infection (dry vs wet gangrene).

cards.q: What is the difference between apoptosis and necrosis?
cards.a:
• Apoptosis: programmed, energy-dependent, no inflammation.
  • Necrosis: accidental, inflammatory.

cards.q: What are the major pathways of apoptosis?
cards.a:
• Intrinsic (mitochondrial): cytochrome c release → caspase-9 → caspase-3
  • Extrinsic (death receptor): FasL/TNF → caspase-8 → caspase-3

cards.q: What is the key executioner caspase in apoptosis?
cards.a: Caspase-3.

cards.q: What protein inhibits apoptosis?
cards.a: Bcl-2 (anti-apoptotic).

cards.q: What protein promotes apoptosis?
cards.a: Bax/Bak (pro-apoptotic).

cards.q: What is the role of p53 in cell injury?
cards.a: Tumor suppressor; induces cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage.

cards.q: What are the two main categories of neoplasia?
cards.a: Benign and Malignant.

cards.q: What are the key differences between benign and malignant tumors?
cards.a:
• Benign: localized, slow-growing, well-differentiated, no metastasis.
  • Malignant: invasive, rapid growth, poorly differentiated, capable of metastasis.

cards.q: What is dysplasia?
cards.a: Disordered growth with loss of uniformity and architectural orientation (pre-malignant).

cards.q: What is carcinoma in situ?
cards.a: Malignant cells confined to epithelium without invasion of basement membrane.

cards.q: What is the most important determinant of tumor behavior?
cards.a: Degree of differentiation (grade) and stage (extent of spread).

cards.q: What is tumor grading based on?
cards.a: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity.

cards.q: What is tumor staging based on?
cards.a: Size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis (TNM system).

cards.q: What is the most common route of metastasis for carcinomas?
cards.a: Lymphatics.

cards.q: What is the most common route of metastasis for sarcomas?
cards.a: Hematogenous (blood).

cards.q: What is the most common site of hematogenous metastasis?
cards.a: Lung and liver.

cards.q: What is the Warburg effect?
cards.a: Cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (aerobic glycolysis).

cards.q: What is tumor angiogenesis?
cards.a: New blood vessel formation induced by tumors (mainly via VEGF).

cards.q: What are the hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan & Weinberg)?
cards.a:
1. Sustaining proliferative signaling
  2. Evading growth suppressors
  3. Resisting cell death
  4. Enabling replicative immortality
  5. Inducing angiogenesis
  6. Activating invasion & metastasis

cards.q: What is the most common cancer in men worldwide?
cards.a: Lung cancer.

cards.q: What is the most common cancer in women worldwide?
cards.a: Breast cancer.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cancer death in men and women?
cards.a: Lung cancer.

cards.q: What tumor marker is used for hepatocellular carcinoma?
cards.a: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).

cards.q: What tumor marker is used for prostate cancer?
cards.a: PSA (prostate-specific antigen).

cards.q: What tumor marker is used for ovarian cancer?
What tumor marker is used for pancreatic cancer?
What tumor marker is used for colorectal cancer?
cards.a: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen).

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia (due to PTHrP or osteolytic metastases).

cards.q: What cancer is associated with SIADH?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What cancer is associated with Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH)?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What cancer is associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy?
cards.a: Lung cancer (non-small cell).

cards.q: What cancer is associated with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What cancer is associated with polycythemia?
cards.a: Renal cell carcinoma (EPO production).

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in children?
cards.a: Pilocytic astrocytoma.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant bone tumor in children?
cards.a: Osteosarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant bone tumor in adults?
cards.a: Metastatic carcinoma (much more common than primary).

cards.q: What is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children?
cards.a: Rhabdomyosarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in adults?
cards.a: Liposarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in children?
cards.a: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in adults?
cards.a: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

cards.q: What is the most common lymphoma in adults in the Western world?
cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

cards.q: What is the most common Hodgkin lymphoma subtype?
cards.a: Nodular sclerosis.

cards.q: What cell is characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Reed-Sternberg cell.

cards.q: What are the classic Reed-Sternberg cell variants?
cards.a:
• Owl-eye — Classic RS cell (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity)
  • Popcorn cell — Lymphocyte predominant
  • Lacunar cell — Nodular sclerosis

cards.q: What is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

cards.q: What is Burkitt lymphoma associated with?
cards.a: EBV and c-MYC translocation t(8;14). Starry sky appearance.

cards.q: What is mantle cell lymphoma associated with?
cards.a: t(11;14) cyclin D1 overexpression.

cards.q: What is follicular lymphoma associated with?
cards.a: t(14;18) BCL-2 overexpression.

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in adults in the Western world?
cards.a: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

cards.q: What is the hallmark of CLL/SLL on smear?
cards.a: Smudge cells.

cards.q: What is the most common myeloproliferative neoplasm?
cards.a: Polycythemia vera (JAK2 mutation).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in untreated chronic myeloid leukemia?
cards.a: Blast crisis.

cards.q: What translocation is diagnostic for CML?
cards.a: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL).

cards.q: What is the most common mutation in myeloproliferative neoplasms?
What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
cards.a: Minimal change disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults?
cards.a: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

cards.q: What is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide?
cards.a: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).

cards.q: What is the classic finding in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
cards.a: Subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, low C3.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)?
cards.a: Pauci-immune (ANCA-associated) GN.

cards.q: What is the most common renal malignancy in adults?
cards.a: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of renal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass (late finding).

cards.q: What paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with renal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Polycythemia (EPO production).

cards.q: What is the most common testicular tumor in young men?
cards.a: Seminoma.

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in seminoma?
cards.a: May have mildly elevated β-hCG.

cards.q: What is the most common germ cell tumor in children?
cards.a: Yolk sac tumor (elevated AFP).

cards.q: What is the most common ovarian tumor in young women?
cards.a: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst).

cards.q: What is the most common malignant ovarian tumor?
cards.a: Serous cystadenocarcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common breast carcinoma?
cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type).

cards.q: What is the most common site of breast cancer?
cards.a: Upper outer quadrant.

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in breast cancer?
cards.a: Axillary lymph node status.

cards.q: What is the most common mutation in hereditary breast cancer?
cards.a: BRCA1 or BRCA2.

cards.q: What is Paget disease of the breast?
cards.a: Eczematous lesion of nipple due to underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the characteristic nuclear feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a:
• Orphan Annie eye nuclei (ground-glass, empty appearing)
  • Nuclear grooves
  • Psammoma bodies

cards.q: What is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma?
cards.a: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children/adolescents?
cards.a: Osteosarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in adults?
cards.a: Multiple myeloma (plasmacytoma).

cards.q: What is the most common metastatic site for osteosarcoma?
cards.a: Lungs.

cards.q: What is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme (grade IV astrocytoma).

cards.q: What is the characteristic histologic feature of glioblastoma?
cards.a: Necrosis with pseudopalisading and endothelial proliferation.

cards.q: What is the most common supratentorial tumor in children?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma.

cards.q: What is the most common posterior fossa tumor in children?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What mutation is found in >95% of polycythemia vera cases?
What is the most common indolent lymphoma?
cards.a: Follicular lymphoma.

cards.q: What translocation is characteristic of follicular lymphoma?
cards.a: t(14;18) — BCL2 overexpression.

cards.q: What is the most common aggressive lymphoma?
cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

cards.q: What virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma in Africa?
cards.a: EBV.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Infection (due to hypogammaglobulinemia) or renal failure.

cards.q: What is the most common skin cancer?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common skin cancer with metastatic potential?
cards.a: Melanoma.

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in melanoma?
cards.a: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion).

cards.q: What is the ABCDE rule for melanoma?
cards.a:
• A — Asymmetry
  • B — Border irregularity
  • C — Color variation
  • D — Diameter >6 mm
  • E — Evolution (change over time)

cards.q: What is the most common type of lung cancer?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma (especially in non-smokers and women).

cards.q: What is the most common lung cancer in smokers?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: What lung cancer is most strongly associated with smoking?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome in small cell lung cancer?
cards.a: SIADH and Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of superior vena cava syndrome?
cards.a: Lung cancer (especially small cell).

cards.q: What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults?
cards.a: Myxoma (usually left atrium).

cards.q: What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in children?
cards.a: Rhabdomyoma (associated with tuberous sclerosis).

cards.q: What is the most common metastatic tumor to the heart?
cards.a: Lung cancer.

cards.q: What are the four major classes of biomolecules?
cards.a:
1. Carbohydrates
  2. Lipids
  3. Proteins
  4. Nucleic acids

cards.q: What is the difference between aldoses and ketoses?
cards.a: Aldoses have aldehyde group (e.g., glucose); ketoses have ketone group (e.g., fructose).

cards.q: Name the three most important hexoses in human metabolism.
cards.a: Glucose, Fructose, Galactose.

cards.q: What is the storage form of glucose in liver and muscle?
cards.a: Glycogen (branched polymer of glucose with α-1,4 and α-1,6 linkages).

cards.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes von Gierke disease (GSD I)?
cards.a: Glucose-6-phosphatase. Cannot release free glucose from liver → severe fasting hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes Pompe disease (GSD II)?
cards.a: Acid α-glucosidase (lysosomal maltase) → cardiomegaly, muscle weakness.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis?
cards.a: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1). Activated by AMP, fructose-2,6-BP; inhibited by ATP, citrate.

cards.q: What is the net ATP yield from complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule?
cards.a: Approximately 30–32 ATP (2 from glycolysis, 2 from TCA, 26–28 from oxidative phosphorylation).

cards.q: What is the key regulatory enzyme of gluconeogenesis?
cards.a: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. Inhibited by fructose-2,6-BP and AMP.

cards.q: Which tissues cannot perform gluconeogenesis and why?
cards.a: Muscle and brain lack glucose-6-phosphatase.

cards.q: What are the three irreversible steps of glycolysis and their gluconeogenic bypass enzymes?
cards.a:
1. Hexokinase → Glucose-6-phosphatase
  2. PFK-1 → Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
  3. Pyruvate kinase → Pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK

cards.q: What is the Cori cycle?
cards.a: Cori cycle: Anaerobic muscle glycolysis → lactate → transported to liver → gluconeogenesis → glucose returned to muscle.

cards.q: What is the pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt) main product in oxidative phase?
cards.a: NADPH (used for fatty acid synthesis, glutathione reduction).

cards.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes classic galactosemia?
cards.a: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Cataracts, hepatomegaly, E. coli sepsis.

cards.q: What is the defect in hereditary fructose intolerance?
cards.a: Aldolase B deficiency → accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate → hypoglycemia, liver damage.

cards.q: What is the committed step of fatty acid synthesis?
cards.a: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (produces malonyl-CoA). Activated by citrate, inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA.

cards.q: Where does fatty acid β-oxidation occur?
cards.a: Mitochondrial matrix.

cards.q: Which cofactor is required for β-oxidation?
cards.a: Carnitine (transports long-chain fatty acyl-CoA into mitochondria).

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis?
cards.a: HMG-CoA reductase (target of statins).

cards.q: What is the function of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)?
cards.a: Hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL on capillary endothelium.

cards.q: Which apolipoprotein activates LPL?
cards.a: ApoC-II.

cards.q: Which apolipoprotein is the ligand for LDL receptor?
What is the defect in familial hypercholesterolemia?
cards.a: LDL receptor mutation → very high LDL, early atherosclerosis.

cards.q: What is the function of LCAT?
cards.a: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol in HDL.

cards.q: What are the ketone bodies?
cards.a: Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone.

cards.q: In which organ are ketone bodies synthesized?
cards.a: Liver mitochondria (from excess acetyl-CoA).

cards.q: Which enzyme is deficient in MCAD deficiency?
cards.a: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase → hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting.

cards.q: What is the urea cycle rate-limiting enzyme?
cards.a: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). Activated by N-acetylglutamate.

cards.q: Which amino acid donates the second nitrogen in urea cycle?
cards.a: Aspartate.

cards.q: What is the defect in ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency?
cards.a: Most common urea cycle disorder → hyperammonemia, orotic aciduria, X-linked.

cards.q: What are the essential amino acids?
cards.a:
Mnemonic: PVT TIM HaLL
  • Phenylalanine
  • Valine
  • Tryptophan
  • Threonine
  • Isoleucine
  • Methionine
  • Histidine
  • Leucine
  • Lysine

cards.q: Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?
cards.a: Leucine and Lysine.

cards.q: Which amino acids are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
cards.a: Isoleucine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, Tyrosine.

cards.q: What is the precursor of catecholamines?
cards.a: Tyrosine.

cards.q: What is the precursor of serotonin?
cards.a: Tryptophan.

cards.q: What is the precursor of heme?
cards.a: Glycine + Succinyl-CoA.

cards.q: Which disease is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase?
cards.a: Phenylketonuria (PKU). Musty odor, fair skin, intellectual disability. Treated with low-phenylalanine diet.

cards.q: What is the defect in alkaptonuria?
cards.a: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency → dark urine, ochronosis, arthritis.

cards.q: What is the most common aminoaciduria?
cards.a: Cystinuria (defective dibasic amino acid transporter).

cards.q: What is the function of tetrahydrofolate (THF)?
cards.a: Carrier of one-carbon units (methyl, methylene, formyl).

cards.q: What is the active form of vitamin B12?
cards.a: Methylcobalamin and deoxyadenosylcobalamin.

cards.q: Which reaction requires both B12 and folate?
cards.a: Homocysteine → Methionine (methionine synthase).

cards.q: What is the defect in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
cards.a: HGPRT deficiency (purine salvage pathway) → hyperuricemia, self-mutilation, gout.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo purine synthesis?
cards.a: Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis?
cards.a: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II).

cards.q: Which drug inhibits dihydrofolate reductase?
cards.a: Methotrexate.

cards.q: Which drug inhibits thymidylate synthase?
cards.a: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU).

cards.q: What is the function of ribonucleotide reductase?
cards.a: Converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.

cards.q: What is the function of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH)?
cards.a:
Converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA. Requires 5 cofactors:
  • TPP (B1 — Thiamine)
  • Lipoic acid
  • CoA (B5 — Pantothenate)
  • FAD (B2 — Riboflavin)
  • NAD (B3 — Niacin)
Mnemonic: Tender Loving Care For Nancy

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1) deficiency — common in alcoholics. Damage to mammillary bodies.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle?
cards.a: Isocitrate dehydrogenase. Inhibited by NADH and ATP; activated by ADP.

cards.q: How many NADH and FADH₂ are produced per acetyl-CoA in one turn of TCA cycle?
cards.a: 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency?
cards.a: Lactic acidosis, neurological deficits. Treated with high-fat diet and thiamine supplementation.

cards.q: Which shuttle transfers reducing equivalents from cytosolic NADH into mitochondria?
cards.a: Malate-aspartate shuttle (yields 2.5 ATP) vs Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (1.5 ATP).

cards.q: What is the defect in Leigh syndrome?
cards.a: Pyruvate dehydrogenase or electron transport chain defects → severe lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration.

cards.q: What are the sources of NADPH in the cell?
cards.a:
1. Pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative phase, via G6PD)
  2. Malic enzyme
  3. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (cytosolic)

cards.q: What is the function of glutathione peroxidase?
cards.a: Reduces H₂O₂ using glutathione (requires selenium).

cards.q: Which enzyme regenerates reduced glutathione?
cards.a: Glutathione reductase (requires NADPH).

cards.q: What is the role of G6PD in RBCs?
cards.a: Generates NADPH → maintains reduced glutathione → protects RBCs from oxidative damage.

cards.q: What triggers hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency?
cards.a: Oxidative stress (fava beans, primaquine, sulfa drugs, infections).

cards.q: What is the Heinz body?
cards.a: Precipitated denatured hemoglobin seen in G6PD deficiency.

cards.q: Which glycogen storage disease presents with painful muscle cramps and myoglobinuria on exercise?
cards.a: McArdle disease (GSD V) — muscle phosphorylase deficiency.

cards.q: Which GSD is characterized by hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia but no lactic acidosis?
cards.a: Hers disease (GSD VI) — liver phosphorylase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the defect in Cori disease (GSD III)?
cards.a: Debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase) deficiency.

cards.q: Name the key allosteric regulators of PFK-1.
cards.a:
• Activators ↑: AMP, Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
  • Inhibitors ↓: ATP, Citrate, Low pH

cards.q: What is the function of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?
cards.a: Powerful activator of PFK-1 (glycolysis) and inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis).

cards.q: Which hormone increases fructose-2,6-BP levels in liver?
cards.a: Insulin (via PFK-2 activation).

cards.q: Which hormone decreases fructose-2,6-BP levels?
cards.a: Glucagon / Epinephrine (via PKA → PFK-2 phosphorylation).

cards.q: What is the main product of the non-oxidative phase of HMP shunt?
cards.a: Ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleotide synthesis).

cards.q: What is the role of transketolase?
cards.a: Transfers 2-carbon units in non-oxidative HMP shunt (requires thiamine).

cards.q: What is essential fructosuria?
cards.a: Benign condition due to fructokinase deficiency.

cards.q: What accumulates in galactokinase deficiency?
cards.a: Galactitol → cataracts.

cards.q: What is the committed step of fatty acid oxidation?
cards.a: Formation of fatty acyl-carnitine by carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I).

cards.q: Which drug inhibits CPT-I?
cards.a: Etomoxir (experimental); malonyl-CoA is physiological inhibitor.

cards.q: What is the final product of odd-chain fatty acid oxidation?
cards.a: Propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (via methylmalonyl-CoA).

cards.q: What vitamin is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase?
cards.a: Vitamin B12.

cards.q: What causes Refsum disease?
cards.a: Deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase → accumulation of phytanic acid.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting step of ketogenesis?
cards.a: HMG-CoA synthase.

cards.q: Why can't the liver use ketone bodies as fuel?
cards.a: Lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase).

cards.q: What is the defect in abetalipoproteinemia?
cards.a: Mutation in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) → no chylomicrons or VLDL.

cards.q: What are the features of Tangier disease?
cards.a: ABCA1 deficiency → very low HDL, orange tonsils, peripheral neuropathy.

cards.q: Which apolipoprotein is deficient in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III)?
cards.a: ApoE (E2/E2 genotype).

cards.q: What is the function of CETP?
cards.a: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein — transfers cholesterol esters from HDL to VLDL/LDL.

cards.q: What is the precursor of nitric oxide (NO)?
cards.a: Arginine (via NOS enzyme).

cards.q: Which amino acid is the precursor of histamine?
cards.a: Histidine.

cards.q: Which amino acid is the precursor of creatine?
cards.a: Glycine + Arginine + Methionine (SAM).

cards.q: What is the defect in homocystinuria (most common form)?
cards.a: Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency → elevated homocysteine and methionine.

cards.q: What is the treatment for cystathionine β-synthase deficiency?
cards.a: Pyridoxine (B6), folate, B12, betaine, and low-methionine diet.

cards.q: What causes maple syrup urine disease?
cards.a: Deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase.

cards.q: Which amino acids are elevated in MSUD?
cards.a: Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine.

cards.q: What is the defect in albinism?
cards.a: Tyrosinase deficiency (cannot convert tyrosine to DOPA).

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis?
cards.a: ALA synthase (requires vitamin B6).

cards.q: Which porphyria presents with photosensitivity and blistering skin lesions?
cards.a: Porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency).

cards.q: Which porphyria presents with acute abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine?
cards.a: Acute intermittent porphyria (porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency).

cards.q: What drug class can precipitate acute porphyria attacks?
cards.a: Barbiturates, anticonvulsants (CYP450 inducers).

cards.q: What is the final product of purine degradation in humans?
cards.a: Uric acid.

cards.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes gout due to overproduction of uric acid?
cards.a: PRPP synthetase overactivity or HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan).

cards.q: What is the difference between leading and lagging strand in DNA replication?
cards.a:
• Leading strand: synthesized continuously (5' → 3').
  • Lagging strand: synthesized discontinuously in Okazaki fragments.

cards.q: Which enzyme synthesizes RNA primers during replication?
cards.a: Primase (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase).

cards.q: What is the function of DNA helicase?
cards.a: Unwinds double helix using ATP.

cards.q: What is the function of DNA topoisomerase II?
cards.a: Relieves supercoiling ahead of replication fork (also called gyrase in bacteria).

cards.q: Which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills gaps with DNA?
cards.a: DNA polymerase I (prokaryotes); Pol δ + Fen1 in eukaryotes.

cards.q: What is the direction of DNA replication?
cards.a: Always 5' → 3'.

cards.q: What are telomeres and what enzyme maintains them?
cards.a: TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends. Maintained by telomerase (reverse transcriptase).

cards.q: What is the defect in xeroderma pigmentosum?
cards.a: Defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) → extreme UV sensitivity and skin cancer.

cards.q: Which DNA repair mechanism fixes double-strand breaks?
cards.a: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or Homologous recombination.

cards.q: What is the most common mutation type caused by UV light?
cards.a: Thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers).

cards.q: What is the central dogma of molecular biology?
cards.a: DNA → RNA → Protein (with reverse transcription in retroviruses).

cards.q: What is the function of RNA polymerase II?
cards.a: Transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes).

cards.q: What are the three types of RNA polymerase in eukaryotes?
cards.a:
• RNA Pol I — rRNA
  • RNA Pol II — mRNA
  • RNA Pol III — tRNA & 5S rRNA
Mnemonic: I make rRNA, II make mRNA, III make tRNA.

cards.q: What is the TATA box?
cards.a: Promoter sequence ~25 bp upstream of transcription start site; binds TBP (part of TFIID).

cards.q: What is the difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic mRNA?
cards.a:
• Prokaryotic: polycistronic, no cap/poly-A tail.
  • Eukaryotic: monocistronic, 5' cap, poly-A tail, splicing.

cards.q: What is alternative splicing?
cards.a: Process by which one gene produces multiple protein isoforms by including/excluding different exons.

cards.q: What is the start codon and what amino acid does it code for?
cards.a: AUG → Methionine (Met).

cards.q: What are the stop codons?
cards.a:
• UAA (ochre)
  • UAG (amber)
  • UGA (opal/umber)

cards.q: What is the wobble hypothesis?
cards.a: Third base of codon can have flexible base-pairing with tRNA anticodon, allowing fewer tRNAs.

cards.q: Which antibiotic inhibits peptidyl transferase on 50S subunit?
cards.a: Chloramphenicol.

cards.q: Which antibiotic blocks translocation on 30S subunit?
cards.a: Tetracyclines.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of erythromycin?
cards.a: Binds 50S subunit and inhibits translocation.

cards.q: What is a frameshift mutation?
cards.a: Insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of 3 → altered reading frame.

cards.q: What is a missense mutation?
cards.a: Single nucleotide change that results in a different amino acid.

cards.q: What is a nonsense mutation?
cards.a: Creates a premature stop codon.

cards.q: What is anticipation in genetics?
cards.a: Increasing severity/earlier onset in successive generations (seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders).

cards.q: Name three trinucleotide repeat disorders.
cards.a:
1. Huntington disease — CAG (chromosome 4)
  2. Fragile X syndrome — CGG (FMR1)
  3. Myotonic dystrophy — CTG

cards.q: What is the function of chaperones in protein folding?
cards.a: Prevent misfolding and aggregation (e.g., heat shock proteins).

cards.q: What is ubiquitin and its role?
cards.a: Tags proteins for degradation by proteasome.

cards.q: What is the defect in α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: Misfolded protein retained in liver → cirrhosis + panacinar emphysema in lungs.

cards.q: What is the function of vitamin A (retinol)?
cards.a: Visual pigments (rhodopsin), epithelial differentiation, gene transcription.

cards.q: What is the function of vitamin D?
cards.a: Calcium and phosphate homeostasis; gene transcription via VDR.

cards.q: What is the active form of vitamin D?
cards.a: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol).

cards.q: Which vitamin is a cofactor for carboxylation reactions?
cards.a: Biotin (B7).

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra?
cards.a: Niacin (B3) — 4 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia, Death.

cards.q: Which vitamin is required for collagen synthesis (hydroxylation)?
cards.a: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

cards.q: What is the function of vitamin K?
cards.a: γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C & S.

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
cards.a: Vitamin A.

cards.q: What is the function of selenium?
cards.a: Component of glutathione peroxidase.

cards.q: What is the function of zinc?
cards.a: Cofactor for many enzymes (carbonic anhydrase, DNA/RNA polymerases); wound healing.

cards.q: What is the function of iodine?
cards.a: Thyroid hormone synthesis.

cards.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis in the fed state?
cards.a: PFK-1 (activated by insulin via fructose-2,6-BP).

cards.q: What is the main fuel for the brain during prolonged starvation?
cards.a: Ketone bodies.

cards.q: Which hormone activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue?
cards.a: Glucagon / Epinephrine (via PKA).

cards.q: What is the Randle cycle (glucose-fatty acid cycle)?
cards.a: Increased fatty acid oxidation inhibits glucose oxidation (via increased acetyl-CoA, citrate, NADH).

cards.q: What is the primary defect in type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: Absolute insulin deficiency (autoimmune β-cell destruction).

cards.q: What is the primary defect in type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: Insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of metformin?
cards.a: Activates AMPK → inhibits gluconeogenesis.

cards.q: What is the function of GLUT4 transporter?
cards.a: Insulin-dependent glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue.

cards.q: What is the function of GLUT2?
cards.a: Bidirectional glucose transport in liver, β-cells, intestine, kidney (high Km).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of sulfonylureas?
cards.a: Close ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels on β-cells → depolarization → insulin release.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors?
cards.a: Block glucose reabsorption in proximal tubule → glucosuria.

cards.q: What is the most common mutation in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: ΔF508 deletion in CFTR gene (impaired chloride channel folding).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Huntington disease?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant; trinucleotide repeat (CAG) on chromosome 4.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Fragile X syndrome?
cards.a: X-linked; CGG repeat in FMR1 gene.

cards.q: What is genomic imprinting?
cards.a: Gene expression depends on parent of origin (e.g., Prader-Willi vs Angelman syndrome on chromosome 15).

cards.q: What is the function of telomerase in cancer?
cards.a: Reactivation allows unlimited replication (immortality).

cards.q: What is the role of oncogenes vs tumor suppressor genes?
cards.a:
• Oncogenes: gain-of-function (one mutated copy sufficient — dominant)
  • Tumor suppressors: loss-of-function (both copies usually lost — recessive, Knudson two-hit hypothesis)

cards.q: What is Li-Fraumeni syndrome?
cards.a: Germline p53 mutation → multiple cancers at young age.

cards.q: What is the defect in HNPCC/Lynch syndrome?
cards.a: Defective DNA mismatch repair (MSH2, MLH1, etc.).

cards.q: What is the function of retinoblastoma (Rb) protein?
cards.a: Tumor suppressor; binds E2F → prevents G1 to S progression.

cards.q: What is the most common enzyme deficiency causing hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: G6PD deficiency.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Wilson disease?
cards.a: Hepatitis, Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, high copper.

cards.q: What is the defect in Wilson disease?
cards.a: ATP7B gene mutation → impaired copper excretion into bile.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Wilson disease?
cards.a: Penicillamine or trientine (copper chelators); zinc.

cards.q: What is hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Iron overload due to HFE gene mutation (C282Y) → bronze diabetes, cirrhosis, arthropathy.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of hereditary hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive.

cards.q: What is the treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Phlebotomy.

cards.q: What is the function of α1-antitrypsin?
cards.a: Inhibits neutrophil elastase in lungs.

cards.q: What are the two major clinical manifestations of α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: Panacinar emphysema (lungs) + cirrhosis (liver).

cards.q: What is the most common inborn error of metabolism?
cards.a: Phenylketonuria (PKU).

cards.q: What is the newborn screening test for PKU?
cards.a: Guthrie test (elevated phenylalanine).

cards.q: What is the treatment for PKU?
cards.a: Low-phenylalanine diet; avoid aspartame.

cards.q: What accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease?
cards.a: GM2 ganglioside (hexosaminidase A deficiency).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Tay-Sachs?
cards.a: Ashkenazi Jewish infant with cherry-red spot, developmental regression, seizures.

cards.q: What is the enzyme deficient in Gaucher disease?
cards.a: Glucocerebrosidase.

cards.q: What is the enzyme deficient in Niemann-Pick disease?
cards.a: Sphingomyelinase.

cards.q: What accumulates in Fabry disease?
cards.a: Ceramide trihexoside (α-galactosidase A deficiency).

cards.q: What is the treatment for Gaucher disease?
cards.a: Enzyme replacement therapy (imiglucerase).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of most lysosomal storage diseases?
cards.a:
Autosomal recessive — except:
  • Fabry disease — X-linked (α-galactosidase A)
  • Hunter syndrome — X-linked (iduronate-2-sulfatase)

cards.q: What is the defect in Hurler syndrome?
cards.a: α-L-iduronidase deficiency (mucopolysaccharidosis).

cards.q: What is the defect in Hunter syndrome?
cards.a: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency (X-linked).

cards.q: What is the major fuel source for RBCs?
cards.a: Glucose (via anaerobic glycolysis).

cards.q: What is the role of 2,3-BPG in hemoglobin?
cards.a: Decreases O₂ affinity → right shift of O₂ dissociation curve.

cards.q: What is the Bohr effect?
cards.a: Increased CO₂ and H⁺ decrease hemoglobin's O₂ affinity (right shift).

cards.q: What is the Haldane effect?
cards.a: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO₂.

cards.q: What is fetal hemoglobin (HbF) composition?
cards.a: α₂γ₂ — higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA (α₂β₂).

cards.q: What is the major hemoglobin in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: HbS (β6 Glu → Val).

cards.q: What triggers sickling in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Deoxygenation, acidosis, dehydration, infection.

cards.q: What is the treatment for sickle cell crisis?
cards.a: Hydration, oxygen, pain control, hydroxyurea (increases HbF).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of megaloblastic anemia?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

cards.q: What is the Schilling test used for?
cards.a: Diagnosing cause of B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia vs malabsorption).

cards.q: What is the function of intrinsic factor?
cards.a: Binds B12 for absorption in terminal ileum.

cards.q: What are the fat-soluble vitamins?
cards.a: A, D, E, K (absorbed with lipids, stored in liver and adipose tissue).

cards.q: What are the water-soluble vitamins?
cards.a: B-complex (B1–B12) and C (not stored in large amounts, excreted in urine).

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia?
cards.a: Vitamin A deficiency.

cards.q: What is the function of Vitamin A (retinol)?
cards.a: Visual pigments (rhodopsin), epithelial differentiation, gene transcription via RAR/RXR.

cards.q: What is the toxicity of excess Vitamin A?
cards.a: Teratogenic (cleft palate, cardiac defects), pseudotumor cerebri, hepatotoxicity.

cards.q: What is the active form of Vitamin D?
cards.a: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol).

cards.q: What does Vitamin D deficiency cause in children vs adults?
cards.a:
• Children: Rickets
  • Adults: Osteomalacia.

cards.q: What is the function of Vitamin E?
cards.a: Antioxidant (protects membranes from free radical damage).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Vitamin E deficiency?
cards.a: Spinocerebellar degeneration, hemolytic anemia, acanthocytosis.

cards.q: What is the function of Vitamin K?
cards.a: γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C & S.

cards.q: What causes Vitamin K deficiency in newborns?
cards.a: Sterile gut + low stores → hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

cards.q: Which vitamin is a cofactor for carboxylation reactions?
cards.a: Biotin (B7).

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1) — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia.

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes beriberi?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1) — wet (cardiac) or dry (neurologic).

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra?
cards.a: Niacin (B3) — 4 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia, Death.

cards.q: What causes pellagra besides dietary deficiency?
cards.a: Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, isoniazid.

cards.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes cheilosis, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis?
cards.a: Riboflavin (B2) deficiency.

cards.q: Which vitamin is required for transamination reactions?
cards.a: Pyridoxine (B6).

cards.q: Which drugs can cause B6 deficiency?
cards.a: Isoniazid, hydralazine, penicillamine.

cards.q: What is the function of Vitamin B12?
cards.a: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine).

cards.q: What causes B12 deficiency besides diet?
cards.a: Pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor deficiency), terminal ileum resection, metformin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of folate deficiency?
cards.a: Poor diet, alcoholism, pregnancy, methotrexate.

cards.q: Why is folate supplementation critical in pregnancy?
cards.a: Prevents neural tube defects.

cards.q: What is the function of Vitamin C?
cards.a: Antioxidant, collagen hydroxylation (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase), iron absorption.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of scurvy?
cards.a: Perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor wound healing.

cards.q: Which mineral is a component of glutathione peroxidase?
cards.a: Selenium.

cards.q: What is the function of Zinc?
cards.a: Cofactor for >300 enzymes, wound healing, taste/smell, immune function.

cards.q: What is acrodermatitis enteropathica?
cards.a: Zinc deficiency — periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea.

cards.q: What is the function of Copper?
cards.a: Component of lysyl oxidase (collagen cross-linking), cytochrome c oxidase.

cards.q: What is Menkes disease?
cards.a: Defective copper absorption (ATP7A) → kinky hair, hypotonia, seizures.

cards.q: What is Wilson disease?
cards.a: Defective copper excretion (ATP7B) → Kayser-Fleischer rings, cirrhosis, basal ganglia damage.

cards.q: What is the function of Iodine?
cards.a: Thyroid hormone synthesis (T3/T4).

cards.q: What is the classic sign of Iodine deficiency?
cards.a: Goiter and cretinism in severe cases.

cards.q: What is the function of Chromium?
cards.a: Enhances insulin action (glucose tolerance factor).

cards.q: What is the function of Fluoride?
cards.a: Strengthens tooth enamel (hydroxyapatite → fluorapatite).

cards.q: What are the clinical features of Kwashiorkor?
cards.a: Edema, fatty liver, skin lesions, normal weight for height (protein deficiency).

cards.q: What are the clinical features of Marasmus?
cards.a: Severe muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, no edema (total calorie deficiency).

cards.q: What is the difference between marasmus and kwashiorkor?
cards.a:
• Marasmus = total calorie deficit
  • Kwashiorkor = protein deficit with adequate calories.

cards.q: What is refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia after refeeding malnourished patients.

cards.q: What is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide?
cards.a: Iron deficiency.

cards.q: What is the daily caloric requirement for an average adult?
cards.a: Approximately 25–30 kcal/kg/day.

cards.q: What is the protein requirement for a healthy adult?
cards.a: 0.8 g/kg/day (higher in stress, pregnancy, growth).

cards.q: What are essential fatty acids?
cards.a: Linoleic acid (ω-6) and α-linolenic acid (ω-3).

cards.q: What is the function of medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs)?
cards.a: Absorbed directly into portal vein, useful in malabsorption syndromes.

cards.q: What is the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for Vitamin A in pregnancy?
cards.a: Avoid excess (teratogenic); use β-carotene instead.

cards.q: What is the role of fiber in the diet?
cards.a: Soluble: lowers cholesterol; Insoluble: increases stool bulk.

cards.q: What is the difference between complete and incomplete proteins?
cards.a: Complete proteins contain all essential amino acids (animal sources, soy, quinoa).

cards.q: What is parenteral nutrition and its major complication?
cards.a: TPN; risk of line infection, cholestasis, and refeeding syndrome.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for obesity?
cards.a: Lifestyle modification (diet + exercise).

cards.q: Which drug is used for weight loss that inhibits fat absorption?
cards.a: Orlistat (pancreatic lipase inhibitor).

cards.q: What is metabolic syndrome?
cards.a: Central obesity + ≥2 of: hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL.

cards.q: What is the DASH diet used for?
cards.a: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension — rich in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, low sodium.

cards.q: What is the Mediterranean diet associated with?
cards.a: Reduced cardiovascular risk and improved longevity.

cards.q: What is the glycemic index?
cards.a: Measure of how quickly a food raises blood glucose.

cards.q: What is the difference between simple and complex carbohydrates?
cards.a: Simple: rapid absorption (sugars); Complex: slower digestion (starches, fiber).

cards.q: What is lactose intolerance due to?
cards.a: Lactase deficiency → osmotic diarrhea, bloating.

cards.q: What is celiac disease?
cards.a: Autoimmune reaction to gluten (gliadin) → villous atrophy in small intestine.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for celiac disease?
cards.a: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA + duodenal biopsy.

cards.q: What is the treatment for celiac disease?
cards.a: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet.

cards.q: What is dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Rapid gastric emptying after gastrectomy → osmotic diarrhea and reactive hypoglycemia.

cards.q: What are the fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies after bariatric surgery?
cards.a: A, D, E, K (due to malabsorption).

cards.q: What is the most common micronutrient deficiency after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 and Iron.

cards.q: What is the role of probiotics?
cards.a: Live microorganisms that confer health benefits when consumed in adequate amounts.

cards.q: What is the function of prebiotics?
cards.a: Non-digestible fibers that promote growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

cards.q: What is the recommended daily fiber intake?
cards.a: 25 g/day for women, 38 g/day for men.

cards.q: What is the WHO recommendation for free sugars?
cards.a: Less than 10% of total energy intake (ideally <5%).

cards.q: What is the function of omega-3 fatty acids?
cards.a: Anti-inflammatory, reduce triglycerides, improve endothelial function.

cards.q: What is the difference between DHA and EPA?
cards.a: Both omega-3; DHA important for brain/retina, EPA more anti-inflammatory.

cards.q: What is the protein-sparing effect of carbohydrates?
cards.a: Carbs prevent breakdown of protein for gluconeogenesis.

cards.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) for pure carbohydrate oxidation?
What is the RQ for pure fat oxidation?
What is the clinical use of indirect calorimetry?
cards.a: Measures resting energy expenditure (REE).

cards.q: What is the Harris-Benedict equation used for?
cards.a: Estimating basal metabolic rate (BMR).

cards.q: What is the stress factor in nutritional requirements during critical illness?
cards.a: Increase caloric needs by 20–50% depending on severity.

cards.q: What is the preferred route of nutrition in critically ill patients?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition (if gut works) over parenteral.

cards.q: What is the major complication of overfeeding in TPN?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia, hepatic steatosis, increased CO₂ production.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is classic in refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Slow refeeding, monitor and replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium.

cards.q: What is the definition of obesity (BMI)?
cards.a: BMI ≥ 30 kg/m².

cards.q: What is sarcopenic obesity?
cards.a: Loss of muscle mass with increased fat mass (common in elderly).

cards.q: What is the role of leptin?
cards.a: Satiety hormone produced by adipocytes; signals to hypothalamus.

cards.q: What is the role of ghrelin?
cards.a: Hunger hormone produced by stomach; increases before meals.

cards.q: Which bariatric surgery has the best long-term weight loss?
cards.a: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (malabsorptive + restrictive).

cards.q: What is the most common nutritional deficiency in alcoholics?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1).

cards.q: What is the Wernicke encephalopathy triad?
cards.a: Confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: High-dose IV thiamine before glucose.

cards.q: What is the function of chromium in nutrition?
cards.a: Enhances insulin sensitivity.

cards.q: What is the function of molybdenum?
cards.a: Cofactor for xanthine oxidase and sulfite oxidase.

cards.q: What is the recommended sodium intake?
cards.a: < 2,300 mg/day (ideally <1,500 mg for hypertensives).

cards.q: What is the DASH diet emphasis?
cards.a: High potassium, magnesium, calcium, fiber; low sodium and saturated fat.

cards.q: What is the Mediterranean diet key components?
cards.a: Olive oil, fish, nuts, fruits, vegetables, moderate red wine.

cards.q: A malnourished patient is started on TPN. Day 2 he develops seizures and muscle weakness. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a: Refeeding syndrome — hypophosphatemia (shift into cells for ATP synthesis).

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormalities define refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and fluid overload.

cards.q: Why must thiamine be given before glucose in alcoholics?
cards.a: Glucose infusion can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine-deficient patients.

cards.q: A patient with short bowel syndrome develops night blindness and dry skin. Which vitamin is deficient?
cards.a: Vitamin A (fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption).

cards.q: A patient on long-term parenteral nutrition develops cholestasis and bone pain. What deficiency is likely?
cards.a: Vitamin D and/or copper deficiency.

cards.q: What is the most common micronutrient deficiency after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass?
cards.a: Iron and Vitamin B12.

cards.q: Why does gastric bypass cause B12 deficiency?
cards.a: Loss of intrinsic factor-producing parietal cells + reduced gastric acid.

cards.q: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and bleeding gums. Which vitamins are likely deficient?
cards.a: Fat-soluble vitamins (especially Vitamin K and Vitamin C if diet is poor).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of orlistat?
cards.a: Pancreatic and gastric lipase inhibitor → reduced dietary fat absorption.

cards.q: What are the major side effects of orlistat?
cards.a: Steatorrhea, fecal incontinence, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.

cards.q: Which medication for weight loss can cause acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Semaglutide / Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonists).

cards.q: What is the preferred nutritional support route in critically ill patients with a functioning gut?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition (maintains gut barrier function).

cards.q: What is the major risk of overfeeding in ICU patients on TPN?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia, hepatic steatosis, increased CO₂ production (respiratory failure risk).

cards.q: A patient with celiac disease develops dermatitis herpetiformis. What is the treatment?
cards.a: Strict gluten-free diet + dapsone.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic biopsy finding in celiac disease?
cards.a: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

cards.q: A patient with Crohn’s disease develops megaloblastic anemia. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 (terminal ileum involvement).

cards.q: What is the difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus on physical exam?
cards.a:
• Kwashiorkor: edema + fatty liver.
  • Marasmus: severe wasting, no edema.

cards.q: What is the classic hair finding in kwashiorkor?
cards.a: Flag sign (alternating dark and light bands).

cards.q: What is the role of medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) in malabsorption syndromes?
cards.a: Absorbed directly into portal vein without needing micelle formation.

cards.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis has failure to thrive. What nutritional intervention is critical?
cards.a: Pancreatic enzyme replacement + high-calorie diet with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of dumping syndrome after gastrectomy?
cards.a: Rapid emptying of hyperosmolar food into small intestine → fluid shift and reactive hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Early vs late dumping syndrome timing?
cards.a:
• Early: <30 min (GI symptoms).
  • Late: 1–3 hours (hypoglycemia).

cards.q: What is the treatment for dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Small frequent meals, separate liquids from solids, complex carbohydrates.

cards.q: A patient with chronic alcoholism has macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which vitamin deficiency?
cards.a: Folate (more common than B12 in alcoholics).

cards.q: What is the most common nutritional deficiency in the United States?
cards.a: Vitamin D deficiency.

cards.q: Which population is at highest risk for Vitamin D deficiency?
cards.a: Elderly, dark-skinned individuals, obese, limited sun exposure.

cards.q: What lab findings confirm Vitamin D deficiency?
cards.a: Low 25-OH vitamin D, elevated PTH, low/normal calcium.

cards.q: A vegan patient develops paresthesias and ataxia. What deficiency is most likely?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 (only found in animal products).

cards.q: What is the best initial test for suspected B12 deficiency?
cards.a: Serum B12 level + methylmalonic acid (elevated in B12 deficiency).

cards.q: What is the function of chromium in glucose metabolism?
cards.a: Component of glucose tolerance factor; enhances insulin signaling.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion (not all present in every case).

cards.q: What is Korsakoff psychosis?
cards.a: Irreversible amnesia and confabulation following untreated Wernicke encephalopathy.

cards.q: Which trace element deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica?
cards.a: Zinc.

cards.q: A patient with Wilson disease is started on treatment. What is the mechanism of penicillamine?
cards.a: Copper chelator.

cards.q: What is the preferred maintenance therapy for Wilson disease?
cards.a: Zinc (blocks intestinal copper absorption).

cards.q: What is the most common inherited disorder of iron metabolism?
cards.a: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE C282Y mutation).

cards.q: What is the treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Therapeutic phlebotomy.

cards.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. What nutritional deficiency contributes?
cards.a: Vitamin D deficiency (impaired 1α-hydroxylation in kidney).

cards.q: What is the role of carnitine in nutrition?
cards.a: Transports long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for β-oxidation.

cards.q: When is carnitine supplementation useful?
cards.a: In carnitine deficiency syndromes or long-term TPN patients.

cards.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) value indicating pure carbohydrate metabolism?
What is the RQ for fat oxidation?
What does a high RQ (>1.0) indicate?
cards.a: Lipogenesis (overfeeding with carbohydrates).

cards.q: What is the indication for parenteral nutrition?
cards.a: Intestinal failure when enteral route is not possible for >7–10 days.

cards.q: What is the major complication of long-term TPN?
cards.a: Intestinal failure-associated liver disease (IFALD) and central line infections.

cards.q: A patient with anorexia nervosa is refed too aggressively. What is the most dangerous complication?
cards.a: Refeeding syndrome leading to fatal hypophosphatemia and cardiac arrhythmias.

cards.q: What is the best initial management for suspected refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Slow refeeding, electrolyte replacement (especially phosphate), close monitoring.

cards.q: What is sarcopenic obesity?
cards.a: Increased fat mass with decreased muscle mass (common in elderly and after bariatric surgery).

cards.q: What hormone is elevated in obesity and contributes to leptin resistance?
cards.a: Leptin (but receptors become resistant).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of liraglutide/semaglutide in weight loss?
cards.a: GLP-1 receptor agonists → increased satiety, delayed gastric emptying, reduced appetite.

cards.q: What is the role of fiber in preventing colon cancer?
cards.a: Increases stool bulk, reduces transit time, binds potential carcinogens.

cards.q: What is the difference between soluble and insoluble fiber?
cards.a:
• Soluble: lowers cholesterol and blood glucose.
  • Insoluble: increases stool bulk and prevents constipation.

cards.q: What is the recommended daily protein intake for a critically ill patient?
cards.a: 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day (higher in burns, trauma).

cards.q: What is the preferred enteral formula for patients with renal failure?
cards.a: Low-electrolyte, high-calorie renal formulas.

cards.q: What is the advantage of polymeric vs elemental enteral formulas?
cards.a: Polymeric: cheaper, better tolerated in patients with intact digestion.

cards.q: A patient with chylothorax is placed on a special diet. What type of diet is used?
cards.a: Low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs).

cards.q: What is the nutritional management of phenylketonuria (PKU)?
cards.a: Phenylalanine-restricted diet + tyrosine supplementation.

cards.q: What is the long-term risk if PKU is untreated?
cards.a: Intellectual disability, seizures, musty odor.

cards.q: What is the difference between classical and operant conditioning?
cards.a:
• Classical (Pavlovian): Involuntary response to a stimulus (bell → salivation).
  • Operant (Skinner): Voluntary behavior modified by consequences (reward/punishment).

cards.q: What is positive reinforcement?
cards.a: Adding a desirable stimulus to increase behavior (e.g., praise for good grades).

cards.q: What is negative reinforcement?
cards.a: Removing an aversive stimulus to increase behavior (e.g., taking pain medication to relieve pain → one takes it more).

cards.q: What is punishment (positive)?
cards.a: Adding an aversive stimulus to decrease behavior (e.g., scolding a child).

cards.q: What is negative punishment?
cards.a: Removing a desirable stimulus to decrease behavior (e.g., taking away video games).

cards.q: What is extinction in behavioral therapy?
cards.a: Withholding the reinforcer until the conditioned response disappears.

cards.q: What is shaping?
cards.a: Rewarding successive approximations toward a desired behavior.

cards.q: What is systematic desensitization?
cards.a: Gradual exposure to feared stimulus while maintaining relaxation — used to treat phobias.

cards.q: What is flooding (implosion therapy)?
cards.a: Direct, prolonged exposure to the maximal feared stimulus without escape — for phobias.

cards.q: What is aversion therapy?
cards.a: Pairing an unwanted behavior with an unpleasant stimulus (e.g., disulfiram + alcohol → nausea).

cards.q: What is token economy?
cards.a: Operant conditioning system where tokens are earned for desired behaviors and exchanged for rewards.

cards.q: What is modeling (observational learning)?
cards.a: Learning by observing and imitating others (Bandura's social learning theory).

cards.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary reinforcers?
cards.a:
• Primary: Innately rewarding (food, water, sex).
  • Secondary (conditioned): Learned reinforcers (money, tokens).

cards.q: Which reinforcement schedule is most resistant to extinction?
cards.a: Variable ratio schedule (e.g., slot machine) — unpredictable reward after variable number of responses.

cards.q: What is Freud's oral stage (age 0–1)?
cards.a: Pleasure centered on the mouth. Fixation → dependency, addictive behavior.

cards.q: What is Freud's anal stage (age 1–3)?
cards.a: Pleasure from retention/expulsion of feces. Fixation → obsessiveness or messiness.

cards.q: What is Freud's phallic stage (age 3–5)?
cards.a: Genitals become focus; Oedipus/Electra complex develops. Fixation → vanity or sexual dysfunction.

cards.q: What is Freud's latency stage (age 5–puberty)?
cards.a: Sexual urges repressed; social/intellectual skills develop.

cards.q: What is Freud's genital stage (puberty onward)?
cards.a: Sexual interests re-emerge with mature focus on opposite-sex relationships.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for infancy (0–1 year)?
cards.a: Trust vs. Mistrust — virtue: Hope.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for toddlerhood (1–3 years)?
cards.a: Autonomy vs. Shame & Doubt — virtue: Will.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for preschool (3–6 years)?
cards.a: Initiative vs. Guilt — virtue: Purpose.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for school age (6–12 years)?
cards.a: Industry vs. Inferiority — virtue: Competence.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for adolescence (12–20 years)?
cards.a: Identity vs. Role Confusion — virtue: Fidelity.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for young adulthood (20–40 years)?
cards.a: Intimacy vs. Isolation — virtue: Love.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for middle adulthood (40–65 years)?
cards.a: Generativity vs. Stagnation — virtue: Care.

cards.q: What is Erikson's stage for old age (65+ years)?
cards.a: Ego Integrity vs. Despair — virtue: Wisdom.

cards.q: What are Piaget's stages of cognitive development?
cards.a:
• Sensorimotor (0–2 yr): object permanence.
  • Preoperational (2–7 yr): symbolic thinking, egocentrism, no conservation.
  • Concrete operational (7–11 yr): conservation, logic with concrete objects.
  • Formal operational (11+ yr): abstract thinking, hypothetical reasoning.
