cards.q: What is object permanence and when does it develop?
cards.a: Understanding that objects exist even when not seen — develops at ~9 months (end of sensorimotor stage).

cards.q: What is conservation in Piaget's theory?
cards.a: Understanding that quantity remains constant despite changes in appearance — develops in concrete operational stage (~7 yr).

cards.q: What is egocentrism in Piaget's preoperational stage?
cards.a: Inability to see the world from another's perspective (not selfishness).

cards.q: What milestones occur at 6 weeks in a newborn?
cards.a: Social smile.

cards.q: What language milestones occur at 6 months?
cards.a: Babbles ('mamama', 'bababa').

cards.q: What language milestones occur at 12 months?
cards.a: First words (1–2 words with meaning).

cards.q: What language milestone occurs at 2 years?
cards.a: 2-word sentences; vocabulary ~50 words.

cards.q: What language milestone occurs at 3 years?
cards.a: 3-word sentences; ~250 words; 75% intelligible to strangers.

cards.q: What motor milestone occurs at 1 year?
cards.a: Walking independently.

cards.q: What fine motor milestone occurs at 9–10 months?
cards.a: Pincer grasp.

cards.q: What is stranger anxiety and when does it appear?
cards.a: Fear of unfamiliar adults, appearing at ~6–9 months.

cards.q: What is separation anxiety and when does it peak?
cards.a: Distress when separated from caregiver, peaks at ~12–18 months.

cards.q: What is Kohlberg's moral development theory?
cards.a:
• Preconventional: obedience/punishment, self-interest.
  • Conventional: conformity, law and order.
  • Postconventional: social contract, universal principles.

cards.q: What is repression (defense mechanism)?
cards.a: Involuntary blocking of painful thoughts/memories from conscious awareness (most basic defense).

cards.q: What is suppression (defense mechanism)?
cards.a: Conscious, deliberate effort to forget or not think about a problem (mature).

cards.q: What is denial (defense mechanism)?
cards.a: Refusing to acknowledge a painful reality (e.g., patient denies cancer diagnosis).

cards.q: What is projection (defense mechanism)?
cards.a: Attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts/feelings to others (e.g., 'She is angry at me', when in fact 'I am angry at her').

cards.q: What is displacement (defense mechanism)?
cards.a: Redirecting emotions from the original target to a safer substitute (e.g., yelling at spouse after being scolded by boss).

cards.q: What is reaction formation?
cards.a: Converting unacceptable impulses into their opposites (e.g., excessive friendliness toward someone you dislike).

cards.q: What is rationalization?
cards.a: Creating logical-sounding excuses to justify unacceptable behavior.

cards.q: What is intellectualization?
cards.a: Using excessive abstract thinking to avoid dealing with the emotional aspects of a situation.

cards.q: What is isolation of affect?
cards.a: Separating a thought from its associated emotion (describes trauma without feeling).

cards.q: What is regression?
cards.a: Reverting to an earlier stage of development under stress (e.g., bedwetting when new sibling arrives).

cards.q: What is sublimation?
cards.a: Redirecting unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities (e.g., aggression → boxing). Mature defense.

cards.q: What is altruism?
cards.a: Dealing with conflicts by meeting the needs of others (e.g., doctor volunteering after experiencing loss). Mature defense.

cards.q: What is humor?
cards.a: Using comedy to express feelings without discomfort. Mature defense.

cards.q: What is splitting (immature defense)?
cards.a: Viewing people as entirely good or entirely bad (common in borderline personality disorder).

cards.q: What is acting out?
cards.a: Expressing unacceptable impulses directly through actions (e.g., temper tantrum) — immature defense.

cards.q: What is undoing?
cards.a: Atoning for unacceptable thoughts with a specific behavior (e.g., OCD rituals).

cards.q: What is identification?
cards.a: Modeling oneself after another person to manage anxiety (e.g., 'Stockholm syndrome').

cards.q: List the mature defense mechanisms.
cards.a:
• SASH:
  • Sublimation
  • Altruism
  • Suppression
  • Humor

cards.q: What are the stages of sleep?
cards.a:
• NREM: N1 (theta), N2 (sleep spindles, K-complexes), N3 (delta — deep sleep).
  • REM: dreaming, atonia, ↑ brain activity, ↑ HR and BP.

cards.q: What EEG findings occur in each sleep stage?
cards.a:
• Awake: beta (alert) / alpha (relaxed).
  • N1: theta.
  • N2: sleep spindles, K-complexes.
  • N3: delta (slow wave).
  • REM: sawtooth waves.

cards.q: What is the most restorative stage of sleep?
cards.a: N3 (slow-wave/delta sleep) — important for physical restoration and memory consolidation.

cards.q: In what sleep stage do most dreams occur?
cards.a: REM sleep.

cards.q: What happens to REM sleep with age?
cards.a: REM sleep decreases with age; delta (N3) sleep also decreases.

cards.q: What are the characteristics of REM sleep?
cards.a:
• Rapid eye movements
  • Erections (penile/clitoral)
  • Muscle atonia
  • Vivid dreaming
  • ↑ Acetylcholine.

cards.q: What neurotransmitter promotes REM sleep?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (cholinergic neurons from pons).

cards.q: What neurotransmitters suppress REM sleep?
cards.a: Serotonin and Norepinephrine.

cards.q: What is insomnia and what is first-line treatment?
cards.a:
• Insomnia: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep for ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months.
  • First-line: CBT-I (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia).

cards.q: What is obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)?
cards.a:
• Repetitive upper airway obstruction during sleep → apneas, hypoxia, EDS.
  • Rx: CPAP.

cards.q: What is narcolepsy?
cards.a:
• Excessive daytime sleepiness with REM abnormalities: cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations.
  • Cause: loss of orexin (hypocretin)-producing neurons.

cards.q: What is cataplexy?
cards.a: Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions (e.g., laughter) — specific to narcolepsy.

cards.q: What are hypnagogic vs. hypnopompic hallucinations?
cards.a:
• Hypnagogic: hallucinations while falling asleep.
  • Hypnopompic: hallucinations while waking up.

cards.q: What is REM sleep behavior disorder?
cards.a: Loss of normal muscle atonia during REM → patient acts out dreams; associated with Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.

cards.q: What are the signs of opioid intoxication?
cards.a:
• CNS depression, miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, constipation, ↓ HR/BP.
  • Antidote: Naloxone.

cards.q: What are the signs of opioid withdrawal?
cards.a: DAWGS: Diarrhea, Anxiety, Watery eyes/rhinorrhea, Goosebumps (piloerection), Sweating, Yawning, Myalgias, Insomnia.

cards.q: What are the signs of alcohol intoxication?
cards.a: Disinhibition, ataxia, slurred speech, sedation, respiratory depression at high doses.

cards.q: What are the signs of alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a:
• Tremors (6–12 h) → seizures (24–48 h) → delirium tremens (48–96 h: confusion, fever, hallucinations, autonomic instability).
  • Tx: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: What is delirium tremens?
cards.a: Severe alcohol withdrawal (48–96 h after cessation): confusion, fever, autonomic instability, hallucinations (visual). Life-threatening — treat with benzodiazepines.

cards.q: What is Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1) deficiency in alcoholics: triad — confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia. Tx: IV thiamine.

cards.q: What is Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a: Chronic thiamine deficiency → bilateral mammillary body lesions → anterograde amnesia + confabulation.

cards.q: What are the signs of benzodiazepine/barbiturate intoxication?
cards.a: CNS depression, ataxia, slurred speech. Benzo: antidote = flumazenil. Barbiturate: no antidote.

cards.q: What are the signs of stimulant (cocaine/amphetamine) intoxication?
cards.a: Euphoria, ↑ HR, ↑ BP, dilated pupils (mydriasis), diaphoresis, hyperthermia, paranoia.

cards.q: What are the signs of cocaine withdrawal?
cards.a: 'Crash': dysphoria, fatigue, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, anhedonia (no physical signs — no antidote needed).

cards.q: What are the signs of PCP intoxication?
cards.a: Belligerence, nystagmus (vertical + horizontal), psychosis, analgesia, ↑ BP/HR; may cause rhabdomyolysis.

cards.q: What are the signs of marijuana intoxication?
cards.a: Euphoria, relaxation, ↑ appetite, dry mouth, red eyes, impaired memory, tachycardia.

cards.q: What are the signs of LSD/hallucinogen intoxication?
cards.a: Visual hallucinations, depersonalization, synesthesia, ↑ HR/BP, no antidote. No physical withdrawal.

cards.q: What are the signs of inhalant intoxication?
cards.a: Euphoria, CNS depression, renal tubular acidosis, methemoglobinemia, 'sudden sniffing death'.

cards.q: What is CAGE questionnaire?
cards.a:
• Screening for alcohol use disorder:
  • Cut down
  • Annoyed
  • Guilty
  • Eye-opener
  • ≥2 yes answers = positive screen.

cards.q: What medications are used for alcohol use disorder?
cards.a: Naltrexone (reduce cravings/relapse), Disulfiram (aversion), Acamprosate (reduce withdrawal symptoms).

cards.q: What medication is used for opioid use disorder (maintenance)?
cards.a: Methadone or Buprenorphine-naloxone (Suboxone).

cards.q: What is the AUDIT tool?
cards.a: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test — 10-question WHO screening instrument for alcohol misuse (more detailed than CAGE).

cards.q: What is the lifetime prevalence of major depressive disorder (MDD)?
cards.a: ~15–17%; twice as common in women than men.

cards.q: What is the most common psychiatric disorder?
cards.a: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) — most common psychiatric diagnosis worldwide.

cards.q: What is the lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia?
cards.a: ~1%; equally affects men and women, but men present earlier (early 20s vs. late 20s).

cards.q: What is the lifetime prevalence of bipolar disorder?
cards.a: ~1–4%; equal in men and women.

cards.q: What are the leading causes of death in various age groups?
cards.a:
• 1–14 yr: accidents
  • 15–24 yr: accidents, then suicide, then homicide
  • 25–64 yr: accidents, then cancer, then heart disease
  • 65+ yr: heart disease, then cancer, then stroke

cards.q: What is the suicide rate by gender and method?
cards.a:
• Women: more attempts, more overdose.
  • Men: more completions, more firearms.

cards.q: What are the strongest risk factors for suicide?
cards.a: Previous attempt (strongest), male sex, older age, chronic illness/pain, depression, substance use, isolation, access to firearms, family history.

cards.q: What is autonomy in medical ethics?
cards.a: Respect for the patient's right to make their own informed decisions.

cards.q: What is beneficence?
cards.a: The duty to act in the patient's best interest.

cards.q: What is non-maleficence?
cards.a: The duty to avoid causing harm ('First, do no harm').

cards.q: What is justice in medical ethics?
cards.a: Fair distribution of healthcare resources and equitable treatment of patients.

cards.q: What are the four components of informed consent?
cards.a:
• DVCR:
  • Disclosure — risks, benefits, alternatives
  • Voluntary — no coercion
  • Competence — decision-making capacity
  • Rational decision based on understanding

cards.q: Who provides consent for a minor in routine medical decisions?
cards.a: Parent or legal guardian.

cards.q: What are the exceptions to parental consent for minors?
cards.a: Minors can consent for: STASH — STIs, Trauma (emergency), Abortion (varies by state), Substance abuse, Health (emancipated minor).

cards.q: What makes a minor 'emancipated'?
cards.a: Married, pregnant, in military, self-supporting/living independently, parent — can give own consent.

cards.q: What is the difference between competence and capacity?
cards.a:
• Competence: legal determination (by court).
  • Capacity: clinical determination (by physician) — can patient understand, appreciate, reason, communicate a choice?

cards.q: What are the components of decision-making capacity?
cards.a: UCAR: Understand information, Communicate choice consistently, Appreciate consequences, Reason through decision.

cards.q: What is the physician's duty to report?
cards.a: Required reporting: child abuse, elder abuse, STIs, TB, gunshot wounds, impaired drivers (state-specific).

cards.q: What is the Tarasoff duty-to-warn?
cards.a: Physician must warn an identifiable third party if patient poses a serious threat of harm to them (Tarasoff v. Regents of UC).

cards.q: What is the rule of double effect?
cards.a: It is ethically permissible to provide treatments (e.g., high-dose morphine in terminal patients) if the intent is to relieve suffering, even if the treatment may hasten death.

cards.q: What is surrogate decision-making hierarchy?
cards.a: Spouse → adult children → parents → siblings → extended family. Decisions should reflect patient's previously expressed wishes.

cards.q: What is an advance directive?
cards.a: Legal document expressing patient's healthcare wishes in advance: includes living will (specific instructions) and durable power of attorney for healthcare (designates a surrogate).

cards.q: What is a DNR order?
cards.a: Do-Not-Resuscitate — patient's right to refuse CPR. Must be honored regardless of physician's opinion if patient has capacity.

cards.q: What is confidentiality in medicine?
cards.a: Physician must keep patient information private. Exceptions: mandatory reporting (abuse, STIs), Tarasoff duty, court orders.

cards.q: Can a physician share patient info with family without consent?
cards.a: No — unless patient consents or is incapacitated (then share only what's needed for care).

cards.q: What are Kübler-Ross's five stages of grief?
cards.a:
• DABDA:
  • Denial
  • Anger
  • Bargaining
  • Depression
  • Acceptance
  • (not always in order; may overlap)

cards.q: What is the difference between normal grief and major depression?
cards.a:
• Normal grief: sadness fluctuates; hallucinations of deceased (not pathologic); responds to distraction.
  • MDD: persistent hopelessness/worthlessness, suicidal ideation, anhedonia, impaired function — requires treatment.

cards.q: What is complicated (prolonged) grief disorder?
cards.a: Grief lasting >12 months with intense longing, difficulty accepting the loss, and impaired functioning. Tx: grief-focused psychotherapy.

cards.q: What is anticipatory grief?
cards.a: Grief that begins before a loss occurs (e.g., when a loved one has terminal illness).

cards.q: What are the first-line antidepressants?
cards.a: SSRIs (e.g., sertraline, fluoxetine) — first-line for MDD, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD.

cards.q: What are the side effects of SSRIs?
cards.a: Sexual dysfunction, GI upset, insomnia, weight changes, serotonin syndrome (with MAOIs — do not combine).

cards.q: What is serotonin syndrome?
cards.a: Triad: Hyperthermia, Neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia), Altered mental status. Most commonly with SSRI + MAOI.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of MAO inhibitors?
cards.a: Inhibit monoamine oxidase → ↑ serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine. Avoid: tyramine-rich foods (hypertensive crisis), pethidine, SSRIs.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of lithium?
cards.a: Stabilizes mood by modulating inositol/IP3 signaling and ion channels. Used in bipolar disorder. Narrow therapeutic window.

cards.q: What are the side effects and toxicity of lithium?
cards.a:
• Side effects: tremor, polyuria (nephrogenic DI), hypothyroidism, weight gain.
  • Toxicity: ataxia, coarse tremor, confusion, arrhythmias, seizures.

cards.q: What antipsychotics are first-generation (typical)?
cards.a: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine — block D2 receptors. Side effects: EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS.

cards.q: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: FALTER: Fever, Altered consciousness, Lead-pipe rigidity, Tachycardia, Elevated CPK, Rhabdomyolysis. Tx: dantrolene + bromocriptine.

cards.q: What antipsychotics are second-generation (atypical)?
cards.a: Clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone — block D2 + 5-HT2. Better for negative symptoms; ↓ EPS.

cards.q: What is the unique side effect of clozapine?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis — requires weekly WBC monitoring. Also: seizures, myocarditis, weight gain.

cards.q: What is tardive dyskinesia?
cards.a: Late-onset involuntary repetitive movements (lip-smacking, tongue protrusion) from chronic D2 blockade. Rx: valbenazine or tetrabenazine.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Enhance GABA-A receptor activity → ↑ Cl⁻ influx → neuronal hyperpolarization. Used for anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, seizures, sedation.

cards.q: What is buspirone used for?
cards.a: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) — partial 5-HT1A agonist. No dependence, no sedation, no cross-tolerance with benzos. Takes 2 weeks.

cards.q: What should you do if a colleague is impaired by substance use?
cards.a: Report to the appropriate authority (department chief, licensing board). Patient safety takes priority over colleague loyalty.

cards.q: What is the physician's obligation when asked to perform a procedure they find morally objectionable?
cards.a: Can refuse but must refer the patient to another physician who can provide the care. Patient welfare must be ensured.

cards.q: What is the 'Captain of the Ship' doctrine?
cards.a: The attending physician is ultimately responsible for the actions of all team members under their supervision.

cards.q: What is Medicare?
cards.a: Federal insurance for age ≥65, certain disabled, and ESRD patients. Parts: A (hospital), B (outpatient), C (Medicare Advantage), D (drugs).

cards.q: What is Medicaid?
cards.a: Joint federal-state insurance for low-income individuals and families. Eligibility varies by state.

cards.q: What is the difference between efficacy and effectiveness of a treatment?
cards.a:
• Efficacy: works in ideal/controlled conditions (RCT).
  • Effectiveness: works in real-world conditions (general population).

cards.q: What is primary prevention?
cards.a: Prevent disease before it occurs (e.g., vaccination, smoking cessation).

cards.q: What is secondary prevention?
cards.a: Detect disease early (e.g., mammography, Pap smear, colonoscopy).

cards.q: What is tertiary prevention?
cards.a: Reduce disability from established disease (e.g., cardiac rehab after MI, physiotherapy).

cards.q: What is lead-time bias?
cards.a: Early detection makes survival time appear longer without actual benefit — common with screening tests.

cards.q: What is length-time bias?
cards.a: Screening preferentially detects slower-growing (less lethal) disease → overestimation of screening benefit.

cards.q: What is the healthy worker effect?
cards.a: Workers are healthier than the general population → underestimates occupational risk in occupational cohort studies.

cards.q: What is attributable risk (risk difference)?
cards.a: Incidence in exposed − Incidence in unexposed. Measures how much disease is due to exposure.

cards.q: What is population attributable risk?
cards.a: Amount of disease in the total population attributable to a particular exposure.

cards.q: What are the five levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
cards.a:
• From bottom to top:
  • 1. Physiological (food, shelter)
  • 2. Safety
  • 3. Love/Belonging
  • 4. Esteem
  • 5. Self-Actualization

cards.q: What is the difference between disease and illness?
cards.a:
• Disease: objective pathological process.
  • Illness: subjective experience of symptoms and dysfunction.

cards.q: What is sick role (Parsons)?
cards.a: Patient is exempted from normal social duties but must seek care and try to recover.

cards.q: What are the two arms of the immune system?
cards.a:
• Innate (non-specific) — immediate, no memory
  • Adaptive (specific) — delayed, has memory (B & T cells)

cards.q: List the main cells of innate immunity.
cards.a: Neutrophils, Macrophages, Dendritic cells, NK cells, Mast cells, Eosinophils, Basophils

cards.q: List the main cells of adaptive immunity.
cards.a: B lymphocytes (humoral) and T lymphocytes (cell-mediated)

cards.q: What are the three lines of defense in immunity?
cards.a:
1. Anatomic/physiologic barriers
  2. Innate immunity
  3. Adaptive immunity

cards.q: What are the major functions of neutrophils?
cards.a: Phagocytosis, NET formation, primary defense against bacteria and fungi

cards.q: What is the role of macrophages in immunity?
cards.a: Phagocytosis, antigen presentation, cytokine production, tissue repair

cards.q: What are the two types of dendritic cells?
cards.a: Conventional DCs (excellent antigen presenters) and Plasmacytoid DCs (produce large amounts of Type I IFN)

cards.q: What is the function of Natural Killer (NK) cells?
cards.a: Kill virus-infected and tumor cells (missing-self recognition via KIRs). Part of innate immunity but have some memory.

cards.q: What are Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs)?
cards.a: Receptors on innate cells that recognize Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns (PAMPs) and Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs). Examples: TLRs, NLRs, RLRs, C-type lectins.

cards.q: Which TLR is located on the cell surface and recognizes LPS?
cards.a: TLR4 (with MD-2 and CD14)

cards.q: Which TLR recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA?
cards.a: TLR9 (endosomal)

cards.q: What is the difference between MHC Class I and Class II?
cards.a:
• MHC I: Present on all nucleated cells, presents to CD8 T cells (endogenous antigens)
  • MHC II: Present on APCs, presents to CD4 T cells (exogenous antigens)

cards.q: Which cells express MHC Class II constitutively?
cards.a: Professional APCs: Dendritic cells, Macrophages, B cells

cards.q: What is the structure of an antibody?
cards.a: Two heavy chains + two light chains. Variable (Fab) region binds antigen, Constant (Fc) region mediates effector functions.

cards.q: Name the five antibody isotypes and their main functions.
cards.a:
• IgM: Primary response, pentamer
  • IgG: Secondary response, crosses placenta, opsonization
  • IgA: Mucosal immunity (dimer)
  • IgE: Parasites & allergy (mast cell degranulation)
  • IgD: B cell receptor

cards.q: What is the function of the classical complement pathway?
cards.a: Activated by antigen-antibody complexes (IgM or IgG)

cards.q: What is the function of the alternative complement pathway?
cards.a: Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 or triggered by microbial surfaces

cards.q: What is the function of the lectin complement pathway?
cards.a: Mannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds microbial carbohydrates

cards.q: What are the three main outcomes of complement activation?
cards.a:
1. Opsonization (C3b)
  2. Inflammation (C3a, C5a)
  3. Membrane Attack Complex (MAC — C5b-9)

cards.q: What is the role of CD4 T helper cells?
cards.a: Orchestrate immune response via cytokine secretion. Subsets: Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, Tfh.

cards.q: What is the master cytokine for Th1 differentiation?
cards.a: IFN-γ (activates macrophages, promotes cell-mediated immunity)

cards.q: What is the master cytokine for Th2 differentiation?
cards.a: IL-4 (promotes humoral immunity, IgE class switching, eosinophil activation)

cards.q: What is the master cytokine for Th17 differentiation?
cards.a: IL-6 + TGF-β (recruits neutrophils, important in autoimmunity and fungal defense)

cards.q: What is the function of Regulatory T cells (Tregs)?
cards.a: Suppress immune response (prevent autoimmunity). Express FoxP3 and CD25.

cards.q: What is the role of T follicular helper (Tfh) cells?
cards.a: Help B cells in germinal centers (class switching, affinity maturation, memory B cell formation)

cards.q: What is the difference between central and peripheral tolerance?
cards.a:
• Central: Negative selection in thymus/bone marrow
  • Peripheral: Anergy, suppression by Tregs, ignorance

cards.q: What are the four types of hypersensitivity reactions?
cards.a:
• Type I: Immediate (IgE)
  • Type II: Cytotoxic (IgG/IgM)
  • Type III: Immune complex
  • Type IV: Delayed (T-cell mediated)

cards.q: Give examples of Type I hypersensitivity.
cards.a: Anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, food allergy

cards.q: Give examples of Type II hypersensitivity.
cards.a: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, Graves disease, Myasthenia gravis

cards.q: Give examples of Type III hypersensitivity.
cards.a: SLE (anti-dsDNA), Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, Serum sickness, Arthus reaction

cards.q: Give examples of Type IV hypersensitivity.
cards.a: Contact dermatitis, TB skin test, Graft rejection, Type 1 diabetes

cards.q: What is the mechanism of Type IV hypersensitivity?
cards.a: T cell mediated (Th1 → macrophage activation or CD8 cytotoxicity)

cards.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
cards.a:
• Active: Host produces antibodies (vaccination, infection)
  • Passive: Pre-formed antibodies given (e.g., RhoGAM, antitoxin)

cards.q: What is immunological memory?
cards.a: Faster, stronger, and more specific response on re-exposure due to memory B and T cells

cards.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary immune response?
cards.a:
• Primary: slow, mostly IgM
  • Secondary: rapid, high-affinity IgG (anamnestic response)

cards.q: What are superantigens?
cards.a: Bacterial toxins (e.g., TSST-1, staphylococcal enterotoxins) that bind MHC II and TCR outside the peptide-binding groove → massive cytokine storm

cards.q: What is the most common primary immunodeficiency?
cards.a: Selective IgA deficiency

cards.q: What is the defect in X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton)?
cards.a: BTK mutation → no mature B cells, absent plasma cells and immunoglobulins

cards.q: What is the defect in SCID (most common form)?
cards.a: IL-2Rγ chain deficiency (X-linked) or ADA deficiency

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia (22q11 deletion)

cards.q: What is the defect in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)?
cards.a: NADPH oxidase deficiency → inability to produce superoxide → recurrent catalase-positive infections

cards.q: What is the nitroblue test used for?
cards.a: Diagnosis of CGD (negative in CGD)

cards.q: What is the defect in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD)?
cards.a: CD18 (β2 integrin) deficiency → delayed umbilical cord separation, poor pus formation

cards.q: What is the defect in Chediak-Higashi syndrome?
cards.a: LYST gene → giant granules, albinism, recurrent infections, neurological issues

cards.q: What is the defect in Job syndrome (Hyper-IgE)?
cards.a: STAT3 mutation → high IgE, eczema, recurrent cold abscesses (Staph), coarse facies

cards.q: What are the two main types of graft rejection?
cards.a: Acute (T-cell mediated) and Chronic (vascular fibrosis, obliterative vasculopathy)

cards.q: What is hyperacute rejection?
cards.a: Pre-existing antibodies (ABO mismatch or anti-HLA) → immediate thrombosis and necrosis

cards.q: What drug class is used for induction immunosuppression?
cards.a: Anti-thymocyte globulin, basiliximab (IL-2R antagonist)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of cyclosporine and tacrolimus?
cards.a: Calcineurin inhibitors → block IL-2 transcription

cards.q: What is the mechanism of sirolimus (rapamycin)?
cards.a: mTOR inhibitor → blocks IL-2 signaling and T cell proliferation

cards.q: What is the mechanism of mycophenolate mofetil?
cards.a: Inhibits IMPDH → blocks purine synthesis in lymphocytes

cards.q: What is the major side effect of long-term steroid use in transplant patients?
cards.a: Osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension, Cushingoid features

cards.q: Which cytokine is known as the 'macrophage activating factor'?
cards.a: IFN-γ (produced by Th1 and NK cells)

cards.q: Which cytokine stimulates IgE class switching and eosinophil activation?
cards.a: IL-5 (Th2 cytokine)

cards.q: Which cytokine is the main growth factor for B cells?
cards.a: IL-4 and IL-13

cards.q: What is the function of IL-2?
cards.a: T cell proliferation and differentiation (autocrine & paracrine)

cards.q: Which cytokine drives Th17 differentiation and is pro-inflammatory?
cards.a: IL-17 and IL-23

cards.q: What is the role of TGF-β in immunity?
cards.a: Anti-inflammatory; promotes Treg differentiation and IgA class switching

cards.q: Which cytokine is produced by Th1 cells and activates macrophages?
cards.a: IFN-γ

cards.q: What is the function of IL-10?
cards.a: Potent anti-inflammatory cytokine (produced by Tregs, Th2, macrophages)

cards.q: What is the major cytokine responsible for fever?
cards.a: IL-1 and TNF-α

cards.q: Which cells produce Type I interferons (IFN-α/β)?
cards.a: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells and virus-infected cells

cards.q: What is the function of Type I interferons?
cards.a: Inhibit viral replication, increase MHC I expression, activate NK cells

cards.q: Give three examples of Type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity.
cards.a:
1. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  2. Goodpasture syndrome
  3. Myasthenia gravis / Graves disease

cards.q: Give three examples of Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity.
cards.a:
1. SLE
  2. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
  3. Serum sickness

cards.q: Give three examples of Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity.
cards.a:
1. TB skin test (PPD)
  2. Contact dermatitis (poison ivy)
  3. Graft rejection

cards.q: What is the Arthus reaction?
cards.a: Localized Type III hypersensitivity — immune complex deposition after antigen injection (e.g., vaccine booster)

cards.q: What is serum sickness?
cards.a: Systemic Type III hypersensitivity — fever, rash, arthralgia, glomerulonephritis after exposure to foreign proteins

cards.q: Which autoimmune disease is associated with anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies?
cards.a: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

cards.q: Which autoimmune disease is associated with anti-CCP antibodies?
cards.a: Rheumatoid Arthritis

cards.q: Which disease is associated with anti-centromere antibodies?
cards.a: Limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome)

cards.q: Which disease is associated with anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies?
cards.a: Diffuse scleroderma

cards.q: Which disease is associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies?
cards.a: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

cards.q: Which disease is associated with anti-GBM antibodies?
cards.a: Goodpasture syndrome

cards.q: Which HLA allele is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: HLA-B27

cards.q: Which HLA alleles are associated with celiac disease?
cards.a: HLA-DQ2 and DQ8

cards.q: Which HLA is associated with rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: HLA-DR4

cards.q: What test is used to diagnose CGD?
cards.a: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry (preferred) or NBT test

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of CGD?
cards.a: Most common is X-linked (gp91phox), also autosomal recessive

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
cards.a: Eczema, Thrombocytopenia (small platelets), Recurrent infections (T+B cell defect)

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
cards.a: WASP gene mutation (X-linked)

cards.q: What is the defect in Ataxia-Telangiectasia?
cards.a: ATM gene (DNA repair defect) → cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, IgA deficiency, increased cancer risk

cards.q: What complement deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infections?
cards.a: Terminal complement deficiency (C5–C9 — MAC deficiency)

cards.q: What complement deficiency is associated with SLE-like syndrome?
cards.a: C1, C2, or C4 deficiency (early classical pathway)

cards.q: What is the most common complement deficiency?
cards.a: C2 deficiency

cards.q: What is hereditary angioedema (HAE)?
cards.a: C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency → uncontrolled bradykinin production → non-pitting edema

cards.q: What is the treatment for hereditary angioedema?
cards.a: C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 antagonist), or ecallantide

cards.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect Coombs test?
cards.a:
• Direct: detects antibodies already on RBCs
  • Indirect: detects antibodies in serum

cards.q: What is the mechanism of Type II hypersensitivity in autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: IgG or IgM against RBC antigens → complement activation or phagocytosis

cards.q: What is the major difference between warm and cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a:
• Warm: IgG, extravascular hemolysis (splenic)
  • Cold: IgM, intravascular hemolysis (complement)

cards.q: What infection is classically associated with cold agglutinin disease?
cards.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae or EBV

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary immunodeficiency worldwide?
cards.a: HIV infection

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of rituximab?
cards.a: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody → B cell depletion

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of infliximab/adalimumab?
cards.a: Anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibodies

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of etanercept?
cards.a: TNF receptor fusion protein (decoy receptor)

cards.q: Name two live attenuated vaccines contraindicated in immunocompromised patients.
cards.a: MMR and Varicella (also oral polio, yellow fever, rotavirus)

cards.q: What type of vaccine is the Hepatitis B vaccine?
cards.a: Recombinant subunit vaccine (HBsAg)

cards.q: What type of vaccine is the Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13)?
cards.a: Conjugate vaccine (polysaccharide + protein carrier)

cards.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunization?
cards.a:
• Active: induces memory (vaccines)
  • Passive: immediate protection, no memory (immunoglobulins)

cards.q: What is the major complication of live vaccines in SCID patients?
cards.a: Vaccine-associated disease / disseminated infection

cards.q: What is tumor immunology's 'cancer immunoediting' concept?
cards.a: Elimination → Equilibrium → Escape phases of tumor-immune interaction

cards.q: Which immune cells are most important for tumor surveillance?
cards.a: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and NK cells

cards.q: What are tumor-specific antigens vs tumor-associated antigens?
cards.a:
• TSA: unique to tumor (e.g., neoantigens)
  • TAA: overexpressed normal proteins (e.g., HER2, MART-1)

cards.q: Name two immune checkpoint molecules targeted in cancer immunotherapy.
cards.a: PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of pembrolizumab / nivolumab?
cards.a: Anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibodies — block PD-1/PD-L1 interaction → unleash T cells against tumors

cards.q: What is the mechanism of ipilimumab?
cards.a: Anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody — blocks inhibitory signal on T cells

cards.q: What is the most common primary immunodeficiency in adults?
cards.a: Selective IgA deficiency

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of selective IgA deficiency?
cards.a: Recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections, anaphylaxis to blood products, increased autoimmune disease

cards.q: What is the defect in Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)?
cards.a: Defective T and B cell development (most common: IL-2Rγ chain or ADA deficiency)

cards.q: What is the treatment for SCID?
cards.a: Bone marrow / stem cell transplant (curative); gene therapy for some forms

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease)?
cards.a: Boys with recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age, absent B cells and plasma cells, low immunoglobulins

cards.q: What is the defect in Hyper-IgM syndrome?
cards.a: Defective CD40 ligand (X-linked) or CD40 → inability to class switch from IgM

cards.q: What infections are common in Hyper-IgM syndrome?
cards.a: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections + opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii)

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)?
cards.a: 70% X-linked (CYBB gene), 30% autosomal recessive

cards.q: What organisms are most common in CGD infections?
cards.a: Catalase-positive organisms: Staph aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in Chediak-Higashi syndrome?
cards.a: Giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes

cards.q: What is the triad of Job syndrome (Autosomal dominant Hyper-IgE syndrome)?
cards.a:
1. High IgE
  2. Eczema
  3. Recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses

cards.q: What gene is mutated in Job syndrome?
cards.a: STAT3

cards.q: What is the defect in Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD-1)?
cards.a: Deficiency of CD18 (β2-integrin) → impaired neutrophil migration

cards.q: What is the classic clinical clue for LAD-1?
cards.a: Delayed separation of umbilical cord + marked leukocytosis without pus formation

cards.q: What complement components are deficient in patients with recurrent Neisseria infections?
cards.a: Terminal complement (C5–C9) — inability to form MAC

cards.q: What is the mechanism of HIV entry into CD4 cells?
cards.a: gp120 binds CD4 + CCR5 (or CXCR4) co-receptor

cards.q: Which cells are primarily destroyed in HIV?
cards.a: CD4+ helper T cells

cards.q: What is the definition of AIDS?
cards.a: CD4 count <200 cells/μL or presence of AIDS-defining illness

cards.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection in AIDS patients with CD4 <200?
cards.a: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)

cards.q: What is the prophylaxis for PCP in HIV patients?
cards.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)

cards.q: What malignancy is strongly associated with HIV/AIDS?
cards.a: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma

cards.q: What is the major difference between allograft, xenograft, and isograft?
cards.a:
• Isograft: identical twin
  • Allograft: same species
  • Xenograft: different species

cards.q: What is hyperacute rejection mediated by?
cards.a: Pre-formed antibodies (ABO or anti-HLA) → immediate complement activation and thrombosis

cards.q: What is the main mechanism of acute cellular rejection?
cards.a: CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells attacking graft

cards.q: What is the main mechanism of chronic rejection?
cards.a: Vascular fibrosis and obliterative arteriopathy (accelerated atherosclerosis)

cards.q: Which immunosuppressant is most associated with nephrotoxicity?
cards.a: Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus (calcineurin inhibitors)

cards.q: Which immunosuppressant is most associated with gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism?
cards.a: Cyclosporine

cards.q: Which immunosuppressant increases risk of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)?
cards.a: All potent immunosuppressants, especially those causing profound T-cell suppression

cards.q: What is the mechanism of azathioprine?
cards.a: Purine analog → inhibits lymphocyte proliferation (converted to 6-MP)

cards.q: What drug interaction is dangerous with azathioprine?
cards.a: Allopurinol (inhibits xanthine oxidase → increased toxicity)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of basiliximab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-2 receptor (CD25) monoclonal antibody — induction therapy

cards.q: What is the function of muromonab-CD3 (OKT3)?
cards.a: Anti-CD3 antibody — depletes T cells (rarely used now)

cards.q: What is graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)?
cards.a: Donor T cells attack recipient tissues (skin, liver, GI tract) after bone marrow transplant

cards.q: What is the difference between acute and chronic GVHD?
cards.a:
• Acute: <100 days, maculopapular rash, diarrhea, jaundice
  • Chronic: >100 days, scleroderma-like skin changes, sicca syndrome

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute GVHD?
cards.a: High-dose corticosteroids ± other immunosuppressants

cards.q: Name two cancers strongly associated with EBV.
cards.a: Burkitt lymphoma and Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

cards.q: Name two cancers strongly associated with HPV.
cards.a: Cervical cancer and Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma

cards.q: Name one cancer associated with Hepatitis B/C.
cards.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

cards.q: What is the role of PD-L1 on tumor cells?
cards.a: Inhibits T cell activation via PD-1 receptor → immune evasion

cards.q: What is immune checkpoint blockade?
cards.a: Therapeutic antibodies that block inhibitory signals (PD-1, CTLA-4) to enhance anti-tumor immunity

cards.q: What is the Warburg effect in tumor immunology?
cards.a: Cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis even in presence of oxygen

cards.q: What are tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs)?
cards.a: Often M2-polarized → promote tumor growth, angiogenesis, and suppress anti-tumor immunity

cards.q: What is the role of regulatory T cells (Tregs) in cancer?
cards.a: Suppress anti-tumor immune response (often increased in tumor microenvironment)

cards.q: What is the most common type of transplant rejection seen in the first week?
cards.a: Hyperacute rejection (if present)

cards.q: What is the most common type of rejection seen months to years later?
cards.a: Chronic rejection

cards.q: What is the classic skin finding in graft-versus-host disease?
cards.a: Maculopapular rash starting on palms, soles, and ears

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in Hashimoto thyroiditis?
cards.a: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in Graves disease?
cards.a: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) — TSH receptor antibody

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in pernicious anemia?
cards.a: Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in primary biliary cholangitis?
cards.a: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA)

cards.q: What is the classic autoantibody in autoimmune hepatitis Type 1?
cards.a: Anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) and ANA

cards.q: What disease is associated with anti-Jo-1 antibodies?
cards.a: Polymyositis / Antisynthetase syndrome

cards.q: What disease is associated with anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La)?
cards.a: Sjögren syndrome

cards.q: What is the HLA association for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus?
cards.a: HLA-DR3 and DR4

cards.q: What is molecular mimicry? Give an example.
cards.a: Immune response against pathogen cross-reacts with self-antigen. Example: Rheumatic fever (Strep M protein mimics cardiac myosin)

cards.q: What is the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever?
cards.a: Type II hypersensitivity — molecular mimicry between group A Strep and heart valves, joints, skin, brain

cards.q: What is the major Jones criterion for rheumatic fever?
cards.a: Carditis, Polyarthritis, Chorea, Erythema marginatum, Subcutaneous nodules

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute rheumatic fever?
cards.a: Penicillin + anti-inflammatory agents (aspirin or corticosteroids)

cards.q: What is the major cause of death in untreated rheumatic heart disease?
cards.a: Mitral stenosis

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of abatacept?
cards.a: CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein — blocks CD28-B7 co-stimulation

cards.q: What is the mechanism of tocilizumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-6 receptor antibody

cards.q: What is the mechanism of ustekinumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-12/IL-23 monoclonal antibody

cards.q: What is the mechanism of secukinumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody

cards.q: Which vaccine type carries risk of reversion to virulence?
cards.a: Live attenuated vaccines

cards.q: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
cards.a: Live vaccines (MMR, Varicella, etc.)

cards.q: What is the only live vaccine given at birth?
cards.a: BCG (in endemic areas)

cards.q: What type of vaccine is the Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine?
cards.a: Conjugate vaccine (polysaccharide linked to protein)

cards.q: What is herd immunity?
cards.a: Indirect protection from infectious disease when a large percentage of population is immune

cards.q: What is the most effective way to prevent measles outbreaks?
cards.a: High MMR vaccination coverage (>95%)

cards.q: What is the difference between killed and live vaccines regarding boosters?
cards.a: Killed vaccines usually require boosters; live vaccines often give lifelong immunity

cards.q: What is the major risk of giving live vaccines to HIV patients with low CD4 counts?
cards.a: Disseminated infection from the vaccine strain

cards.q: What is central tolerance?
cards.a: Elimination of self-reactive lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs (thymus for T cells, bone marrow for B cells)

cards.q: What is peripheral tolerance?
cards.a: Mechanisms outside primary organs: anergy, deletion, suppression by Tregs

cards.q: What transcription factor is essential for Treg development?
cards.a: FoxP3

cards.q: What is AIRE gene defect associated with?
cards.a: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) — candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease

cards.q: What is the function of CTLA-4?
cards.a: Inhibitory receptor on T cells — competes with CD28 for B7 binding

cards.q: What is the function of PD-1/PD-L1 interaction?
cards.a: Inhibits T cell activation and promotes tolerance

cards.q: What is immune privilege? Give examples.
cards.a: Sites with reduced immune surveillance: eye (anterior chamber), brain, testes, fetus

cards.q: What is the role of Fas-FasL in immunity?
cards.a: Induces apoptosis in target cells (important in activation-induced cell death)

cards.q: What is the difference between necrosis and apoptosis in immune context?
cards.a: Necrosis → inflammation; Apoptosis → no inflammation (silent clearance)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary amyloidosis (AA amyloid)?
cards.a: Chronic inflammation (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, TB, familial Mediterranean fever)

cards.q: What is the most common organ affected by amyloidosis?
cards.a: Kidney (proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome)

cards.q: What stain is used to diagnose amyloidosis?
cards.a: Congo red — apple-green birefringence under polarized light

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome in small cell lung cancer?
cards.a: SIADH and Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH)

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in seminoma?
cards.a: β-hCG (mild elevation)

cards.q: What tumor marker is elevated in yolk sac tumor?
cards.a: AFP

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme

cards.q: What is the characteristic histologic feature of glioblastoma?
cards.a: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation

cards.q: What is the most common childhood brain tumor in the posterior fossa?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma

cards.q: What virus is associated with primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS patients?
cards.a: EBV

cards.q: What is the most common route of metastasis for carcinomas?
cards.a: Lymphatic spread

cards.q: What is the most common route of metastasis for sarcomas?
cards.a: Hematogenous spread

cards.q: What is the primary cellular mechanism underlying replicative senescence (Hayflick limit)?
cards.a: Progressive telomere shortening with each cell division. When telomeres become critically short, p53/p21 pathway activates → permanent cell cycle arrest. Telomerase (active in stem/germ cells) prevents this.

cards.q: Compare programmed vs. damage/error theories of aging (high-yield distinction).
cards.a:
• Programmed: Intrinsic genetic clock (telomere shortening, hormonal changes).
  • Damage/Error: Accumulation of insults (free radicals, DNA damage, protein misfolding). Most accepted hybrid is evolutionary senescence theory.

cards.q: What is the free radical theory of aging? Key molecule?
cards.a: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) from mitochondrial metabolism cause cumulative oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids. Antioxidants (superoxide dismutase, catalase) mitigate but decline with age.

cards.q: Define frailty syndrome in geriatrics. Key components (FRAIL mnemonic).
cards.a: Fatigue, Resistance (weakness), Aerobics (endurance), Illness, Loss of weight. Multisystem decline leading to vulnerability to stressors.

cards.q: Physiological change in cardiovascular system with normal aging?
cards.a: ↑ Arterial stiffness (↓ compliance) → ↑ systolic BP, widened pulse pressure. Left ventricular wall thickens; ↓ maximal heart rate (↓ β-adrenergic response).

cards.q: Age-related change in renal function? Clinical implication for drug dosing.
cards.a: ↓ Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~1 mL/min/year after age 30–40 (due to ↓ nephron number). Use Cockcroft-Gault or CKD-EPI (adjusted for age) for dosing renally cleared drugs.

cards.q: What is presbycusis? Most common type and cause.
cards.a: Sensorineural hearing loss (high-frequency first) due to loss of cochlear hair cells and stria vascularis degeneration. Bilateral, progressive.

cards.q: Age-related pulmonary changes increasing infection risk?
cards.a: ↓ Lung elasticity, ↓ vital capacity, ↑ residual volume, ↓ cough reflex, ↓ mucociliary clearance → impaired clearance of pathogens.

cards.q: Gastrointestinal changes in elderly affecting nutrition?
cards.a: ↓ Saliva (xerostomia), ↓ taste/smell, ↓ gastric acid (atrophic gastritis), ↓ motility → constipation, malabsorption, weight loss risk.

cards.q: Musculoskeletal changes with aging? Sarcopenia definition.
cards.a: ↓ Muscle mass/strength (sarcopenia: loss > age-expected), ↓ bone density (osteopenia/porosis), ↓ joint cartilage. Increased fall/fracture risk.

cards.q: Neurological changes in normal aging vs. dementia (key distinction).
cards.a: Normal: Mild ↓ processing speed, mild memory retrieval issues, brain atrophy (esp. hippocampus). Dementia: Significant functional impairment, progressive deficits.

cards.q: Immune system change with aging (immunosenescence)? Clinical effect.
cards.a: ↓ Naive T cells, ↑ memory T cells, ↓ antibody affinity/diversity, chronic low-grade inflammation ('inflammaging') → poorer vaccine response, ↑ infections/autoimmunity/cancer.

cards.q: Pharmacokinetic change in elderly: Volume of distribution for lipophilic drugs?
cards.a: ↑ (due to ↑ body fat percentage) → prolonged half-life and effects of lipophilic drugs (e.g., diazepam, amiodarone).

cards.q: Pharmacodynamic change in elderly: Sensitivity to anticholinergics?
cards.a: ↑ Sensitivity → delirium, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth (BEERS criteria highlight avoidance).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of delirium in hospitalized elderly?
cards.a: Multifactorial: Infection (UTI/pneumonia), medications (anticholinergics, benzos), electrolyte imbalance, surgery, underlying dementia.

cards.q: Define polypharmacy. Key risk in geriatrics.
cards.a: Use of ≥5 medications. Risks: Drug-drug interactions, adverse effects, falls, cognitive impairment, non-adherence.

cards.q: Age-related change in hepatic metabolism? Implication for Phase I drugs.
cards.a: ↓ Phase I metabolism (CYP450 oxidation) more than Phase II (conjugation) → prolonged half-life of drugs like benzodiazepines, warfarin.

cards.q: What is the leading cause of accidental death in elderly?
cards.a: Falls (leading to hip fracture, head injury). Risk factors: Orthostasis, gait instability, medications, vision/hearing loss.

cards.q: Physiological basis of orthostatic hypotension in elderly?
cards.a: Blunted baroreceptor reflex, ↓ vascular compliance, ↓ renin-angiotensin response, volume depletion, autonomic dysfunction.

cards.q: What is the 'failure to thrive' in elderly? Key reversible causes.
cards.a: Weight loss, weakness, apathy. Causes: Depression, medications, malignancy, chronic disease, social isolation, malnutrition.

cards.q: Cellular hallmark of aging: Accumulation of what in lysosomes?
cards.a: Lipofuscin ('age pigment') — indigestible lipid-protein residues from autophagocytosis.

cards.q: Role of sirtuins in aging (high-yield mechanism)?
cards.a: NAD+-dependent deacetylases. Promote longevity by DNA repair, stress resistance, metabolic regulation. Activated by calorie restriction/resveratrol.

cards.q: mTOR pathway in aging? Effect of inhibition?
cards.a: mTOR promotes growth/anabolism. Hyperactivation accelerates aging; inhibition (rapamycin) extends lifespan in models via autophagy.

cards.q: What is epigenetic drift in aging?
cards.a: Age-related changes in DNA methylation/histone modification patterns → altered gene expression without DNA sequence change.

cards.q: Compare caloric restriction vs. intermittent fasting effects on aging.
cards.a: Both extend lifespan in models by ↓ mTOR/insulin signaling, ↑ sirtuins/autophagy, ↓ inflammation/oxidative stress.

cards.q: Most common dementia in elderly? Pathological hallmark.
cards.a: Alzheimer disease — extracellular amyloid-β plaques + intracellular neurofibrillary (tau) tangles.

cards.q: Vascular dementia vs. Alzheimer: Key clinical difference.
cards.a: Vascular: Stepwise decline, focal neuro deficits, history of strokes. Alzheimer: Gradual, prominent memory loss first.

cards.q: Parkinson disease in elderly: Classic triad.
cards.a: Tremor (resting), Rigidity, Bradykinesia (TRAP). Due to dopaminergic neuron loss in substantia nigra.

cards.q: What is the Beers Criteria?
cards.a: List of potentially inappropriate medications in older adults (risk of adverse effects outweigh benefits).

cards.q: Age-related change in endocrine: Thyroid function?
cards.a: Mild ↑ TSH, ↓ T3 (peripheral conversion); clinical hypothyroidism more common but overt function often preserved.

cards.q: Osteoporosis risk factors in elderly (high-yield)?
cards.a: ↓ Estrogen (post-menopause), ↓ vitamin D/calcium absorption, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, corticosteroids, low BMI.

cards.q: Pressure ulcers (decubitus) in elderly: Key prevention?
cards.a: Regular repositioning, pressure-relieving mattresses, nutrition (protein), skin care. Common in immobile/frail patients.

cards.q: What is sundowning? Associated condition.
cards.a: Worsening confusion/agitation in evening. Common in dementia (Alzheimer) patients in hospitals or unfamiliar settings.

cards.q: Physiological change in sleep architecture with aging?
cards.a: ↓ Slow-wave (deep) sleep, ↓ REM, ↑ sleep latency and fragmentation, advanced sleep phase (early to bed/early to rise).

cards.q: Most common malignancy in elderly men vs. women (incidence)?
cards.a: Men: Prostate. Women: Breast (then lung/colorectal). Overall, skin cancers and colorectal also high.

cards.q: Advance directives in geriatrics: Living will vs. durable power of attorney.
cards.a: Living will: Specific treatment wishes. DPOA: Designates surrogate decision-maker.

cards.q: What is the 'geriatric giants' or '4 Is' of geriatrics?
cards.a: Immobility, Instability (falls), Incontinence, Intellectual impairment (dementia/delirium).

cards.q: Pharmacokinetic change: Decreased lean body mass effect on hydrophilic drugs?
cards.a: ↓ Volume of distribution → higher plasma concentration and effects (e.g., digoxin, aminoglycosides).

cards.q: Why is creatinine clearance preferred over serum creatinine for GFR in elderly?
cards.a: ↓ Muscle mass → lower creatinine production → normal serum Cr despite low GFR.

cards.q: Key difference in presentation of MI in elderly vs. young?
cards.a: Atypical: Dyspnea, fatigue, confusion, nausea more common than classic chest pain.

cards.q: What is the leading cause of vision loss in elderly?
cards.a: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (dry > wet). Drusen deposits.

cards.q: Cataracts vs. glaucoma in elderly: Key features.
cards.a: Cataracts: Lens opacity, gradual blurry vision. Glaucoma: Optic neuropathy, peripheral vision loss first (often asymptomatic early).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in elderly (>70)?
cards.a: Calcific (degenerative) aortic stenosis.

cards.q: Mitochondrial theory of aging: Key mechanism?
cards.a: Accumulation of mtDNA mutations → dysfunctional electron transport chain → increased ROS production and energy failure.

cards.q: What is proteostasis collapse in aging?
cards.a: Impaired protein quality control (chaperones, ubiquitin-proteasome system, autophagy) → accumulation of misfolded proteins (e.g., amyloid, tau).

cards.q: Role of IGF-1/insulin signaling in longevity?
cards.a: Reduced signaling (as in caloric restriction) activates FOXO transcription factors → ↑ stress resistance, autophagy, and lifespan.

cards.q: What is inflammaging?
cards.a: Chronic low-grade systemic inflammation in aging due to ↑ pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and senescent cell SASP.

cards.q: SASP — what does it stand for and its effect?
cards.a: Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype: Senescent cells secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, proteases, and growth factors → promotes aging and cancer.

cards.q: Age-related skin changes increasing infection and injury risk?
cards.a: Thinning of epidermis/dermis, ↓ collagen/elastin, ↓ subcutaneous fat, ↓ sweat/sebaceous glands → xerosis, fragility, pressure ulcers.

cards.q: Reproductive changes in aging males (andropause)?
cards.a: Gradual ↓ testosterone (~1%/year after 30), ↓ spermatogenesis, erectile dysfunction, reduced muscle mass/libido.

cards.q: Menopause: Hormonal change and clinical consequences?
cards.a: Ovarian failure → ↓ estrogen/progesterone, ↑ FSH/LH. Leads to hot flashes, osteoporosis, cardiovascular risk ↑, genitourinary syndrome.

cards.q: Most common endocrine disorder in elderly?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism (often subclinical); also high prevalence of diabetes type 2 and osteoporosis.

cards.q: Age-related change in glucose tolerance?
cards.a: Impaired due to ↑ insulin resistance, ↓ β-cell function, and reduced physical activity → higher prevalence of type 2 diabetes.

cards.q: What is sarcopenia? Diagnostic criteria (high-yield)?
cards.a: Progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass + strength. Low muscle mass + low grip strength or slow gait speed.

cards.q: Osteoporosis vs osteomalacia in elderly?
cards.a: Osteoporosis: ↓ bone mass, normal mineralization. Osteomalacia: defective mineralization (often vitamin D deficiency).

cards.q: Most common cause of hip fracture in elderly?
cards.a: Osteoporosis + fall. Intracapsular (femoral neck) or extracapsular (intertrochanteric).

cards.q: Age-related immune change: Thymic involution effect?
cards.a: ↓ Thymic output of naive T cells → reduced response to new antigens and vaccines.

cards.q: Why do elderly have poorer response to vaccines?
cards.a: Immunosenescence: ↓ naive lymphocytes, chronic inflammation, reduced antigen presentation, and lower antibody affinity.

cards.q: Most common infection in long-term care facilities?
cards.a: Urinary tract infection (UTI), followed by pneumonia and skin/soft tissue infections.

cards.q: Delirium vs dementia: Onset and attention?
cards.a: Delirium: Acute onset, fluctuating, impaired attention. Dementia: Insidious, progressive, relatively preserved attention early.

cards.q: Most common reversible cause of dementia-like symptoms in elderly?
cards.a: Depression ('pseudodementia'), medications, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, normal pressure hydrocephalus.

cards.q: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) classic triad?
cards.a: Wet (urinary incontinence), Wobbly (gait apraxia/magnetic gait), Wacky (dementia). Treatable with VP shunt.

cards.q: Lewy body dementia: Key features vs Alzheimer?
cards.a: Visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, extreme sensitivity to antipsychotics.

cards.q: Frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease): Early prominent feature?
cards.a: Personality/behavior changes or language impairment (primary progressive aphasia) with relative sparing of memory early on.

cards.q: Vascular (multi-infarct) dementia: Risk factors and course?
cards.a: Hypertension, diabetes, smoking, prior strokes. Stepwise cognitive decline with focal neurological signs.

cards.q: What is the Clock Drawing Test used for in geriatrics?
cards.a: Screening for visuospatial and executive dysfunction (useful in Alzheimer and vascular dementia).

cards.q: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score suggestive of dementia?
cards.a: ≤23/30 (adjust for education/age). MoCA is more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment.

cards.q: Pharmacologic treatment of Alzheimer disease (first-line)?
cards.a: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) + memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate-severe.

cards.q: Beers Criteria: Why avoid anticholinergics in elderly?
cards.a: High risk of confusion, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and delirium.

cards.q: Why avoid benzodiazepines in elderly (high-yield)?
cards.a: Increased risk of falls, fractures, cognitive impairment, delirium, and dependence.

cards.q: Most common adverse drug reaction in elderly?
cards.a: Falls and delirium (often due to polypharmacy, sedatives, antihypertensives, anticholinergics).

cards.q: Age-related change in pharmacokinetics: Protein binding?
cards.a: ↓ Albumin (especially in illness/malnutrition) → increased free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs (e.g., warfarin, phenytoin).

cards.q: What is the START/STOPP criteria used for?
cards.a: Screening tool to optimize prescribing in older adults (START = start indicated meds, STOPP = stop potentially inappropriate).

cards.q: Leading cause of blindness in elderly in developed countries?
cards.a: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

cards.q: Presbyopia: Cause and age of onset?
cards.a: Loss of lens elasticity → impaired near vision. Begins around age 40–45.

cards.q: Most common cause of conductive hearing loss in elderly?
cards.a: Cerumen impaction (reversible).

cards.q: Physiological change in basal metabolic rate with aging?
cards.a: Decreases due to loss of lean body mass (sarcopenia).

cards.q: Why is vitamin D deficiency common in elderly?
cards.a: ↓ Skin synthesis (less 7-dehydrocholesterol), ↓ sun exposure, ↓ dietary intake, ↓ renal 1α-hydroxylation.

cards.q: Most common nutritional deficiency in elderly?
cards.a: Vitamin D, followed by B12, folate, and protein-calorie malnutrition.

cards.q: What is the Mediterranean diet associated with in aging?
cards.a: Reduced cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, and overall mortality.

cards.q: Role of exercise in preventing frailty?
cards.a: Resistance + aerobic training improves muscle mass, strength, balance, and reduces fall risk.

cards.q: What is the Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA)?
cards.a: Multidimensional evaluation of medical, functional, psychological, and social issues in frail elderly to optimize care.

cards.q: Ethical principle most relevant when discussing goals of care in terminal elderly patients?
cards.a: Autonomy — respect patient wishes via advance directives.

cards.q: What is the most common reason for institutionalization of elderly?
cards.a: Dementia (especially when behavioral issues or caregiver burnout occur).

cards.q: Age-related change in thermoregulation?
cards.a: Impaired (↓ shivering, ↓ sweat response) → higher risk of hypothermia and hyperthermia.

cards.q: Why is aspiration pneumonia common in elderly?
cards.a: ↓ Cough/gag reflex, dysphagia (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), poor dentition, supine positioning.

cards.q: Parkinson disease dementia vs Lewy body dementia timing?
cards.a: Parkinson disease dementia: Motor symptoms ≥1 year before dementia. Lewy body: Dementia early or concurrent with parkinsonism.

cards.q: What malignancy screening is recommended up to what age generally?
cards.a: Individualized; colorectal up to 75–85, breast/mammogram up to 74–75 in average risk (USPSTF).

cards.q: Most important modifiable risk factor for healthy aging?
cards.a: Smoking cessation, followed by physical activity and blood pressure control.

cards.q: What is the concept of 'compression of morbidity'?
cards.a: Delaying the onset of chronic illness so that disability occupies a smaller proportion of total lifespan.

cards.q: Senile (actinic) purpura: Cause?
cards.a: Dermal connective tissue atrophy and fragile blood vessels → easy bruising on forearms/hands.

cards.q: What is the role of senescent cells in aging and disease?
cards.a: They accumulate and secrete SASP (pro-inflammatory factors) → chronic inflammation, tissue dysfunction, and promotion of cancer and degenerative diseases.

cards.q: Name two experimental 'senolytic' agents and their goal.
cards.a: Dasatinib + Quercetin (D+Q). They selectively clear senescent cells to reduce inflammation and improve tissue function.

cards.q: Age-related change in hematopoietic system?
cards.a: ↓ Bone marrow cellularity, ↓ lymphoid progenitors, clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) → increased risk of MDS, leukemia, and anemia.

cards.q: Most common cause of anemia in elderly?
cards.a: Anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, followed by iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, and renal disease.

cards.q: Why is B12 deficiency common in elderly?
cards.a: Atrophic gastritis → ↓ intrinsic factor and acid secretion → impaired absorption.

cards.q: What is the most common solid tumor in men over 70?
cards.a: Prostate cancer.

cards.q: Most common cause of cancer death in elderly (both sexes)?
cards.a: Lung cancer.

cards.q: Herpes zoster (shingles) risk in elderly? Prevention?
cards.a: Reactivation of VZV due to immunosenescence. Prevention: Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) recommended ≥50 years.

cards.q: Pneumococcal vaccination in elderly: Preferred regimen?
cards.a: PCV20 alone or PCV15 followed by PPSV23. Strong recommendation ≥65 years.

cards.q: Physiological change in autonomic nervous system with aging?
cards.a: ↓ Baroreceptor sensitivity and β-adrenergic responsiveness → orthostatic hypotension and blunted heart rate response.

cards.q: What is dysphagia in elderly often due to?
cards.a: Stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, esophageal motility disorders, or medication-induced (pill esophagitis).

cards.q: Fecal incontinence in elderly: Most common cause?
cards.a: Overflow incontinence from fecal impaction (often due to constipation).

cards.q: Urinary incontinence types in elderly women: Most common?
cards.a: Stress incontinence (urethral hypermobility) and urge incontinence (overactive bladder).

cards.q: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: Classic imaging finding?
cards.a: Ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cortical atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo is not the case).

cards.q: What drug class worsens cognition and increases fall risk in elderly?
cards.a: Anticholinergics (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclic antidepressants).

cards.q: Why avoid first-generation antihistamines in elderly?
cards.a: Strong anticholinergic effects → confusion, delirium, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention.

cards.q: Most common drug-induced cause of delirium in hospitalized elderly?
cards.a: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and opioids.

cards.q: What is the CHADS2-VASc score used for in elderly?
cards.a: Stroke risk stratification in atrial fibrillation to guide anticoagulation decision.

cards.q: Why is anticoagulation decision complex in elderly with AF?
cards.a: High stroke risk but also high bleeding risk (HAS-BLED score); fall risk must be weighed.

cards.q: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD): Wet vs dry?
cards.a: Dry (atrophic): Drusen, geographic atrophy (more common). Wet (neovascular): Choroidal neovascularization, treated with anti-VEGF.

cards.q: Glaucoma screening in elderly: Preferred test?
cards.a: Tonometry (intraocular pressure) + fundoscopy/optic nerve evaluation.

cards.q: Cataract surgery indication in elderly?
cards.a: Visual impairment affecting daily function/quality of life.

cards.q: Most common cause of chronic kidney disease in elderly?
cards.a: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: Why adjust dosing of renally cleared drugs in elderly even with normal serum creatinine?
cards.a: GFR declines with age while creatinine production decreases due to sarcopenia.

cards.q: What is the leading preventable cause of disability in elderly?
cards.a: Falls.

cards.q: Components of a multifactorial fall prevention program?
cards.a: Medication review, balance/gait training, vitamin D supplementation, home safety assessment, management of orthostasis/vision.

cards.q: Hip fracture in elderly: Most important predictor of 1-year mortality?
cards.a: Pre-fracture functional status and comorbidities (mortality ~20–30% at 1 year).

cards.q: What is the concept of 'de-prescribing' in geriatrics?
cards.a: Systematic process of tapering or stopping medications where harms outweigh benefits.

cards.q: Polypharmacy definition and major consequence?
cards.a: ≥5 medications. Major consequence: Increased adverse drug events, drug interactions, falls, cognitive impairment, and hospitalization.

cards.q: Malnutrition screening tool commonly used in elderly?
cards.a: Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) or MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool).

cards.q: Why is protein requirement higher in elderly?
cards.a: Anabolic resistance (reduced muscle protein synthesis response) → recommended 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day (higher in illness).

cards.q: What is the Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet?
cards.a: Hybrid diet shown to slow cognitive decline and reduce Alzheimer risk.

cards.q: Role of physical activity in healthy aging?
cards.a: Reduces sarcopenia, improves cognition, cardiovascular health, mood, and reduces frailty and falls.

cards.q: What is 'successful aging' according to Rowe and Kahn?
cards.a: Low probability of disease/disability + high cognitive and physical function + active engagement with life.

cards.q: Ethical issue in elderly care: Therapeutic nihilism?
cards.a: Under-treatment of elderly patients assuming poor prognosis or limited benefit.

cards.q: When can a physician override an elderly patient's refusal of treatment?
cards.a: Only if patient lacks decision-making capacity and no valid advance directive exists.

cards.q: What is the 'Do Not Hospitalize' (DNH) order?
cards.a: Directive for nursing home residents preferring comfort care over hospital transfer.

cards.q: Hospice vs palliative care: Key difference?
cards.a: Hospice: For terminal illness with ≤6 months prognosis, focuses on comfort (no curative intent). Palliative: Can be concurrent with curative treatment.

cards.q: Most common psychiatric disorder in elderly?
cards.a: Depression (often underdiagnosed).

cards.q: Geriatric depression scale (GDS): Advantage?
cards.a: Validated screening tool for depression in elderly that avoids somatic symptoms.

cards.q: Pseudodementia: Key feature?
cards.a: Depression mimicking dementia. Often reversible with antidepressant treatment; patients usually complain of memory loss.

cards.q: REM sleep behavior disorder: Strong association?
cards.a: Synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy).

cards.q: Age-related change in circadian rhythm?
cards.a: Advanced sleep phase syndrome: Earlier sleep and wake times.

cards.q: What is sundowning and management?
cards.a: Increased agitation/confusion in late afternoon/evening in dementia patients. Management: Consistent routine, light exposure, avoid overstimulation.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in elderly with advanced dementia?
cards.a: Pneumonia (aspiration).

cards.q: What is the 'DNR' discussion timing in elderly with frailty?
cards.a: Early goals-of-care discussion, especially before acute illness or surgery.

cards.q: Elder abuse: Most common type?
cards.a: Neglect, followed by psychological and financial abuse.

cards.q: Physician mandatory reporting for elder abuse?
cards.a: Required in most states when reasonable suspicion exists.

cards.q: What is the 'Silver Tsunami'?
cards.a: Rapid increase in elderly population (baby boomers) straining healthcare systems.

cards.q: What is the evolutionary theory of aging (antagonistic pleiotropy)?
cards.a: Genes that confer advantage early in life (reproduction) may have deleterious effects later → natural selection favors early benefits despite late costs.

cards.q: Disposable soma theory of aging?
cards.a: Organism allocates limited resources between reproduction and somatic maintenance; aging results from prioritizing reproduction over long-term repair.

cards.q: Role of AMPK in aging and caloric restriction?
cards.a: Energy sensor activated by low ATP → promotes autophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, and longevity pathways.

cards.q: What is the role of NAD+ decline in aging?
cards.a: Reduced NAD+ levels impair sirtuin activity, DNA repair (PARP), and mitochondrial function → accelerated aging.

cards.q: Hallmarks of aging: List the original 9 (López-Otín).
cards.a: Genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in adults over 85?
cards.a: Heart disease, followed by cancer, stroke, and Alzheimer disease.

cards.q: Age-related cardiovascular change: Aortic stiffness effect?
cards.a: Isolated systolic hypertension and increased pulse pressure.

cards.q: Why is orthostatic hypotension more common in elderly?
cards.a: Impaired baroreflex, reduced vascular compliance, decreased renin-angiotensin response, and polypharmacy.

cards.q: Respiratory change in elderly increasing pneumonia risk?
cards.a: ↓ Mucociliary clearance, ↓ cough reflex, ↓ respiratory muscle strength, and ↑ residual volume.

cards.q: GI change leading to constipation in elderly?
cards.a: Decreased colonic motility, reduced fluid intake, medications (opioids, anticholinergics), and immobility.

cards.q: What is the most common endocrine tumor in elderly?
cards.a: Thyroid nodules (most are benign).

cards.q: Postmenopausal osteoporosis: Primary mechanism?
cards.a: Estrogen deficiency → increased RANKL → enhanced osteoclast activity and bone resorption.

cards.q: Paget disease of bone: Classic lab finding?
cards.a: Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate.

cards.q: Most common primary brain tumor in elderly?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme.

cards.q: Why are elderly more susceptible to drug-induced hyponatremia?
cards.a: Reduced renal free water excretion + common use of thiazides, SSRIs, and carbamazepine.

cards.q: Beers Criteria: Why avoid sliding-scale insulin in elderly?
cards.a: High risk of hypoglycemia without improving glycemic control.

cards.q: What is the strongest predictor of functional decline in elderly?
cards.a: Frailty.

cards.q: Fried Frailty Phenotype: 5 criteria?
cards.a: Unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness (grip strength), slow walking speed, low physical activity.

cards.q: What is the Clinical Frailty Scale used for?
cards.a: Quick bedside assessment of frailty severity and prognosis.

cards.q: Most effective intervention to reduce falls in community-dwelling elderly?
cards.a: Multifactorial exercise programs (balance, strength, gait training).

cards.q: Vitamin D supplementation in elderly: Benefit?
cards.a: Reduces fall risk and hip fracture risk when combined with calcium.

cards.q: What is the concept of 'homeostenosis'?
cards.a: Reduced physiological reserve in multiple organ systems with aging → decreased ability to maintain homeostasis under stress.

cards.q: Why is fever less common in elderly infections?
cards.a: Blunted febrile response due to altered hypothalamic set point and reduced cytokine production.

cards.q: Atypical presentation of pneumonia in elderly?
cards.a: Confusion, functional decline, anorexia, or falls rather than classic fever/cough.

cards.q: Most common valvular disease in elderly?
cards.a: Aortic stenosis (calcific degenerative).

cards.q: Why is digoxin toxicity more common in elderly?
cards.a: Reduced renal clearance and lower lean body mass → higher serum levels.

cards.q: What is the leading iatrogenic cause of morbidity in hospitalized elderly?
cards.a: Delirium.

cards.q: CAM tool: Used for diagnosis of what?
cards.a: Confusion Assessment Method — screening for delirium.

cards.q: Prevention of delirium in hospitalized elderly: Key strategies?
cards.a: Orientation, early mobilization, sleep hygiene, hydration, avoid restraints and high-risk medications.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of reversible cognitive impairment in elderly?
cards.a: Medication side effects.

cards.q: Advance care planning: Difference between living will and POLST?
cards.a: Living will: general wishes. POLST: actionable medical orders for seriously ill patients.

cards.q: Ethical principle of 'substituted judgment'?
cards.a: Surrogate decides based on what the patient would have wanted if competent.

cards.q: When is artificial nutrition ethically withholdable in advanced dementia?
cards.a: When it does not improve quality of life or comfort (per patient values/goals).

cards.q: Elder self-neglect: Most common form of elder mistreatment?
cards.a: Yes — often associated with dementia, depression, or substance use.

cards.q: What is the '4 Ms' framework in Age-Friendly Health Systems?
cards.a: What Matters, Medications, Mentation, Mobility.

cards.q: Compression of morbidity vs. expansion of morbidity?
cards.a: Compression: shorter period of disability at end of life. Expansion: longer period of disability.

cards.q: Most important social determinant of healthy aging?
cards.a: Social engagement and support networks.

cards.q: Why is loneliness a major health risk in elderly?
cards.a: Equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes/day in mortality risk; increases dementia, heart disease, and depression.

cards.q: What is 'ageism' in healthcare?
cards.a: Stereotyping or discrimination against individuals based on age → leads to undertreatment or poor communication.

cards.q: Recommended physical activity for older adults (CDC)?
cards.a: 150 min moderate aerobic + 2 days strength training + balance exercises weekly.

cards.q: Caloric restriction mimetics: Examples?
cards.a: Metformin, rapamycin, resveratrol — activate similar pathways as caloric restriction.

cards.q: What is the role of klotho gene in aging?
cards.a: Klotho protein deficiency accelerates aging; overexpression extends lifespan in mice.

cards.q: Telomerase gene therapy in aging research: Potential benefit?
cards.a: May delay telomere shortening and some age-related diseases (still experimental).

cards.q: Most promising current intervention for healthy aging in humans?
cards.a: Exercise combined with optimal nutrition and social engagement.

cards.q: What is the 'geriatric 5Ms' model?
cards.a: Mobility, Medications, Mind (mentation), Multiccomplexity, Matters Most (what matters to the patient).

cards.q: Final common pathway of many age-related diseases?
cards.a: Chronic inflammation (inflammaging) and cellular senescence.

cards.q: What are the four modes of Mendelian inheritance?
cards.a:
• 1. Autosomal Dominant
  • 2. Autosomal Recessive
  • 3. X-linked Dominant
  • 4. X-linked Recessive

cards.q: Key features of Autosomal Dominant inheritance?
cards.a:
• • Appears in every generation
  • • Male = Female affected
  • • 50% chance to offspring
  • • Often structural proteins or gain-of-function

cards.q: Key features of Autosomal Recessive inheritance?
cards.a:
• • Skips generations
  • • Often enzyme deficiencies
  • • 25% affected, 50% carriers
  • • More common in consanguinity

cards.q: Key features of X-linked Recessive inheritance?
cards.a:
• • More males affected
  • • No male-to-male transmission
  • • All daughters of affected male are carriers
  • • Examples: Hemophilia A/B, Duchenne MD, G6PD

cards.q: Key features of X-linked Dominant inheritance?
cards.a:
• • More females affected
  • • No male-to-male transmission
  • • Affected males transmit to all daughters
  • • Example: Hypophosphatemic rickets

cards.q: What is incomplete penetrance? Give example.
