cards.a: Genotype present but phenotype not expressed. Example: Hereditary Breast-Ovarian Cancer (BRCA1/2) — not all carriers develop cancer.

cards.q: What is variable expressivity? Give example.
cards.a: Different severity in individuals with same genotype. Example: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).

cards.q: What is anticipation? In which disorders is it seen?
cards.a:
• Worsening severity/earlier onset in successive generations due to trinucleotide repeat expansion.
  • Seen in: Huntington, Myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X.

cards.q: What is genomic imprinting? Give examples.
cards.a:
• Gene expression depends on parent of origin.
  • • Prader-Willi: paternal deletion (15q)
  • • Angelman: maternal deletion (15q)

cards.q: What is uniparental disomy (UPD)?
cards.a: Both chromosomes of a pair inherited from one parent. Can cause imprinting disorders (e.g., maternal UPD 15 → Prader-Willi).

cards.q: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) — most common cause?
cards.a: Meiotic nondisjunction (95%) — usually maternal meiosis I. Risk ↑ with advanced maternal age.

cards.q: Cardiac defect most common in Down syndrome?
cards.a: Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD / endocardial cushion defect)

cards.q: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) — classic findings?
cards.a: Rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists, micrognathia, low-set ears, congenital heart disease, severe ID. Most die in first year.

cards.q: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) — classic findings?
cards.a: Cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly, severe ID, congenital heart disease.

cards.q: What is the genetic cause of Fragile X syndrome?
cards.a: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in FMR1 gene on X chromosome → hypermethylation and silencing.

cards.q: Classic physical features of Fragile X syndrome?
cards.a: Long face, large everted ears, macroorchidism (post-puberty), mitral valve prolapse, intellectual disability, autism spectrum features.

cards.q: What is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability?
cards.a: Fragile X syndrome (in males).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Cystic Fibrosis?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — mutation in CFTR gene (most common: ΔF508) on chromosome 7.

cards.q: What is the most common mutation in CF and its effect?
cards.a: ΔF508 — misfolded protein → defective trafficking to cell membrane (Class II mutation).

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for Cystic Fibrosis?
cards.a: Sweat chloride test (>60 mmol/L). Confirm with CFTR genotyping.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Phenylketonuria (PKU)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) or tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor.

cards.q: Classic untreated presentation of PKU?
cards.a: Musty body odor, fair skin/hair, eczema, intellectual disability, seizures. Musty odor from phenylacetic acid.

cards.q: Treatment of classic PKU?
cards.a: Phenylalanine-restricted diet + tyrosine supplementation. Avoid aspartame.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Tay-Sachs disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — deficiency of β-hexosaminidase A → GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

cards.q: Classic findings in Tay-Sachs?
cards.a: Cherry-red spot on macula, progressive neurodegeneration, developmental regression, death by age 4–5. Common in Ashkenazi Jews.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Gaucher disease (most common lysosomal storage disease)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Huntington disease?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in Huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Myotonic dystrophy type 1?
cards.a: CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene on chromosome 19 (autosomal dominant).

cards.q: What is the genetic cause of Prader-Willi syndrome?
cards.a: Lack of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-13 (deletion of paternal copy or maternal UPD).

cards.q: Classic features of Prader-Willi syndrome?
cards.a: Hypotonia & poor feeding in infancy → hyperphagia & obesity in childhood, short stature, hypogonadism, mild-moderate ID.

cards.q: Classic features of Angelman syndrome?
cards.a: “Happy puppet” — severe ID, inappropriate laughter, ataxia, seizures, absent speech.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — frameshift mutation/deletion in Dystrophin gene (Xp21).

cards.q: What is Gower sign?
cards.a: Patient uses hands to “walk up” their legs when rising from floor — classic in Duchenne MD.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Marfan syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutation in FBN1 gene (fibrillin-1) on chromosome 15.

cards.q: Classic cardiovascular complication in Marfan syndrome?
cards.a: Aortic root dilation → aneurysm and dissection (leading cause of death).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Familial Hypercholesterolemia?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutation in LDL receptor gene (most common).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Hemochromatosis (classic form)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — HFE gene mutation (C282Y) on chromosome 6 → increased intestinal iron absorption.

cards.q: What is Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
cards.a: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (allele frequencies remain constant in a population without evolutionary forces).

cards.q: What are the assumptions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
cards.a: No mutation, no selection, no migration, random mating, large population size.

cards.q: What is linkage disequilibrium?
cards.a: Non-random association of alleles at different loci (occurs when loci are close on same chromosome).

cards.q: What is a missense mutation?
cards.a: Single nucleotide change that results in a different amino acid (e.g., sickle cell: Glu → Val).

cards.q: What is a nonsense mutation?
cards.a: Point mutation that creates a premature stop codon → truncated protein.

cards.q: What is a frameshift mutation?
cards.a: Insertion or deletion of nucleotides not divisible by 3 → altered reading frame, usually nonfunctional protein.

cards.q: What is a silent mutation?
cards.a: Nucleotide change that does not change the amino acid (due to degeneracy of genetic code).

cards.q: What is a trinucleotide repeat disorder with anticipation in males?
cards.a: Fragile X syndrome (CGG repeats) — Sherman paradox (more severe when transmitted by mother).

cards.q: What is Lyonization (X-inactivation)?
cards.a: Random inactivation of one X chromosome in females → Barr body. Explains variable expression in female carriers of X-linked disorders.

cards.q: What is mitochondrial inheritance pattern?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance. All offspring of affected mother can be affected; no male-to-offspring transmission. Example: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON).

cards.q: What is a Robertsonian translocation?
cards.a: Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes (13,14,15,21,22) at centromere. Carrier has 45 chromosomes but is phenotypically normal. Increased risk of unbalanced offspring (e.g., translocation Down syndrome).

cards.q: Most common chromosomal cause of spontaneous abortion?
cards.a: Trisomy 16 (most common), followed by other trisomies and monosomy X.

cards.q: What is the genetic mechanism of Cri-du-chat syndrome?
cards.a: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).

cards.q: Classic cry in Cri-du-chat syndrome?
cards.a: High-pitched, cat-like cry.

cards.q: What is the most common inherited cause of mental retardation in males?
cards.a: Fragile X syndrome

cards.q: What is the second most common cause of genetic intellectual disability after Down syndrome?
cards.a: Fragile X syndrome

cards.q: What is the genetic basis of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
cards.a: Imprinting defect at chromosome 11p15 (paternal overexpression of IGF2)

cards.q: Classic features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
cards.a: Macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, Wilms tumor risk

cards.q: What is the genetic mechanism of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome?
cards.a: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 4p

cards.q: What is the genetic mechanism of DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion)?
cards.a: Microdeletion at 22q11.2 (TBX1 gene)

cards.q: CATCH-22 mnemonic for 22q11.2 deletion syndrome?
cards.a: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia (22q11)

cards.q: What is the most common microdeletion syndrome?
cards.a: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge / Velocardiofacial)

cards.q: What is the karyotype in Klinefelter syndrome?
Classic presentation of Klinefelter syndrome?
cards.a: Tall male, gynecomastia, small firm testes, azoospermia, infertility, mild intellectual disability

cards.q: What is the karyotype in Turner syndrome?
cards.a: 45,XO (most common)

cards.q: Classic features of Turner syndrome?
cards.a: Short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, coarctation of aorta, streak ovaries, primary amenorrhea

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Triple X syndrome?
What is the genetic defect in XYY syndrome?
cards.a: 47,XYY — tall stature, acne, normal fertility, possible behavioral issues

cards.q: What is a balanced translocation carrier?
cards.a: Phenotypically normal but increased risk of unbalanced gametes and offspring with chromosomal abnormalities

cards.q: What is the most common Robertsonian translocation?
What is the risk of Down syndrome in a carrier of t(14;21) Robertsonian translocation?
cards.a: Approximately 10–15% (higher if maternal carrier)

cards.q: What is a contiguous gene syndrome?
cards.a: Phenotype caused by deletion or duplication of multiple adjacent genes (e.g., DiGeorge, Williams syndrome)

cards.q: What is Williams syndrome genetic cause?
cards.a: Microdeletion at 7q11.23 (includes elastin gene)

cards.q: Classic features of Williams syndrome?
cards.a: Elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, cocktail party personality, intellectual disability

cards.q: What is the genetic test of choice for diagnosing microdeletion syndromes?
cards.a: FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) or Chromosomal Microarray (CMA)

cards.q: What is chromosomal microarray (CMA) best used for?
cards.a: Detection of copy number variants (deletions/duplications) not visible on standard karyotype

cards.q: What is the difference between karyotyping and FISH?
cards.a: Karyotype: detects large chromosomal abnormalities (>5 Mb). FISH: detects specific smaller deletions/duplications using fluorescent probes

cards.q: What is PCR used for in genetics?
cards.a: Amplification of specific DNA segments (e.g., for trinucleotide repeat disorders, cystic fibrosis genotyping)

cards.q: What is Southern blot used for?
cards.a: Detection of large DNA fragments, trinucleotide repeats (e.g., Fragile X, Myotonic dystrophy)

cards.q: What is the principle of Sanger sequencing?
cards.a: Chain-termination method using dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs)

cards.q: What is next-generation sequencing (NGS) primarily used for?
cards.a: Whole exome or whole genome sequencing — high throughput, identifies point mutations and small indels

cards.q: What is a loss-of-function mutation?
cards.a: Mutation that leads to reduced or absent protein function (usually recessive)

cards.q: What is a gain-of-function mutation?
cards.a: Mutation that gives the protein new or enhanced activity (often dominant)

cards.q: What are oncogenes?
cards.a: Mutated proto-oncogenes that promote cell proliferation (gain-of-function). Need only one mutated copy (dominant)

cards.q: What are tumor suppressor genes?
cards.a: Genes that inhibit cell proliferation. Both copies must be inactivated (Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis)

cards.q: Give examples of proto-oncogenes turned oncogenes.
cards.a: ras (pancreatic, colon cancer), myc (Burkitt lymphoma), HER2/neu (breast cancer)

cards.q: Give examples of tumor suppressor genes.
cards.a: RB1 (retinoblastoma), TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), APC (FAP), BRCA1/2

cards.q: What is Li-Fraumeni syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant germline TP53 mutation → multiple cancers at young age (sarcomas, breast, brain, leukemia)

cards.q: What is the inheritance and defect in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutation in APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC / Lynch syndrome)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — defect in DNA mismatch repair genes (MSH2, MLH1, etc.)

cards.q: What cancers are increased in Lynch syndrome?
cards.a: Colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial

cards.q: What is microsatellite instability (MSI)?
cards.a: Seen in tumors with defective mismatch repair (Lynch syndrome)

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutation in NF1 gene (tumor suppressor) on chromosome 17

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for NF1 (need 2 or more)?
cards.a: ≥6 café-au-lait spots, ≥2 neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, bony lesion, first-degree relative

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in NF2?
cards.a: Mutation in NF2 (merlin) gene on chromosome 22 → bilateral acoustic schwannomas, meningiomas

cards.q: What is pharmacogenetics?
cards.a: Study of how genetic variations affect drug response (e.g., CYP450 polymorphisms)

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of CYP2D6 poor metabolizer?
cards.a: Increased risk of toxicity with codeine, tamoxifen, antidepressants (cannot convert to active form or clear drug)

cards.q: What is G6PD deficiency inheritance and trigger?
cards.a: X-linked recessive. Triggers: fava beans, primaquine, sulfa drugs, infections → hemolytic anemia

cards.q: What is the genetic basis of Warfarin sensitivity?
cards.a: Polymorphisms in VKORC1 and CYP2C9 genes → lower dose requirement

cards.q: What is multifactorial inheritance?
cards.a: Interaction of multiple genes + environment. Examples: Neural tube defects, diabetes type 2, hypertension, schizophrenia

cards.q: What is the recurrence risk pattern in multifactorial diseases?
cards.a: Higher if more relatives affected, more severe in proband, or proband is of the less commonly affected sex

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Wilson disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — mutation in ATP7B gene (copper transport) on chromosome 13

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — mutation in SERPINA1 gene on chromosome 14 (PiZZ genotype worst)

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in hereditary spherocytosis?
cards.a: Mutations in genes encoding red cell membrane proteins (ankyrin, spectrin, band 3)

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Gilbert syndrome?
cards.a: Mild deficiency of UGT1A1 (glucuronyl transferase) → unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, benign

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Crigler-Najjar syndrome Type 1?
cards.a: Complete absence of UGT1A1 → severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, kernicterus risk

cards.q: What is heteroplasmy in mitochondrial diseases?
cards.a: Mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA within a cell. Explains variable expression

cards.q: What is the threshold effect in mitochondrial inheritance?
cards.a: Disease manifests only when mutant mtDNA exceeds a certain percentage in tissues

cards.q: Give examples of mitochondrial diseases.
cards.a: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), MELAS, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre syndrome

cards.q: What is the genetic mechanism of Prader-Willi vs Angelman (summary)?
cards.a:
• Prader-Willi: loss of paternal 15q11-13 genes
  • Angelman: loss of maternal UBE3A gene at 15q11-13

cards.q: What is the inheritance and defect in Hereditary Spherocytosis?
cards.a: Usually autosomal dominant — mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, or band 3. Osmotic fragility test positive.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Familial Hypercholesterolemia?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — LDL receptor mutation (most common).

cards.q: What is the inheritance and defect in Hemochromatosis (classic)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — HFE gene (C282Y) mutation on chromosome 6.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Wilson disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — ATP7B gene mutation (copper transporter).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — SERPINA1 gene (PiZZ genotype most severe).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Gilbert syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive (mild) or dominant — reduced UGT1A1 activity.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Crigler-Najjar Type 1?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — complete UGT1A1 deficiency.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — HGPRT deficiency → hyperuricemia, self-mutilation, gout.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Fabry disease?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — α-galactosidase A deficiency → angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, renal failure.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Hunter syndrome (MPS II)?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency (milder than Hurler).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Hurler syndrome (MPS I)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — α-L-iduronidase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Pompe disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — acid α-glucosidase deficiency → cardiomegaly, hypotonia.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of McArdle disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Type V GSD).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Von Gierke disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Type I GSD).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Galactosemia (classic)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Hereditary Fructose Intolerance?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — aldolase B deficiency.

cards.q: What is Hardy-Weinberg equation for allele frequencies?
cards.a:
• p + q = 1
  • p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (p = dominant allele frequency, q = recessive)

cards.q: How do you calculate carrier frequency for autosomal recessive disease?
cards.a: If disease incidence = q², then carrier frequency ≈ 2pq (≈ 2q if q is small).

cards.q: What does a high inbreeding coefficient (F) increase?
cards.a: Homozygosity for rare recessive alleles → higher incidence of autosomal recessive diseases.

cards.q: What is founder effect?
cards.a: High frequency of a rare allele in a population descended from a small number of ancestors (e.g., Tay-Sachs in Ashkenazi Jews).

cards.q: What is genetic drift?
cards.a: Random change in allele frequencies, more pronounced in small populations.

cards.q: What is the bottleneck effect?
cards.a: Sharp reduction in population size → loss of genetic variation (e.g., cheetahs).

cards.q: What is the difference between penetrance and expressivity?
cards.a:
• Penetrance: % of genotype carriers who show phenotype.
  • Expressivity: degree/severity of phenotype in those who express it.

cards.q: What is pleiotropy?
cards.a: One gene influences multiple seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits (e.g., PKU, Marfan).

cards.q: What is locus heterogeneity?
cards.a: Same phenotype caused by mutations in different genes (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa).

cards.q: What is allelic heterogeneity?
cards.a: Different mutations in the same gene cause the same phenotype (e.g., CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis).

cards.q: What is anticipation and in which disorders is it prominent?
cards.a: Increasing severity/earlier onset in successive generations due to trinucleotide repeat expansion. Seen in Huntington, Myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X.

cards.q: What is a dominant negative mutation?
cards.a: Mutant protein interferes with the function of the wild-type protein (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta).

cards.q: What is haploinsufficiency?
cards.a: Loss of one functional copy of a gene is not enough for normal function (often causes dominant disorders).

cards.q: What is the two-hit hypothesis (Knudson)?
cards.a: Both alleles of a tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated for tumor formation (retinoblastoma, Wilms tumor).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Retinoblastoma?
cards.a: Mutation in RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Retinoblastoma (familial form)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance.

cards.q: What cancers are increased in Li-Fraumeni syndrome?
cards.a: Sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, adrenocortical carcinoma (TP53 mutation).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Xeroderma Pigmentosum?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — defective nucleotide excision repair → extreme UV sensitivity and skin cancers.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Ataxia-Telangiectasia?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — ATM gene (DNA repair) defect.

cards.q: What is Bloom syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — BLM gene (DNA helicase) → photosensitivity, short stature, increased cancer risk.

cards.q: What is Fanconi anemia?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive (mostly) — defective DNA cross-link repair → pancytopenia, thumb/radius abnormalities, increased cancer risk.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Sickle Cell Disease?
cards.a: Point mutation in β-globin gene (Glu6Val) — HbS.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in β-Thalassemia major?
cards.a: Mutations in β-globin gene → reduced or absent β-chain synthesis.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in α-Thalassemia (Hb Bart’s hydrops fetalis)?
cards.a: Deletion of all four α-globin genes (—/—).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Hemophilia A?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — Factor VIII deficiency.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Hemophilia B?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — Factor IX deficiency.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in von Willebrand Disease (most common type)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (usually) — quantitative or qualitative defect in vWF.

cards.q: What is the genetic basis of ABO blood groups?
cards.a: Multiple alleles at a single locus on chromosome 9 (IA, IB, i).

cards.q: What is the Rh blood group inheritance?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant expression of D antigen.

cards.q: What is erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of newborn)?
cards.a: Rh-negative mother sensitized to Rh-positive fetus → anti-D IgG crosses placenta.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Chronic Granulomatous Disease?
cards.a: Most commonly X-linked — NADPH oxidase defect (CYBB gene).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Bruton agammaglobulinemia?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase) mutation.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — WASP gene mutation.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (X-linked form)?
cards.a: Mutation in common γ-chain of IL-2 receptor (IL2RG).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in ADA deficiency?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — adenosine deaminase deficiency (a cause of SCID).

cards.q: What HLA allele is strongly associated with Celiac disease?
cards.a: HLA-DQ2 and DQ8

cards.q: What HLA allele is strongly associated with Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: HLA-B27

cards.q: What HLA alleles are associated with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus?
cards.a: HLA-DR3 and DR4

cards.q: What is the genetic mechanism of imprinting in Prader-Willi syndrome?
cards.a: Loss of paternally expressed genes at 15q11-13.

cards.q: What gene is silenced in Angelman syndrome?
cards.a: UBE3A (maternally expressed in brain).

cards.q: What is DNA methylation’s role in epigenetics?
cards.a: Usually silences gene expression (CpG islands in promoters).

cards.q: What is histone acetylation’s effect on gene expression?
cards.a: Promotes transcription (loosens chromatin structure).

cards.q: What is the most common genetic cause of congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens?
cards.a: Cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutations)

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Kartagener syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — defective dynein arms → primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs inversus, bronchiectasis, infertility.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Polycystic Kidney Disease (adult form)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — PKD1 (chromosome 16) or PKD2 (chromosome 4).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Tuberous Sclerosis?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Somatic mutation in GNAQ gene.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Neurofibromatosis type 2?
cards.a: Mutation in NF2 (merlin) gene on chromosome 22.

cards.q: What is pharmacogenomic testing for before starting abacavir?
cards.a: HLA-B*5701 allele (risk of hypersensitivity reaction).

cards.q: What enzyme deficiency causes malignant hyperthermia susceptibility?
cards.a: Usually ryanodine receptor (RYR1) mutation (autosomal dominant).

cards.q: What is the genetic basis of Long QT syndrome (most common form)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutations in potassium channel genes (KCNQ1, KCNH2).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Brugada syndrome?
cards.a: Usually loss-of-function mutation in sodium channel (SCN5A).

cards.q: What is the recurrence risk for neural tube defects in subsequent pregnancies?
cards.a: 2–5% (higher if previous affected child). Prevent with high-dose folic acid.

cards.q: What is the most common genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
cards.a: Mutation in GJB2 (connexin 26) gene.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Osteogenesis Imperfecta (most common form)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — mutations in type I collagen genes (COL1A1 or COL1A2).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Achondroplasia?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant — gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (classical type)?
cards.a: Mutations in type V collagen genes.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Homocystinuria (classic form)?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — cystathionine β-synthase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Alkaptonuria?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency (ochronosis).

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Maple Syrup Urine Disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive — branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency?
cards.a: X-linked recessive — most common urea cycle disorder.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes (MELAS)?
cards.a: Maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance — MT-TL1 mutation.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers (MERRF)?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance — MT-TK mutation.

cards.q: What is heteroplasmy?
cards.a: Presence of both normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell/tissue → variable phenotypic expression in mitochondrial diseases.

cards.q: What is the threshold effect in mitochondrial disorders?
cards.a: Disease manifests only when the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds a tissue-specific threshold.

cards.q: What are the four main pharmacokinetic processes (ADME)?
cards.a:
• Absorption
  • Distribution
  • Metabolism
  • Excretion

cards.q: Bioavailability (F) definition and formula?
cards.a:
• Fraction of administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.
  • F = AUC_oral / AUC_IV

cards.q: What is the first-pass effect? Which routes avoid it?
cards.a: Metabolism of drug before reaching systemic circulation (mainly hepatic). Avoided by: sublingual, rectal (partial), IV, IM, transdermal, inhalation.

cards.q: Volume of distribution (Vd) formula and clinical meaning?
cards.a:
• Vd = Amount of drug in body / Plasma concentration
  • High Vd = extensive tissue distribution (lipophilic drugs). Low Vd = stays in plasma (hydrophilic).

cards.q: What does a low Vd (< 5 L) indicate?
cards.a: Drug is confined to plasma (e.g., large molecules, highly protein-bound drugs).

cards.q: Half-life (t½) formula?
cards.a: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Clearance (CL)

cards.q: Steady-state concentration is reached after how many half-lives?
cards.a: Approximately 4–5 half-lives (94–97% of steady state).

cards.q: Loading dose formula?
cards.a: Loading dose = Vd × Target concentration / F

cards.q: Maintenance dose formula?
cards.a: Maintenance dose = CL × Target concentration × Dosing interval / F

cards.q: Zero-order elimination — examples?
cards.a: Constant amount eliminated per unit time (saturation kinetics). Examples: Ethanol, Phenytoin (high dose), Aspirin (high dose), Theophylline.

cards.q: Phase I metabolism reactions?
cards.a: Oxidation, Reduction, Hydrolysis (usually by CYP450). Introduces or unmasks polar groups.

cards.q: Phase II metabolism reactions?
cards.a: Conjugation (Glucuronidation, Sulfation, Acetylation, Glutathione, Glycine). Makes drug more water-soluble.

cards.q: Most common CYP450 enzyme involved in drug metabolism?
cards.a: CYP3A4 (metabolizes ~50% of drugs).

cards.q: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (high-yield)?
cards.a: Carbamazepine, Rifampin, Phenytoin, St. John’s Wort, Phenobarbital (CRAP). Also smoking.

cards.q: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (high-yield)?
cards.a: Ketoconazole, Itraconazole, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin, Grapefruit juice, Ritonavir, Cobicistat.

cards.q: What is the therapeutic index?
cards.a: TI = TD50 / ED50 (or LD50/ED50). Higher TI = safer drug.

cards.q: What are competitive antagonists?
cards.a: Bind same site as agonist; can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration. Shift dose-response curve right (e.g., Naloxone at opioid receptors).

cards.q: What are non-competitive (irreversible) antagonists?
cards.a: Bind different site or covalently; cannot be overcome by increasing agonist. Decrease maximal response (Emax).

cards.q: Full agonist vs Partial agonist on dose-response curve?
cards.a: Full agonist: reaches 100% Emax. Partial agonist: reaches lower Emax even at full receptor occupancy.

cards.q: What is potency vs efficacy?
cards.a: Potency: dose required for effect (related to EC50). Efficacy: maximal effect achievable (Emax).

cards.q: Receptor types coupled to G-proteins (major families)?
cards.a: GPCR (7-transmembrane). Gs (↑cAMP), Gi (↓cAMP), Gq (↑IP3/DAG).

cards.q: Ion channel receptors — examples?
cards.a: Nicotinic ACh receptor, GABA-A, Glycine, 5-HT3.

cards.q: Enzyme-linked receptors — examples?
cards.a: Tyrosine kinase receptors (Insulin, EGF, PDGF), JAK-STAT (Cytokines), Guanylate cyclase (ANP, NO).

cards.q: Intracellular (nuclear) receptors — examples?
cards.a: Steroid hormones (Glucocorticoids, Estrogen, Testosterone), Thyroid hormone, Vitamin D, Retinoic acid.

cards.q: Most common mechanism of drug tolerance?
cards.a: Receptor downregulation or desensitization.

cards.q: Tachyphylaxis definition?
cards.a: Rapid development of tolerance after only a few doses (e.g., indirect sympathomimetics like amphetamine, nitrates).

cards.q: What is a prodrug? Give examples.
cards.a: Inactive compound converted to active metabolite. Examples: Codeine → Morphine, Enalapril → Enalaprilat, Levodopa.

cards.q: High-yield Phase II conjugation deficient in neonates?
cards.a: Glucuronidation (e.g., Gray baby syndrome with Chloramphenicol).

cards.q: Drugs highly extracted by liver (high first-pass)?
cards.a: Propranolol, Morphine, Nitroglycerin, Lidocaine.

cards.q: Drugs with high protein binding (>90%)?
cards.a: Warfarin, Phenytoin, Diazepam, Valproate, Aspirin.

cards.q: What displaces warfarin from albumin increasing its effect?
cards.a: Sulfa drugs, NSAIDs, Phenytoin, Valproate.

cards.q: Renal clearance formula?
cards.a: CL_renal = (U × V) / P (urine concentration × urine flow / plasma concentration).

cards.q: pH-dependent drug trapping — weak acids?
cards.a: Weak acids (e.g., Aspirin, Phenobarbital) are ionized (trapped) in alkaline urine → alkalinize urine for overdose.

cards.q: pH-dependent drug trapping — weak bases?
cards.a: Weak bases (e.g., Amphetamines) are ionized in acidic urine → acidify urine for overdose.

cards.q: What is the most common adverse drug reaction type (Type A)?
cards.a: Augmented (dose-dependent, predictable, related to pharmacology).

cards.q: Type B adverse reaction?
cards.a: Bizarre (idiosyncratic, unpredictable, e.g., hypersensitivity, G6PD hemolysis).

cards.q: Drugs causing gingival hyperplasia?
cards.a: Phenytoin, Cyclosporine, Calcium channel blockers (especially Nifedipine).

cards.q: Drugs causing photosensitivity?
cards.a: Tetracyclines, Sulfonamides, Amiodarone, Psoralens, Griseofulvin.

cards.q: Drugs causing lupus-like syndrome?
cards.a: Procainamide, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Quinidine, Minocycline (PHIQ).

cards.q: Drugs causing ototoxicity?
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, Loop diuretics (Furosemide), Cisplatin, Vancomycin.

cards.q: Drugs causing nephrotoxicity (high-yield)?
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, Amphotericin B, Cisplatin, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs (in renal artery stenosis), Contrast dye.

cards.q: Drugs causing hepatotoxicity (high-yield)?
cards.a: Acetaminophen (most common), Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, Statins, Valproate, Alcohol.

cards.q: Most common cause of drug-induced seizures?
cards.a: Bupropion, Imipenem, Isoniazid, Tramadol, Theophylline.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Atropine?
cards.a: Competitive muscarinic receptor antagonist.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Physostigmine?
cards.a: Reversible cholinesterase inhibitor (crosses BBB).

cards.q: What is the antidote for organophosphate poisoning?
cards.a: Atropine (large doses) + Pralidoxime (2-PAM) to regenerate AChE.

cards.q: What receptors do Catecholamines act on (order of potency)?
cards.a:
• Epinephrine: α1 = α2 > β1 > β2
  • NE: α1 = α2 > β1 >> β2

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Cocaine?
cards.a: Blocks reuptake of NE, DA, and 5-HT (sympathomimetic).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Amphetamines?
cards.a: Promote release of NE and DA + inhibit reuptake.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Reserpine?
cards.a: Inhibits VMAT → depletes NE stores (old antihypertensive).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Clonidine?
cards.a: Central α2-agonist → ↓ sympathetic outflow.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bethanechol?
cards.a: Direct muscarinic (M3) agonist. Used for postoperative ileus and urinary retention.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pilocarpine?
cards.a: Direct muscarinic agonist (especially M3). Used for glaucoma and xerostomia.

cards.q: Mechanism and clinical use of Neostigmine?
cards.a: Reversible AChE inhibitor (does NOT cross BBB). Used for myasthenia gravis and reversal of neuromuscular blockade.

cards.q: Mechanism and clinical use of Edrophonium?
cards.a: Short-acting AChE inhibitor. Used in Tensilon test for myasthenia gravis diagnosis.

cards.q: What is the antidote for atropine (antimuscarinic) toxicity?
cards.a: Physostigmine (crosses BBB).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of α1-agonists? Example?
cards.a: Vasoconstriction → ↑ BP. Example: Phenylephrine (nasal decongestant).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of α2-agonists? Example?
cards.a: Central: ↓ sympathetic outflow. Peripheral: ↓ NE release. Example: Clonidine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of β1-selective agonists? Clinical use?
cards.a: ↑ heart rate and contractility. Example: Dobutamine (heart failure, cardiogenic shock).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of β2-agonists? Clinical use?
cards.a: Bronchodilation, uterine relaxation. Examples: Albuterol (asthma), Terbutaline (preterm labor).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Isoproterenol?
cards.a: Non-selective β-agonist (β1 = β2). Used in bradycardia or heart block.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Epinephrine (low dose vs high dose)?
cards.a:
• Low dose: β effects predominate (↑ HR, bronchodilation).
  • High dose: α effects predominate (vasoconstriction).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Norepinephrine?
cards.a: Mainly α1 > β1. Used in septic shock (vasopressor).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Phenoxybenzamine?
cards.a: Non-selective, irreversible α-blocker. Used in pheochromocytoma.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Prazosin?
cards.a: Selective α1-blocker. Used for hypertension and BPH.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Propranolol?
cards.a: Non-selective β-blocker. Uses: HTN, angina, tremor, migraine prophylaxis, hyperthyroidism.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Metoprolol?
cards.a: β1-selective blocker. Preferred in patients with asthma/COPD.

cards.q: Side effects of β-blockers (high-yield)?
cards.a: Bradycardia, AV block, fatigue, erectile dysfunction, masking of hypoglycemia, exacerbation of asthma.

cards.q: What is the treatment for β-blocker overdose?
cards.a: Glucagon (increases cAMP independently of β-receptors).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Atropine?
cards.a: Competitive muscarinic antagonist.

cards.q: Clinical uses of Atropine?
cards.a: Bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning, pupil dilation, antisecretory before surgery.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Scopolamine?
cards.a: Muscarinic antagonist. Used for motion sickness.

cards.q: What are the effects of muscarinic blockade (mnemonic)?
cards.a: Dry as a bone, Red as a beet, Blind as a bat, Mad as a hatter, Hot as a hare.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hexamethonium?
cards.a: Ganglionic blocker (nicotinic antagonist). Rarely used.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Succinylcholine?
cards.a: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (persistent agonist at nicotinic receptors).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rocuronium / Vecuronium?
cards.a: Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (competitive nicotinic antagonists).

cards.q: Reversal of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade?
cards.a: Neostigmine + Glycopyrrolate (or Sugammadex for Rocuronium).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dantrolene?
cards.a: Inhibits Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum. Used in malignant hyperthermia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Baclofen?
cards.a: GABA-B receptor agonist. Used for spasticity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tizanidine?
cards.a: Central α2-agonist. Used for spasticity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Nitroprusside?
cards.a: Releases NO → ↑ cGMP → vasodilation (arterial + venous).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydralazine?
cards.a: Direct arterial vasodilator (↑ cGMP). Used in HTN and heart failure.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Minoxidil?
cards.a: Opens K⁺ channels → hyperpolarization → arterial vasodilation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of ACE inhibitors (e.g., Lisinopril)?
cards.a: Inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ Ang II, ↑ bradykinin.

cards.q: Side effects of ACE inhibitors?
cards.a: Cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia, renal failure (in bilateral renal artery stenosis).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of ARBs (e.g., Losartan)?
cards.a: Block AT1 receptors. No effect on bradykinin (no cough).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Aliskiren?
cards.a: Direct renin inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Calcium channel blockers (Dihydropyridines)?
cards.a: Block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation (e.g., Amlodipine, Nifedipine).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Verapamil / Diltiazem?
cards.a: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs — block Ca²⁺ channels in heart (negative inotrope/chronotrope) and vessels.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Digoxin?
cards.a: Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → ↑ Ca²⁺ via NCX → positive inotrope.

cards.q: Toxicity of Digoxin?
cards.a: Arrhythmias (especially with hypokalemia), visual changes (xanthopsia), GI upset.

cards.q: Antidote for Digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amiodarone?
cards.a: Class III antiarrhythmic (K⁺ channel blocker) with properties of all classes.

cards.q: Major toxicities of Amiodarone?
cards.a: Pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo/hyper), corneal deposits, blue-gray skin, hepatotoxicity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lidocaine?
cards.a: Class Ib antiarrhythmic — Na⁺ channel blocker (preferentially affects ischemic tissue).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Adenosine?
cards.a: Activates A1 receptors → ↑ K⁺ outflow → hyperpolarization. Used for SVT termination.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Magnesium sulfate in torsades de pointes?
cards.a: Stabilizes cardiac membrane.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Statins?
cards.a: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors → ↓ cholesterol synthesis → ↑ LDL receptor expression.

cards.q: Side effects of Statins?
cards.a: Myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, elevated LFTs, teratogenic.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ezetimibe?
cards.a: Inhibits NPC1L1 cholesterol transporter in small intestine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Fibrates (e.g., Gemfibrozil)?
cards.a: PPAR-α agonists → ↑ lipoprotein lipase → ↓ triglycerides.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Niacin?
cards.a: Inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue → ↓ VLDL → ↓ LDL and ↑ HDL.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., Cholestyramine)?
cards.a: Bind bile acids in intestine → ↑ hepatic bile acid synthesis from cholesterol.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Penicillin G / V?
cards.a: Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibits transpeptidation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cephalosporins?
cards.a: Same as penicillins: inhibit cell wall synthesis via PBPs.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vancomycin?
cards.a: Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding D-ala-D-ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin, Tobramycin)?
cards.a: Inhibit protein synthesis by binding 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tetracyclines?
cards.a: Bind 30S subunit → prevent tRNA attachment.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Macrolides (Erythromycin, Azithromycin)?
cards.a: Bind 50S subunit → inhibit translocation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Clindamycin?
cards.a: Binds 50S subunit → inhibits protein synthesis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Linezolid?
cards.a: Binds 50S subunit → inhibits initiation complex formation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Chloramphenicol?
cards.a: Binds 50S subunit → inhibits peptidyl transferase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sulfonamides?
cards.a: Competitive inhibitors of dihydropteroate synthase (PABA analog).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Trimethoprim?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin)?
cards.a: Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Metronidazole?
cards.a: Forms toxic free radicals in anaerobic bacteria and protozoa.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rifampin?
cards.a: Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Isoniazid (INH)?
cards.a: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (requires catalase-peroxidase activation).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pyrazinamide?
cards.a: Disrupts membrane energetics and inhibits fatty acid synthesis (active in acidic pH).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ethambutol?
cards.a: Inhibits arabinosyl transferase (cell wall synthesis).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Tuberculosis (RIPE)?
cards.a: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Isoniazid?
cards.a: Peripheral neuropathy (prevent with Pyridoxine/B6), hepatotoxicity.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Rifampin?
cards.a: Orange-red discoloration of fluids, induces CYP450.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acyclovir / Valacyclovir?
cards.a: Guanosine analog → inhibits viral DNA polymerase (requires viral thymidine kinase).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ganciclovir?
cards.a: Inhibits CMV DNA polymerase (requires viral UL97 kinase).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Oseltamivir?
cards.a: Neuraminidase inhibitor (Influenza A & B).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sofosbuvir?
cards.a: NS5B RNA polymerase inhibitor (Hepatitis C).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amphotericin B?
cards.a: Binds ergosterol → forms pores in fungal membrane.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Amphotericin B?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity, infusion-related reactions, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Azoles (Fluconazole, Itraconazole)?
cards.a: Inhibit lanosterol 14-α-demethylase → ↓ ergosterol synthesis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Echinocandins (Caspofungin)?
cards.a: Inhibit β-glucan synthase → weaken fungal cell wall.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Terbinafine?
cards.a: Inhibits squalene epoxidase (dermatophytes).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Griseofulvin?
cards.a: Disrupts microtubule function → inhibits mitosis in dermatophytes.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methotrexate?
cards.a: Folate analog → inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)?
cards.a: Pyrimidine analog → inhibits thymidylate synthase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cytarabine?
cards.a: Pyrimidine analog → inhibits DNA polymerase.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cisplatin / Carboplatin?
cards.a: Cross-link DNA strands.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Doxorubicin (Adriamycin)?
cards.a: Intercalates DNA, generates free radicals, inhibits topoisomerase II.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Doxorubicin?
cards.a: Cardiotoxicity (cumulative dose-dependent cardiomyopathy).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vincristine / Vinblastine?
cards.a: Inhibit microtubule polymerization (M-phase arrest).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Paclitaxel?
cards.a: Stabilizes microtubules (M-phase arrest).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Etoposide?
cards.a: Inhibits topoisomerase II.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Imatinib?
cards.a: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BCR-ABL).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Trastuzumab (Herceptin)?
cards.a: Monoclonal antibody against HER2/neu.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rituximab?
cards.a: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cyclophosphamide?
cards.a: Alkylating agent → cross-links DNA.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Cyclophosphamide?
cards.a: Hemorrhagic cystitis (prevent with Mesna).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Prednisone / Dexamethasone?
cards.a: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist → gene transcription modulation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tamoxifen?
cards.a: SERM (estrogen antagonist in breast tissue).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Levothyroxine?
cards.a: Synthetic T4.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Propylthiouracil (PTU) / Methimazole?
cards.a: Inhibit thyroid peroxidase → block thyroid hormone synthesis.

cards.q: Which antithyroid drug is preferred in pregnancy?
cards.a: Propylthiouracil (PTU) — lower risk of teratogenicity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Metformin?
cards.a: Activates AMPK → ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑ peripheral glucose uptake.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sulfonylureas (Glipizide)?
cards.a: Close K⁺-ATP channels in β-cells → depolarization → insulin release.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Thiazolidinediones (Pioglitazone)?
cards.a: PPAR-γ agonists → ↑ insulin sensitivity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of GLP-1 agonists (e.g., Exenatide)?
cards.a: ↑ glucose-dependent insulin release, ↓ glucagon, slow gastric emptying.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., Dapagliflozin)?
cards.a: Inhibit glucose reabsorption in proximal tubule → glucosuria.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Insulin?
cards.a: Binds tyrosine kinase receptor → ↑ GLUT4 translocation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Omeprazole / Pantoprazole?
cards.a: Irreversible proton pump (H⁺/K⁺ ATPase) inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cimetidine / Ranitidine?
cards.a: H₂ receptor antagonists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ondansetron?
cards.a: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist (anti-emetic).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Loperamide?
cards.a: μ-opioid agonist in enteric nervous system (antidiarrheal).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lactulose?
cards.a: Osmotic laxative + ammonia trapper (hepatic encephalopathy).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sucralfate?
cards.a: Forms viscous gel in acidic environment → physical barrier over ulcers.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Misoprostol?
cards.a: PGE1 analog → ↑ mucus/bicarbonate, ↓ acid.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acetaminophen?
cards.a: Inhibits COX in CNS (weak peripheral effect).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Aspirin?
cards.a: Irreversible COX-1/2 inhibitor (↓ TXA2).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ibuprofen / Naproxen?
cards.a: Reversible COX-1/2 inhibitors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Celecoxib?
cards.a: Selective COX-2 inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acetylcysteine?
cards.a: Replenishes glutathione (acetaminophen overdose antidote).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Allopurinol?
cards.a: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Febuxostat?
cards.a: Non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Colchicine?
cards.a: Binds tubulin → inhibits microtubule polymerization and neutrophil chemotaxis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Probenecid?
cards.a: Inhibits uric acid reabsorption in proximal tubule.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rasburicase?
cards.a: Recombinant urate oxidase (breaks down uric acid to allantoin).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Furosemide?
cards.a: Inhibits Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in thick ascending limb.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydrochlorothiazide?
cards.a: Inhibits Na⁺-Cl⁻ cotransporter in distal convoluted tubule.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Spironolactone / Eplerenone?
cards.a: Aldosterone receptor antagonists (K⁺-sparing).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mannitol?
cards.a: Osmotic diuretic.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acetazolamide?
cards.a: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ethacrynic acid?
cards.a: Loop diuretic (not a sulfonamide).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SSRIs (e.g., Fluoxetine)?
cards.a: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SNRIs (e.g., Venlafaxine)?
cards.a: Inhibit reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of TCAs (e.g., Amitriptyline)?
cards.a: Inhibit reuptake of NE and 5-HT; also block muscarinic, α1, H1 receptors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of MAOIs?
cards.a: Inhibit monoamine oxidase → ↑ NE, 5-HT, DA.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bupropion?
cards.a: NDRI (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mirtazapine?
cards.a: α2 antagonist + 5-HT2/3 antagonist (increases NE and 5-HT).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lithium?
cards.a: Inhibits inositol monophosphatase and glycogen synthase kinase-3.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Valproate?
cards.a: Increases GABA, blocks Na⁺ channels, inhibits T-type Ca²⁺ channels.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lamotrigine?
cards.a: Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Blocks Na⁺ channels; induces CYP450.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Phenytoin?
cards.a: Blocks Na⁺ channels (zero-order kinetics at high doses).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Enhance GABA-A receptor (↑ Cl⁻ conductance).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Barbiturates?
cards.a: Prolong GABA-A channel opening.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buspirone?
cards.a: 5-HT1A partial agonist (anxiolytic without sedation).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Typical antipsychotics (Haloperidol)?
cards.a: D2 receptor antagonists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Atypical antipsychotics (Risperidone, Olanzapine)?
cards.a: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Clozapine?
cards.a: Atypical antipsychotic with low D2 affinity; used in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Clozapine?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis (requires weekly WBC monitoring).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Levodopa?
cards.a: Dopamine precursor (crosses BBB).

cards.q: Why is Carbidopa given with Levodopa?
cards.a: Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase → ↑ CNS availability of L-DOPA.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Selegiline / Rasagiline?
cards.a: MAO-B inhibitors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Entacapone?
cards.a: COMT inhibitor (prolongs L-DOPA action).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Memantine?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonist (moderate-severe Alzheimer).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Donepezil?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (Alzheimer).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Riluzole?
cards.a: Used in ALS (↓ glutamate release).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Primaquine?
cards.a: Disrupts mitochondrial electron transport in Plasmodium. Used for radical cure of P. vivax/ovale (liver hypnozoites).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Chloroquine?
cards.a: Raises pH in parasite food vacuole → prevents heme polymerization.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Artemisinin derivatives?
cards.a: Generate free radicals → damage parasite proteins.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ivermectin?
cards.a: Increases GABA and glutamate-gated Cl⁻ conductance in nematodes → paralysis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Albendazole / Mebendazole?
cards.a: Inhibits microtubule synthesis (β-tubulin binding).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Praziquantel?
cards.a: Increases Ca²⁺ permeability in trematodes/cestodes → muscle contraction and paralysis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Niclosamide?
cards.a: Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in tapeworms.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pentamidine?
cards.a: Inhibits DNA synthesis and topoisomerase. Used for PCP and African trypanosomiasis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Miltefosine?
cards.a: Alkylphosphocholine → disrupts parasite cell membrane (visceral leishmaniasis).

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Aminoglycosides?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity and Ototoxicity (especially with loop diuretics).

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Vancomycin (rapid infusion)?
cards.a: Red man syndrome (histamine release).

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Linezolid?
cards.a: Thrombocytopenia, optic neuropathy, serotonin syndrome (with SSRIs).

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Chloramphenicol?
cards.a: Gray baby syndrome, aplastic anemia.

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Fluoroquinolones?
cards.a: Tendon rupture (Achilles), cartilage damage (avoid in children/pregnancy), QT prolongation.

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Tetracyclines?
cards.a: Tooth discoloration, photosensitivity, Fanconi syndrome (expired drug).

cards.q: Major adverse effect of Sulfonamides?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, kernicterus in neonates, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

cards.q: Major drug interaction with Rifampin?
cards.a: Strong CYP450 inducer → decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, protease inhibitors.

cards.q: Major drug interaction with Macrolides (except Azithromycin)?
cards.a: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors → increased levels of statins, theophylline, warfarin.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Abacavir?
cards.a: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI).

cards.q: Major toxicity of Abacavir?
cards.a: Hypersensitivity reaction (screen for HLA-B*5701).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Efavirenz?
cards.a: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI).

cards.q: Major side effect of Efavirenz?
cards.a: Neuropsychiatric symptoms, vivid dreams, teratogenic.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Protease inhibitors (e.g., Ritonavir)?
cards.a: Inhibit HIV protease → prevent maturation of virions.

cards.q: Major side effect of Protease inhibitors?
cards.a: Lipodystrophy, hyperglycemia, CYP3A4 inhibition (especially Ritonavir).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Integrase inhibitors (e.g., Raltegravir)?
cards.a: Inhibit HIV integrase → prevent viral DNA integration into host genome.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Enfuvirtide?
cards.a: Fusion inhibitor (blocks gp41).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Maraviroc?
cards.a: CCR5 co-receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydroxychloroquine in lupus?
cards.a: Stabilizes lysosomal membranes, interferes with antigen presentation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mycophenolate mofetil?
cards.a: Inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase → blocks purine synthesis in lymphocytes.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Azathioprine?
cards.a: Purine analog → inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tacrolimus / Cyclosporine?
cards.a: Calcineurin inhibitors → block IL-2 transcription.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sirolimus (Rapamycin)?
cards.a: mTOR inhibitor → blocks T-cell proliferation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Basiliximab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-2 receptor (CD25) monoclonal antibody.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Natalizumab?
cards.a: Anti-α4-integrin antibody → prevents lymphocyte migration into CNS (MS, Crohn’s).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Infliximab / Adalimumab?
cards.a: Anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibodies.

cards.q: Major risk with Anti-TNF agents?
cards.a: Reactivation of latent TB, opportunistic infections.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Anakinra?
cards.a: IL-1 receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tocilizumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-6 receptor antibody.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ustekinumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-12/IL-23 monoclonal antibody.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Secukinumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Omalizumab?
cards.a: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody (asthma, urticaria).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Eculizumab?
cards.a: Anti-C5 monoclonal antibody (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, aHUS).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Depletes B cells (anti-CD20).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase + anti-inflammatory effects at low dose.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Leflunomide?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase → blocks pyrimidine synthesis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sulfasalazine?
cards.a: Anti-inflammatory + antibacterial (cleaved to 5-ASA + sulfapyridine).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydroxychloroquine in RA?
cards.a: Lysosomal alkalinization and interference with antigen processing.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Finasteride?
cards.a: 5α-reductase inhibitor → ↓ dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Used in BPH and male pattern baldness.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Flutamide / Bicalutamide?
cards.a: Androgen receptor antagonists. Used in prostate cancer.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Leuprolide?
cards.a: GnRH agonist (continuous use → downregulation). Used in prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sildenafil / Tadalafil?
cards.a: PDE-5 inhibitors → ↑ cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation in corpus cavernosum.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tamsulosin?
cards.a: α1A-selective blocker (prostate smooth muscle). Used in BPH.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Oxybutynin / Tolterodine?
cards.a: Muscarinic antagonists. Used for urge incontinence / overactive bladder.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Desmopressin (DDAVP)?
cards.a: V2 receptor agonist → ↑ aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting duct (central DI, nocturnal enuresis).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Demeclocycline?
cards.a: Tetracycline derivative that causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (used in SIADH).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Conivaptan / Tolvaptan?
cards.a: V2 receptor antagonists (aquaretics). Used in SIADH.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Octreotide?
cards.a: Somatostatin analog. Used in acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, variceal bleeding.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Propylthiouracil (PTU) vs Methimazole?
cards.a: Both inhibit thyroid peroxidase. PTU also inhibits peripheral T4 → T3 conversion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Radioactive Iodine (I-131)?
cards.a: Destroys thyroid follicular cells via β-emission.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cinacalcet?
cards.a: Calcimimetic → activates CaSR in parathyroid → ↓ PTH secretion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Zoledronate)?
cards.a: Inhibit osteoclast activity → ↓ bone resorption.

cards.q: Major side effect of Bisphosphonates?
cards.a: Esophagitis (oral), osteonecrosis of jaw, atypical femoral fractures.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Teriparatide?
cards.a: Recombinant PTH (1-34) → anabolic effect on bone (intermittent dosing).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Denosumab?
cards.a: Anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody → inhibits osteoclast differentiation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Raloxifene?
cards.a: SERM: agonist on bone, antagonist on breast/uterus.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Calcitonin?
cards.a: Inhibits osteoclast activity. Used in hypercalcemia and osteoporosis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Orlistat?
cards.a: Pancreatic and gastric lipase inhibitor → ↓ fat absorption.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Osmotic laxative + acidifies colon → traps NH4+.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Rifaximin?
cards.a: Non-absorbable antibiotic. Used in hepatic encephalopathy and traveler’s diarrhea.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Alosetron?
cards.a: 5-HT3 antagonist. Used in severe IBS-D (women only).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lubiprostone?
cards.a: ClC-2 chloride channel activator → ↑ intestinal fluid secretion (IBS-C, opioid constipation).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Teduglutide?
cards.a: GLP-2 analog → promotes intestinal growth in short bowel syndrome.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Montelukast / Zafirlukast?
cards.a: Leukotriene receptor (CysLT1) antagonists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Theophylline?
cards.a: Non-selective PDE inhibitor + adenosine receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Theophylline?
cards.a: Narrow therapeutic index: seizures, arrhythmias, nausea.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cromolyn?
cards.a: Mast cell stabilizer. Used in asthma prophylaxis.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ipratropium / Tiotropium?
cards.a: Muscarinic antagonists (bronchodilators).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pseudoephedrine?
cards.a: α-adrenergic agonist → nasal vasoconstriction (decongestant).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dextromethorphan?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonist (antitussive).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Guaifenesin?
cards.a: Expectorant → ↑ respiratory tract fluid volume.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acetylcysteine in acetaminophen overdose?
cards.a: Replenishes glutathione + direct binding of toxic metabolite NAPQI.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Fomepizole?
cards.a: Alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor. Used in methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pralidoxime (2-PAM)?
cards.a: Regenerates acetylcholinesterase in organophosphate poisoning.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Flumazenil?
cards.a: Competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Naloxone / Naltrexone?
cards.a: Opioid receptor antagonists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Physostigmine in anticholinergic toxicity?
cards.a: Reversible cholinesterase inhibitor that crosses BBB.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vitamin K in warfarin overdose?
cards.a: Replenishes vitamin K stores → restores clotting factors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Protamine sulfate?
cards.a: Binds heparin → neutralizes it.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Idarucizumab?
cards.a: Specific reversal agent for Dabigatran.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Andexanet alfa?
cards.a: Reversal agent for Factor Xa inhibitors (Rivaroxaban, Apixaban).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methylene blue?
cards.a: Reduces methemoglobin to hemoglobin.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Deferoxamine?
cards.a: Iron chelator.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dimercaprol (BAL)?
cards.a: Chelator for heavy metals (arsenic, gold, lead, mercury).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of EDTA?
cards.a: Chelator for lead and calcium.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Penicillamine?
cards.a: Chelator for copper (Wilson disease), lead, and rheumatoid arthritis.

cards.q: What is the volume of distribution (Vd) clinical implication for highly lipophilic drugs?
cards.a: Very high Vd (> body water volume) — extensive tissue distribution (e.g., amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin).

cards.q: What is the effect of hypoalbuminemia on highly protein-bound drugs?
cards.a: Increased free (active) fraction → higher risk of toxicity (e.g., phenytoin, warfarin).

cards.q: Zero-order kinetics drugs (high-yield list)?
cards.a: Phenytoin (high dose), Ethanol, Aspirin (high dose), Theophylline.

cards.q: Drugs with narrow therapeutic index (high-yield)?
cards.a: Digoxin, Lithium, Theophylline, Phenytoin, Warfarin, Aminoglycosides, Vancomycin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of drug-induced torsades de pointes?
cards.a: Drugs that prolong QT interval (e.g., antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron).

cards.q: Drugs that cause serotonin syndrome (high-yield combination)?
cards.a: MAOIs + SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs + Meperidine, Linezolid + SSRIs.

cards.q: Drugs that cause malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Succinylcholine + volatile anesthetics (halothane, isoflurane). Treated with dantrolene.

cards.q: Drugs causing drug-induced lupus (high-yield)?
cards.a: Procainamide, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Quinidine, Minocycline.

cards.q: Drugs causing gynecomastia (high-yield)?
cards.a: Spironolactone, Cimetidine, Ketoconazole, Digoxin, Estrogens, Anti-androgens.

cards.q: Drugs causing orange-red body fluids?
cards.a: Rifampin.

cards.q: Drugs causing blue-gray skin discoloration?
cards.a: Amiodarone.

cards.q: Drugs causing retinopathy (high-yield)?
cards.a: Chloroquine / Hydroxychloroquine, Hydroxychloroquine requires eye exams.

cards.q: Drugs causing optic neuritis?
cards.a: Ethambutol, Linezolid, Isoniazid (with B6 deficiency).

cards.q: Drugs causing peripheral neuropathy (high-yield)?
cards.a: Isoniazid, Metronidazole, Vincristine, Paclitaxel, Nitrofurantoin, Didanosine.

cards.q: Drugs causing pseudomembranous colitis?
cards.a: Clindamycin, Cephalosporins, Fluoroquinolones, Ampicillin.

cards.q: Drugs causing interstitial nephritis?
cards.a: Methicillin, NSAIDs, PPIs, Sulfonamides, Rifampin.

cards.q: Drugs causing Fanconi syndrome?
cards.a: Expired tetracyclines, Ifosfamide, Tenofovir.

cards.q: Drugs contraindicated in pregnancy (high-yield categories)?
cards.a: ACEi/ARBs, Statins, Tetracyclines, Fluoroquinolones, Aminoglycosides, Warfarin, Isotretinoin, Thalidomide.

cards.q: Drugs safe in pregnancy (high-yield)?
cards.a: Penicillins, Cephalosporins, Azithromycin, Acetaminophen, Heparin, Insulin, Labetalol, Methyldopa.

cards.q: Drugs that require dose adjustment in renal failure (high-yield)?
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, Vancomycin, Digoxin, Lithium, Methotrexate, Allopurinol.

cards.q: Drugs that require dose adjustment in hepatic failure?
cards.a: Phenytoin, Valproate, Theophylline, Lidocaine, Propranolol.

cards.q: Most common mechanism of pharmacokinetic drug interaction?
cards.a: CYP450 enzyme induction or inhibition.

cards.q: Strongest CYP3A4 inducers?
cards.a: Rifampin, Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, St. John’s Wort.

cards.q: Strongest CYP3A4 inhibitors?
cards.a: Ketoconazole, Itraconazole, Ritonavir, Clarithromycin, Grapefruit juice.

cards.q: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) inducers vs inhibitors effect?
cards.a: Inducers decrease drug absorption/effect. Inhibitors increase drug levels (e.g., verapamil, quinidine).

cards.q: What is the effect of grapefruit juice on drug levels?
cards.a: Inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and P-gp → increased bioavailability of many drugs.

cards.q: Warfarin drug interactions (high-yield)?
cards.a:
• Increased effect: Amiodarone, TMP-SMX, Metronidazole, Fluconazole.
  • Decreased effect: Rifampin, Carbamazepine, Vitamin K.

cards.q: What is pharmacodynamics?
cards.a: What the drug does to the body (receptor interaction, dose-response).

cards.q: What is pharmacokinetics?
cards.a: What the body does to the drug (ADME).

cards.q: Phase I vs Phase II metabolism summary?
cards.a:
• Phase I: oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis (CYP450).
  • Phase II: conjugation (makes more polar).

cards.q: Most common Phase II reaction?
cards.a: Glucuronidation.

cards.q: Drugs metabolized by zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses?
cards.a: Phenytoin, Ethanol.

cards.q: What is bioavailability?
cards.a: Fraction of administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.

cards.q: What route has 100% bioavailability?
cards.a: Intravenous (IV).

cards.q: What is extraction ratio?
cards.a: Fraction of drug removed from blood by liver in one pass. High extraction = high first-pass effect.

cards.q: Drugs with high hepatic extraction (high first-pass)?
cards.a: Morphine, Propranolol, Nitroglycerin, Lidocaine.

cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation used for?
cards.a: To determine ionization state of weak acids/bases and predict distribution/trapping.

cards.q: Ionization of weak acids in alkaline environment?
cards.a: More ionized (A⁻) → trapped in alkaline urine (e.g., aspirin overdose → alkalinize urine).

cards.q: Ionization of weak bases in acidic environment?
cards.a: More ionized (BH⁺) → trapped in acidic urine (e.g., amphetamine overdose).

cards.q: What is the blood-brain barrier permeability rule?
cards.a: Lipid-soluble, non-ionized, low molecular weight drugs cross more easily.

cards.q: What is receptor reserve?
cards.a: Maximal response can be achieved with only partial receptor occupancy (spare receptors).

cards.q: What is efficacy?
cards.a: Maximal effect a drug can produce (Emax), independent of dose.

cards.q: What is potency?
cards.a: Dose required to produce 50% of maximal effect (EC50). Lower EC50 = higher potency.

cards.q: Full agonist vs partial agonist on log dose-response curve?
cards.a: Full agonist reaches 100% Emax. Partial agonist has lower Emax.

cards.q: Competitive antagonist effect on dose-response curve?
cards.a: Shifts curve to the right (↑ EC50), no change in Emax.

cards.q: Non-competitive antagonist effect on dose-response curve?
cards.a: Decreases Emax, no change or slight right shift in EC50.

cards.q: What is an inverse agonist?
cards.a: Binds receptor and produces opposite effect of constitutive activity (e.g., some antihistamines at H1).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of microcytic anemia worldwide?
cards.a: Iron deficiency anemia (due to blood loss, poor intake, or malabsorption)

cards.q: What are the lab findings in iron deficiency anemia?
cards.a: ↓ Serum iron, ↓ Ferritin, ↑ TIBC, ↑ Transferrin, ↓ MCV, ↑ RDW, hypochromic microcytic RBCs on smear

cards.q: What is the best initial test and most accurate test for iron deficiency?
cards.a:
Best initial: Serum ferritin
Most accurate: Bone marrow iron stain (absent stores)

cards.q: What causes sideroblastic anemia? Key lab finding?
cards.a:
Defect in heme synthesis (e.g., ALA synthase deficiency, lead poisoning, isoniazid, alcohol).
Key: Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain + ↑ serum iron/ferritin

cards.q: What are the causes of macrocytic anemia? Differentiate megaloblastic vs non-megaloblastic.
cards.a:
Megaloblastic (DNA synthesis defect): B12/folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxyurea).
Non-megaloblastic: Liver disease, hypothyroidism, alcohol, reticulocytosis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of B12 deficiency in the US?
cards.a: Pernicious anemia (autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → ↓ intrinsic factor)

cards.q: How do you differentiate B12 vs folate deficiency clinically and on labs?
cards.a:
B12: neurologic symptoms (subacute combined degeneration), ↑ methylmalonic acid + homocysteine.
Folate: No neuro symptoms, only ↑ homocysteine

cards.q: What is the Schilling test used for?
cards.a: Diagnosing the cause of B12 malabsorption (pernicious anemia vs ileal disease vs bacterial overgrowth)

cards.q: What are the peripheral smear findings in megaloblastic anemia?
cards.a: Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes), Howell-Jolly bodies

cards.q: What is the treatment for B12 deficiency neurological symptoms?
cards.a: Intramuscular cyanocobalamin (1 mg daily for 1 week, then weekly, then monthly)

cards.q: What is the most common inherited hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Hereditary spherocytosis (ankyrin/spectrin defect)

cards.q: What are the classic findings in hereditary spherocytosis?
cards.a: Spherocytes on smear, ↑ MCHC, negative Coombs, ↑ osmotic fragility test, gallstones, splenomegaly

cards.q: What is the treatment for hereditary spherocytosis?
cards.a: Folate supplementation + splenectomy (definitive)

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic smear finding in G6PD deficiency?
cards.a: Bite cells and Heinz bodies (after oxidant stress)

cards.q: What triggers hemolysis in G6PD deficiency?
cards.a: Infection, fava beans, drugs (primaquine, sulfa, dapsone, nitrofurantoin)

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of G6PD deficiency?
cards.a: X-linked recessive (more common in African & Mediterranean populations)

cards.q: What are the smear findings in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Sickle cells, Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells

cards.q: What is the most common acute complication in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis (most common), acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19)

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic test for sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Hemoglobin electrophoresis (HbS)

cards.q: What is hydroxyurea used for in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Increases HbF → decreases sickling and frequency of crises

cards.q: What are the two major types of thalassemia?
cards.a: α-thalassemia (gene deletion) and β-thalassemia (point mutations)

cards.q: What is the clinical picture of HbH disease?
cards.a: Three α-gene deletion → moderate hemolytic anemia, HbH (β4 tetramers)

cards.q: What is hydrops fetalis in thalassemia?
cards.a: Four α-gene deletion (—/—) → lethal in utero (Bart's hemoglobin — γ4 tetramers)

cards.q: What is the treatment for β-thalassemia major (Cooley anemia)?
cards.a: Lifelong transfusions + iron chelation (deferasirox, deferoxamine)

cards.q: What are the smear findings in thalassemia?
cards.a: Microcytic hypochromic RBCs, target cells, basophilic stippling, teardrop cells

cards.q: What is the most common cause of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm type)?
cards.a: IgG-mediated (positive direct Coombs test). Associated with SLE, CLL, drugs (penicillin, methyldopa)

cards.q: What is the treatment for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Steroids (first-line), rituximab, splenectomy, IVIG

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: IgM-mediated (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV, Waldenström macroglobulinemia)

cards.q: What is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria?
cards.a: Donath-Landsteiner antibody (biphasic IgG). Seen after viral infections or syphilis

cards.q: What are the lab findings in PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria)?
cards.a: CD55/CD59 deficiency on flow cytometry, hemolytic anemia (dark urine in morning), pancytopenia, venous thrombosis (especially hepatic veins)

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for PNH?
cards.a: Eculizumab or ravulizumab (complement C5 inhibitors)

cards.q: What are the causes of aplastic anemia?
cards.a: Idiopathic, drugs (chloramphenicol, NSAIDs), radiation, viruses (parvovirus B19, EBV, hepatitis), PNH, Fanconi anemia

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for severe aplastic anemia in young patients?
cards.a: Allogeneic bone marrow transplant

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in children?
cards.a: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)

cards.q: What are the key markers in B-ALL vs T-ALL?
cards.a:
B-ALL: TdT+, CALLA (CD10)+, CD19+.
T-ALL: CD2,3,5,7+

cards.q: What is the most common translocation in ALL with good prognosis?
cards.a: t(12;21) — TEL-AML1

cards.q: What are Auer rods pathognomonic for?
cards.a: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), especially M3 (acute promyelocytic leukemia)

cards.q: What is the translocation in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and its treatment?
cards.a:
t(15;17) — PML-RARA.
Treatment: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) + arsenic trioxide

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in adults in the Western world?
cards.a: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

cards.q: What is the characteristic immunophenotype of CLL?
What is Richter transformation?
cards.a: CLL transforming into aggressive large cell lymphoma (poor prognosis)

cards.q: What is the Philadelphia chromosome and its significance?
cards.a: t(9;22) → BCR-ABL fusion → seen in CML (and some ALL/AML)

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)?
cards.a: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib)

cards.q: What are the phases of CML?
cards.a: Chronic phase → accelerated phase → blast crisis

cards.q: What are the hallmark cells in Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, CD20−)

cards.q: What is the most common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Nodular sclerosis

cards.q: What is the treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: ABVD chemotherapy ± radiation

cards.q: What are the most common indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas?
cards.a: Follicular lymphoma (t(14;18) — BCL2 overexpression)

cards.q: What is the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

cards.q: What virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma?
cards.a: EBV (endemic form) + t(8;14) — c-MYC translocation (starry sky pattern)

cards.q: What is multiple myeloma classic presentation (CRAB)?
cards.a: Calcium elevation, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions

cards.q: What are the key lab findings in multiple myeloma?
cards.a: M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), Bence-Jones proteins (urine), rouleaux formation on smear, lytic lesions on X-ray

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Infection (due to immunosuppression)

cards.q: What is Waldenström macroglobulinemia?
cards.a: IgM paraproteinemia (hyperviscosity syndrome) — lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

cards.q: What is the treatment for hyperviscosity in Waldenström?
cards.a: Plasmapheresis

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
cards.a: Autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet GPIIb/IIIa → splenic macrophage destruction of platelets

cards.q: Classic presentation and treatment of acute ITP in children?
cards.a: Often follows viral infection; self-limited. Treatment: Observation or IVIG/steroids if severe bleeding

cards.q: What is the treatment of chronic ITP in adults?
cards.a: First-line: Corticosteroids. Second-line: Rituximab, splenectomy, thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag)

cards.q: What are the lab findings in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)?
cards.a: Thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), ↑ LDH, ↑ indirect bilirubin, normal coagulation studies, neurologic symptoms, fever, renal involvement (pentad)

cards.q: What is the deficient enzyme in TTP?
cards.a: ADAMTS13 (von Willebrand factor cleaving protease)

cards.q: What is the urgent treatment for TTP?
cards.a: Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) + glucocorticoids. Avoid platelet transfusion

cards.q: What is the difference between TTP and HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome)?
cards.a: HUS: More renal failure, often after E. coli O157:H7 (Shiga toxin). Less neurologic involvement than TTP

cards.q: What are the vitamin K–dependent clotting factors?
cards.a: II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C & S)

cards.q: Which clotting factor has the shortest half-life?
cards.a: Factor VII

cards.q: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
cards.a: von Willebrand disease (vWD)

cards.q: What are the lab findings in von Willebrand disease?
cards.a: ↑ Bleeding time, normal PT, normal or ↑ aPTT, ↓ vWF antigen/activity, ↓ Factor VIII (in type 2N/3)
