cards.q: Treatment of mild von Willebrand disease?
cards.a: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases vWF from endothelial cells

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Hemophilia A and B?
cards.a: X-linked recessive

cards.q: Hemophilia A vs Hemophilia B — deficient factor?
cards.a:
A: Factor VIII
B: Factor IX (Christmas disease)

cards.q: What is the mixing study result in hemophilia?
cards.a: aPTT corrects with mixing study (factor deficiency), does NOT correct in inhibitors

cards.q: What is the most common site of bleeding in hemophilia?
cards.a: Hemarthrosis (joints)

cards.q: Treatment of hemophilia?
cards.a: Recombinant factor replacement. Prophylaxis in severe cases

cards.q: What is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
cards.a: Widespread activation of coagulation → consumption of platelets and clotting factors → thrombosis + bleeding

cards.q: Lab findings in DIC?
cards.a: ↓ Platelets, ↑ PT/PTT, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer/FDP, schistocytes

cards.q: Most common triggers of DIC?
cards.a: Sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism), malignancy (especially acute promyelocytic leukemia)

cards.q: What is the most common hereditary thrombophilia?
cards.a: Factor V Leiden mutation (resistance to activated protein C)

cards.q: What is the second most common inherited thrombophilia?
cards.a: Prothrombin G20210A mutation

cards.q: What is the classic triad of Virchow?
cards.a:
1. Endothelial injury
2. Stasis
3. Hypercoagulability

cards.q: What is the best initial test for suspected DVT?
cards.a: Compression duplex ultrasound

cards.q: What is the most accurate test for pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute DVT/PE?
cards.a: Low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) or unfractionated heparin → warfarin or DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban)

cards.q: Which anticoagulant is safe in pregnancy?
cards.a: Heparin and LMWH (does not cross placenta)

cards.q: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
cards.a: Antibodies against heparin-PF4 complex → platelet activation and consumption. Paradoxical thrombosis

cards.q: Diagnosis of HIT?
cards.a: 4T score + serotonin release assay or anti-PF4 antibody ELISA

cards.q: Treatment of HIT?
cards.a: Stop heparin immediately + start direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban or bivalirudin)

cards.q: What is the reversal agent for warfarin?
cards.a: Vitamin K + Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)

cards.q: What is the reversal for dabigatran?
cards.a: Idarucizumab

cards.q: What is the reversal for rivaroxaban/apixaban?
cards.a: Andexanet alfa

cards.q: What is the most common cause of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)?
cards.a: Anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies in donor plasma (usually multiparous female donors)

cards.q: What is febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Caused by cytokines or recipient antibodies to donor WBCs. Treated with acetaminophen

cards.q: What is the most common transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction

cards.q: What is acute hemolytic transfusion reaction caused by?
cards.a: ABO incompatibility (preformed IgM antibodies) → intravascular hemolysis

cards.q: What is the most common cause of delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Anamnestic response to minor antigens (Kidd, Kell, Duffy)

cards.q: What blood product is used to treat bleeding in thrombocytopenia?
cards.a: Platelet concentrate

cards.q: What blood product is used to treat coagulopathy with low fibrinogen?
cards.a: Cryoprecipitate

cards.q: What is the indication for fresh frozen plasma (FFP)?
cards.a: Coagulation factor deficiency, reversal of warfarin, DIC

cards.q: What is polycythemia vera?
cards.a: Myeloproliferative neoplasm with JAK2 mutation → ↑ RBC mass (erythrocytosis)

cards.q: Classic symptoms and findings in polycythemia vera?
cards.a: Pruritus (especially after hot shower), ruddy complexion, splenomegaly, ↑ uric acid, erythromelalgia

cards.q: What is the treatment for polycythemia vera?
cards.a: Phlebotomy (first-line) + low-dose aspirin + hydroxyurea (if high risk)

cards.q: What mutation is found in >95% of polycythemia vera cases?
cards.a: JAK2 V617F

cards.q: What are the three major myeloproliferative neoplasms?
cards.a:
1. Polycythemia vera
2. Essential thrombocythemia
3. Primary myelofibrosis

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in primary myelofibrosis?
cards.a: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) and leukoerythroblastic reaction on smear + bone marrow fibrosis

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for essential thrombocythemia in high-risk patients?
cards.a: Hydroxyurea + low-dose aspirin

cards.q: What is the most common myeloproliferative neoplasm?
cards.a: Polycythemia vera

cards.q: What is the classic triad of symptoms in essential thrombocythemia?
cards.a: Thrombosis, hemorrhage, and erythromelalgia (burning pain in extremities)

cards.q: What mutation is found in ~50% of essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis?
cards.a: JAK2 V617F (also CALR or MPL mutations in JAK2-negative cases)

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic test for primary myelofibrosis?
cards.a: Bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis (dry tap) + leukoerythroblastic reaction on peripheral smear

cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary polycythemia?
cards.a: Hypoxia (COPD, high altitude, sleep apnea, right-to-left shunt)

cards.q: How do you differentiate polycythemia vera from secondary polycythemia?
cards.a:
PV: ↓ EPO, JAK2 mutation positive.
Secondary: ↑ EPO

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Oxygen, hydration, analgesia, antibiotics, transfusion/exchange transfusion

cards.q: What is the most common organism causing osteomyelitis in sickle cell patients?
cards.a: Salmonella

cards.q: What is the hand-foot syndrome in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Dactylitis (painful swelling of hands and feet) — often the first manifestation in infants

cards.q: What is the most common functional asplenia cause in adults?
cards.a: Sickle cell disease (autosplenectomy)

cards.q: What vaccines are required in asplenic patients?
cards.a: Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPSV23), meningococcal, Hib, and annual influenza

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: IgG antibodies coat RBCs → extravascular hemolysis in spleen

cards.q: What is the direct Coombs test (DAT) used for?
cards.a: Detects antibodies or complement bound to RBC surface

cards.q: What drugs classically cause drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Penicillin, cephalosporins, methyldopa, quinidine

cards.q: What is the treatment for cold agglutinin disease?
cards.a: Avoid cold exposure + rituximab (if severe). Steroids are usually ineffective

cards.q: What infection is most commonly associated with cold agglutinin disease?
cards.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

cards.q: What is the characteristic smear finding in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA)?
cards.a: Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs)

cards.q: What are the five causes of MAHA?
cards.a: TTP, HUS, DIC, malignant hypertension, prosthetic heart valves, HELLP syndrome

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of hereditary elliptocytosis?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (spectrin defect)

cards.q: What is pyruvate kinase deficiency?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive glycolytic enzyme defect → chronic hemolytic anemia, ↑ 2,3-BPG

cards.q: What is the smear finding in lead poisoning?
cards.a: Basophilic stippling

cards.q: What is the treatment for lead poisoning?
cards.a: EDTA or succimer (DMSA) chelation

cards.q: What is Fanconi anemia?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive DNA repair defect → pancytopenia, thumb/radius abnormalities, café-au-lait spots, increased risk of AML

cards.q: What is the most common cause of aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease?
cards.a: Parvovirus B19

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia overall in adults?
cards.a: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

cards.q: What is the characteristic finding on flow cytometry in CLL?
cards.a: CD5+, CD23+, CD19+, CD20 dim

cards.q: What is smudge cells on peripheral smear associated with?
cards.a: CLL

cards.q: What is the most common translocation in follicular lymphoma?
cards.a: t(14;18) — BCL2 overexpression

cards.q: What is the histologic pattern in follicular lymphoma?
cards.a: Nodular/follicular pattern with centrocytes and centroblasts

cards.q: What virus is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma?
cards.a: HTLV-1

cards.q: What is the most common primary CNS lymphoma association?
cards.a: EBV in immunocompromised patients (HIV)

cards.q: What is the treatment regimen for non-Hodgkin lymphoma (DLBCL)?
cards.a: R-CHOP (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin, Prednisone)

cards.q: What is the Ann Arbor staging system used for?
cards.a: Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma

cards.q: What is the B symptom triad in lymphoma?
cards.a: Fever, night sweats, weight loss (>10% in 6 months)

cards.q: What is the Reed-Sternberg cell variant seen in nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma?
cards.a: Lacunar cells

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome in multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia

cards.q: What is rouleaux formation on blood smear associated with?
cards.a: Multiple myeloma (due to paraprotein)

cards.q: What is the CRAB criteria for multiple myeloma?
cards.a: HyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions

cards.q: What is the diagnostic test for multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Serum protein electrophoresis (M-spike) + urine protein electrophoresis + bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells)

cards.q: What is the most common heavy chain in multiple myeloma?
cards.a: IgG

cards.q: What is amyloidosis AL type associated with?
cards.a: Plasma cell dyscrasias (multiple myeloma, Waldenström)

cards.q: What is the treatment for multiple myeloma?
cards.a: Bortezomib-based regimens, lenalidomide, daratumumab, autologous stem cell transplant

cards.q: What is Waldenström macroglobulinemia (lymphoplasmacytic)?
cards.a: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma producing IgM → hyperviscosity syndrome

cards.q: What is the treatment for symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenström?
cards.a: Plasmapheresis

cards.q: What is the most common bleeding disorder in uremia?
cards.a: Qualitative platelet dysfunction (due to uremic toxins)

cards.q: What is the treatment for bleeding in uremic patients?
cards.a: Desmopressin (DDAVP) or cryoprecipitate

cards.q: What is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state in Caucasians?
cards.a: Factor V Leiden

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of heparin?
cards.a: Binds antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of low molecular weight heparin (LMWH)?
cards.a: Primarily inhibits factor Xa (more predictable than unfractionated heparin)

cards.q: What is the antidote for heparin overdose?
cards.a: Protamine sulfate

cards.q: What is the mechanism of warfarin?
cards.a: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → decreases synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X, Protein C & S)

cards.q: Why does warfarin initially cause a pro-thrombotic state?
cards.a: Protein C (short half-life) decreases faster than the procoagulant factors

cards.q: What is the target INR for most patients on warfarin?
What is the target INR for patients with mechanical heart valves?
What are direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) and their targets?
cards.a:
Rivaroxaban/Apixaban/Edoxaban: Factor Xa inhibitors
Dabigatran: Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor

cards.q: What is the reversal agent for unfractionated heparin?
cards.a: Protamine sulfate

cards.q: What is the most common cause of inherited thrombophilia in pregnancy?
cards.a: Factor V Leiden

cards.q: What is antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)?
cards.a: Autoantibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein) → arterial/venous thrombosis + recurrent miscarriages

cards.q: What is the lupus anticoagulant paradox?
cards.a: Prolongs aPTT in vitro but causes hypercoagulability in vivo

cards.q: What is the treatment for antiphospholipid syndrome?
cards.a: Warfarin (INR 2–3) or LMWH + low-dose aspirin in pregnancy

cards.q: What is the most common acquired cause of thrombophilia?
cards.a: Antiphospholipid syndrome

cards.q: What are the lab findings in DIC?
cards.a: ↑ PT/PTT, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes

cards.q: What is the most common trigger for acute DIC?
cards.a: Sepsis

cards.q: What is the treatment for DIC?
cards.a: Treat underlying cause + supportive care (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets if bleeding)

cards.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary hemostasis?
cards.a:
Primary: platelet plug formation
Secondary: coagulation cascade (fibrin clot)

cards.q: What test evaluates the intrinsic pathway?
cards.a: aPTT (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII)

cards.q: What test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?
cards.a: PT (factor VII)

cards.q: What test evaluates the common pathway?
cards.a: Both PT and aPTT (factors X, V, II, I)

cards.q: What is the bleeding time test used for?
cards.a: Assesses platelet function (prolonged in vWD, thrombocytopenia, aspirin use)

cards.q: What is the most common bleeding disorder in von Willebrand disease type 1?
cards.a: Quantitative deficiency of vWF

cards.q: What is the most severe form of von Willebrand disease?
cards.a: Type 3 (complete absence of vWF)

cards.q: What is the treatment for type 2B vWD?
cards.a: Avoid DDAVP (can worsen thrombocytopenia)

cards.q: What is the most common malignancy associated with DIC?
cards.a: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (M3 AML)

cards.q: What is the characteristic chromosomal translocation in APL?
cards.a: t(15;17) — PML-RARA fusion

cards.q: What is the specific treatment for APL?
cards.a: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) + arsenic trioxide

cards.q: What is the risk of ATRA induction in APL?
cards.a: Differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of eosinophilia?
cards.a: Allergic reactions / parasitic infections

cards.q: What malignancy is associated with Philadelphia chromosome?
cards.a: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)

cards.q: What is the blast percentage that defines blast crisis in CML?
cards.a: >20% blasts in blood or bone marrow

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for CML in chronic phase?
cards.a: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib first-line)

cards.q: What is the most common translocation in Burkitt lymphoma?
cards.a: t(8;14) — MYC overexpression

cards.q: What is the histologic appearance of Burkitt lymphoma?
cards.a: Starry sky pattern (macrophages with apoptotic debris among lymphoblasts)

cards.q: What is the most aggressive lymphoma?
cards.a: Burkitt lymphoma

cards.q: What is the most common indolent lymphoma?
cards.a: Follicular lymphoma

cards.q: What virus is strongly associated with primary effusion lymphoma?
cards.a: HHV-8 (in HIV patients)

cards.q: What is the most common cause of superior vena cava syndrome?
cards.a: Lung cancer (small cell)

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome in small cell lung cancer?
cards.a: SIADH

cards.q: What is tumor lysis syndrome?
cards.a: Massive cell death after chemotherapy → hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, acute kidney injury

cards.q: What is the prophylaxis for tumor lysis syndrome?
cards.a: Allopurinol or rasburicase + hydration + urinary alkalinization

cards.q: What is the most common leukemia in infants?
cards.a: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)

cards.q: What is the prognosis of ALL with t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome?
cards.a: Poor prognosis

cards.q: What is the most common childhood solid tumor metastasis to bone marrow?
cards.a: Neuroblastoma

cards.q: What is the characteristic finding in hairy cell leukemia?
cards.a: Hairy projections on B cells, TRAP positive, splenomegaly, pancytopenia

cards.q: What is the treatment for hairy cell leukemia?
cards.a: Cladribine or pentostatin

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in CLL?
cards.a: Infection

cards.q: What is the most common cause of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia in children?
cards.a: Viral infection

cards.q: What is Evans syndrome?
cards.a: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia + immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

cards.q: What is the embryological origin of the CNS?
cards.a: Neuroectoderm (neural plate → neural tube). Neural crest cells give rise to PNS ganglia, Schwann cells, meninges, and adrenal medulla.

cards.q: What are the three primary brain vesicles?
cards.a:
Prosencephalon (forebrain) → Telencephalon + Diencephalon
Mesencephalon (midbrain)
Rhombencephalon (hindbrain) → Metencephalon + Myelencephalon

cards.q: What adult structures derive from the telencephalon?
cards.a: Cerebral hemispheres, cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, hippocampus, amygdala, olfactory bulbs.

cards.q: What adult structures derive from the diencephalon?
cards.a: Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (pineal), subthalamus, neurohypophysis.

cards.q: What adult structures derive from the mesencephalon?
cards.a: Midbrain (tectum, tegmentum, cerebral peduncles, substantia nigra, red nucleus).

cards.q: What adult structures derive from the metencephalon?
cards.a: Pons + Cerebellum.

cards.q: What adult structure derives from the myelencephalon?
cards.a: Medulla oblongata.

cards.q: What is the most common site for lumbar puncture in adults?
cards.a: L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace (spinal cord ends at L1–L2 in adults; L3 in infants).

cards.q: What layers are penetrated during LP (superficial to deep)?
cards.a: Skin → Subcut. tissue → Supraspinous lig. → Interspinous lig. → Ligamentum flavum → Epidural space → Dura → Arachnoid → Subarachnoid space (CSF).

cards.q: What is the function of the Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscus pathway?
cards.a: Fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception. Decussates in medulla (internal arcuate fibers).

cards.q: Where are the first-order neurons of DCML located?
cards.a: Dorsal root ganglia. Ascend ipsilaterally in fasciculus gracilis (lower body) or cuneatus (upper body).

cards.q: Where does the spinothalamic tract decussate?
cards.a: Anterior white commissure at or 1–2 segments above entry level (anterolateral system).

cards.q: What sensations are carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract?
cards.a: Pain and temperature.

cards.q: What sensations are carried by the anterior spinothalamic tract?
cards.a: Crude (light) touch and pressure.

cards.q: What are the classic findings in Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection)?
cards.a:
Ipsilateral: UMN weakness, loss of vibration/proprioception (DCML), loss of tactile discrimination.
Contralateral: Loss of pain/temperature (spinothalamic) starting 1–2 segments below lesion.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries). Supplies anterior horns, corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts.

cards.q: What is the Artery of Adamkiewicz?
cards.a: Major radicular artery supplying the lower thoracic and lumbar cord (usually left, T9–T12). Damage → anterior spinal artery syndrome.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of anterior spinal artery occlusion?
cards.a: Bilateral loss of motor function + pain/temperature below lesion. Preserved dorsal column sensations (vibration/proprioception).

cards.q: Which cranial nerve is the only one to exit the brainstem dorsally?
cards.a: CN IV (Trochlear nerve) — decussates in superior medullary velum.

cards.q: Which cranial nerve is the only purely motor nerve that innervates a muscle on the contralateral side?
cards.a: CN IV (superior oblique).

cards.q: What is the function of CN III (Oculomotor)?
cards.a: Motor to all extraocular muscles except LR (CN VI) and SO (CN IV). Parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle (pupillary constriction + accommodation).

cards.q: What is the result of a CN III lesion?
cards.a: Down-and-out eye, ptosis, mydriasis (dilated pupil), loss of accommodation.

cards.q: What is the function of CN VI (Abducens)?
cards.a: Lateral rectus muscle (abduction). Most commonly affected in raised ICP (long intracranial course).

cards.q: What is the result of a CN VI lesion?
cards.a: Medial strabismus (inability to abduct affected eye).

cards.q: Which nucleus is the motor nucleus for CN IX, X, XI (cranial root)?
cards.a: Nucleus ambiguus (branchiomotor to pharynx/larynx).

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue?
cards.a: CN VII via chorda tympani (to nucleus solitarius).

cards.q: Which cranial nerve carries taste from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue?
cards.a: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) to nucleus solitarius.

cards.q: What is the afferent and efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
cards.a:
Afferent: CN II
Efferent: CN III (parasympathetic fibers from Edinger-Westphal nucleus).

cards.q: What is the triad of Horner syndrome?
cards.a:
1. Ptosis (Müller’s muscle)
2. Miosis (dilator pupillae)
3. Anhidrosis (facial sweating). Caused by sympathetic chain interruption.

cards.q: Where is the lesion in central Horner syndrome vs. peripheral?
cards.a:
Central: brainstem/spinal cord (e.g., Wallenberg).
Peripheral: cervical sympathetic chain, superior cervical ganglion, carotid sheath.

cards.q: What artery occlusion causes Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome?
cards.a: PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar artery) or vertebral artery.

cards.q: List key findings in Wallenberg syndrome.
cards.a:
Ipsilateral: Horner’s, facial pain/temp loss, ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus).
Contralateral: body pain/temp loss.

cards.q: What is the most common site of saccular (berry) aneurysm?
cards.a: Anterior communicating artery (junction with ACA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the primary visual cortex?
cards.a: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) (calcarine branch). Macular sparing in PCA stroke due to MCA collateral.

cards.q: What artery supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere and lower limb motor/sensory cortex?
cards.a: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

cards.q: What artery supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere (face/arm motor/sensory, Broca’s, Wernicke’s)?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery (MCA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the internal capsule?
cards.a: Lenticulostriate branches of MCA (putaminal and caudate branches) + anterior choroidal artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
cards.a: Basal ganglia (putamen) due to Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriate arteries.

cards.q: What structure is the major relay for all sensory information except olfaction?
cards.a: Thalamus (specific nuclei: VPL, VPM, LGN, MGN, etc.).

cards.q: What is the function of the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus?
cards.a: Somatosensory input from body (spinothalamic and DCML) → postcentral gyrus.

cards.q: What is the function of the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus?
cards.a: Somatosensory input from face (trigeminothalamic) + taste.

cards.q: What thalamic nucleus receives input from the mammillary bodies?
cards.a: Anterior nucleus (part of Papez circuit — memory).

cards.q: What is the function of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)?
cards.a: Visual information from retina → primary visual cortex (calcarine fissure).

cards.q: What is the function of the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)?
cards.a: Auditory information from inferior colliculus → primary auditory cortex (Heschl’s gyrus).

cards.q: What nucleus is the primary motor relay from cerebellum to cortex?
cards.a: Ventrolateral (VL) nucleus of thalamus.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the thalamus?
cards.a: Posterior communicating artery + thalamoperforating branches of PCA + anterior choroidal artery.

cards.q: What are the components of the basal ganglia?
cards.a: Striatum (caudate + putamen), globus pallidus (externa + interna), subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra (pars compacta + reticulata).

cards.q: What is the direct pathway of the basal ganglia?
cards.a: Striatum (D1 receptors) → inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits thalamus → facilitates movement (excitatory to cortex).

cards.q: What is the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia?
cards.a: Striatum (D2 receptors) → inhibits GPe → disinhibits STN → excites GPi → inhibits thalamus → inhibits movement.

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is depleted in Parkinson disease?
cards.a: Dopamine from substantia nigra pars compacta (nigrostriatal pathway).

cards.q: What is the classic lesion in Huntington disease?
cards.a: Atrophy of striatum (especially caudate nucleus) → decreased GABA and ACh.

cards.q: What is the function of the subthalamic nucleus?
cards.a: Excitatory (glutamate) to GPi. Lesion → hemiballismus.

cards.q: What artery supplies the internal capsule and basal ganglia?
cards.a: Lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the midbrain?
cards.a: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and branches of the basilar artery (paramedian and circumferential branches).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the pons?
cards.a: Basilar artery (paramedian, short circumferential, and long circumferential branches including AICA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the medulla?
cards.a: Vertebral arteries and branches (PICA supplies lateral medulla).

cards.q: What cranial nerves exit at the pontomedullary junction?
cards.a: CN VI, VII, VIII.

cards.q: What is the location of the facial colliculus?
cards.a: Floor of the 4th ventricle in the pons. Formed by the facial nerve fibers looping around the abducens nucleus.

cards.q: What nucleus is located in the floor of the 4th ventricle at the level of the upper medulla?
cards.a: Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII).

cards.q: What is the function of the inferior olivary nucleus?
cards.a: Major source of climbing fibers to the cerebellum. Involved in motor learning.

cards.q: What are the three cerebellar peduncles and their main connections?
cards.a:
Superior: Cerebellum → midbrain (dentatorubrothalamic).
Middle: Pontine nuclei → cerebellum (corticopontocerebellar).
Inferior: Spinal cord/olivary → cerebellum.

cards.q: What is the function of the dentate nucleus?
cards.a: Major output nucleus of the lateral cerebellar hemisphere (planning and execution of skilled movements).

cards.q: What is the function of the fastigial nucleus?
cards.a: Vermis output — regulation of axial and proximal muscles, balance, and eye movements.

cards.q: What are the deep cerebellar nuclei (from lateral to medial)?
cards.a: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial (Don't Eat Greasy Foods).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a cerebellar hemisphere lesion?
cards.a: Ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion?
cards.a: Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, nystagmus.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the superior surface of the cerebellum?
cards.a: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the inferior surface of the cerebellum?
cards.a: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA).

cards.q: What artery is most commonly involved in lateral pontine syndrome?
cards.a: AICA.

cards.q: What are the key findings in AICA syndrome (lateral pontine)?
cards.a: Ipsilateral facial paralysis (CN VII), hearing loss/tinnitus (CN VIII), ataxia, Horner syndrome, contralateral pain/temp loss.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of locked-in syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral ventral pontine infarction (basilar artery occlusion) sparing the tegmentum.

cards.q: What structure is damaged in central pontine myelinolysis?
cards.a: Basis pontis (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts) — usually due to rapid correction of hyponatremia.

cards.q: What is the function of the locus ceruleus?
cards.a: Major noradrenergic nucleus in the pons. Involved in arousal, attention, and stress response.

cards.q: What is the function of the raphe nuclei?
cards.a: Major serotonergic nuclei in the brainstem. Modulate mood, sleep, and pain.

cards.q: Where is the substantia nigra located and what is its function?
cards.a: Midbrain. Pars compacta produces dopamine for nigrostriatal pathway.

cards.q: Where is the red nucleus located and what is its function?
cards.a: Midbrain tegmentum. Involved in motor coordination (rubrospinal tract).

cards.q: What is the Edinger-Westphal nucleus?
cards.a: Parasympathetic nucleus of CN III in the midbrain. Controls pupillary constriction and accommodation.

cards.q: What is the pretectal area responsible for?
cards.a: Pupillary light reflex (connects optic tract to Edinger-Westphal nuclei bilaterally).

cards.q: What structure is damaged in Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome)?
cards.a: Posterior commissure and pretectal area — vertical gaze palsy (especially upward), light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus.

cards.q: What is Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Midbrain base lesion (CN III + corticospinal tract) — ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.

cards.q: What is Benedikt syndrome?
cards.a: Midbrain tegmentum (CN III + red nucleus) — ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia/tremor.

cards.q: What are the layers of the cerebral cortex (from superficial to deep)?
cards.a: Molecular, External granular, External pyramidal, Internal granular, Internal pyramidal, Multiform (May Every Engineer In Italy Make Money).

cards.q: Which cortical layer is the major output layer to subcortical structures?
cards.a: Layer V (internal pyramidal) — gives rise to corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticostriatal tracts.

cards.q: Which cortical layer receives the bulk of thalamic input?
cards.a: Layer IV (internal granular).

cards.q: What is the primary motor cortex location and blood supply?
cards.a: Precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4) — supplied by MCA (lateral) and ACA (medial/leg).

cards.q: What is the primary somatosensory cortex location?
cards.a: Postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3,1,2).

cards.q: What is Broca’s area location and function?
cards.a: Inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann 44/45) — motor speech production (dominant hemisphere).

cards.q: What is Wernicke’s area location and function?
cards.a: Superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann 22) — language comprehension.

cards.q: What artery supplies Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery (superior division for Broca’s, inferior for Wernicke’s).

cards.q: What is the arcuate fasciculus?
cards.a: White matter tract connecting Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas. Lesion → conduction aphasia.

cards.q: What are the key features of conduction aphasia?
cards.a: Fluent speech, intact comprehension, but poor repetition. Often with phonemic paraphasias.

cards.q: What is the function of the frontal eye fields (Brodmann 8)?
cards.a: Voluntary conjugate horizontal eye movements to the contralateral side.

cards.q: What is Gerstmann syndrome?
cards.a: Dominant parietal lobe (angular gyrus) lesion — agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.

cards.q: What is the function of the hippocampus?
cards.a: Formation of new declarative (episodic) memories. Part of the Papez circuit.

cards.q: What is the Papez circuit (memory circuit)?
cards.a: Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus → entorhinal cortex → hippocampus.

cards.q: What structure is damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a: Mammillary bodies (and dorsomedial thalamus) due to thiamine deficiency.

cards.q: What is the major output tract of the hippocampus?
cards.a: Fornix.

cards.q: What is the amygdala responsible for?
cards.a: Emotional processing, fear conditioning, and emotional memory.

cards.q: What is Kluver-Bucy syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral amygdala lesion — hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia.

cards.q: What are the lateral and medial lemnisci?
cards.a:
Lateral = auditory pathway.
Medial = dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.

cards.q: What is the reticular formation responsible for?
cards.a: Arousal, attention, sleep-wake cycle, and autonomic functions (RAS — reticular activating system).

cards.q: What are the two main types of hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Communicating (impaired absorption) and Non-communicating/obstructive (blockage within ventricular system).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Aqueductal stenosis.

cards.q: What is the flow of CSF?
cards.a: Lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → foramina of Luschka (lateral) & Magendie (median) → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → superior sagittal sinus.

cards.q: Where are most arachnoid granulations located?
cards.a: Superior sagittal sinus.

cards.q: What is the clinical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Wet, Wobbly, Wacky — urinary incontinence, gait apraxia (magnetic gait), dementia.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, most commonly at the anterior communicating artery.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache, often described as 'worst headache of my life', meningismus, photophobia, altered mental status.

cards.q: What CSF finding is diagnostic of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Xanthochromia (yellowish discoloration due to bilirubin) after 6–12 hours. Also elevated RBCs that do not clear in successive tubes.

cards.q: What is the most common complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Vasospasm (delayed cerebral ischemia) occurring 4–14 days after bleed. Treated with nimodipine.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) — WHO grade IV astrocytoma. Butterfly lesion crossing corpus callosum.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in children?
cards.a: Pilocytic astrocytoma (posterior fossa) followed by medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with bitemporal hemianopia?
cards.a: Pituitary adenoma (compresses optic chiasm).

cards.q: What tumor is associated with Homer-Wright rosettes?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma (primitive neuroectodermal tumor, posterior fossa).

cards.q: What tumor shows perivascular pseudorosettes and is often in the 4th ventricle in children?
cards.a: Ependymoma.

cards.q: What is the most common supratentorial tumor in children?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma — derived from Rathke pouch remnants, calcified, causes bitemporal hemianopia and endocrine dysfunction.

cards.q: What histology is classic for oligodendroglioma?
cards.a: Fried egg appearance (perinuclear halos) and chicken-wire vasculature. Often has 1p/19q codeletion.

cards.q: What tumor is strongly associated with NF2?
cards.a: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas).

cards.q: What is the most common intracranial tumor in patients with AIDS?
cards.a: Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated, ring-enhancing).

cards.q: What is the ring-enhancing lesion differential in AIDS patients?
cards.a: Toxoplasmosis (most common), Primary CNS lymphoma, abscess, PML (non-enhancing usually).

cards.q: What is the histology of meningioma?
cards.a: Whorls and psammoma bodies. Strongly attached to dura. Expresses EMA.

cards.q: What is the most common location for meningioma?
cards.a: Parasagittal region or convexities.

cards.q: What tumor shows Antoni A and Antoni B areas with Verocay bodies?
cards.a: Schwannoma.

cards.q: What is the most common peripheral nerve sheath tumor?
cards.a: Schwannoma (arises from Schwann cells, S-100 positive).

cards.q: What cranial nerve is most commonly affected by schwannoma?
cards.a: Vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) — vestibular schwannoma.

cards.q: What is the inheritance and classic skin finding in Neurofibromatosis Type 1?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (NF1 gene, chromosome 17). >=6 café-au-lait spots.

cards.q: What is the inheritance and classic finding in Neurofibromatosis Type 2?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (NF2 gene, chromosome 22). Bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of tuberous sclerosis?
cards.a:
1. Facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum)
2. Seizures
3. Intellectual disability. Also cortical tubers, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA).

cards.q: What is Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in V1 distribution + leptomeningeal angiomatosis + glaucoma + seizures. Tram-track calcifications on CT.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric posterior fossa tumor?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary spinal cord tumor in adults?
cards.a: Ependymoma (especially myxopapillary in filum terminale).

cards.q: What is syringomyelia?
cards.a: Central canal dilation (syrinx) in cervical cord. Classic cape-like bilateral loss of pain and temperature (crossing spinothalamic fibers).

cards.q: What condition is syringomyelia most commonly associated with?
cards.a: Chiari I malformation.

cards.q: What is Chiari I malformation?
cards.a: Cerebellar tonsils herniate >5 mm below foramen magnum. Associated with syringomyelia.

cards.q: What is Chiari II malformation?
cards.a: Cerebellar vermis + tonsils herniate through foramen magnum + myelomeningocele.

cards.q: What is Dandy-Walker malformation?
cards.a: Agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis + cystic dilation of 4th ventricle + enlarged posterior fossa. Associated with hydrocephalus.

cards.q: What neural tube defect is associated with elevated maternal AFP and acetylcholinesterase?
cards.a: Anencephaly or open spina bifida (myelomeningocele).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates?
cards.a: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in young adults?
cards.a: Neisseria meningitidis.

cards.q: What organism causes meningitis with India ink positive CSF?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans.

cards.q: What is the classic CSF finding in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
cards.a: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with normal WBC count.

cards.q: What is tabes dorsalis?
cards.a: Tertiary neurosyphilis — demyelination of dorsal columns and dorsal roots → loss of proprioception/vibration, Argyll Robertson pupils, positive Romberg.

cards.q: What is the pathology in subacute combined degeneration?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency — demyelination of dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal tracts.

cards.q: What is the classic finding in myasthenia gravis on repetitive nerve stimulation?
cards.a: Decremental response.

cards.q: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer. Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Incremental response on high-frequency stimulation.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy overall?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus (distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?
cards.a: Most commonly autosomal dominant (CMT1 — demyelinating).

cards.q: What is the pathology in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
cards.a: Combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration. Loss of anterior horn cells and corticospinal tract degeneration. TDP-43 inclusions.

cards.q: What is the most common motor neuron disease in children?
cards.a: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) — SMN1 gene deletion.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Thiamine (B1) deficiency — mammillary body hemorrhage/necrosis, periventricular petechiae, confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia.

cards.q: What is the classic EEG finding in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)?
cards.a: Periodic sharp wave complexes.

cards.q: What protein is deposited in cerebral amyloid angiopathy?
cards.a: Abeta (amyloid-beta) — causes lobar hemorrhages in elderly.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of lobar hemorrhage in elderly patients?
cards.a: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

cards.q: What is the pathology of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
cards.a: JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes → demyelination. Seen in severely immunocompromised patients.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery (branch of maxillary artery) usually due to temporal bone fracture. Lens-shaped (biconvex) hyperdensity on CT.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Rupture of bridging veins. Crescentic (concave) hyperdensity that crosses suture lines but not dural reflections. Common in elderly and alcoholics.

cards.q: What is the characteristic CT appearance of an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines.

cards.q: What is the characteristic CT appearance of a subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Crescentic (banana-shaped) hyperdensity that crosses suture lines.

cards.q: What is the most common site of a contrecoup injury?
cards.a: Inferior frontal and anterior temporal lobes (against the rough surfaces of the skull base).

cards.q: What is diffuse axonal injury (DAI) pathologically characterized by?
cards.a: Axonal retraction balls (best seen with beta-APP immunohistochemistry). Caused by shear forces in high-speed trauma.

cards.q: What is the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Gait disturbance (magnetic gait), urinary incontinence, dementia ('wet, wobbly, wacky').

cards.q: What is the treatment for normal pressure hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of communicating hydrocephalus in adults?
cards.a: Subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis (impaired CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations).

cards.q: What is the most common site of obstruction in non-communicating hydrocephalus in children?
cards.a: Cerebral aqueduct (aqueductal stenosis).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the anterior limb of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Anterior cerebral artery (medial striate branches) and some MCA lenticulostriates.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the posterior limb of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery lenticulostriate branches + anterior choroidal artery.

cards.q: What is the clinical effect of a lesion in the anterior limb of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Primarily frontal lobe disconnection symptoms (e.g., abulia, personality changes).

cards.q: What is the clinical effect of a lesion in the genu of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Contralateral facial weakness (corticobulbar fibers).

cards.q: What is the clinical effect of a lesion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal) and hemisensory loss.

cards.q: What artery supplies the lateral medulla?
cards.a: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

cards.q: What artery supplies the medial medulla?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery.

cards.q: What is the most common site of lacunar infarcts?
cards.a: Basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, and pons (small vessel disease due to hypertension).

cards.q: What is the pathology of lacunar infarcts?
cards.a: Lipohyalinosis and microatheroma of small penetrating arteries.

cards.q: What syndrome results from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery in the spinal cord?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery syndrome — bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function.

cards.q: What is the most common demyelinating disease of the CNS?
cards.a: Multiple sclerosis.

cards.q: What are the classic MRI findings in multiple sclerosis?
cards.a: Periventricular white matter lesions perpendicular to the ventricles ('Dawson’s fingers'), ovoid lesions, and involvement of corpus callosum, spinal cord, and optic nerves.

cards.q: What CSF finding is characteristic of multiple sclerosis?
cards.a: Oligoclonal bands (IgG) on electrophoresis.

cards.q: What is the most common site of involvement in multiple sclerosis?
cards.a: Optic nerve (optic neuritis) and periventricular white matter.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
cards.a: Immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy).

cards.q: What antibody is associated with Miller-Fisher variant of GBS?
cards.a: Anti-GQ1b — ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ascending paralysis in children?
cards.a: Guillain-Barré syndrome.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of myotonic dystrophy type 1?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant with anticipation (CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene).

cards.q: What are the classic features of myotonic dystrophy?
cards.a: Myotonia, frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy, cardiac conduction defects, distal muscle weakness.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked dystrophin gene mutation → absent dystrophin → pseudohypertrophy of calves, Gowers sign.

cards.q: What is the difference between Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy?
cards.a:
Duchenne: complete absence of dystrophin (severe, early onset).
Becker: partial dystrophin function (milder, later onset).

cards.q: What is the most common mitochondrial myopathy?
cards.a: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of mitochondrial diseases?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: Mitochondrial DNA deletion — progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction block.

cards.q: What is the most common leukodystrophy?
cards.a: Metachromatic leukodystrophy — arylsulfatase A deficiency.

cards.q: What is the enzyme deficient in Krabbe disease?
cards.a: Galactocerebrosidase — globoid cells on histology.

cards.q: What storage disease shows 'crumpled tissue paper' macrophages?
cards.a: Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency).

cards.q: What disease shows cherry-red spot on macula?
cards.a: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) and Niemann-Pick disease.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of adrenoleukodystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked — ABCD1 mutation, accumulation of very long chain fatty acids.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Marchiafava-Bignami disease?
cards.a: Demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum — seen in chronic alcoholics.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of central pontine myelinolysis?
cards.a: Locked-in syndrome or spastic quadriparesis following rapid correction of hyponatremia.

cards.q: What toxin causes bilateral globus pallidus necrosis and parkinsonism?
cards.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Wilson disease?
cards.a: ATP7B mutation → copper accumulation in basal ganglia (especially putamen) and liver. Kayser-Fleischer rings.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of viral encephalitis with temporal lobe involvement?
What are Cowdry type A inclusions seen in?
cards.a: HSV encephalitis (eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions).

cards.q: What prion disease is associated with cannibalism?
cards.a: Kuru.

cards.q: What is the classic EEG finding in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
cards.a: Periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz.

cards.q: What CSF marker is elevated in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
cards.a: 14-3-3 protein.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome?
cards.a: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration?
cards.a: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) — breast/ovarian cancer.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of intracerebral hemorrhage in young adults?
cards.a: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) or hypertension (in older adults).

cards.q: What is the characteristic histology of pilocytic astrocytoma?
cards.a: Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. Most common pediatric brain tumor in cerebellum.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with 'chicken-wire' vasculature and fried-egg appearance?
cards.a: Oligodendroglioma.

cards.q: What is the most common extra-axial brain tumor?
cards.a: Meningioma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary CNS lymphoma histology?
cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, often perivascular.

cards.q: What virus is associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
cards.a: JC virus (polyomavirus).

cards.q: What is the treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis in AIDS?
cards.a: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin.

cards.q: What is the most common metastatic brain tumors?
cards.a: Lung > Breast > Melanoma > Kidney > GI (lung most common overall).

cards.q: What is the classic location for central pontine myelinolysis?
cards.a: Basis pontis.

cards.q: What vitamin deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Friedreich ataxia?
cards.a: GAA trinucleotide repeat in frataxin gene → mitochondrial dysfunction. Degeneration of dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of Friedreich ataxia?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary) regarding pain/temp loss?
cards.a: Ipsilateral face + contralateral body.

cards.q: What structure is damaged in pure motor hemiparesis lacunar stroke?
cards.a: Posterior limb of internal capsule or basis pontis.

cards.q: What structure is damaged in ataxic hemiparesis lacunar stroke?
cards.a: Basis pontis or internal capsule.

cards.q: What is the function of the nucleus solitarius?
cards.a: Visceral sensory and taste (CN VII, IX, X).

cards.q: What is the function of the nucleus ambiguus?
cards.a: Motor to pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles (CN IX, X, XI cranial root).

cards.q: What is the function of the dorsal motor nucleus of vagus?
cards.a: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to thoracic and abdominal viscera.

cards.q: What is the most common site of hypertensive hemorrhage in the brainstem?
cards.a: Pons.

cards.q: What is the classic finding in a PCA stroke?
cards.a: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

cards.q: What is the classic finding in an ACA stroke?
cards.a: Contralateral lower extremity weakness and sensory loss.

cards.q: What is the classic finding in an MCA stroke (dominant hemisphere)?
cards.a: Contralateral hemiparesis (face/arm > leg), aphasia (if dominant), hemineglect (if non-dominant).

cards.q: What artery is occluded in 'top of the basilar' syndrome?
cards.a: Basilar artery tip affecting midbrain and thalami.

cards.q: What is Anton syndrome?
cards.a: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness (occipital lobe lesion).

cards.q: What is Balint syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral parietal-occipital lesions → optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, simultanagnosia.

cards.q: What is Gerstmann syndrome location?
cards.a: Dominant inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the hippocampus?
cards.a: Anterior choroidal artery and posterior cerebral artery branches.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy?
cards.a: Hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis).

cards.q: What structure is damaged in prosopagnosia?
cards.a: Fusiform gyrus (face recognition area).

cards.q: What is the function of the supramarginal gyrus?
cards.a: Language (dominant) and spatial awareness.

cards.q: What is the function of the angular gyrus?
cards.a: Reading, writing, and calculation (dominant hemisphere).

cards.q: What is the most common site of embolic stroke?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery territory.

cards.q: What is the most common site of lacunar stroke?
cards.a: Lenticulostriate territory (basal ganglia/internal capsule).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a putaminal hemorrhage?
cards.a: Contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss, possible aphasia or neglect.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of thalamic hemorrhage?
cards.a: Contralateral hemisensory loss, possible hemiparesis if internal capsule involved.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of cerebellar hemorrhage?
cards.a: Ataxia, headache, vomiting, possible hydrocephalus.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric supratentorial tumor?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric infratentorial tumor?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma or pilocytic astrocytoma.

cards.q: What tumor shows 'pseudopalisading' necrosis and endothelial proliferation?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with ' Homer-Wright rosettes'?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with 'perivascular pseudorosettes'?
cards.a: Ependymoma.

cards.q: What tumor shows psammoma bodies?
cards.a: Meningioma.

cards.q: What is the most common sellar/suprasellar tumor in children?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in HIV patients?
cards.a: Primary CNS lymphoma.

cards.q: What is the treatment for primary CNS lymphoma?
cards.a: High-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy ± radiation.

cards.q: What is the most common complication after subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Vasospasm (treated prophylactically with nimodipine).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of non-traumatic subdural hematoma in elderly?
cards.a: Brain atrophy with stretching of bridging veins.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epidural hematoma in children?
cards.a: Skull fracture with middle meningeal artery laceration.

cards.q: What are the major components of a typical neuron?
cards.a:
Dendrites (receive signals) → Cell body (soma) (integrates) → Axon hillock (action potential initiation) → Axon (conducts) → Axon terminals (synaptic release).
Note: Myelin sheath + Nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons.

cards.q: What is the resting membrane potential of a neuron and its primary cause?
cards.a:
-70 mV.
Maintained by:
• High K+ permeability (leak channels)
• Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in)
• Large intracellular anions.

cards.q: Describe the phases of an action potential with ion movements.
cards.a:
1. Resting (-70 mV)
2. Depolarization: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ influx (+30 mV)
3. Peak
4. Repolarization: Na+ channels inactivate, K+ channels open → K+ efflux
5. Hyperpolarization (afterhyperpolarization)
6. Return to resting.

cards.q: What is the absolute vs relative refractory period?
cards.a:
Absolute: No new AP possible (Na+ channels inactivated).
Relative: Stronger-than-normal stimulus can trigger AP (some Na+ channels recovered, membrane hyperpolarized).

cards.q: What determines conduction velocity in axons?
cards.a:
1. Axon diameter (larger = faster)
2. Myelination (saltatory conduction via Nodes of Ranvier).
Myelinated axons conduct at 5-120 m/s vs 0.5-10 m/s unmyelinated.

cards.q: What is saltatory conduction and its advantage?
cards.a:
Action potential jumps between Nodes of Ranvier.
Advantages: Faster conduction + energy efficient (less Na+/K+ pumping needed).

cards.q: List the major ion channels involved in action potential generation.
cards.a:
• Voltage-gated Na+ channels (depolarization)
• Voltage-gated K+ channels (repolarization)
• Leak K+ channels (resting potential)
• Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (presynaptic terminal).

cards.q: Compare EPSP vs IPSP.
cards.a:
EPSP (Excitatory): Depolarizing (Na+/Ca2+ influx) — brings closer to threshold.
IPSP (Inhibitory): Hyperpolarizing (Cl- influx or K+ efflux) — moves away from threshold.
Summation (spatial + temporal) determines firing.

cards.q: What are the steps of chemical synaptic transmission?
cards.a:
1. AP arrives at terminal → Ca2+ influx
2. Vesicle fusion (SNARE proteins) → neurotransmitter release
3. Binding to postsynaptic receptors
4. Postsynaptic potential change
5. Neurotransmitter removal (reuptake, degradation, diffusion).

cards.q: Name the major excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in CNS.
cards.a:
Excitatory: Glutamate (NMDA, AMPA, kainate receptors)
Inhibitory: GABA (GABA-A/Cl-, GABA-B), Glycine.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin vs tetanus toxin?
cards.a:
Botulinum: Cleaves SNARE proteins → blocks ACh release at NMJ (flaccid paralysis).
Tetanus: Blocks inhibitory (GABA/glycine) release in spinal cord (spastic paralysis).

cards.q: Describe the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) transmission.
cards.a:
Motor neuron → ACh release → binds nicotinic receptors → Na+ influx → end-plate potential → muscle AP → contraction.
Degraded by acetylcholinesterase.

cards.q: What are the types of acetylcholine receptors?
cards.a:
Nicotinic: Ligand-gated ion channels (NMJ, autonomic ganglia).
Muscarinic: G-protein coupled (parasympathetic effectors).

cards.q: What is temporal vs spatial summation?
cards.a:
Temporal: Multiple signals from same synapse in quick succession.
Spatial: Simultaneous signals from different synapses.

cards.q: What is long-term potentiation (LTP)?
cards.a:
Persistent strengthening of synapses based on recent patterns of activity.
Key: NMDA receptor activation → Ca2+ influx → AMPA receptor insertion (glutamate, hippocampus).

cards.q: What is the difference between myelinated and unmyelinated axons in PNS vs CNS?
cards.a:
PNS: Schwann cells (one axon per cell).
CNS: Oligodendrocytes (one cell myelinates multiple axons).

cards.q: List the sensory receptor types and adequate stimuli.
cards.a:
• Mechanoreceptors (touch/pressure)
• Thermoreceptors (temperature)
• Nociceptors (pain)
• Chemoreceptors (taste, smell, blood gases)
• Photoreceptors (vision)
• Proprioceptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs).

cards.q: What is the law of specific nerve energies?
cards.a: A sensory nerve is excited by only one type of stimulus and produces only one sensation regardless of how it is stimulated. (Muller's law)

cards.q: Describe the pathway for fine touch, vibration, proprioception.
cards.a:
Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscus pathway:
1st neuron: dorsal root ganglion → dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus) → medulla (nucleus gracilis/cuneatus) → decussation (internal arcuate fibers) → medial lemniscus → thalamus (VPL) → somatosensory cortex.

cards.q: Describe the anterolateral (spinothalamic) pathway.
cards.a:
Pain, temperature, crude touch.
1st neuron → dorsal horn → decussation in anterior white commissure → lateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus (VPL) → cortex.

cards.q: What is the somatotopic organization in the primary somatosensory cortex?
cards.a: Homunculus — medial = lower limb, lateral = face (homunculus is upside-down and distorted).

cards.q: What are the two main visual pathways after the lateral geniculate nucleus?
cards.a:
Dorsal stream (where/how — parietal lobe, motion/spatial).
Ventral stream (what — temporal lobe, object recognition).

cards.q: What is the function of rods vs cones?
cards.a:
Rods: Low light (scotopic), high sensitivity, no color, peripheral vision.
Cones: Color (photopic), high acuity, central (fovea).

cards.q: What is the pathway of the pupillary light reflex?
cards.a: Retina → optic nerve → pretectal nucleus → Edinger-Westphal nucleus → CN III (parasympathetic) → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae (bilateral constriction).

cards.q: What is the auditory pathway (brief)?
cards.a: Cochlea (hair cells) → cochlear nerve (CN VIII) → cochlear nuclei → superior olivary complex → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus → primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus).

cards.q: What is the function of the vestibular system?
cards.a: Detects head position and acceleration (semicircular canals for angular, utricle/saccule for linear).

cards.q: What is the stretch (myotatic) reflex pathway?
cards.a: Muscle spindle (Ia afferent) → dorsal root → monosynaptic to alpha motor neuron → muscle contraction (e.g., knee jerk — L3/L4).

cards.q: What is the inverse stretch (Golgi tendon) reflex?
cards.a: Golgi tendon organ (Ib afferent) → inhibits alpha motor neuron (via inhibitory interneuron) to protect against excessive tension.

cards.q: What is the withdrawal (flexor) reflex?
cards.a: Polysynaptic nociceptive reflex — withdraws limb from painful stimulus + crossed extensor reflex for balance.

cards.q: Compare upper motor neuron (UMN) vs lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions.
cards.a:
UMN: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, clonus.
LMN: Flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia/areflexia, fasciculations, atrophy.

cards.q: What are the major descending motor pathways?
cards.a:
• Corticospinal (pyramidal) — voluntary skilled movement
• Vestibulospinal — balance/posture
• Reticulospinal — locomotion/posture
• Rubrospinal — flexor tone (less prominent in humans).

cards.q: What is the function of the basal ganglia?
cards.a: Initiation and modulation of voluntary movement, procedural learning, reward.

cards.q: What is the direct vs indirect pathway in basal ganglia?
cards.a:
Direct (facilitates movement): Striatum → inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits thalamus.
Indirect (inhibits movement): Striatum → GPe → STN → GPi → inhibits thalamus.

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is lost in Parkinson disease?
cards.a: Dopamine from substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum (nigrostriatal pathway).

cards.q: What is the function of the cerebellum?
cards.a: Coordination of movement, error correction, motor learning, balance.

cards.q: What are the three functional divisions of the cerebellum?
cards.a:
1. Vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular) — balance/eye movements
2. Spinocerebellum (vermis + intermediate) — limb/trunk coordination
3. Cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) — planning/sequencing.

cards.q: What are the clinical signs of cerebellar dysfunction?
cards.a: DANISH: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia.

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the brain (major arteries)?
cards.a:
• Anterior cerebral (ACA)
• Middle cerebral (MCA)
• Posterior cerebral (PCA)
Formed by internal carotid + vertebrobasilar systems → Circle of Willis.

cards.q: What is the function of the hypothalamus?
cards.a: Homeostasis (temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, autonomic control, endocrine via pituitary).

cards.q: What is the reticular activating system (RAS)?
cards.a: Brainstem nuclei (locus ceruleus, raphe, etc.) that maintain arousal and consciousness.

cards.q: What are the stages of sleep and their EEG patterns?
cards.a:
• Wake: Beta → Alpha
• N1: Theta
• N2: Sleep spindles + K-complexes
• N3: Delta (slow-wave)
• REM: Beta-like (paradoxical), sawtooth waves, atonia.

cards.q: What neurotransmitters promote wakefulness vs sleep?
cards.a:
Wake: Norepinephrine, Serotonin, Histamine, Orexin/Hypocretin, Acetylcholine.
Sleep: GABA, Adenosine, Melatonin.

cards.q: What is the Papez circuit (limbic system)?
cards.a: Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nuclei → cingulate gyrus → entorhinal cortex → hippocampus.

cards.q: What is the role of the hippocampus?
cards.a: Formation of new declarative (explicit) memories (episodic + semantic).

cards.q: What is the role of the amygdala?
cards.a: Emotional processing, especially fear and aggression; emotional tagging of memories.

cards.q: What is Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a:
Thiamine deficiency (alcoholics):
• Wernicke: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia
• Korsakoff: anterograde/retrograde amnesia + confabulation (mammillary body damage).

cards.q: What is the difference between Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia?
cards.a:
Broca's (non-fluent/expressive): frontal (inferior frontal gyrus) — good comprehension, poor production.
Wernicke's (fluent/receptive): temporal (superior temporal gyrus) — poor comprehension, fluent but nonsensical speech.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of tetrodotoxin (TTX) and saxitoxin?
cards.a: Block voltage-gated Na+ channels → prevent depolarization → paralysis. Found in pufferfish (TTX) and shellfish (saxitoxin).

cards.q: What is the effect of local anesthetics (e.g., lidocaine) on nerves?
cards.a: Block voltage-gated Na+ channels from inside the axon (use-dependent) → prevent action potential propagation. Small-diameter and myelinated fibers affected first.

cards.q: Which fibers have the highest conduction velocity?
cards.a: A-alpha fibers (proprioception, motor to skeletal muscle) — largest diameter, heavily myelinated.

cards.q: Classify peripheral nerve fibers by diameter and function (Erlanger-Gasser classification).
cards.a:
A-alpha: Proprioception, skeletal motor (fastest)
A-beta: Touch, pressure
A-delta: Sharp pain, temperature
C: Dull pain, temperature, postganglionic autonomic (slowest, unmyelinated).

cards.q: What is Wallerian degeneration?
cards.a: Degeneration of the distal portion of an axon after injury. Occurs in PNS (Schwann cells help regeneration) and CNS (limited regeneration).

cards.q: What is the difference between regeneration in PNS vs CNS?
cards.a:
PNS: Schwann cells form Bands of Bungner, release growth factors → good regeneration.
CNS: Oligodendrocytes inhibit regeneration (Nogo, MAG), glial scar formation.

cards.q: Name the excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters and their receptors.
cards.a:
Glutamate and Aspartate.
Receptors: Ionotropic (AMPA, NMDA, Kainate) and Metabotropic (mGluR).

cards.q: What is the role of NMDA receptors in excitotoxicity?
cards.a: High Ca2+ permeability. Overactivation (e.g., ischemia) → excessive Ca2+ influx → cell death via enzymes, free radicals, and mitochondrial damage.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter is primarily used by the nigrostriatal pathway?
cards.a: Dopamine (substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum).

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter is used by the locus ceruleus?
cards.a: Norepinephrine — involved in arousal, attention, and stress response.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter is used by the raphe nuclei?
cards.a: Serotonin (5-HT) — mood, sleep, appetite, pain modulation.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines and barbiturates?
cards.a:
Both potentiate GABA-A receptor (Cl- influx).
Benzos: increased frequency of channel opening.
Barbiturates: increased duration of opening.

cards.q: What is the difference between ionotropic and metabotropic receptors?
cards.a:
Ionotropic: Ligand-gated ion channels (fast).
Metabotropic: G-protein coupled receptors (slower, second messengers).

cards.q: What second messenger is increased by norepinephrine on beta-adrenergic receptors?
cards.a: cAMP (via Gs protein → adenylate cyclase).

cards.q: What is the effect of ACh on muscarinic M1 vs M2 receptors?
cards.a:
M1 (Gq): increased IP3/DAG (excitation).
M2 (Gi): decreased cAMP (inhibitory, heart).

cards.q: Describe the crossed extensor reflex.
cards.a: Polysynaptic reflex accompanying withdrawal reflex: ipsilateral flexion + contralateral extension to maintain posture/balance.

cards.q: What is the Babinski sign and what does it indicate?
cards.a: Dorsiflexion of big toe + fanning of other toes on plantar stimulation. Indicates UMN lesion (corticospinal tract damage) in adults.

cards.q: What is clonus and its clinical significance?
cards.a: Rhythmic oscillations due to hyperreflexia from loss of UMN inhibition. Seen in UMN lesions.

cards.q: What is decorticate vs decerebrate posturing?
cards.a:
Decorticate: Flexion of upper limbs, extension of lower (lesion above red nucleus).
Decerebrate: Extension of all limbs (lesion below red nucleus, worse prognosis).

cards.q: What is the function of the spinocerebellar tracts?
cards.a: Carry unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs to cerebellum for coordination.

cards.q: What is the blood-brain barrier (BBB) composed of?
cards.a: Tight junctions between endothelial cells + astrocyte foot processes + pericytes. Allows lipid-soluble molecules, glucose (GLUT1), amino acids.

cards.q: What areas of the brain lack a BBB?
cards.a: Circumventricular organs: area postrema (vomiting center), neurohypophysis, pineal gland, median eminence.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of CSF production and absorption?
cards.a: Produced by choroid plexus (Na+/K+ ATPase) → ventricles → subarachnoid space → absorbed by arachnoid granulations into dural venous sinuses.

cards.q: What is normal CSF pressure and composition?
cards.a:
Pressure: 70-180 mm H2O.
Clear, protein 15-45 mg/dL, glucose approx 2/3 blood, few lymphocytes.

cards.q: What is the function of the thalamus?
cards.a: Major sensory relay station (except olfaction) to cortex. Also involved in arousal and motor control.

cards.q: What is the function of the hypothalamus in temperature regulation?
cards.a:
Anterior hypothalamus: heat dissipation (parasympathetic).
Posterior hypothalamus: heat conservation/production (sympathetic).

cards.q: What nucleus produces orexin/hypocretin and its clinical importance?
cards.a: Lateral hypothalamus. Loss → narcolepsy with cataplexy.

cards.q: What is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)?
cards.a: Master circadian pacemaker in hypothalamus. Receives input from retina via retinohypothalamic tract.

cards.q: What are the major components of the limbic system?
cards.a: Hippocampus, amygdala, fornix, mammillary bodies, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, septum.

cards.q: What is Kluver-Bucy syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral amygdala lesions → hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia.

cards.q: What is the role of the prefrontal cortex?
cards.a: Executive function, decision making, personality, working memory, social behavior.

cards.q: What artery occlusion classically causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing?
cards.a: Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) — supplies calcarine cortex (occipital lobe).

cards.q: What is Anton-Babinski syndrome?
cards.a: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness (lesion in occipital lobe + association areas).

cards.q: What is the function of the frontal eye fields (Brodmann area 8)?
cards.a: Conjugate horizontal eye movements to the opposite side. Lesion → ipsilateral gaze deviation.

cards.q: What is Gerstmann syndrome?
cards.a: Dominant parietal lobe lesion (angular gyrus): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.

cards.q: What is neglect syndrome and which side is more common?
cards.a: Usually right parietal lesion → left-sided neglect (patient ignores left side of space/body).

cards.q: What is the difference between conduction aphasia and global aphasia?
cards.a:
Conduction: Arcuate fasciculus lesion — fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition.
Global: Large MCA territory — non-fluent, poor comprehension, poor repetition.

cards.q: What is the primary neurotransmitter of the sympathetic nervous system?
cards.a: Norepinephrine (postganglionic). Preganglionic: Acetylcholine (nicotinic).

cards.q: What is the primary neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (both pre- and postganglionic).

cards.q: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on the heart?
cards.a: Increased heart rate (chronotropy), increased contractility (inotropy), increased conduction velocity via beta-1 receptors.

cards.q: What cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibers?
cards.a: CN III (Edinger-Westphal), CN VII (superior salivatory), CN IX (inferior salivatory), CN X (dorsal motor nucleus + nucleus ambiguus).

cards.q: What is Horner syndrome and its classic triad?
cards.a: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Caused by interruption of sympathetic supply to head (e.g., Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection).

cards.q: What is the pathway for pupillary dilation (sympathetic)?
cards.a: Hypothalamus → ciliospinal center (C8-T2) → superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid plexus → dilator pupillae.

cards.q: What is the Argyll Robertson pupil?
cards.a: Accommodates but does not react to light (light-near dissociation). Classic in neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis).

cards.q: What is the Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect)?
cards.a: Swinging flashlight test: affected pupil dilates when light is swung to it. Indicates optic nerve or severe retinal damage.

cards.q: What is the accommodation reflex pathway?
cards.a: Cortex → Edinger-Westphal nucleus → CN III → ciliary ganglion → ciliary muscle (lens rounding) + sphincter pupillae (miosis) + convergence.

cards.q: What is the function of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus?
cards.a: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons for pupillary constriction and lens accommodation (CN III).

cards.q: What structure is responsible for vertical gaze?
cards.a: Rostral interstitial nucleus of MLF (riMLF) and interstitial nucleus of Cajar.

cards.q: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)?
cards.a: Lesion of MLF → ipsilateral adduction deficit + contralateral nystagmus on abduction. Classic in multiple sclerosis.

cards.q: What is one-and-a-half syndrome?
cards.a: PPRF (or abducens nucleus) + ipsilateral MLF lesion → ipsilateral gaze palsy + INO → only contralateral abduction remains.

cards.q: What is the function of the basal ganglia in Parkinson disease (direct vs indirect pathway imbalance)?
cards.a: Dopamine loss → decreased direct pathway (D1) + increased indirect pathway (D2) → increased GPi inhibition of thalamus → bradykinesia/rigidity.

cards.q: What are the cardinal features of Parkinson disease?
cards.a: TRAP: Tremor (resting), Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia/Bradykinesia, Postural instability.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Huntington disease?
cards.a: Loss of GABAergic neurons in striatum (especially caudate) → chorea, cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms.

cards.q: What is hemiballismus and its lesion location?
cards.a: Wild flinging movements of proximal limbs. Classic lesion: contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is primarily used by Purkinje cells of the cerebellum?
cards.a: GABA (inhibitory output to deep cerebellar nuclei).

cards.q: What is the output nucleus of the cerebellum?
cards.a: Deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, interposed, fastigial) → thalamus and brainstem.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of a cerebellar hemisphere lesion?
cards.a: Ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, decomposition of movement.

cards.q: What is the clinical presentation of a midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion?
cards.a: Truncal ataxia, gait instability, nystagmus.

cards.q: What is the clinical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)?
cards.a:
Wet, Wobbly, Wacky:
• Urinary incontinence
• Gait ataxia (magnetic gait)
• Dementia (reversible with shunt).

cards.q: What is the difference between communicating and non-communicating hydrocephalus?
cards.a:
Communicating: Impaired CSF absorption (e.g., post-SAH, meningitis).
Non-communicating (obstructive): Blockage within ventricular system (e.g., aqueductal stenosis, tumor).

cards.q: What is syringomyelia and its classic sensory loss?
cards.a: Central canal dilation (often with Chiari I). Cape-like bilateral loss of pain and temperature (crossing spinothalamic fibers) with preserved touch/vibration.

cards.q: What is tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) and its key findings?
cards.a: Demyelination of dorsal columns + dorsal roots → loss of proprioception/vibration, Argyll Robertson pupils, positive Romberg sign, ataxia, lightning pains.

cards.q: What is subacute combined degeneration and its cause?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency → demyelination of dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal tracts → loss of vibration/proprioception + UMN signs (spastic paresis).

cards.q: What is the pathology in multiple sclerosis (MS)?
cards.a: Autoimmune demyelination (oligodendrocytes) in CNS white matter → plaques. Relapsing-remitting course common. Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign.

cards.q: What is Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) classic CSF finding?
cards.a: Albuminocytologic dissociation (increased protein, normal WBC count). Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) — ascending paralysis, areflexia.

cards.q: What is myasthenia gravis? Key clinical features and test.
cards.a: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors. Fatigable weakness (worse with activity), ptosis, diplopia, bulbar symptoms. Improves with edrophonium (Tensilon test) or ice pack test.

cards.q: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)?
cards.a: Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. Associated with small cell lung cancer. Weakness improves with activity. Decreased DTRs.

cards.q: What is the difference in repetitive nerve stimulation between MG and LEMS?
cards.a:
MG: Decremental response.
LEMS: Incremental response (facilitation) at high-frequency stimulation.

cards.q: What is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors.

cards.q: What is the effect of curare vs succinylcholine at the NMJ?
cards.a:
Curare: Competitive antagonist (non-depolarizing blocker).
Succinylcholine: Depolarizing blocker (initial fasciculations then paralysis).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin at the NMJ?
cards.a: Cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25 or synaptobrevin) → prevents ACh vesicle release → flaccid paralysis.

cards.q: What is the role of the muscle spindle vs Golgi tendon organ?
cards.a:
Muscle spindle (Ia, II): Detects muscle length/stretch (stretch reflex).
Golgi tendon organ (Ib): Detects muscle tension (inverse myotatic reflex).

cards.q: What is the function of alpha vs gamma motor neurons?
cards.a:
Alpha: Innervate extrafusal fibers (force generation).
Gamma: Innervate intrafusal fibers (maintain spindle sensitivity during contraction).

cards.q: What is the jaw jerk reflex and its significance?
cards.a: Masseter stretch reflex (CN V). Hyperreflexia suggests UMN lesion above the pons.

cards.q: What is the cremasteric reflex and its spinal level?
cards.a: Stroking medial thigh → testicular elevation. Mediated by L1-L2. Absent in UMN lesions or testicular torsion.

cards.q: What is the anal wink reflex and its significance?
cards.a: Contraction of external anal sphincter on stroking perianal skin (S2-S4). Tests sacral spinal cord integrity.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of dementia overall?
cards.a: Alzheimer disease — amyloid plaques (Abeta) and neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau).

cards.q: What is the pathology in frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease)?
cards.a: Pick bodies (tau inclusions), frontal and temporal lobe atrophy → personality changes, disinhibition, language deficits.

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is lost in Alzheimer disease (nucleus basalis of Meynert)?
cards.a: Acetylcholine.

cards.q: What is the function of the locus ceruleus?
cards.a: Major source of norepinephrine in the brain — arousal, attention, stress response.

cards.q: What is REM sleep behavior disorder associated with?
cards.a: Loss of normal muscle atonia during REM. Strong predictor of future synucleinopathies (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia).

cards.q: What are the EEG waves in different sleep stages?
cards.a:
Wake: Beta/Alpha
N1: Theta
N2: Sleep spindles + K-complexes
N3: Delta (slow wave)
REM: Beta-like (sawtooth waves).

cards.q: What is the effect of benzodiazepines on sleep architecture?
cards.a: Decrease slow-wave sleep (N3) and REM sleep.

cards.q: What is the reticular formation?
cards.a: Network of neurons in brainstem tegmentum involved in arousal, autonomic control, reflexes, and motor control.
