cards.q: What is central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination)?
cards.a: Rapid correction of hyponatremia → demyelination of basis pontis → locked-in syndrome, quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy.

cards.q: What is Wernicke encephalopathy triad?
cards.a: Confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia (due to thiamine deficiency). Mammillary body hemorrhage.

cards.q: What is the function of the fornix?
cards.a: Major output tract of hippocampus → mammillary bodies (Papez circuit).

cards.q: What is the blood supply of the internal capsule?
cards.a: Lenticulostriate branches of MCA (Charcot's artery of cerebral hemorrhage).

cards.q: What is the most common site of lacunar infarcts?
cards.a: Basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons (small vessel disease from hypertension).

cards.q: What artery supplies the lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome)?
cards.a: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery.

cards.q: List key features of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
cards.a:
Ipsilateral: Horner syndrome, facial pain/temp loss, ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness.
Contralateral: body pain/temp loss.

cards.q: What is the artery most commonly involved in MCA stroke?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery — contralateral hemiparesis (face/arm > leg), aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant).

cards.q: What is Broca's area blood supply?
cards.a: Superior division of MCA.

cards.q: What is the function of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA)?
cards.a: Supplies medial aspect of hemispheres including leg/foot area of motor and sensory cortex.

cards.q: What is locked-in syndrome and its lesion location?
cards.a: Ventral pontine lesion (basilar artery occlusion) → quadriplegia + anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm, most commonly at anterior communicating artery.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Lucid interval after head trauma → lens-shaped hyperdensity on CT (middle meningeal artery).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Crescent-shaped hyperdensity, crosses suture lines, elderly/alcoholics (bridging veins).

cards.q: What is central cord syndrome?
cards.a: Hyperextension injury in elderly with spondylosis → upper extremity weakness greater than lower, cape-like sensory loss.

cards.q: What is anterior spinal artery syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral loss of motor function + pain/temperature below lesion. Spares dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception).

cards.q: What is Brown-Sequard syndrome?
cards.a:
Hemisection of spinal cord:
Ipsilateral: motor loss + loss of vibration/proprioception.
Contralateral: loss of pain/temperature (starts 1-2 levels below).

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) — aggressive, ring-enhancing, butterfly lesion.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in children?
cards.a: Pilocytic astrocytoma (often cerebellar) or medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with bitemporal hemianopia?
cards.a: Pituitary adenoma compressing optic chiasm.

cards.q: What is the most common tumor of the pineal region?
cards.a: Germinoma (in young males).

cards.q: What is paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration associated with?
cards.a: Anti-Yo antibodies (breast/ovarian cancer) or small cell lung cancer (anti-Hu).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates?
cards.a: Group B Streptococcus.

cards.q: What organism causes meningitis with India ink positive CSF?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans (especially in AIDS).

cards.q: What is the most common viral cause of encephalitis with temporal lobe involvement?
cards.a: HSV-1 — Cowdry type A inclusions.

cards.q: What is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by?
cards.a: JC virus reactivation in immunocompromised patients → demyelination, bizarre astrocytes.

cards.q: What CSF finding is classic in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Cloudy CSF, increased neutrophils, increased protein, decreased glucose, increased opening pressure.

cards.q: What is the treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis in AIDS?
cards.a: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of viral meningitis?
cards.a: Enteroviruses (Coxsackie, Echovirus). Usually self-limited.

cards.q: What is the classic CSF finding in viral (aseptic) meningitis?
cards.a: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal-to-mildly elevated protein, normal glucose.

cards.q: What is the treatment for HSV encephalitis?
cards.a: Intravenous Acyclovir immediately (even before PCR confirmation).

cards.q: What prion disease is associated with cannibalism?
cards.a: Kuru (Papua New Guinea).

cards.q: What are the key features of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)?
cards.a: Rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG, spongiform change on histology, 14-3-3 protein in CSF.

cards.q: What is the inheritance and deficient enzyme in metachromatic leukodystrophy?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive, arylsulfatase A deficiency → sulfatide accumulation → demyelination.

cards.q: What is the deficient enzyme in Krabbe disease?
cards.a: Galactocerebrosidase → globoid cells on histology.

cards.q: What disease shows cherry-red spot on macula?
cards.a: Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A deficiency) and Niemann-Pick disease.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of adrenoleukodystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked — ABCD1 mutation → very long chain fatty acid accumulation.

cards.q: What is Chiari type 1 malformation?
cards.a: Caudal displacement of cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum → syringomyelia, headache, ataxia.

cards.q: What is Dandy-Walker malformation?
cards.a: Agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis + cystic dilation of 4th ventricle + enlarged posterior fossa.

cards.q: What neural tube defect is prevented by folic acid?
cards.a: Spina bifida and anencephaly.

cards.q: What is holoprosencephaly associated with?
cards.a: Failure of forebrain cleavage. Seen in trisomy 13 and fetal alcohol syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
cards.a: Basal ganglia / putamen (Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms).

cards.q: What is cerebral amyloid angiopathy associated with?
cards.a: Lobar hemorrhages in elderly, associated with Alzheimer disease (Abeta deposition in vessel walls).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ischemic stroke in young adults?
cards.a: Cardioembolism or carotid/vertebral artery dissection.

cards.q: What is the pathology of lacunar infarcts?
cards.a: Hypertensive small vessel disease (lipohyalinosis).

cards.q: What tumor is associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome?
cards.a: Hemangioblastoma (cerebellum, spinal cord).

cards.q: What is tuberous sclerosis associated with?
cards.a: Cortical tubers, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas.

cards.q: What is Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Port-wine stain (V1 distribution), leptomeningeal angiomatosis, tram-track calcifications, seizures, glaucoma.

cards.q: What is neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) diagnostic criteria?
cards.a: 6 or more cafe-au-lait spots, 2 or more neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules.

cards.q: What is the most common intramedullary spinal cord tumor in adults?
cards.a: Ependymoma.

cards.q: What is the most common intradural extramedullary spinal tumor?
cards.a: Meningioma and schwannoma.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epidural abscess?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus (often from vertebral osteomyelitis).

cards.q: What is the most common demyelinating disease of the CNS?
cards.a: Multiple sclerosis.

cards.q: What is the most common demyelinating disease of the PNS?
cards.a: Guillain-Barre syndrome.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with Miller-Fisher variant of GBS?
cards.a: Anti-GQ1b — ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic EMG finding in myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Thymoma (also thymic hyperplasia).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy overall?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus (distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy).

cards.q: What is Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?
cards.a: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN). Pes cavus, hammer toes, inverted champagne bottle legs.

cards.q: What is inclusion body myositis?
cards.a: Most common myopathy in patients over 50 years. Distal weakness (finger flexors, quadriceps), rimmed vacuoles on biopsy.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked dystrophin gene mutation → absent dystrophin → pseudohypertrophy of calves.

cards.q: What is myotonic dystrophy type 1?
cards.a: CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene. Myotonia, frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy, cardiac conduction defects.

cards.q: What is the most common mitochondrial myopathy?
cards.a: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of mitochondrial diseases?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: Mitochondrial DNA deletion → ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction block.

cards.q: What is the most common seizure type in children?
cards.a: Febrile seizures.

cards.q: What is hippocampal sclerosis associated with?
cards.a: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.

cards.q: What is Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
cards.a: Childhood epileptic encephalopathy with multiple seizure types, intellectual disability, slow spike-and-wave on EEG.

cards.q: What is West syndrome?
cards.a: Infantile spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, developmental regression. Treated with ACTH.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in neurofibromatosis type 1?
cards.a: NF1 gene (chromosome 17) — neurofibromin (tumor suppressor).

cards.q: What is the most common primary spinal cord tumor?
cards.a: Ependymoma (especially myxopapillary type in filum terminale).

cards.q: What is anterior horn cell disease?
cards.a: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) — combined upper and lower motor neuron signs.

cards.q: What protein aggregates in most cases of ALS?
What is the most common motor neuron disease in children?
cards.a: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) — SMN1 gene deletion.

cards.q: What is the pathology in polio?
cards.a: Destruction of anterior horn cells → asymmetric flaccid paralysis.

cards.q: What is the most common acquired myopathy?
cards.a: Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis.

cards.q: What is the classic skin finding in dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Anti-Mi-2.

cards.q: What is the second most common cause of dementia?
cards.a: Vascular (multi-infarct) dementia.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome?
cards.a: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (small cell lung cancer).

cards.q: What antibody is seen in paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration?
cards.a: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) — breast/ovarian cancer.

cards.q: What is limbic encephalitis often associated with?
cards.a: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) — small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
cards.a: JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes.

cards.q: What is HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy?
cards.a: Demyelination of dorsal and lateral columns → spastic paraparesis and sensory ataxia.

cards.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection affecting the CNS in AIDS?
cards.a: Toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of fungal meningitis?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans.

cards.q: What stain highlights the Cryptococcus capsule?
cards.a: India ink or mucicarmine.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of brain abscess in immunocompetent adults?
cards.a: Contiguous spread from sinusitis/otitis (Streptococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes).

cards.q: What is neurocysticercosis and its treatment?
cards.a: Taenia solium larval cysts in brain. Treatment: Albendazole + steroids.

cards.q: What organism causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis via cribriform plate?
cards.a: Naegleria fowleri — rapidly fatal.

cards.q: What is the function of the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)?
cards.a: Receives visceral sensory input (taste, baroreceptors, chemoreceptors) via CN VII, IX, X.

cards.q: What is the function of the nucleus ambiguus?
cards.a: Motor innervation to pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles (CN IX, X) — swallowing and speech.

cards.q: What nucleus provides parasympathetic outflow to the heart?
cards.a: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus and nucleus ambiguus (CN X).

cards.q: What is the role of the periaqueductal gray (PAG)?
cards.a: Modulation of pain (descending inhibition via endogenous opioids), autonomic control, and defensive behavior.

cards.q: What is the role of the substantia nigra pars reticulata?
cards.a: Major output nucleus of basal ganglia (GABAergic, inhibitory to thalamus).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the hippocampus?
cards.a: Anterior choroidal artery and posterior cerebral artery branches.

cards.q: What is the most common site of embolic stroke?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery territory.

cards.q: What structure is damaged in central pontine myelinolysis?
cards.a: Basis pontis (oligodendrocytes particularly vulnerable to osmotic shifts).

cards.q: What is the most sensitive test for early Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: PET scan showing temporoparietal hypometabolism or amyloid PET imaging.

cards.q: What CSF biomarker is decreased in Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: Abeta-42 (decreased), total tau and phospho-tau increased.

cards.q: What is the function of the dentate nucleus?
cards.a: Output from lateral cerebellar hemisphere to contralateral thalamus (planning of movement).

cards.q: What is the fastigial nucleus responsible for?
cards.a: Vermis output — regulation of axial and proximal muscles, balance.

cards.q: What is the clinical sign of a lesion in the flocculonodular lobe?
cards.a: Truncal ataxia, nystagmus, vertigo (vestibulocerebellum).

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is used by climbing fibers in the cerebellum?
cards.a: Glutamate (from inferior olivary nucleus).

cards.q: What neurotransmitter is used by mossy fibers in the cerebellum?
cards.a: Glutamate.

cards.q: What is the only excitatory neuron in the cerebellar cortex?
cards.a: Granule cell.

cards.q: What is the only output neuron of the cerebellar cortex?
cards.a: Purkinje cell (GABAergic, inhibitory).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a cerebellar stroke?
cards.a: Vertigo, ataxia, nystagmus, ipsilateral limb dysmetria.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acquired nystagmus?
cards.a: Multiple sclerosis or drug toxicity (e.g., phenytoin, alcohol).

cards.q: What is downbeat nystagmus associated with?
cards.a: Chiari malformation or craniocervical junction lesions.

cards.q: What is the function of the superior colliculus?
cards.a: Visual reflex orientation (saccadic eye movements toward stimuli).

cards.q: What is the function of the inferior colliculus?
cards.a: Auditory reflex orientation.

cards.q: What is the role of the red nucleus?
cards.a: Facilitates flexor tone in upper limbs (rubrospinal tract — less prominent in humans).

cards.q: What is the neurotransmitter of the olivocochlear bundle?
cards.a: Acetylcholine (inhibitory feedback to outer hair cells).

cards.q: What is the pathway for conscious proprioception from the lower limb?
cards.a: Fasciculus gracilis → nucleus gracilis → medial lemniscus.

cards.q: What is the pathway for conscious proprioception from the upper limb?
cards.a: Fasciculus cuneatus → nucleus cuneatus → medial lemniscus.

cards.q: What is the location of the primary auditory cortex?
cards.a: Heschl's gyrus (transverse temporal gyrus, Brodmann area 41).

cards.q: What is the location of the primary visual cortex?
cards.a: Calcarine sulcus (Brodmann area 17) in occipital lobe.

cards.q: What is the location of the primary somatosensory cortex?
cards.a: Postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3,1,2).

cards.q: What is the location of the primary motor cortex?
cards.a: Precentral gyrus (Brodmann area 4).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the primary motor and sensory cortex for the lower limb?
cards.a: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

cards.q: What is the blood supply to the face and arm areas of motor/sensory cortex?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery (MCA).

cards.q: What structure connects Wernicke's area to Broca's area?
cards.a: Arcuate fasciculus.

cards.q: What is the dominant hemisphere for language in most right-handed people?
cards.a: Left hemisphere.

cards.q: What is prosopagnosia and its lesion location?
cards.a: Inability to recognize faces. Lesion in fusiform gyrus (ventral visual stream).

cards.q: What is alexia without agraphia and its lesion?
cards.a: Left occipital lobe + splenium of corpus callosum (disconnection syndrome).

cards.q: What is the function of the cingulate gyrus?
cards.a: Emotional processing, attention, pain perception, and motivation (part of Papez circuit).

cards.q: What is the major output of the amygdala?
cards.a: Stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway.

cards.q: What is the major input to the hippocampus?
cards.a: Entorhinal cortex (via perforant pathway).

cards.q: What is the major output of the hippocampus?
cards.a: Fornix (to mammillary bodies and septal nuclei).

cards.q: What structure is damaged in Korsakoff psychosis?
cards.a: Mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus.

cards.q: What is the effect of a lesion in the mammillary bodies?
cards.a: Anterograde amnesia (Korsakoff syndrome).

cards.q: What is the role of the ventral tegmental area (VTA)?
cards.a: Dopaminergic reward pathway (mesolimbic system).

cards.q: What is the mesolimbic pathway?
cards.a: VTA → nucleus accumbens — involved in reward and addiction.

cards.q: What is the mesocortical pathway?
cards.a: VTA → prefrontal cortex — involved in motivation and cognition.

cards.q: What nucleus produces dopamine for the nigrostriatal pathway?
cards.a: Substantia nigra pars compacta.

cards.q: What are the major neurotransmitters in the CNS and their primary roles?
cards.a:
Glutamate: Major excitatory (NMDA, AMPA, kainate).
GABA: Major inhibitory (GABA-A, GABA-B).
Dopamine: Reward, movement, emotion.
Serotonin (5-HT): Mood, sleep, appetite.
Norepinephrine: Arousal, attention.
Acetylcholine: Memory, attention (basal forebrain).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors → ↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening → hyperpolarization.

cards.q: Clinical uses of Benzodiazepines (high-yield)?
cards.a: Anxiety, insomnia, seizures (status epilepticus), alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms, procedural sedation.

cards.q: What is the antidote for Benzodiazepine overdose?
cards.a: Flumazenil (competitive GABA-A antagonist). Caution in chronic users (seizure risk).

cards.q: Compare short-acting vs long-acting Benzodiazepines (examples + uses).
cards.a:
Short: Midazolam, Triazolam (procedural sedation, insomnia).
Long: Diazepam, Chlordiazepoxide (alcohol withdrawal, anxiety).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Barbiturates?
cards.a: Positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A → ↑ duration of Cl⁻ channel opening (at high doses: direct GABA-A agonists).

cards.q: Why are Barbiturates more dangerous than Benzodiazepines in overdose?
cards.a: They can cause respiratory depression and coma even without GABA; have lower therapeutic index and induce CYP450.

cards.q: Mechanism and use of Zolpidem / Zaleplon / Eszopiclone?
cards.a: Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics (Z-drugs). Bind GABA-A α1 subunit → sedation with less muscle relaxation / anticonvulsant effect.

cards.q: First-line drug for status epilepticus?
cards.a: Lorazepam (IV Benzodiazepine) → followed by Fosphenytoin or Valproate if persists.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Phenytoin?
cards.a: Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (use-dependent) → inhibits high-frequency firing.

cards.q: Classic side effects of Phenytoin?
cards.a: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, megaloblastic anemia, CYP450 inducer, teratogenic (fetal hydantoin syndrome).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Na⁺ channel blocker (similar to Phenytoin). Also used for trigeminal neuralgia.

cards.q: What is the major toxicity of Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis / aplastic anemia, SIADH, teratogenic (neural tube defects), CYP450 auto-inducer.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Valproate?
cards.a: Multiple: ↑ GABA (inhibits GABA transaminase), Na⁺ channel blocker, T-type Ca²⁺ channel blocker.

cards.q: Major toxicities of Valproate?
cards.a: Hepatotoxicity (especially children), pancreatitis, teratogenic (neural tube defects), weight gain, tremor.

cards.q: Drug of choice for absence (petit mal) seizures?
cards.a: Ethosuximide (blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic neurons).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lamotrigine?
cards.a: Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and inhibits glutamate release.

cards.q: Major side effect of Lamotrigine?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (especially with rapid titration or Valproate co-administration).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Levetiracetam?
cards.a: Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A → modulates neurotransmitter release.

cards.q: Why is Levetiracetam popular for epilepsy?
cards.a: Broad-spectrum, minimal drug interactions, no hepatic metabolism, safe in pregnancy.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Topiramate?
cards.a: Multiple: Na⁺ channel blocker, GABA enhancer, AMPA/kainate antagonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.

cards.q: Clinical uses of Topiramate (beyond seizures)?
cards.a: Migraine prophylaxis, weight loss (appetite suppression), alcohol dependence.

cards.q: First-line treatment for tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures?
cards.a: Valproate (broad spectrum) or Lamotrigine / Levetiracetam.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of typical antipsychotics (e.g., Haloperidol, Chlorpromazine)?
cards.a: D2 receptor antagonists (mesolimbic pathway → ↓ positive symptoms).

cards.q: Major side effects of high-potency typical antipsychotics (e.g., Haloperidol)?
cards.a: Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia. Also NMS.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of atypical antipsychotics (e.g., Olanzapine, Risperidone)?
cards.a: D2 + 5-HT2A receptor antagonists (better negative symptom control, lower EPS risk).

cards.q: Metabolic side effects of atypical antipsychotics?
cards.a: Weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia (especially Olanzapine and Clozapine).

cards.q: Which atypical antipsychotic requires weekly WBC monitoring?
cards.a: Clozapine (risk of agranulocytosis).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SSRIs?
cards.a: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition → ↑ synaptic 5-HT.

cards.q: Common side effects of SSRIs?
cards.a: Sexual dysfunction, GI upset, insomnia, serotonin syndrome (with MAOIs), withdrawal syndrome.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SNRIs (Venlafaxine, Duloxetine)?
cards.a: Inhibit reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine.

cards.q: Clinical use of Duloxetine?
cards.a: Depression, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of TCAs (Amitriptyline, Imipramine)?
cards.a: Inhibit reuptake of NE and 5-HT + block muscarinic, α1, H1 receptors.

cards.q: Classic toxicities of TCAs?
cards.a: Anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention), sedation, orthostatic hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias (wide QRS), lethal in overdose.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of MAOIs (Phenelzine, Selegiline)?
cards.a: Inhibit monoamine oxidase → ↑ NE, 5-HT, DA stores.

cards.q: What is the major risk with MAOIs?
cards.a: Tyramine crisis (hypertensive crisis) with aged cheese, wine, cured meats. Also serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bupropion?
cards.a: NDRI (norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor). Also nicotinic antagonist.

cards.q: Unique uses and side effects of Bupropion?
cards.a: Depression, smoking cessation. Low sexual side effects. Lowers seizure threshold.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mirtazapine?
cards.a: α2 antagonist + 5-HT2/3 antagonist → ↑ NE and 5-HT release. Also H1 antagonist.

cards.q: Why is Mirtazapine useful in certain patients?
cards.a: Sedating + increases appetite (good for elderly, cancer cachexia, insomnia).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lithium?
cards.a: Inhibits inositol monophosphatase and GSK-3 → mood stabilization.

cards.q: Classic side effects and monitoring for Lithium?
cards.a: Tremor, nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism, Ebstein's anomaly (teratogenic), narrow therapeutic index. Monitor levels, TSH, creatinine.

cards.q: First-line mood stabilizer in pregnancy?
cards.a: Lamotrigine (relatively safer than Lithium or Valproate).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buspirone?
cards.a: 5-HT1A partial agonist. Anxiolytic without sedation or dependence.

cards.q: Treatment of acute agitation / psychosis?
cards.a: IM Haloperidol + Lorazepam + Diphenhydramine (or atypical like Olanzapine).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Memantine?
cards.a: Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist. Used in moderate-severe Alzheimer's.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Donepezil?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → ↑ ACh in Alzheimer's.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Levodopa/Carbidopa in Parkinson's?
cards.a: Levodopa crosses BBB → converted to Dopamine. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase.

cards.q: Major long-term complication of Levodopa?
cards.a: On-off phenomenon and dyskinesias.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pramipexole / Ropinirole?
cards.a: Non-ergot D2/D3 dopamine receptor agonists.

cards.q: Side effect of Dopamine agonists?
cards.a: Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality), somnolence.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Selegiline / Rasagiline?
cards.a: MAO-B inhibitors → prevent dopamine breakdown.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Entacapone?
cards.a: COMT inhibitor → prolongs Levodopa action (prevents peripheral metabolism).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amantadine in Parkinson's?
cards.a: Increases dopamine release + NMDA antagonist (also used for dyskinesias).

cards.q: Treatment of acute dystonic reaction (from antipsychotics)?
cards.a: Benzatropine (anticholinergic) or Diphenhydramine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Trihexyphenidyl / Benztropine?
cards.a: Central muscarinic (M1) antagonists. Used to treat drug-induced parkinsonism and EPS.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tetrabenazine?
cards.a: VMAT2 inhibitor → depletes dopamine stores. Used in Huntington's chorea and tardive dyskinesia.

cards.q: First-line treatment for essential tremor?
cards.a: Propranolol (non-selective β-blocker). Alternative: Primidone.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Riluzole?
cards.a: Decreases glutamate release and blocks Na⁺ channels. Used in ALS to slow progression.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Baclofen?
cards.a: GABA-B receptor agonist in spinal cord → inhibits monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflexes. Used for spasticity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tizanidine?
cards.a: Central α2-adrenergic agonist → increases presynaptic inhibition of motor neurons.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dantrolene?
cards.a: Inhibits Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle. Used in malignant hyperthermia and spasticity.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Dantrolene + supportive care (cooling, hyperventilation, stop triggering agents).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Opioids (e.g., Morphine)?
cards.a: Agonists at μ, κ, δ opioid receptors → Gi-coupled → ↓ cAMP, ↑ K⁺ conductance, ↓ Ca²⁺ influx.

cards.q: Classic side effects of Opioids?
cards.a: Respiratory depression, miosis, constipation, sedation, euphoria, dependence.

cards.q: Antidote for Opioid overdose?
cards.a: Naloxone (pure opioid receptor antagonist). Short-acting.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tramadol?
cards.a: Weak μ-opioid agonist + inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.

cards.q: Why is Tramadol contraindicated with SSRIs?
cards.a: Risk of serotonin syndrome.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Local Anesthetics (e.g., Lidocaine)?
cards.a: Block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in inactivated state → prevent action potential propagation.

cards.q: Why are local anesthetics less effective in infected tissue?
cards.a: Acidic environment → more ionized form → less penetration into nerve.

cards.q: What is the maximum safe dose of Lidocaine with epinephrine?
cards.a: 7 mg/kg (without epi: 4–5 mg/kg).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Succinylcholine?
cards.a: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker → persistent agonist at nicotinic receptors → Phase I then Phase II block.

cards.q: Complication of Succinylcholine?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia (especially in burns, trauma, neuromuscular disease), malignant hyperthermia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (e.g., Rocuronium)?
cards.a: Competitive antagonists at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: Reversal agent for non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade?
cards.a: Neostigmine (AChE inhibitor) + Glycopyrrolate or Sugammadex (for Rocuronium/Vecuronium).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of General Anesthetics – Inhaled (e.g., Halothane, Isoflurane)?
cards.a: Enhance GABA-A activity and inhibit NMDA receptors → CNS depression.

cards.q: What determines speed of induction for inhaled anesthetics?
cards.a: Blood:gas partition coefficient (lower solubility = faster induction/recovery).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Propofol?
cards.a: Potentiates GABA-A receptor. Rapid onset, short duration.

cards.q: Side effect of Propofol infusion?
cards.a: Propofol infusion syndrome (metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure) – especially in children/critically ill.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ketamine?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonist. Produces dissociative anesthesia.

cards.q: Unique advantage of Ketamine?
cards.a: Maintains respiratory drive and cardiovascular stability. Bronchodilator. Useful in asthmatics and shock.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Etomidate?
cards.a: GABA-A agonist. Minimal cardiovascular depression.

cards.q: Side effect of Etomidate?
cards.a: Adrenal suppression (inhibits 11β-hydroxylase).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Midazolam in anesthesia?
cards.a: Benzodiazepine – GABA-A potentiation. Used for premedication and procedural sedation.

cards.q: Treatment of migraine (acute)?
cards.a: Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists), NSAIDs, Dihydroergotamine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Triptans?
cards.a: 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists → cranial vasoconstriction + inhibit trigeminal nerve activation.

cards.q: Contraindication for Triptans?
cards.a: Coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, basilar migraine, recent MAOI use.

cards.q: Prophylaxis for migraine?
cards.a: Propranolol, Topiramate, Amitriptyline, Valproate, CGRP antagonists (Erenumab).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of ADHD stimulants (Methylphenidate, Amphetamines)?
cards.a: Increase release and block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in prefrontal cortex.

cards.q: Non-stimulant treatment for ADHD?
cards.a: Atomoxetine (selective NE reuptake inhibitor), Guanfacine/Clonidine (α2 agonists), Bupropion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Caffeine?
cards.a: Adenosine receptor antagonist → ↑ alertness, mild stimulant.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Nicotine?
cards.a: Agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (peripheral and central).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Varenicline?
cards.a: Partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors → reduces craving and withdrawal.

cards.q: Treatment of alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Long-acting Benzodiazepines (Chlordiazepoxide or Diazepam) + Thiamine, Folate, Multivitamins.

cards.q: Drug used for maintenance of alcohol abstinence?
cards.a: Disulfiram (aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor), Naltrexone, Acamprosate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Disulfiram?
cards.a: Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase → accumulation of acetaldehyde → flushing, nausea, tachycardia.

cards.q: Treatment of opioid dependence?
cards.a: Methadone (long-acting μ agonist), Buprenorphine (partial agonist), Naltrexone.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cocaine?
cards.a: Blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.

cards.q: Classic toxicity of Cocaine?
cards.a: Sympathomimetic effects, myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures, perforated nasal septum.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amphetamines?
cards.a: Promote release of catecholamines from presynaptic terminals + inhibit reuptake.

cards.q: Treatment of benzodiazepine and barbiturate withdrawal?
cards.a: Long-acting benzodiazepine taper (e.g., Diazepam).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of PCP (Phencyclidine)?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonist. Causes violent behavior, nystagmus, hypertension.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of LSD?
cards.a: 5-HT2A receptor agonist → hallucinations and altered perception.

cards.q: Treatment of serotonin syndrome?
cards.a: Cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist), supportive care, benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Anticholinergics in Parkinson's (e.g., Benztropine)?
cards.a: Restore dopamine-acetylcholine balance in striatum by blocking muscarinic receptors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Carbidopa?
cards.a: Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor → increases Levodopa availability to brain.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Haloperidol (high-potency typical antipsychotic)?
cards.a: Strong D2 receptor antagonist. High risk of EPS, low risk of metabolic side effects.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Chlorpromazine (low-potency typical)?
cards.a: D2 antagonist with strong anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and α1-blocking effects → more sedation and orthostatic hypotension.

cards.q: What is Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: Life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics: rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, altered mental status, ↑ CK.

cards.q: Treatment of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Stop antipsychotic + Dantrolene or Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist) + supportive cooling.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Risperidone?
cards.a: D2 + 5-HT2A antagonist. Dose-dependent EPS risk.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Quetiapine?
cards.a: Atypical antipsychotic with low D2 affinity. Strong H1 and α1 blockade → sedation.

cards.q: Which atypical antipsychotic is best for negative symptoms?
cards.a: Clozapine (most effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of SSRIs (e.g., Fluoxetine, Sertraline, Escitalopram)?
cards.a: Selective inhibition of serotonin reuptake (SERT) → increased synaptic 5-HT.

cards.q: Which SSRI has the longest half-life?
cards.a: Fluoxetine (and its active metabolite norfluoxetine) → least likely to cause discontinuation syndrome.

cards.q: Which SSRI is most likely to cause sexual dysfunction?
cards.a: All SSRIs, but Paroxetine is often worst (also most anticholinergic).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Venlafaxine?
cards.a: SNRI – inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake (at higher doses also dopamine).

cards.q: Withdrawal syndrome with Venlafaxine?
cards.a: Severe discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, electric shocks, irritability) due to short half-life.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amitriptyline?
cards.a: TCA – inhibits NE and 5-HT reuptake + strong anticholinergic and H1 blockade.

cards.q: Clinical uses of Amitriptyline (beyond depression)?
cards.a: Neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis, insomnia, chronic tension headache.

cards.q: TCA overdose classic presentation?
cards.a: Anticholinergic toxicity + wide QRS, seizures, coma, arrhythmias (Na⁺ channel blockade).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Phenelzine?
cards.a: Irreversible non-selective MAO inhibitor (MAO-A and MAO-B).

cards.q: Dietary restriction with MAOIs?
cards.a: Avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, red wine) → hypertensive crisis.

cards.q: Advantage of Bupropion over SSRIs?
cards.a: No sexual dysfunction, promotes weight loss, helps with smoking cessation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Trazodone?
cards.a: 5-HT2A antagonist + weak SERT inhibition. Strong H1 blockade.

cards.q: Clinical use of low-dose Trazodone?
cards.a: Insomnia (highly sedating).

cards.q: Narrow therapeutic index drug with tremor, polyuria, and thyroid dysfunction?
cards.a: Lithium.

cards.q: Teratogenic effect of Lithium?
cards.a: Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid valve malformation).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Valproate as mood stabilizer?
cards.a: Increases GABA levels, inhibits histone deacetylase, blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.

cards.q: Which mood stabilizer is most teratogenic?
cards.a: Valproate (neural tube defects, fetal valproate syndrome).

cards.q: Advantage of Lamotrigine in bipolar disorder?
cards.a: Particularly effective against depressive episodes with lower risk of mania induction.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Carbamazepine as mood stabilizer?
cards.a: Na⁺ channel blocker. Also induces its own metabolism (auto-inducer).

cards.q: Drug used for rapid cycling bipolar disorder?
cards.a: Valproate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors → increase acetylcholine in Alzheimer's disease.

cards.q: Drug used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease?
cards.a: Memantine (often combined with donepezil).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Selegiline (low dose)?
cards.a: Selective MAO-B inhibitor → increases dopamine in Parkinson's.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Entacapone / Tolcapone?
cards.a: COMT inhibitors → prevent peripheral breakdown of Levodopa.

cards.q: Why is Tolcapone rarely used?
cards.a: Hepatotoxicity (requires monitoring).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pramipexole?
cards.a: D3 > D2 dopamine receptor agonist.

cards.q: First-line treatment for Parkinson's in young patients?
cards.a: Dopamine agonists (Pramipexole/Ropinirole) to delay Levodopa use.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bromocriptine?
cards.a: Ergot-derived D2 agonist (older agent, less commonly used now).

cards.q: Treatment of acute dystonia from antipsychotics?
cards.a: Benzatropine (anticholinergic) IM or Diphenhydramine.

cards.q: Treatment of akathisia?
cards.a: β-blockers (Propranolol) or Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Baclofen for spasticity?
cards.a: GABA-B agonist → presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferents in spinal cord.

cards.q: Intrathecal use of which drug for severe spasticity?
cards.a: Baclofen pump.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vigabatrin?
cards.a: Irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase → ↑ GABA levels. Used in infantile spasms.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Vigabatrin?
cards.a: Permanent visual field constriction (requires regular ophthalmologic monitoring).

cards.q: Drug of choice for infantile spasms?
cards.a: ACTH or Vigabatrin (especially in tuberous sclerosis).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tiagabine?
cards.a: GABA reuptake inhibitor (GAT-1) → ↑ synaptic GABA.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Gabapentin / Pregabalin?
cards.a: Bind α2δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ glutamate release. Used in neuropathic pain and seizures.

cards.q: Clinical uses of Pregabalin?
cards.a: Neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, generalized anxiety disorder, partial seizures.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Felbamate?
cards.a: NMDA antagonist + enhances GABA. Reserved for refractory epilepsy due to toxicity.

cards.q: Major toxicity of Felbamate?
cards.a: Aplastic anemia and hepatic failure.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Stiripentol?
cards.a: Enhances GABA-A and inhibits CYP enzymes. Used in Dravet syndrome.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cannabidiol (Epidiolex)?
cards.a: Modulates GPR55 and TRPV1 receptors, enhances GABA, reduces excitotoxicity. Used in Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Aripiprazole?
cards.a: D2 partial agonist (stabilizes dopamine signaling) + 5-HT1A partial agonist + 5-HT2A antagonist.

cards.q: Advantage of Aripiprazole?
cards.a: Lower risk of metabolic side effects and hyperprolactinemia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Brexpiprazole and Cariprazine?
cards.a: D2 and 5-HT1A partial agonists (newer atypicals).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lurasidone?
cards.a: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonist with 5-HT7 antagonism. Low metabolic risk.

cards.q: Which antipsychotic is approved for bipolar depression?
cards.a: Quetiapine and Lurasidone.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Esketamine?
cards.a: NMDA receptor antagonist (S-enantiomer of ketamine). Used for treatment-resistant depression.

cards.q: Administration route of Esketamine?
cards.a: Intranasal spray under medical supervision.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vortioxetine?
cards.a: Multimodal: SERT inhibition + 5-HT1A agonist + 5-HT3 antagonist.

cards.q: Advantage of Vortioxetine?
cards.a: Improves cognitive function in depression.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vilazodone?
cards.a: SSRI + 5-HT1A partial agonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Atomoxetine?
cards.a: Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI). First-line non-stimulant for ADHD.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Guanfacine / Clonidine in ADHD?
cards.a: α2A-adrenergic agonists → improve prefrontal cortex function and reduce hyperactivity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Modafinil?
cards.a: Weak dopamine reuptake inhibitor + orexin activation. Used for narcolepsy and shift-work sleep disorder.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Sodium Oxybate (GHB)?
cards.a: GABA-B agonist + weak agonist at GHB receptors. Used in narcolepsy (cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pitolisant?
cards.a: Histamine H3 receptor inverse agonist → increases histamine release. Used in narcolepsy.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Solriamfetol?
cards.a: Dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Used in narcolepsy and OSA-related sleepiness.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Suvorexant?
cards.a: Dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA). Used for insomnia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ramelteon?
cards.a: Melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist. Used for sleep-onset insomnia.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for alcohol withdrawal seizures?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines (Lorazepam or Diazepam).

cards.q: Drug used to reduce craving in alcohol use disorder?
cards.a: Naltrexone (opioid antagonist) or Acamprosate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acamprosate?
cards.a: Normalizes glutamate neurotransmission (NMDA antagonist + GABA agonist).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buprenorphine?
cards.a: Partial μ-opioid agonist + κ antagonist. Used in opioid use disorder.

cards.q: Advantage of Buprenorphine over Methadone?
cards.a: Ceiling effect on respiratory depression → safer in overdose.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methadone?
cards.a: Long-acting full μ-opioid agonist. Used in opioid maintenance therapy.

cards.q: Treatment of opioid overdose in pregnant patient?
cards.a: Naloxone (still first-line; benefits outweigh risks).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Naloxone vs Naltrexone?
cards.a: Both pure opioid antagonists. Naloxone: short-acting (IV/IM). Naltrexone: long-acting (oral/IM).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Flumazenil?
cards.a: Competitive GABA-A receptor antagonist. Reverses benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Contraindication for Flumazenil?
cards.a: Chronic benzodiazepine use or suspected TCA co-ingestion (risk of seizures).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Physostigmine in anticholinergic toxicity?
cards.a: Tertiary amine AChE inhibitor that crosses BBB.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cyproheptadine?
cards.a: H1 and 5-HT2 receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dantrolene in malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) → inhibits Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Triggering agents for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Volatile anesthetics (halothane, isoflurane) + Succinylcholine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bromocriptine in neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
cards.a: Dopamine D2 agonist → restores central dopamine signaling.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amantadine in tardive dyskinesia?
cards.a: NMDA antagonist + increases dopamine release.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Valbenazine / Deutetrabenazine?
cards.a: VMAT2 inhibitors. Used for tardive dyskinesia.

cards.q: Most common cause of drug-induced parkinsonism?
cards.a: Typical antipsychotics (especially high-potency) and Metoclopramide.

cards.q: Treatment of drug-induced parkinsonism?
cards.a: Reduce dose or switch to atypical + Benztropine or Amantadine.

cards.q: What is the most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) — WHO grade 4 astrocytoma. Butterfly lesion crossing corpus callosum, ring-enhancing on MRI, pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation on histology.

cards.q: What is the hallmark histologic feature of glioblastoma?
cards.a: Pseudopalisading necrosis + microvascular proliferation (endothelial hyperplasia).

cards.q: What genetic alterations are classic in primary GBM?
cards.a: IDH-wildtype, EGFR amplification, PTEN loss, TERT promoter mutation.

cards.q: Most common primary brain tumor in children?
cards.a: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade 1) — often cerebellar, cystic with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, BRAF fusion.

cards.q: What are Rosenthal fibers?
cards.a: Eosinophilic corkscrew-shaped inclusions in pilocytic astrocytoma and Alexander disease.

cards.q: Most common supratentorial tumor in children?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma (adamantinomatous type) — calcified, Rathke pouch remnant, wet keratin, cholesterol clefts.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with 'fried egg' appearance and chicken-wire capillaries?
cards.a: Oligodendroglioma (WHO grade 2/3). IDH-mutant + 1p/19q codeletion.

cards.q: What is the most common CNS lymphoma type and its key feature?
cards.a: Primary CNS Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma. Strongly associated with EBV in immunocompromised. Perivascular cuffing, angiocentric growth.

cards.q: What tumor shows Homer-Wright rosettes and is a primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET)?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma — cerebellar, midline, drop metastases via CSF.

cards.q: What is the most common sellar tumor?
cards.a: Pituitary adenoma. Prolactinoma is the most common functioning type.

cards.q: What tumor arises from Rathke pouch remnants and shows 'motor-oil' fluid?
cards.a: Craniopharyngioma.

cards.q: What are the two main types of meningioma histology?
cards.a:
1. Whorls + psammoma bodies (classic)
2. Syncytial / fibroblastic.

cards.q: What is the inheritance and chromosome for Neurofibromatosis type 1?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant, chromosome 17 (NF1 gene, neurofibromin).

cards.q: What is the inheritance and chromosome for Neurofibromatosis type 2?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant, chromosome 22 (NF2 gene, merlin).

cards.q: Bilateral acoustic schwannomas are pathognomonic for which disease?
cards.a: Neurofibromatosis type 2.

cards.q: What is the most common peripheral nerve sheath tumor?
cards.a: Schwannoma — Antoni A (Verocay bodies) + Antoni B areas, S-100 positive.

cards.q: What CNS tumor is associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome?
cards.a: Hemangioblastoma — cerebellar, highly vascular, stromal cells with lipid droplets, associated with polycythemia.

cards.q: What is the most common metastatic brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Lung cancer (especially small cell), followed by breast, melanoma, colorectal, kidney.

cards.q: What is the histologic hallmark of Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: Senile (amyloid) plaques (Aβ) and neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau).

cards.q: What protein is primarily found in neurofibrillary tangles?
cards.a: Tau protein (hyperphosphorylated).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in Parkinson disease?
cards.a: Lewy bodies (α-synuclein) in substantia nigra pars compacta.

cards.q: Loss of which pigmented neurons causes Parkinson disease?
cards.a: Dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra pars compacta.

cards.q: What are the key features of Huntington disease?
cards.a: CAG repeats on chromosome 4 (HTT gene), atrophy of caudate nucleus (loss of GABA neurons), chorea, dementia.

cards.q: What disease shows 'spongiform encephalopathy' and prion protein plaques?
cards.a: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of most prion diseases?
cards.a: Mostly sporadic; some autosomal dominant (familial CJD).

cards.q: What is the most common demyelinating disease?
cards.a: Multiple Sclerosis (MS).

cards.q: What are the key histologic findings in MS plaques?
cards.a: Periventricular white matter plaques, loss of myelin (Luxol fast blue stain), relative axonal preservation, macrophage infiltration.

cards.q: What CSF finding is characteristic of MS?
cards.a: Oligoclonal bands (IgG) on electrophoresis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of viral encephalitis in the US?
cards.a: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) — temporal lobe predilection.

cards.q: What are Cowdry inclusions seen in?
cards.a: HSV encephalitis (intr nuclear eosinophilic inclusions).

cards.q: What organism causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
cards.a: JC virus (polyomavirus) in immunocompromised patients.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in PML?
cards.a: Demyelination with bizarre astrocytes and oligodendrocytes with ground-glass nuclear inclusions.

cards.q: What parasite causes ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS patients?
cards.a: Toxoplasma gondii.

cards.q: What is the most common fungal CNS infection in AIDS?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans — soap-bubble lesions, mucicarmine positive capsule.

cards.q: What is the classic CSF finding in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: ↑ Neutrophils, ↑ Protein, ↓ Glucose, ↑ Opening pressure.

cards.q: What is the classic CSF finding in viral meningitis?
cards.a: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly ↑ protein.

cards.q: What are the three layers of meninges from outer to inner?
cards.a: Dura mater → Arachnoid mater → Pia mater.

cards.q: What is the most common site of epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Temporal/parietal (middle meningeal artery rupture).

cards.q: What is the classic CT appearance of epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Lens-shaped (biconvex).

cards.q: What is the classic CT appearance of subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Crescent-shaped (concave).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm.

cards.q: Most common location for berry aneurysm?
cards.a: Anterior communicating artery.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ischemic stroke?
cards.a: Atherosclerosis (thrombotic) or cardioembolism.

cards.q: What are the two major types of cerebral edema?
cards.a:
1. Cytotoxic (intracellular, e.g., ischemia)
2. Vasogenic (extracellular, BBB disruption, e.g., tumor).

cards.q: What stain is used to demonstrate myelin loss in MS?
cards.a: Luxol fast blue.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric brain tumor in the posterior fossa?
cards.a: Medulloblastoma.

cards.q: What tumor shows 'true rosettes' (Flexner-Wintersteiner) and is associated with retinoblastoma gene?
cards.a: Retinoblastoma (also pineoblastoma in trilateral disease).

cards.q: What tumor arises from ependymal cells and often causes hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Ependymoma — perivascular pseudorosettes, true ependymal rosettes. Most common in 4th ventricle in children.

cards.q: What is the characteristic location and histology of choroid plexus papilloma?
cards.a: Lateral ventricles (children) or 4th ventricle (adults). Papillary fronds with fibrovascular core, CSF overproduction possible.

cards.q: What CNS tumor is associated with tuberous sclerosis?
cards.a: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) — located at foramen of Monro.

cards.q: What is the most common pineal region tumor?
cards.a: Germinoma — highly radiosensitive, elevated β-hCG and AFP in some germ cell tumors.

cards.q: What tumor shows 'Zellballen' pattern and is S-100 positive?
cards.a: Paraganglioma (pheochromocytoma of head/neck).

cards.q: What is the second most common primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Meningioma — dural-based, extra-axial, psammoma bodies.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in meningiomas?
cards.a: NF2 gene (merlin) on chromosome 22.

cards.q: What is the most aggressive pediatric brain tumor?
cards.a: ATRT (Atypical Teratoid/Rhabdoid Tumor) — SMARCB1/INI1 loss.

cards.q: What neurodegenerative disease shows 'ballooned neurons' and Pick bodies?
cards.a: Pick disease (frontotemporal dementia) — tau-positive Pick bodies.

cards.q: What is the classic clinical tetrad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Wet, Wobbly, Wacky — urinary incontinence, gait apraxia (magnetic gait), dementia.

cards.q: What protein aggregates in Lewy body dementia?
cards.a: α-Synuclein (Lewy bodies).

cards.q: What disease shows 'negri bodies' in hippocampal neurons?
cards.a: Rabies encephalitis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of subdural hematoma in elderly?
cards.a: Brain atrophy → bridging vein tear after minor trauma.

cards.q: What is diffuse axonal injury (DAI) pathologically characterized by?
cards.a: Axonal swellings (retraction balls) — seen best with β-APP stain. Caused by shear injury in high-speed trauma.

cards.q: What is the most common site of cerebral contusion?
cards.a: Inferior frontal and anterior temporal lobes (coup-contrecoup).

cards.q: What vascular malformation has 'nidus' and high risk of hemorrhage?
cards.a: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of lobar hemorrhage in elderly?
cards.a: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Aβ deposition in vessel walls).

cards.q: What are lacunar infarcts classically associated with?
cards.a: Hypertension and lipohyalinosis — small vessel disease. Common locations: basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons.

cards.q: What syndrome results from anterior spinal artery occlusion?
cards.a: Anterior spinal artery syndrome — bilateral loss of motor + pain/temp (spares dorsal columns).

cards.q: What is the most common demyelinating disease of the peripheral nervous system?
cards.a: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy).

cards.q: What CSF finding is classic in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
cards.a: Albuminocytologic dissociation (↑ protein, normal WBC).

cards.q: What antibody is associated with Miller-Fisher variant of GBS?
cards.a: Anti-GQ1b — ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy overall?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus (distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy).

cards.q: What neuropathy is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?
cards.a: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN) — demyelinating (CMT1) or axonal (CMT2), pes cavus, hammer toes.

cards.q: What is the pathology in myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in myasthenia gravis on EMG?
cards.a: Decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

cards.q: What tumor is associated with myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Thymoma (thymic hyperplasia also common).

cards.q: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer — autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.

cards.q: What is the difference in repetitive stimulation between MG and LEMS?
cards.a:
MG: decremental response.
LEMS: incremental response (facilitation) at high frequency.

cards.q: What is the most common leukodystrophy?
cards.a: Metachromatic leukodystrophy — arylsulfatase A deficiency, sulfatide accumulation.

cards.q: What is the enzyme deficient in Krabbe disease?
cards.a: Galactocerebrosidase — globoid cells on histology.

cards.q: What disease shows 'cherry red spot' on macula?
cards.a: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) and Niemann-Pick.

cards.q: What storage disease shows 'crumpled tissue paper' macrophages?
cards.a: Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency).

cards.q: What is the inheritance and deficient enzyme in adrenoleukodystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked — ABCD1 mutation, very long chain fatty acids accumulation.

cards.q: What congenital malformation features downward displacement of cerebellar vermis and tonsils through foramen magnum?
cards.a: Chiari type 1 malformation (type 2 has myelomeningocele).

cards.q: What is Dandy-Walker malformation?
cards.a: Agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis + cystic dilation of 4th ventricle + enlarged posterior fossa.

cards.q: What neural tube defect is associated with elevated maternal AFP and acetylcholinesterase?
cards.a: Anencephaly or open spina bifida (myelomeningocele).

cards.q: What is the most common site of syringomyelia?
cards.a: Cervical spinal cord — central canal dilation, cape-like loss of pain/temp (crossing fibers).

cards.q: What is the classic association of syringomyelia?
cards.a: Chiari type 1 malformation or trauma/tumor.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates?
cards.a: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).

cards.q: What organism causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients with India ink positive CSF?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans.

cards.q: What is the most common viral cause of aseptic meningitis?
cards.a: Enteroviruses (esp. Coxsackie, Echovirus).

cards.q: What is tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) characterized by?
cards.a: Demyelination of dorsal columns and dorsal roots — loss of proprioception/vibration, Argyll Robertson pupils, positive Romberg.

cards.q: What is general paresis of the insane (neurosyphilis)?
cards.a: Chronic meningoencephalitis with personality changes, dementia, Argyll Robertson pupils.

cards.q: What are the histologic features of tuberculous meningitis?
cards.a: Basilar exudates, caseating granulomas, cranial nerve palsies.

cards.q: What is the most common space-occupying lesion in AIDS patients?
cards.a: Toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions).

cards.q: What is the treatment for cerebral toxoplasmosis in AIDS?
cards.a: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin.

cards.q: What virus causes subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)?
cards.a: Measles virus — persistent defective infection years after initial infection.

cards.q: What are Negri bodies diagnostic of?
cards.a: Rabies.

cards.q: What prion disease is associated with cannibalism in Papua New Guinea?
cards.a: Kuru.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cerebral abscess in immunocompetent adults?
cards.a: Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species (often from contiguous spread — sinusitis/otitis).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of brain abscess in adults?
cards.a: Contiguous spread from sinusitis/otitis/mastoiditis (Streptococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes).

cards.q: What is the classic ring-enhancing lesion differential in AIDS patients (MASS)?
cards.a: Metastasis, Abscess, Stroke (toxoplasmosis), Subacute (PML, lymphoma).

cards.q: What is the treatment for neurocysticercosis?
cards.a: Albendazole + steroids (to reduce inflammation from dying cysts).

cards.q: What organism causes amebic meningoencephalitis via cribriform plate?
cards.a: Naegleria fowleri (primary amebic meningoencephalitis — rapidly fatal).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of viral encephalitis with temporal lobe involvement?
What are Cowdry type A inclusions seen in?
cards.a: HSV encephalitis (eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions).

cards.q: What prion disease presents with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and 14-3-3 protein in CSF?
cards.a: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

cards.q: What is the characteristic EEG finding in CJD?
cards.a: Periodic sharp wave complexes.

cards.q: What is the pathology of Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Thiamine deficiency — mammillary body hemorrhage/necrosis, periventricular petechiae, confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia.

cards.q: What is Korsakoff psychosis?
cards.a: Chronic sequela of Wernicke — anterograde/retrograde amnesia, confabulation (mammillary body damage).

cards.q: What is central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome) associated with?
cards.a: Rapid correction of hyponatremia — locked-in syndrome, demyelination of basis pontis.

cards.q: What toxin causes basal ganglia necrosis and parkinsonism?
cards.a: Carbon monoxide (globus pallidus lesions) or MPTP.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Marchiafava-Bignami disease?
cards.a: Demyelination/necrosis of corpus callosum — seen in chronic alcoholics.

cards.q: What vitamin deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency — dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal tracts.

cards.q: What is the pathology of pellagra (niacin deficiency)?
cards.a: Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia — neuronal degeneration in cortex and anterior horns.

cards.q: What is the most common seizure type in children?
cards.a: Febrile seizures.

cards.q: What is hippocampal sclerosis associated with?
cards.a: Temporal lobe epilepsy — neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 and dentate gyrus.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of status epilepticus in adults?
cards.a: Anticonvulsant noncompliance or stroke.

cards.q: What is Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
cards.a: Childhood epileptic encephalopathy — multiple seizure types, intellectual disability, slow spike-and-wave on EEG.

cards.q: What is West syndrome (infantile spasms)?
cards.a: Flexor spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, developmental regression — treated with ACTH.

cards.q: What is the pathology of tuberous sclerosis complex?
cards.a: Cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA, renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas.

cards.q: What is Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Port-wine stain (trigeminal distribution), leptomeningeal angiomatosis, tram-track calcifications, glaucoma, seizures.

cards.q: What is von Hippel-Lindail disease?
cards.a: Hemangioblastomas (cerebellar/spinal), renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, retinal angiomas.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in tuberous sclerosis?
cards.a: TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of neurofibromatosis type 1?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant (NF1 gene, chromosome 17).

cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria highlights for NF1?
cards.a: ≥6 café-au-lait spots, ≥2 neurofibromas, axillary freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, sphenoid dysplasia.

cards.q: What peripheral nerve tumor is seen in NF1?
cards.a: Plexiform neurofibroma (risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor).

cards.q: What is the most common primary spinal cord tumor?
cards.a: Ependymoma (especially myxopapillary in filum terminale).

cards.q: What is the most common intramedullary spinal cord tumor in adults?
cards.a: Ependymoma.

cards.q: What is the most common intradural extramedullary spinal tumor?
cards.a: Meningioma and schwannoma.

cards.q: What is syringomyelia classically associated with?
cards.a: Chiari I malformation or trauma.

cards.q: What is the classic sensory loss in syringomyelia?
cards.a: Cape-like distribution (loss of pain and temperature, preserved touch/vibration).

cards.q: What is anterior horn cell disease?
cards.a: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) — combined UMN + LMN signs.

cards.q: What is the pathology in ALS?
cards.a: Loss of anterior horn cells and corticospinal tract degeneration.

cards.q: What protein aggregates in ALS?
cards.a: TDP-43 (most cases).

cards.q: What is the most common motor neuron disease in children?
cards.a: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) — SMN1 gene deletion.

cards.q: What is polio virus pathology?
cards.a: Destruction of anterior horn cells — asymmetric flaccid paralysis.

cards.q: What is the most common acquired myopathy?
cards.a: Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis.

cards.q: What is the classic skin finding in dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Anti-Mi-2.

cards.q: What is inclusion body myositis?
cards.a: Most common myopathy in patients >50 — distal weakness (finger flexors, quadriceps), rimmed vacuoles.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: Dystrophin gene mutation (X-linked) — absent dystrophin, pseudohypertrophy of calves.

cards.q: What is Becker muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: Partial dystrophin function — milder, later onset than Duchenne.

cards.q: What is myotonic dystrophy type 1?
cards.a: CTG repeats in DMPK gene — myotonia, frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy, cardiac conduction defects.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of myotonic dystrophy?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant with anticipation.

cards.q: What stain highlights nemaline rods in nemaline myopathy?
cards.a: Gomori trichrome.

cards.q: What is the most common mitochondrial myopathy?
cards.a: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes).

cards.q: What is the inheritance of mitochondrial diseases?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance.

cards.q: What is the pathology in Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: Mitochondrial deletion — ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction block.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of epidural abscess?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus (often from vertebral osteomyelitis).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, dementia ('wet, wobbly, wacky').

cards.q: What is communicating hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Impaired CSF absorption (e.g., post-meningitis, SAH) — all ventricles enlarged.

cards.q: What is non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Blockage within ventricular system (e.g., aqueductal stenosis, tumor).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Aqueductal stenosis.

cards.q: What is Dandy-Walker malformation associated with?
cards.a: Hydrocephalus, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, enlarged posterior fossa.

cards.q: What neural tube defect is prevented by folic acid supplementation?
cards.a: Spina bifida and anencephaly.

cards.q: What is holoprosencephaly associated with?
cards.a: Failure of forebrain cleavage — seen in trisomy 13, fetal alcohol syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ischemic stroke in young adults?
cards.a: Cardioembolism or dissection.

cards.q: What is the pathology of lacunar infarcts?
cards.a: Hypertensive small vessel disease — lipohyalinosis.

cards.q: What artery supplies the lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome)?
cards.a: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

cards.q: What is the classic finding in Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome?
cards.a: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, facial pain/temp loss, contralateral body pain/temp loss, ataxia, dysphagia.

cards.q: What artery occlusion causes contralateral hemiparesis and aphasia (if dominant)?
cards.a: Middle cerebral artery (MCA).

cards.q: What artery supplies the medial aspect of the hemispheres and lower limbs?
cards.a: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

cards.q: What is the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
cards.a: Putamen / basal ganglia (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms).

cards.q: What is the most common site of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms?
cards.a: Small penetrating arteries in basal ganglia.

cards.q: What is cerebral amyloid angiopathy associated with?
cards.a: Lobar hemorrhages in elderly, Alzheimer disease.

cards.q: What is the most common primary CNS vasculitis?
cards.a: Primary angiitis of CNS.

cards.q: What is Binswanger disease?
cards.a: Subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy — multiple lacunar infarcts and white matter demyelination in hypertensive patients.

cards.q: What is the pathology of multi-infarct dementia?
cards.a: Stepwise cognitive decline due to multiple cortical infarcts.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of dementia overall?
cards.a: Alzheimer disease.

cards.q: What is the second most common cause of dementia?
cards.a: Vascular (multi-infarct) dementia.

cards.q: What protein is deposited in cerebral amyloid angiopathy?
cards.a: Aβ (amyloid-beta).

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome?
cards.a: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (small cell lung cancer).

cards.q: What antibody is seen in paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration?
cards.a: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) — associated with breast/ovarian cancer.

cards.q: What is limbic encephalitis associated with?
cards.a: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) — small cell lung cancer.

cards.q: What is the pathology of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
cards.a: JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes — demyelination, bizarre astrocytes.

cards.q: What is the treatment for PML?
cards.a: Restore immune function (e.g., stop immunosuppression, start ART in HIV).

cards.q: What is HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) formerly called?
cards.a: AIDS dementia complex — subcortical dementia.

cards.q: What is vacuolar myelopathy in HIV?
cards.a: Demyelination of dorsal and lateral columns — spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia.

cards.q: What is the most common opportunistic infection in AIDS affecting CNS?
cards.a: Toxoplasmosis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of fungal meningitis?
cards.a: Cryptococcus neoformans.

cards.q: What stain highlights Cryptococcus capsule?
cards.a: Mucicarmine or India ink.

cards.q: What are the 4 major dopamine pathways and their clinical relevance?
cards.a:
1. Mesolimbic: VTA → Nucleus accumbens → Positive symptoms of schizophrenia; reward/addiction
2. Mesocortical: VTA → Prefrontal cortex → Negative/cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia
3. Nigrostriatal: Substantia nigra → Striatum → Movement (↓DA = Parkinsonism, EPS)
4. Tuberoinfundibular: Hypothalamus → Pituitary → DA inhibits prolactin (D₂ blockade → ↑ Prolactin)

cards.q: What is the synthesis pathway of dopamine?
cards.a:
Tyrosine → (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting step, requires BH₄) → L-DOPA → (DOPA decarboxylase) → Dopamine (DA)
Then → (dopamine β-hydroxylase) → Norepinephrine
Then → (PNMT, in adrenal medulla only) → Epinephrine
VMAT2 packages catecholamines into vesicles

cards.q: What is the synthesis pathway of serotonin (5-HT)?
cards.a:
Tryptophan → (tryptophan hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → 5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) → (aromatic amino acid decarboxylase) → Serotonin (5-HT)
Serotonin → (MAO + aldehyde dehydrogenase) → 5-HIAA (urinary metabolite, measured in carcinoid syndrome)

cards.q: What are the two types of monoamine oxidase (MAO) and their substrates?
cards.a:
MAO-A: Metabolizes Serotonin (5-HT), Norepinephrine (NE), Epinephrine, and Tyramine
MAO-B: Metabolizes Dopamine (DA) and Phenylethylamine
Both types metabolize Tyramine.
Selegiline = selective MAO-B inhibitor at low doses (used in Parkinson's disease).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of GABA-A receptors and how do drugs modulate it?
cards.a:
GABA-A = Ligand-gated Cl⁻ channel → Cl⁻ influx → hyperpolarization → CNS depression
Benzodiazepines: ↑ FREQUENCY of Cl⁻ channel opening (GABA must be present)
Barbiturates: ↑ DURATION of Cl⁻ channel opening (can open independently at high doses)
Alcohol: ↑ GABA-A + blocks NMDA
GABA-B: Gi-coupled (baclofen acts here)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of NMDA receptors and which drugs target them?
cards.a:
NMDA receptors = Ionotropic glutamate receptors (require glutamate + glycine + membrane depolarization)
At rest: blocked by Mg²⁺; conducts Ca²⁺, Na⁺, K⁺
NMDA antagonists used clinically:
• Memantine → Alzheimer's disease
• Ketamine → anesthesia / treatment-resistant depression
• Amantadine → Parkinson's, NMS
• Alcohol → CNS depression
• PCP → drug of abuse (dissociative hallucinogen)

cards.q: What are the two types of cholinergic receptors and their pharmacological relevance?
cards.a:
Muscarinic (M₁–M₅): G-protein coupled; in CNS, heart, glands, smooth muscle
• Blocked by TCAs, low-potency antipsychotics → anticholinergic side effects (SLUDGE opposite: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia)
Nicotinic (Nm, Nn): Ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels
• Nm: Neuromuscular junction
• Nn: Autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla
• Vareniclne, nicotine act at α4β2 nAChR

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of SSRIs?
cards.a:
Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
Block the serotonin transporter (SERT) on presynaptic neurons → ↑ 5-HT in synapse
Delayed therapeutic effect (2–6 weeks): Due to initial 5-HT₁A autoreceptor negative feedback → with chronic use, autoreceptors desensitize → net ↑ serotonergic neurotransmission + neuroplastic changes (↑ BDNF, hippocampal neurogenesis)

cards.q: List all 6 SSRIs with their unique features.
cards.a:
Fluoxetine (Prozac) — longest t½ (~1 week incl. norfluoxetine); least discontinuation syndrome; strong CYP2D6 inhibitor
Sertraline (Zoloft) — broadest indications; safest in pregnancy; minimal drug interactions
Paroxetine (Paxil) — most anticholinergic; most sedating; strongest CYP2D6 inhibitor; worst discontinuation; Category D in pregnancy
Citalopram (Celexa) — most selective SERT; QT prolongation at high doses
Escitalopram — S-enantiomer of citalopram; fewest interactions
Fluvoxamine — primarily OCD; strong CYP1A2 inhibitor

cards.q: What are the common side effects of SSRIs?
cards.a:
GI: Nausea, diarrhea (take with food; improves in weeks)
Sexual: ↓ libido, anorgasmia, delayed ejaculation (most common cause of non-compliance)
CNS: Insomnia, headache, initial anxiety
Metabolic: Weight gain (long-term)
Bleeding: ↓ platelet serotonin → ↓ platelet aggregation (caution with NSAIDs/warfarin)
SIADH / Hyponatremia (especially elderly)
Cardiac: QT prolongation (citalopram/escitalopram at high doses)

cards.q: What are the indications for SSRIs?
cards.a:
Depression: Major depressive disorder (first-line)
Anxiety disorders: GAD, panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, OCD, specific phobias
Others: Bulimia nervosa (fluoxetine — only FDA-approved antidepressant for bulimia), PMDD, hot flashes
First-line for most depressive and anxiety disorders due to safety profile

cards.q: What is serotonin syndrome?
cards.a:
Excess serotonergic activity — Classic Triad:
1. Altered mental status (agitation, confusion)
2. Autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension)
3. Neuromuscular abnormalities (tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, clonus — most specific)
Common triggers: SSRI + MAOI, linezolid, tramadol, meperidine, DXM, St. John's Wort
Treatment: Stop offending drug, benzos, cyproheptadine (5-HT₂A antagonist), cooling

cards.q: What is SSRI discontinuation syndrome?
cards.a:
Abrupt cessation of SSRIs (especially short-acting) → withdrawal-like symptoms
Mnemonic FINISH:
Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance/dizziness, Sensory disturbances (electric shock 'brain zaps'), Hyperarousal
Worst with: Paroxetine (shortest t½, no active metabolite)
Least risk: Fluoxetine (longest t½)
Management: Restart and taper slowly

cards.q: What are CYP interactions among SSRIs?
cards.a:
Fluoxetine: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → ↑ TCAs, haloperidol, codeine (↓ efficacy of codeine → ↓ morphine production)
Paroxetine: Strongest CYP2D6 inhibitor (even stronger than fluoxetine)
Fluvoxamine: CYP1A2, 2C19, 3A4 inhibitor → ↑ theophylline, warfarin, clozapine
Sertraline: Mild CYP2D6 inhibitor (minimal clinical significance)
Escitalopram/Citalopram: Minimal CYP interactions (preferred when avoiding drug interactions)

cards.q: What is the safety of SSRIs in pregnancy?
cards.a:
Generally preferred antidepressants in pregnancy
Sertraline: Preferred (most safety data; safest in pregnancy and lactation)
Paroxetine: Category D — avoid (associated with cardiac malformations, particularly VSD)
Fluoxetine: Category C; long t½ may affect neonate longer
Third-trimester exposure: Neonatal adaptation syndrome (transient jitteriness, irritability, respiratory distress)
PPHN risk: Small increased risk with 3rd-trimester SSRIs
Untreated maternal depression carries significant risks — always weigh risk vs. benefit

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of SNRIs?
cards.a:
Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)
Block both SERT (serotonin transporter) and NET (norepinephrine transporter)
→ ↑ synaptic 5-HT and NE
Advantage over SSRIs:
• NE pathway involved in descending pain modulation → benefit for pain disorders
• Broader efficacy for some patients
Drugs: Venlafaxine, Desvenlafaxine, Duloxetine, Levomilnacipran

cards.q: What are the unique properties of venlafaxine?
cards.a:
Dose-dependent NE reuptake inhibition:
• Low dose (<150 mg/day): Primarily SSRI-like
• Medium dose (150–225 mg): SNRI
• High dose (>225 mg): NE dominates
Side effects: Dose-dependent hypertension (monitor BP), sweating, tachycardia
Worst discontinuation syndrome among antidepressants (short t½)
Indications: MDD, GAD, social anxiety, panic disorder, fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain

cards.q: What are the unique properties of duloxetine?
cards.a:
Balanced 5-HT and NE reuptake inhibition
FDA-approved indications (mnemonic D-MAN):
Depression (MDD), Musculoskeletal pain/fibromyalgia, Anxiety (GAD), Neuropathy (diabetic peripheral)
+ Stress urinary incontinence (NE → ↑ urethral sphincter tone)
Caution: Hepatotoxicity — avoid in liver disease and significant alcohol use
Side effects: Nausea (most common), hypertension
Avoid: Within 14 days of MAOIs; uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma

cards.q: What side effects are unique to SNRIs compared to SSRIs?
cards.a:
Shared with SSRIs: Nausea, sexual dysfunction, insomnia, headache
Unique to SNRIs (NE-mediated):
• Hypertension (esp. venlafaxine at high doses — dose-dependent)
• Tachycardia
• Diaphoresis (sweating)
• Urinary hesitancy/retention (NE → α₁ stimulation → ↑ urethral sphincter tone)
• Dry mouth
Risk of serotonin syndrome with MAOIs (contraindicated)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)?
cards.a:
Primary therapeutic: Block SERT and NET → ↑ NE and 5-HT (NE > 5-HT for most)
Receptor blockade causing side effects:
• α₁-adrenergic: Orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia
• H₁ histamine: Sedation, weight gain
• Muscarinic (M₁): Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, confusion
• Na⁺ channels: Cardiac toxicity in overdose (QRS widening)

cards.q: Classify TCAs into tertiary and secondary amines.
cards.a:
Tertiary Amines (more anticholinergic, more sedating, more α₁ blockade):
• Amitriptyline — most sedating; migraine prophylaxis
• Imipramine — enuresis in children, panic disorder
• Clomipramine — most serotonergic; drug of choice for OCD (before SSRIs)
• Doxepin — most antihistaminergic; insomnia, pruritus
Secondary Amines (better tolerated, more NE selective):
• Nortriptyline — least orthostatic hypotension; therapeutic window 50–150 ng/mL
• Desipramine — most NE selective; least sedating; ADHD (alt)

cards.q: What are the features of TCA overdose (the 3 Cs)?
cards.a:
3 Cs of TCA overdose:
1. Convulsions (seizures)
2. Coma
3. Cardiac arrhythmias (wide QRS, ventricular tachycardia, QT prolongation)
ECG: QRS >100 ms → seizure risk; QRS >160 ms → arrhythmia risk
Mechanism: Na⁺ channel blockade (like Class IA antiarrhythmic) → widened QRS → VT, VF
Also: Anticholinergic signs (hyperthermia, tachycardia), hypotension (α₁ blockade)
