cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for TCA overdose with cardiac toxicity?
cards.a:
IV Sodium Bicarbonate (NaHCO₃)
Mechanisms of benefit:
1. Alkalinization (↑ pH) → alters TCA protein binding → ↑ ionization → ↓ Na⁺ channel binding affinity → ↑ cardiac conduction
2. Sodium loading → overcomes Na⁺ channel blockade (pharmacological competition)
Goal: Serum pH 7.45–7.55; NaHCO₃ boluses IV
Also: Benzodiazepines for seizures; supportive care
Avoid: Physostigmine (can worsen arrhythmias), flumazenil

cards.q: What are unique clinical uses of specific TCAs?
cards.a:
Amitriptyline: Migraine prophylaxis, neuropathic pain, insomnia
Imipramine: Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) in children, panic disorder
Clomipramine: OCD (most serotonergic TCA; was drug of choice before SSRIs)
Doxepin: Insomnia, pruritus, urticaria (strongest antihistamine among TCAs)
Nortriptyline: Smoking cessation (alternative to bupropion); therapeutic window 50–150 ng/mL
Desipramine: ADHD (alternative); most noradrenergic; least sedating

cards.q: What are contraindications to TCAs?
cards.a:
Absolute:
• MAOIs within 14 days (serotonin syndrome / hypertensive crisis risk)
• Acute/recent MI (Na⁺ channel block → arrhythmia)
• QTc prolongation / Torsades risk
Relative:
• Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — urinary retention
• Narrow-angle glaucoma — ↑ intraocular pressure
• Elderly — falls (orthostatic hypotension), anticholinergic delirium
• Active suicidality — narrow therapeutic index, lethal in overdose
Key: TCAs are among most dangerous antidepressants in overdose

cards.q: Which TCA has a true therapeutic window (curvilinear dose-response)?
cards.a:
Nortriptyline
Therapeutic window: 50–150 ng/mL
• Below 50 ng/mL → insufficient efficacy
• Above 150 ng/mL → toxicity WITHOUT additional benefit
This 'inverted-U' (curvilinear) relationship is unique among antidepressants
Serum level monitoring is required for nortriptyline (unlike most other antidepressants where levels are used only for toxicity detection)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of MAOIs?
cards.a:
Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)
Inhibit MAO enzyme → ↓ breakdown of NE, 5-HT, and DA → ↑ monoamine levels
Types:
• Irreversible non-selective: Phenelzine, Tranylcypromine (weeks to recover — requires new MAO enzyme synthesis)
• Reversible inhibitor of MAO-A (RIMA): Moclobemide (competitive; less tyramine risk)
• Selective MAO-B: Selegiline (at low doses — used in Parkinson's disease)

cards.q: What are the indications and clinical uses for MAOIs?
cards.a:
Atypical depression (classic indication — mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity)
Treatment-resistant depression
Panic disorder, social anxiety disorder (phenelzine)
PTSD
Neurological: Parkinson's disease (selegiline — MAO-B inhibitor)
Rarely used for depression now due to serious drug and food interactions; reserved for treatment failures

cards.q: Why must patients on MAOIs avoid tyramine-rich foods (the Cheese Effect)?
cards.a:
Mechanism (Cheese/Tyramine Effect):
• Normally, MAO in GI tract and liver metabolizes dietary tyramine before systemic absorption
• MAOIs block GI MAO → tyramine absorbed intact → enters noradrenergic terminals → displaces NE from vesicles → massive NE release → hypertensive crisis
Tyramine-rich foods to avoid: Aged cheeses, wine (especially red), beer, fermented meats, soy sauce, fava beans, aged/smoked fish, sauerkraut
Symptoms: Severe throbbing headache, severe hypertension → risk of stroke, intracranial hemorrhage

cards.q: What are the most dangerous drug interactions with MAOIs?
cards.a:
MAOI + Serotonergic agents → Serotonin Syndrome:
• SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, meperidine (most dangerous), tramadol, dextromethorphan (DXM), St. John's Wort
MAOI + Sympathomimetics → Hypertensive Crisis:
• Amphetamines, cocaine, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, tyramine (food)
MAOI + Meperidine: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED → life-threatening serotonin syndrome + hyperthermia
Washout rule: 14 days after MAOI before starting serotonergic drug; 5 weeks if stopping fluoxetine before starting MAOI

cards.q: How do phenelzine and tranylcypromine differ?
cards.a:
Phenelzine (Nardil): Irreversible non-selective MAOI; also inhibits GABA transaminase → mildly anxiolytic/GABA-like; more weight gain; more anticholinergic
Tranylcypromine (Parnate): Irreversible non-selective MAOI; structurally related to amphetamine → mildly stimulating; more insomnia, less sedation; less weight gain
Both require strict dietary restrictions and 14-day washout period

cards.q: What is special about selegiline as an MAO inhibitor?
cards.a:
Selective MAO-B inhibitor at low doses (≤10 mg/day)
• Selective MAO-B inhibition → ↑ DA → used in early Parkinson's disease
• No dietary tyramine restriction at low doses (MAO-A is still intact)
• At high doses → loses MAO-B selectivity → inhibits MAO-A → tyramine dietary restrictions needed
Transdermal selegiline patch (Emsam): Approved for MDD
• Bypasses GI MAO → less tyramine risk at 6 mg/24h dose
• Minimal dietary restrictions at lowest dose

cards.q: What is moclobemide (RIMA) and how does it differ from irreversible MAOIs?
cards.a:
Reversible Inhibitor of MAO-A (RIMA)
• Competitively inhibits MAO-A only (reversible)
• Tyramine can displace it from the enzyme → dietary restrictions MUCH less strict
• Fewer drug interactions
Advantages: Safer than irreversible MAOIs; shorter washout (~24h vs 14 days)
Available: Canada, UK, Australia (NOT available in USA)
Indications: Depression, social anxiety disorder
Side effects: Insomnia, nausea, headache

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of bupropion?
cards.a:
Norepinephrine-Dopamine Reuptake Inhibitor (NDRI)
• Blocks NET (norepinephrine transporter) and DAT (dopamine transporter)
• Does NOT inhibit SERT → no serotonergic side effects (no sexual dysfunction)
• Also blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) → aids smoking cessation
• Active metabolite: Hydroxybupropion (longer half-life)
Key advantages: No sexual dysfunction, no weight gain (often promotes weight loss), activating (beneficial for fatigue/hypersomnia)

cards.q: What are the FDA-approved indications and key features of bupropion?
cards.a:
FDA-approved: MDD, Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), Smoking cessation (Zyban)
Off-label: ADHD (adults), SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction (add-on), bipolar depression (with mood stabilizer), weight loss (Contrave = bupropion + naltrexone)
Advantages over SSRIs: No sexual dysfunction, no weight gain, activating
Contraindications: Seizure disorder, anorexia/bulimia nervosa (electrolyte imbalances → ↑ seizure risk), abrupt alcohol/BZD withdrawal, within 14 days of MAOI
Key risk: Lowers seizure threshold (dose-dependent)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and side effects of mirtazapine?
cards.a:
Noradrenergic and Specific Serotonergic Antidepressant (NaSSA)
• α₂ presynaptic antagonist → blocks auto/heteroreceptors → ↑ NE and 5-HT release
• 5-HT₂ and 5-HT₃ antagonism → no sexual dysfunction; antiemetic
• H₁ antagonism → sedation, weight gain
Paradox: MORE sedating at LOW doses (more H₁ effect relative to NE)
Key benefits: Good for depression + insomnia + weight loss (anorexia/cachexia); no sexual dysfunction; fast onset
Rare: Agranulocytosis (monitor CBC if fever/sore throat)

cards.q: What is the mechanism and key side effect of trazodone?
cards.a:
Mechanism:
• 5-HT₂A and 5-HT₂C receptor antagonist (primary)
• Weak SERT inhibitor
• H₁ antagonist (sedation) + α₁ antagonist (orthostatic hypotension)
Primary clinical use: Insomnia (at low doses 50–100 mg) — most common psychiatric use
Also: Depression (300–600 mg), anxiety
Unique and dangerous side effect: Priapism (prolonged painful erection, due to α₁ blockade → venous engorgement) — medical emergency; treated with aspiration/injection
Also: Orthostatic hypotension, sedation

cards.q: What is the mechanism of vortioxetine and its clinical advantage?
cards.a:
Multimodal antidepressant:
• SERT inhibitor (↑ 5-HT)
• 5-HT₁A partial agonist (anxiolytic effect)
• 5-HT₃, 5-HT₇, 5-HT₁D antagonist
• 5-HT₁B partial agonist
Unique clinical advantage: May improve cognitive function (executive function, memory, concentration) — differentiating feature vs. SSRIs
FDA approved: MDD
Side effects: Nausea (most common), fewer sexual side effects than SSRIs

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of typical (first-generation) antipsychotics?
cards.a:
D₂ receptor antagonism across all 4 dopamine pathways:
• Mesolimbic D₂ blockade → ↓ positive symptoms (therapeutic)
• Mesocortical D₂ blockade → worsens negative symptoms (adverse)
• Nigrostriatal D₂ blockade → EPS (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia)
• Tuberoinfundibular D₂ blockade → ↑ Prolactin → galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction

cards.q: How do high-potency and low-potency typical antipsychotics differ?
cards.a:
High-potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine):
• High D₂ affinity → MORE EPS
• LESS anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, α₁-blocking effects
• Less sedation, less orthostatic hypotension
Low-potency (chlorpromazine, thioridazine):
• Lower D₂ affinity → LESS EPS
• MORE anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, α₁-blocking effects
• More sedation, more orthostatic hypotension
Rule: High potency = High EPS; Low potency = Low EPS + more other side effects

cards.q: What are the 4 types of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and their timing? (4-2-4 rule)
cards.a:
Mnemonic: '4 hours / 4 days / 4 weeks / 4 months'
1. Acute Dystonia (within 4 hours–4 days): Sustained involuntary muscle contraction (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, opisthotonos, trismus)
2. Akathisia (4 days–4 weeks): Subjective motor restlessness; unable to sit still; pacing
3. Drug-induced Parkinsonism (4 weeks–4 months): Bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait
4. Tardive Dyskinesia (>4 months, often years): Repetitive involuntary movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, choreiform)

cards.q: How is antipsychotic-induced acute dystonia treated?
cards.a:
Acute dystonia = sudden sustained involuntary muscle spasm
Examples: Oculogyric crisis (eye deviation upward), torticollis (neck twisting), opisthotonos, trismus (jaw clenching)
Treatment:
• Benztropine (Cogentin) — anticholinergic; IM or IV for acute episode
• Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — anticholinergic; IM or IV
• Trihexyphenidyl — oral maintenance
Mechanism: Anticholinergics restore DA/ACh balance in nigrostriatal tract
Risk factors: Young males, high-potency antipsychotics, first antipsychotic exposure, cocaine use

cards.q: How is antipsychotic-induced akathisia treated?
cards.a:
Akathisia = intense inner restlessness; cannot remain still; pacing, shifting weight
Commonly misdiagnosed as psychosis worsening (can worsen outcomes if antipsychotic dose ↑)
Treatment:
• Propranolol (β-blocker, lipophilic) — first-line
• Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) — second-line
• Mirtazapine (5-HT₂A antagonism helps)
• Reduce antipsychotic dose or switch to atypical
Anticholinergics (benztropine) have limited efficacy for akathisia

cards.q: What is tardive dyskinesia (TD) and how is it treated?
cards.a:
Tardive Dyskinesia = involuntary repetitive movements after prolonged D₂ blockade
Movements: Lip smacking, tongue protrusion (fly-catcher), grimacing, choreiform limb movements
Mechanism: Dopamine receptor supersensitivity (↑ D₂ receptor density) after chronic blockade
Risk: Older women, longer duration, higher dose
Treatment:
• Valbenazine (Ingrezza) — FDA approved for TD
• Deutetrabenazine (Austedo) — FDA approved for TD and Huntington's chorea
• Tetrabenazine (off-label)
• Switch to clozapine
• Anticholinergics WORSEN TD — avoid

cards.q: What are the features of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a:
FEVER mnemonic:
Fever (hyperthermia >38–40°C)
Encephalopathy (confusion, altered consciousness)
Vitals unstable (tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis)
Elevated CPK (↑↑ → rhabdomyolysis → renal failure)
Rigidity ('lead-pipe' rigidity — most specific feature)
Labs: ↑ WBC, ↑ LFTs, ↑ creatinine, metabolic acidosis
Onset: Hours to weeks after starting/increasing antipsychotic
Mortality: 5–20% if untreated

cards.q: How is Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) treated?
cards.a:
STOP antipsychotic immediately
Supportive: ICU admission, IV fluids, aggressive cooling
Specific pharmacotherapy:
• Dantrolene — inhibits sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺ release → ↓ rigidity and hyperthermia
• Bromocriptine or amantadine — DA agonists → restore dopaminergic tone
• Benzodiazepines — for agitation
Monitor: CPK, creatinine (for rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria)
Resume antipsychotic: Wait ≥2 weeks; use lower-potency or atypical agent; monitor closely

cards.q: What are the unique side effects of chlorpromazine and thioridazine?
cards.a:
Chlorpromazine (low-potency):
• Corneal and lens deposits (high doses → visual changes)
• Photosensitivity (use sunscreen)
• Purple-gray skin discoloration (prolonged high doses)
• Most sedating typical antipsychotic
Thioridazine (low-potency):
• Pigmentary retinopathy → night blindness, permanent vision loss
• QTc prolongation → Torsades de Pointes (most cardiotoxic typical antipsychotic)
• Retrograde ejaculation
Mnemonic: Thioridazine → Retinal damage

cards.q: What are the unique features of haloperidol?
cards.a:
High-potency typical antipsychotic (highly D₂ selective)
• Most EPS of all antipsychotics
• Least anticholinergic, least sedating, least orthostatic hypotension
Uses: Schizophrenia, acute psychosis (IM), delirium (IV in ICU — off label), Tourette's syndrome, acute agitation
Long-acting injectable (decanoate): Monthly dosing for compliance
Key risk: QT prolongation (especially IV); monitor ECG
Most common long-term risk: Tardive dyskinesia

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics?
cards.a:
5-HT₂A + D₂ receptor antagonism (dual blockade)
Why 5-HT₂A blockade matters:
• Nigrostriatal: 5-HT₂A blockade → ↑ DA release → offsets D₂ blockade → ↓ EPS
• Mesocortical: 5-HT₂A blockade in PFC → ↑ DA → improves negative symptoms
Vs. typical antipsychotics:
• Less EPS, less tardive dyskinesia
• May improve negative/cognitive symptoms
• More metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia)
• Variable prolactin elevation

cards.q: What are the indications and required monitoring for clozapine?
cards.a:
Indications:
• Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed ≥2 antipsychotics) — most effective antipsychotic overall
• Suicidal ideation in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder
Required monitoring (REMS program):
• ANC before starting
• Weekly ANC for first 6 months
• Every 2 weeks for 6 months
• Monthly thereafter if stable
Stop clozapine if: ANC <1,500 (mild neutropenia); ANC <500 (severe — absolute contraindication)

cards.q: What is clozapine-induced agranulocytosis?
cards.a:
Incidence: ~1–2% of patients
Mortality: High if untreated
Mechanism: Proposed — reactive nitrenium metabolite damages granulocytes; immune-mediated hapten mechanism; direct bone marrow toxicity
Risk factors: Female sex, older age, concurrent carbamazepine (synergistic risk), HLA-DQB1 variants
Clinical: Fever, sore throat, oral ulcers → CBC urgently
Management: Stop clozapine immediately; G-CSF (filgrastim) to stimulate granulocyte production; supportive care
Never rechallenge if severe agranulocytosis occurred

cards.q: What are other serious side effects of clozapine beyond agranulocytosis?
cards.a:
Metabolic: Most weight gain of all antipsychotics; dyslipidemia; insulin resistance; type 2 diabetes
Cardiac: Myocarditis (1–3 months after starting; potentially fatal); cardiomyopathy; QT prolongation
Neurological: Seizures (most seizurogenic antipsychotic — dose-dependent, especially >600 mg/day)
Autonomic: Hypersalivation/sialorrhea (characteristic; treat with sublingual atropine drops or clonidine); constipation (ileus risk)
Other: Sedation (most sedating atypical), urinary incontinence, hypotension
Note: Does NOT significantly elevate prolactin

cards.q: What are the key features of olanzapine?
cards.a:
Mechanism: D₂ + 5-HT₂A + H₁ + M₁ + α₁ blockade
Second highest metabolic risk (after clozapine):
• Major weight gain
• Dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, new-onset type 2 diabetes
Uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar I mania, acute agitation (IM), bipolar depression (+ fluoxetine = Symbyax)
Formulations: Oral, ODT (orally disintegrating tablet), IM (acute agitation), LAI (long-acting injectable)
WARNING: Do NOT combine IM olanzapine + IM/IV benzodiazepine → risk of respiratory depression/death

cards.q: What are the key features of risperidone?
cards.a:
Mechanism: D₂ + 5-HT₂A + α₁ + H₁ blockade
Unique feature: Highest prolactin elevation among atypical antipsychotics (retains significant D₂ blockade in tuberoinfundibular pathway)
→ Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis
EPS risk: Higher than most atypicals but less than typical antipsychotics
Uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, irritability in autism spectrum disorder (FDA approved)
Paliperidone = active metabolite of risperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone)
LAI formulations available (Risperdal Consta, Invega Sustenna/Trinza)

cards.q: What are the key features of quetiapine?
cards.a:
Mechanism: D₂ + 5-HT₂A + H₁ + α₁ + M₁ blockade (very low D₂ affinity)
Least EPS of all antipsychotics (lowest D₂ affinity)
Most sedating atypical antipsychotic (strong H₁ blockade)
Unique concern: Cataract formation (lens opacities — slit-lamp exam recommended every 6 months)
Uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania, bipolar depression (FDA approved), adjunct for MDD, insomnia (off-label)
Low prolactin elevation (low D₂ affinity)
Metabolic effects: Significant weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia

cards.q: What is the unique mechanism and advantages of aripiprazole?
cards.a:
Partial D₂ agonist + 5-HT₂A antagonist + 5-HT₁A partial agonist
D₂ partial agonism:
• Mesolimbic (overactive DA) → functional antagonist → ↓ positive symptoms
• Mesocortical (underactive DA) → functional agonist → ↑ DA → improves negative symptoms
Clinical advantages over other atypicals:
• No prolactin elevation (partial agonism)
• Minimal weight gain
• Minimal metabolic effects
• Less sedation, less QT prolongation
Indications: Schizophrenia, bipolar I, MDD augmentation, Tourette's, autism, agitation

cards.q: What is the key safety concern with ziprasidone?
cards.a:
Mechanism: D₂ + 5-HT₂A + 5-HT₁A partial agonist + mild SERT/NET inhibitor
Key concern: QTc prolongation — greatest QTc prolongation among atypical antipsychotics → risk of Torsades de Pointes
→ Baseline and monitoring ECG required; avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs
Advantages:
• Minimal weight gain and metabolic effects (best metabolic profile after aripiprazole among atypicals)
• Mild antidepressant-like effects (SERT/NET inhibition)
Must be taken with food (≥500 kcal meal doubles bioavailability)

cards.q: Rank atypical antipsychotics by metabolic risk (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia).
cards.a:
Highest → Lowest metabolic risk:
1. Clozapine (worst overall)
2. Olanzapine (close second)
3. Quetiapine
4. Risperidone / Paliperidone
5. Ziprasidone (minimal)
6. Aripiprazole (minimal)
Mnemonic for worst two: 'CO' = Clozapine, Olanzapine
Monitoring for all atypicals: Fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panel, BMI, waist circumference at baseline and every 3 months

cards.q: Which antipsychotics cause the most and least prolactin elevation?
cards.a:
Most prolactin elevation:
• Risperidone (highest among atypicals)
• Paliperidone
• Typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine)
Minimal/No prolactin elevation:
• Aripiprazole (partial D₂ agonist — minimal functional blockade of tuberoinfundibular pathway)
• Quetiapine (very low D₂ affinity)
• Clozapine
Clinical effects of ↑ prolactin: Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, infertility, ↓ libido, osteoporosis (long-term)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines?
cards.a:
Bind to GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine site (between α and γ subunits) → allosteric potentiation of GABA
→ Increase the FREQUENCY of Cl⁻ channel opening
→ ↑ Cl⁻ influx → hyperpolarization → CNS depression
Key point: BZDs REQUIRE GABA to work (cannot activate GABA-A independently)
BZD binding site: α1 subunit (sedation/hypnosis), α2 subunit (anxiolytic/muscle relaxant), α5 subunit (memory/cognition)

cards.q: Compare the mechanisms of benzodiazepines vs barbiturates.
cards.a:
PropertyBenzodiazepinesBarbiturates
GABA-A effect↑ Cl⁻ channel FREQUENCY↑ Cl⁻ channel DURATION
GABA required?YesNo (at high doses)
Therapeutic indexWide (safe)Narrow (dangerous)
Overdose antidoteFlumazenilNone
Respiratory depressionMildSevere/fatal
CYP inductionNoYes (strong)

cards.q: Which benzodiazepines are safest in liver disease (LOT mnemonic)?
cards.a:
LOT Mnemonic — Glucuronidation only (Phase II; bypass hepatic CYP enzymes):
Lorazepam (Ativan)
Oxazepam (Serax)
Temazepam (Restoril)
Why safe: These drugs undergo glucuronidation only → no active metabolites → not affected by CYP inhibitors/inducers → safe in hepatic impairment, elderly, patients on complex drug regimens
Lorazepam also preferred in status epilepticus (predictable IV absorption) and alcohol withdrawal with liver disease

cards.q: List long-acting vs short-acting benzodiazepines and their uses.
cards.a:
Long-acting (t½ >24h; active metabolites):
• Diazepam — anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, seizures, muscle spasm
• Chlordiazepoxide — alcohol withdrawal
• Clonazepam — panic disorder, seizures (absence, myoclonic), social anxiety
• Flurazepam — insomnia (avoid in elderly)
Short-acting:
• Lorazepam — status epilepticus (IV); alcohol withdrawal with liver disease
• Alprazolam — panic disorder (most misused BZD)
• Triazolam — insomnia (shortest t½; severe discontinuation syndrome)
• Midazolam — procedural sedation (fastest onset IV)

cards.q: What are the indications for benzodiazepines?
cards.a:
1. Anxiety disorders: GAD, panic disorder (acute), social anxiety
2. Seizures: Status epilepticus (lorazepam IV — first line), febrile seizures
3. Alcohol withdrawal: Chlordiazepoxide, diazepam (prevent DTs and seizures)
4. Insomnia: Short-term only
5. Procedural sedation/anesthesia induction: Midazolam
6. Muscle spasm: Diazepam
7. Acute agitation, akathisia (lorazepam)
Not recommended: Long-term anxiety (dependence, cognitive impairment, tolerance)

cards.q: What is flumazenil and what are its limitations?
cards.a:
Competitive GABA-A benzodiazepine receptor antagonist
Use: Reversal of BZD-induced sedation/overdose
Route: IV only
Onset: 1–2 minutes; Duration: Very short (30–60 min) → BZD may outlast it → re-sedation occurs → repeated dosing needed
Limitations/Contraindications:
• Can precipitate seizures in BZD-dependent patients (acute withdrawal)
• Does NOT reverse barbiturates or other CNS depressants
• Contraindicated in patients whose seizures are being controlled with BZDs
• Not recommended for mixed overdoses

cards.q: What are the features and management of benzodiazepine withdrawal?
cards.a:
Onset: Short-acting BZDs (hours–days after stopping); long-acting (days–weeks)
Symptoms (opposite of BZD effects — GABA hypoactivity):
• Anxiety, panic, insomnia, irritability, dysphoria
• Tremor, diaphoresis, palpitations
• Seizures (life-threatening — like alcohol withdrawal)
• Psychosis (severe cases)
Management:
• Slow taper with long-acting BZD (diazepam); ~10% reduction per week
• Carbamazepine or valproate as adjuncts
KEY: BZD withdrawal CAN be FATAL (unlike opioid withdrawal)

cards.q: What is buspirone and how is it used?
cards.a:
Mechanism: 5-HT₁A partial agonist (presynaptic somatodendritic autoreceptor agonist → ↓ 5-HT firing; postsynaptic partial agonist)
Also: Partial D₂ agonist (minor)
FDA indication: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
Key features:
• Delayed onset (2–4 weeks) — NOT for acute anxiety
• No sedation, no tolerance, no physical dependence, no withdrawal
• No interaction with alcohol or CNS depressants
• No anticonvulsant or muscle relaxant effect
Important: Does NOT work well in patients previously on BZDs (withdrawal symptoms perceived as treatment failure)

cards.q: What are the Z-drugs (non-BZD GABA-A hypnotics)?
cards.a:
Non-BZD hypnotics — bind GABA-A at BZD site but selective for BZ1 (ω1) subunit:
• Zolpidem (Ambien) — most prescribed; selective BZ1; sedative; next-day impairment at higher doses; sleepwalking, sleep-driving, complex sleep behaviors
• Zaleplon — shortest t½ (~1h); use only for sleep onset
• Eszopiclone (Lunesta) — longer t½ (~6h); sleep onset and maintenance
Advantages vs. BZDs: Less muscle relaxation, less anticonvulsant effect, less tolerance
Side effects: Anterograde amnesia (especially with alcohol), sleepwalking, sleep-eating, Schedule IV controlled substances

cards.q: What are ramelteon and suvorexant used for?
cards.a:
Ramelteon (Rozerem): Melatonin receptor agonist (MT₁ and MT₂) in suprachiasmatic nucleus
• Reduces sleep latency; no dependence, no tolerance, no controlled substance status
• Avoid with fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor → ↑ ramelteon levels significantly)
• Approved for chronic insomnia, circadian rhythm disorders
Suvorexant (Belsomra): Orexin (hypocretin) receptor antagonist (OX₁R + OX₂R)
• Blocks wake-promoting orexin signaling → promotes sleep
• Sleep onset and maintenance
• Schedule IV; next-day drowsiness; do not drive

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of lithium?
cards.a:
Multiple proposed mechanisms (exact mechanism unknown):
1. Inhibits inositol monophosphatase → depletes free inositol → ↓ IP₃ and DAG → ↓ phosphoinositide (PIP₂) signaling ('inositol depletion hypothesis')
2. Inhibits GSK-3β (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta) → ↑ neuroprotection, ↑ neurogenesis
3. Inhibits protein kinase C (PKC)
4. Modulates neurotransmitter release (NE, DA, 5-HT)
Net result: Mood stabilization in bipolar disorder (mania and maintenance)

cards.q: What are the clinical indications for lithium?
cards.a:
FDA-approved:
• Bipolar I disorder — acute mania and maintenance (gold standard for prevention of relapse)
• Acute manic episodes
Off-label:
• Bipolar depression (partially effective)
• Augmentation in treatment-resistant MDD
• Cluster headache prevention
• Aggression/impulsivity in brain injury
• Stimulates granulopoiesis → leukocytosis
KEY: Lithium ↓ suicide risk in bipolar disorder — one of very few drugs with this demonstrated effect

cards.q: What is the therapeutic range for lithium?
cards.a:
Therapeutic range (drawn 12h after last dose — steady state):
• Acute mania: 0.8–1.2 mEq/L
• Maintenance: 0.6–1.0 mEq/L
• Mild–moderate toxicity: >1.5 mEq/L
• Severe toxicity: >2.0 mEq/L
Narrow therapeutic index → frequent monitoring required
Also monitor: BMP (renal function, electrolytes), TSH (thyroid), CBC, ECG, urinalysis
Monitoring frequency: Serum levels every 3–6 months when stable

cards.q: What are the signs and symptoms of lithium toxicity?
cards.a:
Early/Mild (1.5–2.0 mEq/L): Fine tremor, nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia
Moderate (2.0–2.5 mEq/L): Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, muscle twitching, ECG changes
Severe (>2.5 mEq/L): Seizures, delirium, coma, cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension
Mnemonic SALTD: Sedition (confusion), Ataxia, Large (coarse) tremor, Tachycardia, Diarrhea
Treatment: IV normal saline (Na⁺ competes with Li⁺ for reabsorption), hold lithium, hemodialysis if severe

cards.q: What renal effects does lithium cause?
cards.a:
1. Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (NDI) — most common renal effect
• Li⁺ enters principal cells via ENaC → impairs cAMP-mediated ADH signaling → ↓ aquaporin-2 insertion → polyuria, polydipsia
Treatment of Li⁺-induced NDI: Amiloride (blocks ENaC → prevents Li⁺ entry into principal cells), low-salt diet, thiazides (paradoxically reduce urine output by ↑ proximal tubular reabsorption)
2. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis → CKD with long-term use
Monitor: Creatinine, eGFR every 3–6 months

cards.q: What thyroid effects does lithium cause?
cards.a:
1. Hypothyroidism — most common (20–40% of long-term users)
Mechanism: Li⁺ inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis, release, and peripheral T₄→T₃ conversion → ↑ TSH → goiter
2. Hyperthyroidism — rare (<2%)
Management:
• Check TSH at baseline, then every 6 months
• If hypothyroidism: Add levothyroxine — do NOT stop lithium if otherwise effective
• Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is treatable and NOT a reason to discontinue lithium
Women are at higher risk for lithium-induced hypothyroidism

cards.q: What are the pregnancy risks with lithium?
cards.a:
Teratogenicity:
• Associated with Ebstein anomaly (downward displacement of tricuspid valve into right ventricle) — risk ~0.1% (small but real)
• Other cardiac defects
Note: Risk was historically overestimated; absolute risk is small
Neonatal effects: Lithium toxicity (floppiness/hypotonia, cyanosis, bradycardia, respiratory distress)
Management: Risk-benefit discussion; if continued → lowest effective dose, divided doses, frequent serum monitoring; fetal echocardiogram at 18–22 weeks; avoid large doses in labor (fetal lithium toxicity risk)

cards.q: Which drugs increase lithium serum levels and why?
cards.a:
↑ Lithium levels (↓ renal excretion):
• NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) → ↓ renal prostaglandins → ↓ GFR → ↓ Li⁺ clearance
• Thiazide diuretics → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → compensatory ↑ proximal tubular Li⁺ reabsorption
• ACE inhibitors / ARBs → ↓ aldosterone → Na⁺ loss → ↑ Li⁺ reabsorption
• Dehydration / low-sodium diet
• Tetracyclines
Mnemonic: 'NSAIDs, Thiazides, ACEi → ↑ Lithium → Toxicity'
Safe pain reliever: Acetaminophen (does not affect lithium levels)

cards.q: Which drugs decrease lithium serum levels?
cards.a:
↓ Lithium levels (↑ renal excretion):
• Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor → ↑ HCO₃⁻ excretion with Li⁺)
• Theophylline (↑ renal Li⁺ clearance)
• Caffeine (↑ Na⁺ and Li⁺ excretion)
• Loop diuretics (furosemide — less effect than thiazides)
• High-sodium diet (Na⁺ and Li⁺ compete for proximal tubular reabsorption → ↑ Li⁺ excreted)
Clinical pearl: Fluctuating dietary sodium is a major cause of lithium level variability
Renal handling: Li⁺ filtered freely; 60–80% reabsorbed in proximal tubule (like Na⁺)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action and side effects of valproate?
cards.a:
Mechanism:
1. Na⁺ channel blockade (voltage-gated) → ↓ sustained repetitive firing
2. ↑ GABA (inhibits GABA transaminase → ↓ GABA breakdown; ↑ GABA synthesis)
3. T-type Ca²⁺ channel blockade (absence seizures)
Indications: Bipolar disorder (all phases, especially mania), epilepsy (broad spectrum), migraine prophylaxis
Side effects: Weight gain, tremor, alopecia (hair loss), GI upset, sedation
Serious: Hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, PCOS features in females
Teratogenicity: HIGHEST risk of all antiepileptics/mood stabilizers

cards.q: What is the teratogenic risk of valproate?
cards.a:
Highest teratogenic risk of all antiepileptics and mood stabilizers
Neural tube defects (NTDs): Risk ~1–2% (spina bifida — highest of any antiepileptic drug)
Fetal valproate syndrome: Cognitive impairment (dose-dependent IQ reduction), ASD risk ↑, craniofacial abnormalities, limb defects
Other defects: Cardiac, cleft palate, hypospadias
Management: Avoid in women of childbearing age when alternatives exist; if used → high-dose folic acid (4–5 mg/day) pre-conception
Drug interaction: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation → ↑ lamotrigine levels 2× → ↑ SJS risk → reduce lamotrigine dose 50%

cards.q: What are the mechanism and serious side effects of carbamazepine?
cards.a:
Mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → ↓ sustained repetitive neuronal firing
Indications: Bipolar disorder (especially rapid cycling), epilepsy (partial and tonic-clonic), trigeminal neuralgia
Serious adverse effects:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)/TEN → associated with HLA-B*1502 allele (esp. Han Chinese — genetic testing recommended)
• Aplastic anemia + agranulocytosis (monitor CBC)
• SIADH → hyponatremia
• Teratogenicity (neural tube defects, cleft palate)
• Auto-inducer of CYP3A4 (induces own metabolism → dose must be ↑ over first 4–6 weeks)

cards.q: What are key drug interactions with carbamazepine?
cards.a:
Carbamazepine = potent CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 INDUCER
→ ↓ blood levels of many co-administered drugs:
• Oral contraceptives → ↓ efficacy → unintended pregnancy
• Warfarin → ↓ anticoagulation
• Antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, TCAs
• Lamotrigine → ↓ lamotrigine levels significantly → need higher lamotrigine dose
Auto-induction: Induces its own metabolism → initial dose insufficient → must titrate up over weeks
Drugs that ↑ carbamazepine levels: CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, fluoxetine, grapefruit juice) → toxicity risk

cards.q: What is the mechanism and clinical profile of lamotrigine?
cards.a:
Mechanism:
• Na⁺ channel blocker (voltage-gated)
• Inhibits glutamate release (presynaptic)
Indications:
• Bipolar disorder — especially bipolar depression and maintenance (superior to other mood stabilizers for depressive phase)
• Epilepsy (broad spectrum: partial, absence, myoclonic, Lennox-Gastaut)
Key concern: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
• Risk greatly reduced by slow titration (gradual dose escalation over 6+ weeks)
• Risk greatly increased by valproate (inhibits lamotrigine metabolism → ↑ levels 2× → ↑ SJS risk)
• Any new rash → strongly consider stopping lamotrigine

cards.q: Compare lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine for bipolar disorder.
cards.a:
DrugManiaDepressionMaintenanceKey risk
Lithium++++++ (gold std)NDI, thyroid, Ebstein, toxicity
Valproate++++++Teratogenicity (highest), hepatotox
Carbamazepine++++SJS (HLA-B*1502), aplastic anemia
Lamotrigine-/+++++++SJS (slow titration prevents)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of methylphenidate for ADHD?
cards.a:
Blocks reuptake of dopamine (DAT) and norepinephrine (NET) from the synapse
• More selective for DAT than NET
• Does NOT cause significant vesicular catecholamine release (unlike amphetamines)
→ ↑ prefrontal cortex DA and NE → ↑ attention, executive function, impulse control
Formulations: Short-acting (Ritalin: 3–5h), intermediate (Ritalin LA), long-acting (Concerta/Metadate: 8–12h)
Schedule II controlled substance

cards.q: How do amphetamines work for ADHD (amphetamine, dextroamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine)?
cards.a:
Mechanism — more powerful than methylphenidate:
1. Reverse monoamine transporters (DAT, NET) → actively pump DA and NE OUT of the presynaptic neuron into the synapse
2. Displace catecholamines from vesicles via VMAT2 displacement
3. Weakly inhibit MAO
→ Much greater DA and NE release than methylphenidate
Drugs: Adderall (mixed amphetamine salts), Dexedrine (dextroamphetamine), Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine — prodrug; lower abuse potential)
All Schedule II

cards.q: What is atomoxetine and how does it differ from stimulants for ADHD?
cards.a:
Selective Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor (NRI)
• Blocks NET only → ↑ NE in prefrontal cortex
• No significant DAT blockade → no abuse/addiction potential
• Not a controlled substance
Advantages:
• Good for ADHD + comorbid anxiety
• Good for ADHD + tic disorders (stimulants can worsen tics)
Disadvantages:
• Delayed onset (4–6 weeks) — not immediately effective
• Hepatotoxicity (rare but serious)
• Black box warning: suicidal ideation in pediatric patients
• Can raise BP and HR

cards.q: What are the side effects of stimulant medications (methylphenidate, amphetamines)?
cards.a:
Cardiovascular: ↑ HR, ↑ BP, palpitations (screen for cardiac conditions before prescribing)
GI/Metabolic: ↓ Appetite, weight loss, nausea, abdominal cramps
CNS: Insomnia (give in morning; avoid late dosing), headache, irritability, rebound effect when wearing off
Growth: Possible growth suppression in children (drug holidays considered)
Psychiatric: Exacerbate anxiety, tics, psychosis (rare)
Abuse potential: Schedule II — monitor for diversion
Contraindications: Bipolar without mood stabilizer, active psychosis, within 14 days of MAOI, structural cardiac defects

cards.q: How are guanfacine and clonidine used in ADHD?
cards.a:
Central α₂-adrenergic receptor agonists
→ ↑ postsynaptic NE signaling in prefrontal cortex → ↑ attention and impulse control
Guanfacine (Intuniv): More selective α₂A subtype; less sedating; preferred over clonidine for ADHD
Clonidine (Kapvay): Less selective; more sedating; also useful for sleep in ADHD
Uses:
• Alone or adjunct to stimulants
• ADHD + tic disorders / Tourette's (do NOT worsen tics)
• ADHD + hypertension
Side effects: Sedation, hypotension, bradycardia; abrupt discontinuation → rebound hypertension
Not controlled substances

cards.q: What are the three opioid receptor types and their effects?
cards.a:
ReceptorEffects of agonismKey drugs
μ (mu)Analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, constipation, miosis, physical dependenceMorphine, fentanyl, heroin
κ (kappa)Analgesia, dysphoria, sedation, miosisButorphanol, nalbuphine
δ (delta)Analgesia, mood modulationEnkephalins
All are Gi-coupled → ↓ cAMP → ↑ K⁺ conductance (hyperpolarization) + ↓ Ca²⁺ conductance (↓ neurotransmitter release)

cards.q: What is the classic triad of opioid overdose and its treatment?
cards.a:
Classic Opioid Toxidrome:
1. Miosis (pinpoint pupils) — due to μ/κ receptor stimulation of Edinger-Westphal nucleus
2. Respiratory depression — most dangerous; cause of death
3. CNS depression / Coma
Additional: Bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, hyporeflexia, constipation
Treatment: Naloxone (Narcan)
• IV, IM, or intranasal
• Onset: 1–2 minutes
• Duration: 30–90 min → opioid may outlast naloxone → repeated dosing or infusion needed

cards.q: What is naloxone and what are its limitations?
cards.a:
Pure competitive opioid receptor antagonist (μ > κ > δ)
Onset: 1–5 min (IV fastest)
Duration: 30–90 min (SHORT) → may need repeated dosing for long-acting opioids
Uses: Acute opioid overdose reversal, opioid-induced respiratory depression during surgery, diagnosis of opioid use disorder
Precautions:
• May precipitate acute opioid withdrawal → agitation, pain, vomiting, tachycardia, pulmonary edema (rare)
• Does NOT reverse non-opioid CNS depressants (alcohol, benzos, barbiturates)
• No oral bioavailability (used to prevent abuse of buprenorphine/naloxone in Suboxone)

cards.q: What is naltrexone and how does it differ from naloxone?
cards.a:
Pure competitive opioid receptor antagonist (like naloxone, but longer acting)
Key differences from naloxone:
• Oral bioavailability (naloxone is essentially inactive orally)
• Duration: 24–72 hours
Uses:
• Opioid use disorder (OUD) maintenance — blocks euphoria of opioids → prevents relapse
• Alcohol use disorder (AUD) — blocks endorphin-mediated reward → ↓ craving
• Long-acting injectable (Vivitrol) — once monthly
• Combined with bupropion: Contrave (weight loss)
Contraindication: Current opioid use (precipitates withdrawal); acute hepatitis/severe liver failure

cards.q: What are the pharmacological properties of methadone?
cards.a:
Full μ-opioid agonist + additional properties:
• NMDA receptor antagonist → useful for neuropathic pain; reduces opioid tolerance
• Long half-life: 24–36 hours (prevents withdrawal; once-daily dosing)
Uses: OUD maintenance treatment, chronic/neuropathic pain, opioid detoxification
Key risks:
• QTc prolongation → Torsades de Pointes (ECG monitoring required)
• Accumulation → delayed toxicity (long t½)
• Many CYP3A4 interactions
Dispensed daily from federally licensed clinics (DEA-regulated)

cards.q: What is buprenorphine and why is it used in opioid use disorder?
cards.a:
Partial μ-opioid agonist + κ-opioid antagonist
Pharmacology:
• High receptor affinity → displaces full agonists from μ-receptors
• Partial agonism → ceiling effect on respiratory depression (safer in overdose than full agonists)
• Suppresses withdrawal without full euphoria
Formulations for OUD:
• Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) — sublingual; naloxone prevents IV abuse
• Buprenorphine alone (Subutex) — for pregnant patients
KEY: Can be prescribed in office-based setting (vs. methadone which requires specialized clinic)
Caution: If given before sufficient opioid clearance → precipitates withdrawal

cards.q: What is the mechanism and key risks of tramadol?
cards.a:
Dual mechanism:
1. Weak μ-opioid receptor agonist (prodrug → active O-desmethyltramadol via CYP2D6)
2. NE and 5-HT reuptake inhibitor (SNRI-like)
Key risks:
• Serotonin syndrome — especially with SSRIs, MAOIs, TCAs (dangerous combination)
• Lowers seizure threshold (contraindicated in epilepsy)
• Schedule IV; some abuse potential
• CYP2D6 poor metabolizers → ↓ efficacy; ultra-rapid metabolizers → opioid toxicity
AVOID with MAOIs — life-threatening serotonin syndrome

cards.q: Why is meperidine (pethidine) dangerous with MAOIs?
cards.a:
Meperidine is unique — it has serotonergic properties (SERT inhibitor)
Metabolized to normeperidine (neurotoxic; lowers seizure threshold; renally cleared)
MAOI + Meperidine = ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED
→ Excitatory serotonin syndrome: Hyperthermia, agitation, rigidity, myoclonus, seizures
In patients on MAOIs needing opioid analgesia: Use morphine (not serotonergic)
Also avoid with MAOIs: Tramadol, fentanyl (mild serotonergic properties)
Normeperidine accumulation: Risk in renal failure → seizures (avoid meperidine in renal failure regardless of MAOIs)

cards.q: Why do opioids cause constipation and how is it treated?
cards.a:
Mechanism: μ-opioid receptors in myenteric plexus (Auerbach's) → ↓ ACh release → ↓ peristalsis + ↑ anal sphincter tone + ↑ water absorption → hard, dry, infrequent stool
KEY: Tolerance does NOT develop to opioid constipation (unlike tolerance to analgesia, euphoria, miosis, respiratory depression)
Treatment:
• Methylnaltrexone (Relistor) — peripheral-restricted μ-opioid antagonist; no BBB crossing → reverses GI effects without reversing analgesia
• Naloxegol — similar peripheral μ-antagonist
• Stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl)
• Lubiprostone (FDA approved for OIC)

cards.q: What are the signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal?
cards.a:
Mechanism: Opioids suppress locus coeruleus NE neurons; withdrawal → NE hyperactivity
Symptoms (onset: 8–24h for short-acting; 36–48h for long-acting):
• Anxiety, irritability, insomnia, yawning
• Lacrimation, rhinorrhea, diaphoresis
• Tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
• Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps
• Myalgia, arthralgia, piloerection ('gooseflesh' / cold turkey), restless leg
• Mydriasis (dilated pupils — opposite of intoxication)
KEY: NOT life-threatening (unlike alcohol/BZD withdrawal)
Treatment: Methadone, buprenorphine, clonidine (for autonomic symptoms)

cards.q: Compare medications used for opioid use disorder (OUD).
cards.a:
DrugClassSettingKey advantageKey risk
MethadoneFull μ agonistSpecialized clinic (daily dispensing)Strong withdrawal suppressionQT prolongation, overdose risk
Buprenorphine/ naloxonePartial μ agonistOffice-based (monthly visits)Safer ceiling effectPrecipitates w/d if too early
Naltrexone (Vivitrol)Pure antagonistOffice/monthly IMNo physical dependenceMust be opioid-free 7–10 days first

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of ethanol in the CNS?
cards.a:
Ethanol ENHANCES inhibitory neurotransmission:
• ↑ GABA-A receptor activity → ↑ Cl⁻ influx → CNS depression
• Inhibits NMDA glutamate receptors → ↓ excitatory neurotransmission
Also: ↑ Dopamine in nucleus accumbens (reward), ↑ endorphin release (euphoria), ↑ adenosine
Tolerance/Dependence mechanism: Chronic alcohol → NMDA receptor upregulation + GABA-A downregulation → brain becomes hyperexcitable → when alcohol stops → WITHDRAWAL (GABA↓, NMDA ↑ unopposed → CNS excitation → seizures)

cards.q: What is the metabolic pathway of ethanol and its clinical consequences?
cards.a:
Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH)
↓ Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) — NAD⁺ → NADH
Acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) — toxic (flushing, nausea)
↓ Aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) — NAD⁺ → NADH
Acetate → CO₂ + H₂O
↑ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio consequences:
• ↑ Lactate (pyruvate → lactate) → lactic acidosis
• ↓ Gluconeogenesis → hypoglycemia
• ↑ Lipid synthesis → fatty liver, hypertriglyceridemia
• ↑ Ketone production
High-dose/chronic: CYP2E1 (MEOS pathway) — also produces free radicals → oxidative stress

cards.q: What is the mechanism of disulfiram (Antabuse)?
cards.a:
Irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)
Alcohol → Acetaldehyde (accumulates, cannot be metabolized) → Disulfiram reaction
Disulfiram reaction: Flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, palpitations, hypotension (sometimes severe)
Clinical use: Alcohol use disorder — aversion therapy (patient avoids alcohol to avoid reaction)
Important: Alcohol found in mouthwash, hand sanitizers, sauces, vanilla extract → reaction
Drugs causing disulfiram-like reaction: Metronidazole, cefotetan, cefamandole, chlorpropamide (mechanism: ALDH inhibition or similar)
Avoid in: Severe cardiovascular disease, psychosis, pregnancy

cards.q: What is Wernicke encephalopathy and how is it treated?
cards.a:
Cause: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency — classically in chronic alcoholism
Classic Triad (CAO):
• Confusion (global confusion, altered mental status)
• Ataxia (cerebellar/gait ataxia)
• Ophthalmoplegia (lateral gaze palsy/nystagmus/6th nerve palsy)
Pathology: Petechial hemorrhages in mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, thalamus
Treatment: IV Thiamine BEFORE glucose (giving glucose first depletes remaining thiamine → precipitates/worsens Wernicke's)
Give thiamine 100 mg IV, then glucose

cards.q: How does Korsakoff syndrome differ from Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a:
Korsakoff psychosis = chronic irreversible sequela of untreated Wernicke encephalopathy
Pathology: Permanent damage to mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus
Key features:
• Anterograde amnesia (cannot form NEW memories)
• Retrograde amnesia (cannot recall PAST events)
• Confabulation (unconscious fabrication of memories to fill gaps — not intentional lying)
• Intact consciousness and general cognition
Treatment: Thiamine — may partially improve; severe cases largely irreversible
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Used when both present simultaneously

cards.q: What is the timeline of alcohol withdrawal and how is it managed?
cards.a:
Timeline after last drink:
• 6–12h: Tremor, anxiety, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea
• 12–24h: Alcoholic hallucinosis (visual/auditory hallucinations; clear sensorium)
• 24–48h: SEIZURES (grand mal — potentially fatal)
• 48–72h: Delirium Tremens (DTs) — confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability, hyperthermia
DTs mortality: ~5–15% untreated
Treatment (first-line: Benzodiazepines): Chlordiazepoxide (preferred), diazepam; use lorazepam if liver disease (LOT mnemonic)
Also: IV thiamine, electrolyte replacement, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics for hallucinations

cards.q: How does naltrexone help in alcohol use disorder (AUD)?
cards.a:
Mechanism:
Alcohol → ↑ endorphin/enkephalin release → ↑ DA in nucleus accumbens → reward/euphoria
Naltrexone blocks μ-opioid receptors → blocks alcohol-induced endorphin reward → ↓ craving, ↓ pleasurable effects of drinking → ↓ relapse rate
Clinical evidence: ↓ heavy drinking days, ↓ relapse rate
Forms: Oral (daily) or IM injection (Vivitrol — monthly)
Contraindication: Active opioid use, acute hepatitis, severe liver failure
Vs. Disulfiram: Disulfiram = deterrent (makes drinking unpleasant); Naltrexone = anticraving (reduces desire/reward from drinking)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of acamprosate in alcohol use disorder?
cards.a:
Structural analog of GABA
Mechanism:
• NMDA receptor modulation (partial antagonism — reduces glutamate hyperactivity of protracted alcohol withdrawal)
• GABA-A receptor positive modulation
→ Reduces conditioned cravings, dysphoria, anxiety during abstinence ('protracted abstinence syndrome')
Uses: Maintaining abstinence after detoxification; does NOT treat acute withdrawal
Advantages: Renally excreted → safe in liver disease (unlike naltrexone and disulfiram)
Disadvantages: 3× daily dosing; ineffective if patient continues drinking
Contraindicated in severe renal impairment

cards.q: What is the mechanism of cocaine's CNS effects?
cards.a:
Mechanism:
1. Blocks DAT, NET, and SERT → ↑ synaptic DA, NE, and 5-HT (reuptake inhibition)
2. Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → local anesthetic effect
DA-mediated: Euphoria, increased energy, decreased appetite, alertness
NE-mediated (sympathomimetic): Tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction, mydriasis, hyperthermia
Cardiovascular toxicity: MI (coronary vasospasm + ↑ O₂ demand), arrhythmias (Na⁺ channel block), stroke, aortic dissection
Withdrawal: 'Crash' — hypersomnia, hyperphagia, depression, anhedonia (NOT life-threatening)

cards.q: How is cocaine intoxication and cardiovascular toxicity managed?
cards.a:
Benzodiazepines — first-line (reduce sympathetic drive, treat anxiety and seizures)
Hypertension: Phentolamine (α-blocker); nitroprusside; nitroglycerin
Chest pain / MI: Aspirin, nitroglycerin, phentolamine; consider coronary angiography
Hyperthermia: Active cooling
AVOID β-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) — leave α-adrenergic receptors unopposed → paradoxical worsening of hypertension and coronary vasospasm ('unopposed α stimulation')
Labetalol (α + β blocker) may be used with caution
No specific antidote exists for cocaine toxicity

cards.q: What is the mechanism and presentation of PCP intoxication?
cards.a:
PCP (Phencyclidine) = NMDA receptor antagonist (non-competitive; binds within open ion channel)
Also: DA, sigma receptor agonist; anticholinergic effects
Clinical presentation (dose-dependent):
• Low dose: Euphoria, dissociation
• Moderate: Agitation, violence, nystagmus (horizontal, vertical, OR rotary — pathognomonic), tachycardia, hypertension, analgesia
• High: Coma, seizures, respiratory depression
Key features: Apparent superhuman strength (analgesia + stimulation), bizarre behavior, self-destructive acts
Treatment: Benzodiazepines (for agitation); minimize stimulation; supportive care

cards.q: What is the mechanism of LSD and other classical hallucinogens?
cards.a:
LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide):
Mechanism: 5-HT₂A receptor partial agonist — primarily in prefrontal cortex and visual cortex → altered serotonergic signaling → hallucinations, synesthesia
Same mechanism (5-HT₂A agonists):
• Psilocybin (magic mushrooms)
• Mescaline (peyote)
• DMT
Physical effects: Mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia, mild sympathomimetic effects
No physical dependence; no withdrawal syndrome
HPPD (flashbacks): Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder
Treatment of 'bad trip': Benzodiazepines; calm environment ('talking down'); avoid antipsychotics if possible

cards.q: What is the mechanism and toxicity of MDMA ('ecstasy')?
cards.a:
MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine)
Mechanism:
1. Massively releases 5-HT, DA, and NE from presynaptic terminals (via reversal of transporters)
2. Inhibits SERT, DAT, NET (reuptake inhibition)
→ Predominantly 5-HT release → empathy, emotional closeness, euphoria
Toxicity:
• Hyperthermia — life-threatening (rhabdomyolysis, DIC, renal failure)
• Hyponatremia — SIADH + excessive water intake at raves
• Serotonin syndrome (especially if combined with MAOIs)
• Tachycardia, hypertension, bruxism (jaw clenching)
Long-term: Serotonergic neurotoxicity (↓ 5-HT)

cards.q: What is the mechanism of THC and its CNS effects?
cards.a:
THC (Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol) = active compound in cannabis
Mechanism: Agonist at CB₁ (CNS) and CB₂ (immune/peripheral) cannabinoid receptors
CB₁ = Gi-coupled → ↓ cAMP, ↓ neurotransmitter release
→ ↑ DA in nucleus accumbens → reward
CNS effects: Euphoria, relaxation, ↑ appetite (ghrelin), ↓ nausea, short-term memory impairment, altered time perception
Medical uses: Chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting, appetite stimulation (AIDS/cancer), chronic pain, MS spasticity
Adverse effects: Amotivational syndrome, psychosis (predisposed), cannabis use disorder, cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome

cards.q: What is the mechanism of nicotine dependence and smoking cessation treatments?
cards.a:
Nicotine: Agonist at α4β2 nicotinic AChRs (nAChRs) in VTA → ↑ DA in nucleus accumbens → reward and dependence
Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy:
1. Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT): Patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler — reduces withdrawal
2. Bupropion (Zyban): Blocks DAT/NET + nAChR antagonism → reduces craving and withdrawal (also used with NRT)
3. Varenicline (Chantix): Partial α4β2 nAChR agonist → partial DA release (reduces withdrawal) + blocks nicotine → reduces reward; most effective single agent for smoking cessation
Warning: Neuropsychiatric effects (black box warning — monitor mood changes)

cards.q: Compare mechanisms and key features of drugs of abuse.
cards.a:
DrugMechanismWithdrawal fatal?Antidote
Opioidsμ-opioid agonistNoNaloxone
CocaineDAT/NET/SERT blockNoNone (BZDs symptomatic)
AlcoholGABA-A ↑, NMDA blockYES (DTs)BZDs
BZDsGABA-A ↑ frequencyYES (seizures)Flumazenil (limited)
PCPNMDA antagonistNoBZDs (symptomatic)
LSD5-HT₂A agonistNoBZDs (symptomatic)
MDMA5-HT/DA/NE releaseNoSupportive
CannabisCB₁/CB₂ agonistNoNone

cards.q: What are the diagnostic features of serotonin syndrome?
cards.a:
Hunter Criteria (requires serotonergic agent PLUS at least one of):
• Spontaneous clonus
• Inducible clonus + agitation or diaphoresis
• Ocular clonus + agitation or diaphoresis
• Tremor + hyperreflexia
• Hypertonia + temp >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus
Classic features:
• Hyperthermia, agitation, diaphoresis
• Clonus (most specific sign), myoclonus, tremor, hyperreflexia
• Tachycardia, hypertension, diarrhea, mydriasis
Onset: Hours (fast) after serotonergic drug addition/combination
Treatment: Stop drug, BZDs, cyproheptadine (5-HT₂A antagonist), cooling

cards.q: What drug combinations most commonly cause serotonin syndrome?
cards.a:
High-risk combinations:
• SSRI + MAOI — most dangerous (contraindicated; 14-day washout required)
• SSRI + Linezolid (antibiotic with MAOI activity)
• SSRI + Methylene blue (MAOI activity)
• SSRI + Tramadol (weak SERT inhibitor + μ agonist)
• SSRI + Meperidine (SERT inhibitor)
• SSRI + Dextromethorphan (DXM) (weak SERT inhibitor)
• SSRI + St. John's Wort (SERT inhibitor — herbal)
• SSRI + Triptans (5-HT₁B/₁D agonists — debated but possible)
• MDMA (massive 5-HT release)

cards.q: What are the diagnostic features of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a:
NMS = Idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics (D₂ blockade)
Classic Tetrad:
1. Hyperthermia (>38°C, often >40°C)
2. Lead-pipe muscular rigidity — most specific feature (cogwheel rigidity)
3. Altered consciousness / Encephalopathy
4. Autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis, tachypnea)
Labs: ↑↑ CPK (rhabdomyolysis → AKI), ↑ WBC, metabolic acidosis
Onset: Days to weeks after starting/increasing antipsychotic (within 2 weeks typically)
Mortality: 5–20% untreated; cause of death = respiratory failure, renal failure, arrhythmia

cards.q: How do you differentiate serotonin syndrome from NMS?
cards.a:
FeatureSerotonin SyndromeNMS
Cause↑ Serotonergic drugsD₂ blockade (antipsychotics)
OnsetHours (FAST)Days–weeks (SLOW)
RigidityMild or absentSevere 'lead-pipe'
ReflexesHyperreflexia, clonusNormal or ↓
PupilsMydriasisNormal
Bowel soundsHyperactive (diarrhea)Hypoactive
CPKMildly ↑Markedly ↑↑
TreatmentCyproheptadine + BZDsDantrolene + Bromocriptine

cards.q: What are VMAT2 inhibitors and when are they used?
cards.a:
VMAT2 = Vesicular Monoamine Transporter 2
• Packages catecholamines (DA, NE, 5-HT) into vesicles for storage
VMAT2 inhibitors → ↓ vesicular DA storage → ↓ presynaptic DA → ↓ hyperkinetic movements
FDA-approved drugs:
• Valbenazine (Ingrezza) — FDA approved for Tardive Dyskinesia
• Deutetrabenazine (Austedo) — FDA approved for Tardive Dyskinesia AND Huntington's chorea
• Tetrabenazine (Xenazine) — FDA approved for Huntington's chorea
Side effects: Depression/suicidality (↓ DA), sedation, parkinsonism
Contraindication: Active suicidality; combined with MAOIs

cards.q: Why do antidepressants take 2–6 weeks to show therapeutic effect?
cards.a:
Immediate effect: SERT block → ↑ synaptic 5-HT (within hours)
BUT delayed therapy due to:
1. Presynaptic 5-HT₁A autoreceptors initially 'sense' ↑ 5-HT → negative feedback → ↓ serotonergic neuron firing rate → initial blunting of effect
2. With chronic use → 5-HT₁A autoreceptors desensitize/downregulate → net ↑ serotonergic output
3. Downstream neuroplastic changes take weeks: ↑ BDNF, hippocampal neurogenesis, synaptic remodeling
Clinical implication: Adequate trial = adequate dose for at least 4–6 weeks before declaring treatment failure

cards.q: What are the indications, mechanism, and side effects of ECT?
cards.a:
Indications:
• Severe treatment-resistant MDD (failed ≥2 antidepressants)
• Psychotic depression
• Severe suicidality (requires rapid response)
• Catatonia (all types — most responsive)
• Severe refractory mania
• Severe depression in pregnancy (safest option)
Mechanism: Not fully known; ↑ neurotrophic factors (BDNF), ↑ neuroplasticity, ↓ HPA axis dysregulation, normalization of monoaminergic activity
Side effects: Anterograde and retrograde amnesia (most common concern; usually transient), headache, muscle aches, confusion post-procedure, perioperative cardiovascular effects
No absolute contraindications

cards.q: What augmentation strategies are used for treatment-resistant depression (TRD)?
cards.a:
When SSRI/SNRI monotherapy fails ≥2 adequate trials:
1. Lithium augmentation — most evidence-based classical strategy
2. Atypical antipsychotic augmentation (FDA-approved add-ons):
• Aripiprazole + SSRI/SNRI
• Quetiapine + SSRI/SNRI
• Olanzapine + fluoxetine (Symbyax — bipolar depression)
3. Add bupropion to SSRI (NE/DA augmentation)
4. Mirtazapine + venlafaxine ('California Rocket Fuel')
5. Thyroid hormone (T₃) augmentation
6. Switch to different antidepressant class
7. ECT — for refractory or severe cases

cards.q: Summarize receptor blockade and associated side effects of psychiatric drugs.
cards.a:
Receptor blockedSide effectsKey drugs
D₂EPS, ↑ prolactinTypical antipsychotics
5-HT₂A↓ EPS, ↓ sexual dysfunction, weight gainAtypicals, mirtazapine
H₁Sedation, weight gain, ↑ appetiteTCAs, mirtazapine, quetiapine
M₁ (muscarinic)Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, tachycardia, confusionTCAs, low-potency antipsychotics, paroxetine
α₁Orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, sexual dysfunctionTCAs, antipsychotics, trazodone
α₂ (presynaptic)↑ NE and 5-HT release (therapeutic)Mirtazapine

cards.q: What are the highest-yield single drug-toxicity associations in USMLE Psychopharmacology?
cards.a:
Must-know associations:
• Clozapine → Agranulocytosis (weekly CBC) + Seizures (most seizurogenic) + Sialorrhea
• Lithium → Ebstein anomaly (fetus), Nephrogenic DI, Hypothyroidism; toxicity: NaHCO₃ / NS / dialysis
• Valproate → Neural tube defects (highest risk), Alopecia, Hepatotoxicity, Pancreatitis
• Carbamazepine → SJS (HLA-B*1502), SIADH, Aplastic anemia; autoinducer
• Lamotrigine → SJS (slow titration prevents it); best for bipolar depression
• Bupropion → Seizures (avoid in eating disorders), No sexual dysfunction, Smoking cessation
• Trazodone → Priapism
• Aripiprazole → Partial D₂ agonist; no prolactin elevation; least metabolic effects
• Paroxetine → Category D in pregnancy; worst discontinuation syndrome
• Fluoxetine → Longest t½; least discontinuation syndrome; approved for bulimia

cards.q: What are the two types of bone ossification? Give examples of each.
cards.a:
1. Intramembranous ossification: Direct mesenchymal → bone (flat bones: skull, clavicle).
2. Endochondral ossification: Mesenchyme → cartilage model → bone (long bones, vertebrae, base of skull).

cards.q: What zones are present in the epiphyseal growth plate (from epiphysis to diaphysis)?
cards.a:
Resting → Proliferative → Hypertrophic → Calcified → Ossification zone.
Longitudinal growth occurs primarily in the proliferative zone.

cards.q: What is the most common site of hematogenous osteomyelitis in children?
cards.a: Metaphysis of long bones (especially distal femur, proximal tibia) due to sluggish blood flow in sinusoidal vessels.

cards.q: Most common organism causing osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease patients?
cards.a: Salmonella species (followed by Staphylococcus aureus).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic radiographic finding in osteoid osteoma?
cards.a: Nidus surrounded by reactive sclerotic bone. Night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs.

cards.q: What is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children/adolescents?
cards.a: Osteosarcoma (metaphysis of long bones, especially distal femur). Codman triangle + sunburst appearance on X-ray.

cards.q: What is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in adults >40 years?
cards.a: Chondrosarcoma (pelvis, proximal femur, humerus). Calcified 'popcorn' or 'ring-and-arc' appearance.

cards.q: What translocation is associated with Ewing sarcoma?
cards.a: t(11;22) → EWS-FLI1 fusion. Onion-skin periosteal reaction on X-ray.

cards.q: What is the characteristic histologic finding in giant cell tumor of bone?
cards.a: Multinucleated giant cells in a background of mononuclear stromal cells. Epiphyseal location in adults.

cards.q: What is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in adults?
cards.a: Liposarcoma (especially in retroperitoneum and thigh).

cards.q: What is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children?
cards.a: Rhabdomyosarcoma (embryonal type most common).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: X-linked recessive, onset ~2–5 years, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, elevated CK, wheelchair by age 12.

cards.q: What protein is deficient in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
cards.a: Dystrophin (frameshift mutation). Becker has partial function (in-frame mutation).

cards.q: What is the most common site of myasthenia gravis weakness?
cards.a: Ocular muscles (ptosis, diplopia). Fatigable weakness improves with rest.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding on ice pack test or edrophonium test in myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Improvement in ptosis/weakness.

cards.q: What autoantibodies are present in myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Anti-AChR (most common), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic association with myasthenia gravis?
cards.a: Thymoma (also thymic hyperplasia).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for myasthenic crisis?
cards.a: Plasmapheresis or IVIG + supportive ventilation.

cards.q: What is the difference between myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)?
cards.a:
MG: Proximal weakness worsens with repetition, bulbar/ocular common.
LEMS: Proximal weakness improves with repetition, autonomic symptoms, associated with small cell lung cancer, anti-P/Q voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel antibodies.

cards.q: What is the most common inflammatory myopathy in adults >50 years?
cards.a: Inclusion body myositis (distal weakness, finger flexors, quadriceps, poor response to steroids).

cards.q: What autoantibodies are associated with dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Anti-Mi-2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-γ (malignancy association).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic skin finding in dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Gottron papules (over knuckles) and heliotrope rash.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for polymyositis/dermatomyositis?
cards.a: High-dose corticosteroids (± methotrexate or azathioprine).

cards.q: What is the most common crystal arthropathy?
cards.a: Gout (monosodium urate crystals).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding on polarized light microscopy in gout?
cards.a: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals.

cards.q: What joint is most commonly affected in acute gout (podagra)?
cards.a: 1st metatarsophalangeal joint.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute gout attack?
cards.a: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or corticosteroids. Avoid starting allopurinol during acute attack.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of colchicine?
cards.a: Inhibits microtubule polymerization → ↓ neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis of urate crystals.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pseudogout (CPPD deposition disease)?
cards.a: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals – positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.

cards.q: What conditions are associated with chondrocalcinosis (pseudogout)?
cards.a: Hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatasia, aging.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in septic arthritis in adults?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in septic arthritis in young sexually active adults?
cards.a: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (disseminated gonococcal infection).

cards.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic test for septic arthritis?
cards.a: Joint aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis (WBC >50,000 with >75% PMNs).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)?
cards.a: Arthritis, urethritis, conjunctivitis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'). Associated with HLA-B27.

cards.q: What HLA association is strongest in ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: HLA-B27. Sacroiliitis (bilateral), bamboo spine, enthesitis.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: NSAIDs. TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) or IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) for refractory disease.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic X-ray finding in ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Bamboo spine (syndesmophytes) and sacroiliitis.

cards.q: What autoantibody is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Anti-CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies (more specific than RF).

cards.q: What are the classic deformities in advanced rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Ulnar deviation of fingers, swan-neck deformity, boutonnière deformity, rheumatoid nodules.

cards.q: What is the most common extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Rheumatoid nodules (subcutaneous, over extensor surfaces).

cards.q: What is the first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Methotrexate.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase → ↓ purine/pyrimidine synthesis.

cards.q: What is the most serious side effect of methotrexate?
cards.a: Hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression. Folic acid supplementation reduces toxicity.

cards.q: What are the seronegative spondyloarthropathies?
cards.a: Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD-associated, Reactive arthritis — all associated with HLA-B27, negative RF, asymmetric oligoarthritis, enthesitis, uveitis.

cards.q: What is the characteristic rash in psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: Silver-scaled plaques. Pencil-in-cup deformity on X-ray.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the femoral head in the US?
cards.a: Corticosteroid use (also sickle cell disease, alcoholism, trauma).

cards.q: What is the earliest radiographic sign of osteonecrosis?
cards.a: Normal X-ray (MRI is most sensitive – shows 'double-line sign').

cards.q: What is the most common joint involved in osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Knee (followed by hip, DIP/PIP joints of hands, first CMC joint).

cards.q: What are the classic radiographic findings in osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts.

cards.q: What is Heberden's node vs Bouchard's node?
cards.a:
Heberden's: DIP joints.
Bouchard's: PIP joints (both in OA).

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for osteoarthritis pain?
cards.a: Acetaminophen → topical NSAIDs → oral NSAIDs (with PPI if high GI risk).

cards.q: What are the two main cells responsible for bone remodeling? Their origins?
cards.a:
Osteoblasts: Derived from mesenchymal stem cells (build bone).
Osteoclasts: Derived from monocyte-macrophage lineage (resorb bone).

cards.q: What is the role of RANKL and OPG in bone remodeling?
cards.a:
RANKL (from osteoblasts) binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast activation.
OPG (osteoprotegerin) is a decoy receptor that inhibits RANKL.

cards.q: What hormone stimulates osteoclast activity indirectly?
cards.a: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) → ↑ RANKL expression on osteoblasts.

cards.q: What is the effect of estrogen on bone?
cards.a: Inhibits RANKL and promotes OPG → ↓ osteoclast activity. Deficiency (post-menopause) → osteoporosis.

cards.q: What are the radiographic findings in osteoporosis?
cards.a: ↓ Bone density, vertebral compression fractures, codfish vertebrae.

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis?
cards.a: Bisphosphonates (alendronate, zoledronate).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of bisphosphonates?
cards.a: Incorporate into hydroxyapatite → induce osteoclast apoptosis.

cards.q: Major side effects of oral bisphosphonates?
cards.a: Esophageal irritation/ulceration, osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare), atypical femoral fractures.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of denosumab?
cards.a: Monoclonal antibody against RANKL → inhibits osteoclast differentiation.

cards.q: What is teriparatide and when is it used?
cards.a: Recombinant PTH (1-34) — anabolic agent. Used in severe osteoporosis or patients who failed bisphosphonates.

cards.q: What is the difference between osteoporosis and osteomalacia?
cards.a:
Osteoporosis: Normal mineralization, ↓ bone mass.
Osteomalacia: Defective mineralization (vitamin D deficiency, low Ca/Phos).

cards.q: What is the radiographic finding in osteomalacia / rickets?
cards.a: Looser zones (pseudofractures) in adults; rachitic rosary, bowing of legs in children.

cards.q: What is Paget disease of bone? Classic lab finding?
cards.a: Disordered bone remodeling (↑ osteoclast then ↑ osteoblast activity). Markedly ↑ alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphorus.

cards.q: What is the most common complication of Paget disease?
cards.a: High-output heart failure, osteosarcoma (rare), hearing loss (skull involvement).

cards.q: Treatment of symptomatic Paget disease?
cards.a: Bisphosphonates (zoledronate is preferred).

cards.q: What is the most common fracture in children?
cards.a: Clavicle fracture (birth trauma or falls).

cards.q: What is Salter-Harris classification used for?
cards.a: Classification of physeal (growth plate) fractures in children.

cards.q: Which Salter-Harris fracture type has the worst prognosis?
cards.a: Type V (crush injury to growth plate).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of limping in a child 3–10 years old?
cards.a: Transient synovitis (post-viral).

cards.q: What is Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease?
cards.a: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children 4–8 years old.

cards.q: What is slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)? Classic patient?
cards.a: Displacement of femoral head on neck. Overweight adolescent male (10–16 years). Pain in knee or hip.

cards.q: What is the treatment for SCFE?
cards.a: Surgical pinning (percutaneous).

cards.q: What is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)? Best screening test?
cards.a: Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers in newborns. Confirmed by ultrasound (<6 months).

cards.q: What is the most common benign bone tumor?
cards.a: Osteochondroma (exostosis). Malignant transformation rare (<1%).

cards.q: What is the most common malignant bone tumor of the pelvis in adolescents?
cards.a: Ewing sarcoma.

cards.q: What is the characteristic histology of osteosarcoma?
cards.a: Osteoid production by malignant cells.

cards.q: What is the most common site of metastasis for osteosarcoma?
cards.a: Lungs.

cards.q: What autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) arthritis?
cards.a: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith.

cards.q: What is Jaccoud arthropathy?
cards.a: Deformities in SLE that are reducible (non-erosive).

cards.q: What is the classic hand deformity in rheumatoid arthritis at the MCP joints?
cards.a: Ulnar deviation.

cards.q: What is the difference between rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis regarding DIP joints?
cards.a: RA spares DIP joints. OA commonly affects DIP (Heberden nodes).

cards.q: What is the most common vasculitis associated with hepatitis B?
cards.a: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)?
cards.a: Pulmonary involvement (interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension).

cards.q: What autoantibody is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome)?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: What autoantibody is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for acute gout in a patient with renal failure?
cards.a: Colchicine (dose-adjusted) or intra-articular/systemic corticosteroids.

cards.q: What drug is used for gout prophylaxis?
cards.a: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) or febuxostat. Start after acute attack resolves.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of probenecid?
cards.a: Inhibits uric acid reabsorption in proximal tubule (uricosuric).

cards.q: What is pseudogout most commonly associated with in elderly patients?
cards.a: Degenerative joint disease.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in prosthetic joint infection (early <3 months)?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus or coagulase-negative staphylococci.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in osteomyelitis in IV drug users?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute osteomyelitis?
cards.a: Empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam) after cultures.

cards.q: What is Charcot joint?
cards.a: Neurogenic arthropathy (most commonly in diabetes) → painless joint destruction.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of septic bursitis?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus (prepatellar or olecranon bursitis).

cards.q: What is Osgood-Schlatter disease?
cards.a: Apophysitis of tibial tuberosity in adolescent athletes. Pain with activity, swelling over tibial tuberosity.

cards.q: What is Sever disease?
cards.a: Calcaneal apophysitis (heel pain in children).

cards.q: What is the most common site of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Lower leg (anterior compartment) after tibial fracture.

cards.q: What are the 6 P's of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Pain (out of proportion), Paresthesia, Pallor, Paralysis, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Fasciotomy.

cards.q: What is the most common shoulder dislocation type?
cards.a: Anterior dislocation (95%). Risk of axillary nerve injury.

cards.q: What nerve is most commonly injured in humeral shaft fracture?
cards.a: Radial nerve (wrist drop).

cards.q: What nerve is injured in anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.a: Axillary nerve (deltoid paralysis, loss of sensation over lateral shoulder).

cards.q: What is the most common carpal bone fractured?
cards.a: Scaphoid. Snuffbox tenderness. Risk of avascular necrosis (proximal pole).

cards.q: What is the most common ligament injured in ankle sprain?
cards.a: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL).

cards.q: What is the most common nerve injury in supracondylar humerus fracture in children?
cards.a: Anterior interosseous nerve (branch of median nerve) → inability to make OK sign.

cards.q: What is the most common complication of supracondylar fracture?
cards.a: Volkmann ischemic contracture (due to brachial artery injury or compartment syndrome).

cards.q: What is Colles fracture? Classic deformity?
cards.a: Distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation. 'Dinner fork' deformity.

cards.q: What is Smith fracture?
cards.a: Distal radius fracture with volar (palmar) angulation. 'Garden spade' deformity.

cards.q: What is a Boxer fracture?
cards.a: Fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck. Common in punch injuries.

cards.q: What is the most common site of stress fracture in athletes?
cards.a: Tibia (posterior medial aspect).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pathologic fracture in adults?
cards.a: Metastatic bone disease (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid).

cards.q: What is the most common primary bone malignancy in patients >40 years old?
cards.a: Multiple myeloma (lytic lesions, CRAB features).

cards.q: What malignancy is associated with Paget disease of bone?
cards.a: Osteosarcoma (rare, <1%).

cards.q: What is the histologic hallmark of rhabdomyosarcoma?
cards.a: Rhabdomyoblasts with cross-striations.

cards.q: What is the most common location of synovial sarcoma?
cards.a: Near joints/tendons in young adults (lower extremity).

cards.q: What is the characteristic translocation in synovial sarcoma?
cards.a: t(X;18) — SYT-SSX fusion.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of atraumatic knee effusion in young adults?
cards.a: ACL tear (anterior cruciate ligament).

cards.q: What is the Lachman test used for?
cards.a: Assessing ACL integrity (most sensitive test).

cards.q: What is the unhappy triad of the knee?
cards.a: ACL tear + MCL tear + medial meniscus tear.

cards.q: What is the most common meniscus injury?
cards.a: Medial meniscus (more fixed, less mobile).

cards.q: What is the McMurray test used for?
cards.a: Detecting meniscal tears.

cards.q: What is the most common shoulder injury in older adults?
cards.a: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus most commonly affected).

cards.q: What test is used for supraspinatus tear?
cards.a: Empty can test (Jobe test).

cards.q: What is the most common site of rotator cuff tear?
cards.a: Supraspinatus tendon insertion on greater tuberosity.

cards.q: What is frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)? Classic patient?
cards.a: Painful restriction of both active and passive shoulder motion. Common in diabetics and after immobility.

cards.q: What is De Quervain tenosynovitis?
cards.a: Inflammation of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Positive Finkelstein test.

cards.q: What is trigger finger?
cards.a: Stenosing tenosynovitis of flexor tendon sheath. Painful clicking or locking of finger.

cards.q: What is Dupuytren contracture? Associations?
cards.a: Palmar fascia fibrosis → flexion contracture of 4th/5th fingers. Associated with alcoholism, diabetes, smoking, Northern European descent.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital foot deformity?
cards.a: Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus).

cards.q: What is the treatment for congenital clubfoot?
cards.a: Ponseti method (serial casting + Achilles tenotomy).

cards.q: What is genu varum vs genu valgum?
cards.a:
Genu varum: Bowlegs (normal until age 2).
Genu valgum: Knock-knees (normal ages 2–7).

cards.q: What is Blount disease?
cards.a: Pathologic tibia vara (growth disturbance of proximal medial tibial physis) in obese children.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant soft tissue tumor in children?
cards.a: Rhabdomyosarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric bone tumor?
cards.a: Osteosarcoma (second most common is Ewing sarcoma).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of back pain in children/adolescents?
cards.a: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture, especially L5).

cards.q: What is spondylolisthesis?
cards.a: Forward slippage of one vertebra on another (commonly L5 on S1).

cards.q: What is cauda equina syndrome? Classic triad?
cards.a: Saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, lower extremity weakness. Surgical emergency.

cards.q: What is the most sensitive test for ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Sacroiliac joint tenderness or positive Schober test.

cards.q: What extra-articular manifestation is most common in ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Anterior uveitis (acute, unilateral).
