cards.q: What is the strongest HLA association in psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: HLA-B27 (especially with axial involvement).

cards.q: What is dactylitis?
cards.a: 'Sausage digit' — seen in psoriatic arthritis and reactive arthritis.

cards.q: What skin finding is pathognomonic for dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Gottron papules and heliotrope rash.

cards.q: What is the most common malignancy associated with dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Ovarian cancer (also breast, lung, GI).

cards.q: What autoantibody is associated with polymyositis?
cards.a: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) — associated with antisynthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic's hands, Raynaud).

cards.q: What is inclusion body myositis? Key clinical feature?
cards.a: Distal weakness (finger flexors, quadriceps), asymmetric, poor response to immunosuppression. Affects older males.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for giant cell arteritis?
cards.a: High-dose corticosteroids (prednisone) immediately — do not wait for biopsy.

cards.q: What is the most feared complication of giant cell arteritis?
cards.a: Blindness (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy).

cards.q: What is polymyalgia rheumatica? Classic presentation?
cards.a: Pain and stiffness in shoulders and hips in patients >50. Associated with giant cell arteritis.

cards.q: What lab finding is markedly elevated in both polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis?
cards.a: ESR and CRP.

cards.q: What is the treatment for mild rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Methotrexate + short-term low-dose steroids.

cards.q: What biologic agent targets TNF-α and is commonly used in RA, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of rituximab in RA?
cards.a: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody → B-cell depletion.

cards.q: What is the most common side effect of long-term corticosteroid use in rheumatologic disease?
cards.a: Osteoporosis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate in rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase → impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells (anti-inflammatory at low doses via adenosine release).

cards.q: What supplement is given with methotrexate to reduce toxicity?
cards.a: Folic acid (or folinic acid/leucovorin in high-dose regimens).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of leflunomide?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase → blocks pyrimidine synthesis in lymphocytes.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of sulfasalazine?
cards.a: Cleaved into 5-ASA (anti-inflammatory) and sulfapyridine (antibacterial). Used in RA and IBD.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of hydroxychloroquine in rheumatic diseases?
cards.a: Alkalinizes lysosomes → interferes with antigen processing and TLR signaling.

cards.q: What is the major toxicity of hydroxychloroquine?
cards.a: Retinopathy (requires baseline and annual eye exams).

cards.q: What biologic is a CTLA-4 Ig fusion protein used in RA?
cards.a: Abatacept — inhibits T-cell co-stimulation.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of tocilizumab?
cards.a: Anti-IL-6 receptor antibody.

cards.q: What is the risk of using TNF inhibitors?
cards.a: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis and opportunistic infections.

cards.q: What is the screening required before starting TNF inhibitors?
cards.a: Quantiferon-TB Gold or PPD + chest X-ray.

cards.q: What is the embryologic origin of skeletal muscle?
cards.a: Paraxial mesoderm → somites → myotomes.

cards.q: What is the embryologic origin of limb bones?
cards.a: Lateral plate mesoderm (somatic layer) + neural crest contribution to digits.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital limb defect?
cards.a: Polydactyly.

cards.q: What syndrome is associated with absent radii and thumbs?
cards.a: Fanconi anemia or Holt-Oram syndrome.

cards.q: What is the most common muscular dystrophy overall?
cards.a: Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

cards.q: What is the genetic defect in myotonic dystrophy type 1?
cards.a: CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in DMPK gene (anticipation phenomenon).

cards.q: What is the classic hand finding in myotonic dystrophy?
cards.a: Grip myotonia (cannot release handshake) and frontal balding, cataracts, testicular atrophy.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant.

cards.q: What is the treatment for statin-induced myopathy?
cards.a: Discontinue statin + supportive care. Check CK levels.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is Brodie abscess?
cards.a: Subacute osteomyelitis — walled-off abscess in bone.

cards.q: What is Garre sclerosing osteomyelitis?
cards.a: Chronic non-suppurative osteomyelitis with marked periosteal reaction.

cards.q: What is the most common location for Ewing sarcoma?
cards.a: Diaphysis of long bones (especially femur) and pelvis.

cards.q: What is the onion-skin appearance on X-ray associated with?
cards.a: Ewing sarcoma.

cards.q: What is the most common benign bone tumor in children?
cards.a: Osteochondroma.

cards.q: What is the most common primary bone tumor in the spine?
cards.a: Hemangioma (benign).

cards.q: What is the characteristic X-ray finding in osteoid osteoma?
cards.a: Central radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense sclerotic bone.

cards.q: What relieves the night pain of osteoid osteoma?
cards.a: NSAIDs (due to high prostaglandin production).

cards.q: What is the most common site for giant cell tumor of bone?
cards.a: Epiphysis of long bones (around knee) in young adults.

cards.q: What is the characteristic X-ray appearance of chondrosarcoma?
cards.a: Popcorn calcifications or ring-and-arc pattern.

cards.q: What is the most common soft tissue tumor in adults?
cards.a: Lipoma.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant soft tissue tumor in adults?
cards.a: Liposarcoma.

cards.q: What is the treatment for disseminated gonococcal infection?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin (for possible chlamydia co-infection).

cards.q: What crystal is found in pseudogout?
cards.a: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) — positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.

cards.q: What conditions predispose to calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?
cards.a: Hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatasia.

cards.q: What is the most common joint affected in hemochromatosis arthropathy?
cards.a: 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints.

cards.q: What is the classic radiographic sign of calcium pyrophosphate deposition?
cards.a: Chondrocalcinosis (linear calcification of cartilage).

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute pseudogout?
cards.a: NSAIDs or intra-articular corticosteroids.

cards.q: What is the most common organism causing Lyme arthritis?
cards.a: Borrelia burgdorferi.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Lyme arthritis?
cards.a: Doxycycline (or amoxicillin in children/pregnant patients).

cards.q: What is Whipple disease joint involvement?
cards.a: Migratory arthritis, often precedes GI symptoms. Caused by Tropheryma whipplei.

cards.q: What is the treatment for Whipple disease?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone followed by long-term trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of monoarticular arthritis in young adults?
cards.a: Trauma or septic arthritis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of polyarticular arthritis in young adults?
cards.a: Viral (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis B) or rheumatoid arthritis.

cards.q: What is Still disease (systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis)?
cards.a: High spiking fever, evanescent salmon-colored rash, arthritis, leukocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for systemic JIA?
cards.a: NSAIDs + systemic corticosteroids; biologics (anakinra, tocilizumab) for refractory disease.

cards.q: What autoantibody is associated with drug-induced lupus?
cards.a: Anti-histone antibodies.

cards.q: What drugs classically cause drug-induced lupus?
cards.a: Procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, minocycline.

cards.q: What is the most common manifestation of SLE in the musculoskeletal system?
cards.a: Non-erosive arthritis (Jaccoud arthropathy).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in SLE patients?
cards.a: Infection (due to immunosuppression) and cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute lupus flare with severe organ involvement?
cards.a: High-dose corticosteroids ± cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of avascular necrosis of the femoral head in adults?
cards.a: Corticosteroid use (chronic high dose) and alcohol abuse.

cards.q: What is the earliest MRI finding in avascular necrosis?
cards.a: Double-line sign on T2-weighted images.

cards.q: What is the most common site of osteochondritis dissecans?
cards.a: Lateral aspect of medial femoral condyle.

cards.q: What is the most common direction of hip dislocation?
cards.a: Posterior dislocation (dashboard injury). Risk of sciatic nerve injury.

cards.q: What is the most common nerve injured in posterior hip dislocation?
cards.a: Sciatic nerve.

cards.q: What is the most common fracture in elderly patients after a fall?
cards.a: Femoral neck fracture.

cards.q: What is the major complication of femoral neck fracture?
cards.a: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

cards.q: What is the treatment for displaced femoral neck fracture in elderly patients?
cards.a: Hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement.

cards.q: What is the most common pelvic fracture in elderly patients after minor trauma?
cards.a: Pubic rami fracture.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of pathologic fracture in metastatic bone disease?
cards.a: Breast cancer (lytic lesions).

cards.q: What primary cancers cause blastic bone metastases?
cards.a: Prostate cancer (most common), carcinoid, Hodgkin lymphoma.

cards.q: What cancers cause lytic bone metastases?
cards.a: Breast, lung, thyroid, kidney, multiple myeloma.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for localized osteosarcoma?
cards.a: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide surgical resection + adjuvant chemotherapy.

cards.q: What is the most common site of Ewing sarcoma metastasis?
cards.a: Lungs and bones.

cards.q: What is the characteristic gross appearance of giant cell tumor on X-ray?
cards.a: Soap bubble appearance on X-ray.

cards.q: What is the most common hand tumor?
cards.a: Ganglion cyst.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant hand tumor?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the characteristic translocation in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma?
cards.a: t(2;13) or t(1;13) — PAX3/7-FOXO1 fusion.

cards.q: What is the treatment for rhabdomyosarcoma?
cards.a: Multimodal: surgery, chemotherapy (VAC regimen), and radiation.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of septic arthritis in prosthetic joints?
cards.a: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis).

cards.q: What is the most sensitive test for prosthetic joint infection?
cards.a: Synovial fluid culture and alpha-defensin test.

cards.q: What is the most common organism in diabetic foot osteomyelitis?
cards.a: Polymicrobial (Staph aureus + Gram-negatives + anaerobes).

cards.q: What is Charcot arthropathy most commonly associated with?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute gout in a patient on warfarin?
cards.a: Colchicine or corticosteroids (avoid NSAIDs).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of febuxostat?
cards.a: Non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor (alternative to allopurinol).

cards.q: What is the most common extra-articular manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Acute anterior uveitis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of death in ankylosing spondylitis?
cards.a: Cardiovascular complications (aortic regurgitation, heart block).

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for axial spondyloarthritis refractory to NSAIDs?
cards.a: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept) or IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic skin lesion in psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: Silvery scales on extensor surfaces.

cards.q: What is the characteristic radiographic finding in psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: Pencil-in-cup deformity.

cards.q: What is the treatment for severe psoriatic arthritis?
cards.a: Methotrexate, TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab), or IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of reactive arthritis?
cards.a: Chlamydia trachomatis (urogenital) or GI pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia).

cards.q: What is the classic triad of reactive arthritis?
cards.a: Arthritis + conjunctivitis + urethritis.

cards.q: What HLA is strongly associated with reactive arthritis?
cards.a: HLA-B27.

cards.q: What is the most common manifestation of SLE in joints?
cards.a: Non-erosive, non-deforming arthritis.

cards.q: What is Libman-Sacks endocarditis?
cards.a: Non-bacterial verrucous endocarditis in SLE (mitral valve most common).

cards.q: What is the most specific autoantibody for drug-induced lupus?
cards.a: Anti-histone antibody.

cards.q: What is the treatment for mild SLE?
cards.a: Hydroxychloroquine ± low-dose prednisone.

cards.q: What is the most specific antibody for diffuse systemic sclerosis?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

cards.q: What is the most specific antibody for limited systemic sclerosis (CREST)?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: What is the treatment for scleroderma renal crisis?
cards.a: ACE inhibitors (captopril).

cards.q: What are the layers of the epidermis from deepest to superficial?
cards.a:
Stratum basale (germinativum) → Stratum spinosum → Stratum granulosum → Stratum lucidum (thick skin only) → Stratum corneum.
Mnemonic: Boys Say Girls Love Cookies.

cards.q: What cells are found in the stratum basale and what is their function?
cards.a: Melanocytes (produce melanin, neural crest origin) and stem cells of keratinocytes. Mitotically active layer. Merkel cells (touch) and melanocytes also present.

cards.q: What is the function of Langerhans cells and where are they primarily located?
cards.a: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells) of the skin; important in contact dermatitis. Primarily in stratum spinosum.

cards.q: What protein is produced in the stratum granulosum and what is its function?
cards.a: Keratohyalin granules (contain filaggrin) and lamellar bodies (lipid-rich, form waterproof barrier). Keratinocytes lose nuclei here.

cards.q: What is the embryologic origin of melanocytes?
cards.a: Neural crest cells. Migrate to epidermis during development.

cards.q: What is the most common type of skin cancer?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) (>75% of cases). Locally invasive, rarely metastasizes ('rodent ulcer').

cards.q: What is the classic clinical and histologic description of basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Pearly papule with telangiectasias, rolled borders, central ulceration. Histology: basaloid cells in nests with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact.

cards.q: What is the most common location for basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Sun-exposed areas, especially face (nose, cheeks).

cards.q: What mutation is most commonly associated with basal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: PTCH1 (Hedgehog pathway) loss-of-function mutation.

cards.q: What is the second most common skin cancer and its precursor?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Precursor: actinic keratosis.

cards.q: What are key risk factors and histologic features of squamous cell carcinoma?
cards.a: UV exposure, immunosuppression, chronic wounds. Histology: keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, atypical keratinocytes invading dermis.

cards.q: What virus is strongly associated with SCC in immunocompromised patients?
cards.a: HPV (especially types 16, 18).

cards.q: What is the ABCDE rule used for?
cards.a:
Clinical suspicion of melanoma:
• Asymmetry
• Border irregularity
• Color variation
• Diameter >6 mm
• Evolving

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in melanoma?
cards.a: Breslow depth (thickness in mm).

cards.q: What mutation is commonly targeted in metastatic melanoma therapy?
cards.a: BRAF V600E mutation (vemurafenib, dabrafenib).

cards.q: What are the four major subtypes of melanoma?
cards.a:
1. Superficial spreading (most common)
2. Nodular (most aggressive)
3. Lentigo maligna
4. Acral lentiginous (palms/soles, common in darker skin).

cards.q: What skin finding is pathognomonic for psoriasis?
cards.a: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding after scale removal) and silvery scales on extensor surfaces.

cards.q: What are the histologic features of psoriasis?
cards.a: Regular acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, thinned suprapapillary plates, dilated dermal capillaries.

cards.q: What HLA association is strongest in psoriasis?
cards.a: HLA-Cw6.

cards.q: What is the Koebner phenomenon?
cards.a: Development of psoriatic lesions at sites of trauma. Seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo.

cards.q: What are the classic flexural erythematous lesions with satellite pustules in infants?
cards.a: Candidal diaper dermatitis.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of tinea capitis in the US?
cards.a: Trichophyton tonsurans.

cards.q: What is a Wood's lamp finding in tinea versicolor?
cards.a: Yellow-green fluorescence (Malassezia furfur).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in tinea corporis on KOH prep?
cards.a: Septate hyphae with branching.

cards.q: What organism causes 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH prep?
cards.a: Malassezia furfur (tinea versicolor).

cards.q: What is the classic distribution of atopic dermatitis (eczema) in infants vs. older children?
cards.a:
Infants: Face, extensor surfaces.
Older children/adults: Flexural surfaces (antecubital, popliteal fossae).

cards.q: What is the major criterion for diagnosis of atopic dermatitis?
cards.a: Pruritus (itch that rashes).

cards.q: What is the triad of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma called?
cards.a: Atopic triad (atopy).

cards.q: What are the 5 P's of lichen planus?
cards.a: Pruritic, Polygonal, Purple, Papules, Plate-like (Wickham striae).

cards.q: What is the histologic finding in lichen planus?
cards.a: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at dermoepidermal junction, saw-tooth rete ridges, Civatte bodies.

cards.q: What is the most common bullous disease?
cards.a: Bullous pemphigoid (elderly patients).

cards.q: Differentiate bullous pemphigoid vs. pemphigus vulgaris (clinical and immunofluorescence).
cards.a:
Pemphigoid: Tense bullae, elderly, subepidermal split, linear IgG/C3 at basement membrane (negative Nikolsky).
Pemphigus: Flaccid bullae, oral involvement, intraepidermal (suprabasal) split, IgG against desmogleins (positive Nikolsky).

cards.q: What autoantibodies are in pemphigus vulgaris?
cards.a: Anti-desmoglein 3 (and 1) — IgG against desmosomes.

cards.q: What is the target antigen in bullous pemphigoid?
cards.a: Hemidesmosomes (BP180 / BP230).

cards.q: What skin finding is seen in dermatitis herpetiformis?
cards.a: Pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). Strongly associated with celiac disease.

cards.q: What immunofluorescence pattern is seen in dermatitis herpetiformis?
cards.a: Granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae.

cards.q: What is the treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis?
cards.a: Dapsone + gluten-free diet.

cards.q: What is acantholysis?
cards.a: Loss of cohesion between keratinocytes due to desmosome destruction (seen in pemphigus).

cards.q: What drug class classically causes Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN?
cards.a: Aromatic anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin), sulfa drugs, allopurinol, NSAIDs.

cards.q: What is the difference between SJS and TEN?
cards.a:
SJS: <10% body surface area detachment.
TEN: >30% BSA. Overlap 10–30%.

cards.q: What is Nikolsky sign positive in?
cards.a: Pemphigus vulgaris, SJS/TEN, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

cards.q: What is the causative organism and toxin in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus producing exfoliative toxin (cleaves desmoglein 1).

cards.q: What is the cleavage plane in SSSS vs. bullous impetigo?
cards.a: SSSS: granular layer (intraepidermal, superficial). Bullous impetigo: also superficial but localized.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of erythema multiforme?
cards.a: HSV infection (especially recurrent).

cards.q: What are target lesions characteristic of?
cards.a: Erythema multiforme.

cards.q: What skin manifestation is associated with celiac disease?
cards.a: Dermatitis herpetiformis.

cards.q: What is the most common skin finding in sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on nose/ears) and erythema nodosum.

cards.q: What is Gottron papules pathognomonic for?
cards.a: Dermatomyositis.

cards.q: What is the heliotrope rash?
cards.a: Periorbital violaceous erythema in dermatomyositis.

cards.q: What autoantibody is most specific for dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Anti-Mi-2.

cards.q: What is the classic hand finding in systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)?
cards.a: Sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST)?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I).

cards.q: What is the most common drug causing fixed drug eruption?
cards.a: Tetracyclines, NSAIDs, sulfonamides.

cards.q: What is acanthosis nigricans associated with?
cards.a: Insulin resistance / diabetes, obesity, and internal malignancy (especially GI adenocarcinoma).

cards.q: What is the most common benign skin lesion?
cards.a: Seborrheic keratosis ('stuck-on' appearance).

cards.q: What is the sign of Leser-Trélat?
cards.a: Sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses — paraneoplastic (GI malignancy).

cards.q: What is the difference between a junctional, compound, and intradermal nevus?
cards.a:
Junctional: at dermoepidermal junction.
Compound: junctional + dermal.
Intradermal: only dermis (most common adult type).

cards.q: What is the causative organism of impetigo and its classic lesion?
cards.a:
Staphylococcus aureus (most common) or Streptococcus pyogenes.
Classic: Honey-crusted erosions around mouth/nose in children.

cards.q: Differentiate bullous impetigo from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS).
cards.a:
Bullous impetigo: Localized, toxin-producing S. aureus, subcorneal split.
SSSS: Generalized, remote focus of infection, cleavage in granular layer, no organisms in skin.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of cellulitis?
cards.a: Streptococcus pyogenes (beta-hemolytic) or Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: What is necrotizing fasciitis Type 1 vs Type 2?
cards.a:
Type 1: Polymicrobial (diabetics, post-surgery).
Type 2: Group A Strep (± S. aureus). 'Flesh-eating' with rapid spread along fascia.

cards.q: What is the treatment for necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.a: Immediate surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin).

cards.q: What virus causes molluscum contagiosum and what is the classic lesion?
cards.a: Poxvirus. Pearly, umbilicated papules. Central core contains molluscum bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies).

cards.q: What is the most common viral exanthem in children?
cards.a: Varicella (chickenpox) — caused by VZV. Successive crops of lesions in different stages.

cards.q: What are the complications of varicella in adults/immunocompromised?
cards.a: Pneumonia, encephalitis, disseminated disease, bacterial superinfection.

cards.q: What is herpes zoster (shingles) and its classic distribution?
cards.a: Reactivation of VZV in a single dermatome. Painful grouped vesicles on erythematous base.

cards.q: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?
cards.a: Herpes zoster oticus (CN VII + VIII involvement) → facial palsy, ear pain, vesicles in external auditory canal, hearing loss.

cards.q: What is the treatment for herpes zoster?
cards.a: Oral acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir within 72 hours + analgesics. IV acyclovir for disseminated/Ramsay Hunt.

cards.q: What skin finding is pathognomonic for measles (rubeola)?
cards.a: Koplik spots (white spots on buccal mucosa) preceding the maculopapular rash.

cards.q: What is hand-foot-mouth disease caused by?
cards.a: Coxsackie A16 (or enterovirus 71). Vesicles on palms, soles, and oral mucosa.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of roseola infantum (exanthem subitum)?
cards.a: High fever for 3–5 days followed by a maculopapular rash as fever defervesces (HHV-6).

cards.q: What is erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) caused by?
cards.a: Parvovirus B19. 'Slapped cheek' rash + lace-like reticular rash on trunk/extremities.

cards.q: What complication can parvovirus B19 cause in patients with chronic hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Aplastic crisis (transient red cell aplasia).

cards.q: What is the most common dermatophyte infection of the feet?
cards.a: Tinea pedis (athlete’s foot). Caused by Trichophyton species.

cards.q: What is onychomycosis and its most common cause?
cards.a: Fungal infection of the nail. Most common: Trichophyton rubrum.

cards.q: What is the KOH preparation finding for dermatophytes?
cards.a: Septate hyphae with branching at acute angles.

cards.q: What is the treatment for tinea capitis?
cards.a: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine (topical agents ineffective). Selenium sulfide shampoo as adjunct.

cards.q: What is pityriasis rosea? Classic finding?
cards.a: Herald patch followed by Christmas tree distribution of oval salmon-colored papules with collarette scale. Self-limited.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of alopecia areata?
cards.a: Autoimmune (T-cell mediated attack on hair follicles). Associated with other autoimmune diseases.

cards.q: What is the exclamation mark hair sign?
cards.a: Seen in alopecia areata — short broken hairs at periphery of patch.

cards.q: What is telogen effluvium?
cards.a: Diffuse hair shedding 2–4 months after a physiologic stressor (pregnancy, surgery, illness, crash dieting).

cards.q: What is androgenetic alopecia (male/female pattern baldness)?
cards.a: DHT-mediated miniaturization of hair follicles. Treatment: minoxidil, finasteride (males).

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic nail finding in psoriasis?
cards.a: Pitting, oil-drop spots, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis.

cards.q: What is Beau’s lines?
cards.a: Transverse grooves in nails due to temporary arrest of nail growth (systemic illness, chemotherapy).

cards.q: What is clubbing associated with?
cards.a: Chronic hypoxia (lung disease, congenital heart disease, lung cancer, IBD).

cards.q: What is vitiligo?
cards.a: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes → depigmented macules. Associated with other autoimmune diseases (thyroid, DM1, pernicious anemia).

cards.q: What is melasma?
cards.a: Hyperpigmented macules on face (malar distribution), triggered by pregnancy, OCPs, sun exposure ('mask of pregnancy').

cards.q: What is the most common pigmentary disorder in dark-skinned individuals?
cards.a: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

cards.q: What is the most common type of ichthyosis?
cards.a: Ichthyosis vulgaris — autosomal dominant, associated with atopic dermatitis, 'fish-scale' appearance.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of lamellar ichthyosis?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive (TGM1 mutation). Collodion baby at birth.

cards.q: What skin finding is seen in tuberous sclerosis?
cards.a: Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas), ash-leaf spots (hypopigmented macules), shagreen patch.

cards.q: What is the most common neurocutaneous syndrome?
cards.a: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease).

cards.q: What are café-au-lait spots and their significance?
cards.a: Hyperpigmented macules. ≥6 spots >5 mm (prepubertal) or >15 mm (postpubertal) suggestive of NF1.

cards.q: What is Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in V1 distribution + leptomeningeal angiomatosis + glaucoma + seizures.

cards.q: What is the most common malignant skin tumor in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma (defect in nucleotide excision repair).

cards.q: What drug is associated with photosensitivity and lupus-like syndrome?
cards.a: Hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid (anti-histone antibodies).

cards.q: What is the most common drug eruption?
cards.a: Morbilliform (exanthematous) drug eruption.

cards.q: What is DRESS syndrome?
cards.a: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms — fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, organ involvement (liver most common).

cards.q: What is the most common organism causing hot tub folliculitis?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for acne vulgaris?
cards.a: Topical retinoids (first-line). Combinations with benzoyl peroxide or antibiotics for moderate disease. Oral acne isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic.

cards.q: What is hidradenitis suppurativa?
cards.a: Chronic suppurative inflammation of apocrine glands (axillae, groin). Painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts.

cards.q: What is the most common cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins) and lupus pernio.

cards.q: What is pyoderma gangrenosum associated with?
cards.a: Inflammatory bowel disease (UC > Crohn), rheumatoid arthritis, hematologic malignancies. Painful ulcer with violaceous undermined borders.

cards.q: What is the pathognomonic finding in erythema nodosum?
cards.a: Tender, erythematous subcutaneous nodules on anterior shins (panniculitis). Does NOT ulcerate.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic skin finding?
cards.a: Acanthosis nigricans (GI adenocarcinoma) and dermatomyositis.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern and classic triad of incontinentia pigmenti?
cards.a: X-linked dominant (lethal in males). Triad: vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → hypopigmented stages along Blaschko lines. Associated with dental, ocular, and CNS abnormalities.

cards.q: What is the most common genodermatosis?
cards.a: Neurofibromatosis type 1.

cards.q: What are Lisch nodules?
cards.a: Iris hamartomas seen in NF1.

cards.q: What is the most common tumor in NF1?
cards.a: Optic glioma and plexiform neurofibromas.

cards.q: What is the classic cardiac tumor in tuberous sclerosis?
cards.a: Cardiac rhabdomyoma.

cards.q: What is the inheritance of xeroderma pigmentosum?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive. Defect in nucleotide excision repair → extreme photosensitivity and skin cancers.

cards.q: What is the defect in albinism?
cards.a: Tyrosinase deficiency or defective melanin synthesis/transport (oculocutaneous or ocular types).

cards.q: What is Waardenburg syndrome?
cards.a: White forelock, heterochromia iridis, sensorineural deafness, dystopia canthorum (PAX3 mutation).

cards.q: What is the most common ichthyosis?
cards.a: Ichthyosis vulgaris (autosomal dominant, filaggrin mutation). Associated with atopic dermatitis.

cards.q: What is the presentation of a collodion baby?
cards.a: Lamellar ichthyosis (autosomal recessive). Tight, shiny membrane at birth that cracks and peels.

cards.q: What skin finding is associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?
cards.a: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (lips, buccal mucosa, perioral) + hamartomatous polyps.

cards.q: What is Gardner syndrome?
cards.a: Familial adenomatous polyposis + osteomas, desmoid tumors, epidermoid cysts, congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE).

cards.q: What is the most common cutaneous manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum.

cards.q: What is necrobiosis lipoidica associated with?
cards.a: Diabetes mellitus. Yellow-brown plaques on shins with central atrophy and telangiectasias.

cards.q: What is pretibial myxedema associated with?
cards.a: Graves disease (hyperthyroidism) — non-pitting waxy plaques on shins.

cards.q: What skin finding is seen in pellagra (niacin deficiency)?
cards.a: Casals necklace (photosensitive dermatitis in C3–C4 distribution) + diarrhea, dementia.

cards.q: What is the classic skin finding in scurvy (vitamin C deficiency)?
cards.a: Perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding, poor wound healing.

cards.q: What is acrodermatitis enteropathica?
cards.a: Zinc deficiency — periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea.

cards.q: What is the most common drug causing photosensitivity?
cards.a: Tetracyclines, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, thiazides, fluoroquinolones.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of fixed drug eruption?
cards.a: NSAIDs, tetracyclines, sulfonamides. Oval erythematous to violaceous plaque that recurs at the same site.

cards.q: What is the treatment for severe acne with nodulocystic lesions?
cards.a: Oral isotretinoin (requires iPLEDGE program due to teratogenicity).

cards.q: What is the major side effect of isotretinoin?
cards.a: Teratogenicity (CNS, cardiac, craniofacial malformations), hyperlipidemia, hepatotoxicity, dry skin/mucosa.

cards.q: What is rosacea?
cards.a: Chronic facial erythema, telangiectasias, papules/pustules (no comedones), rhinophyma in advanced cases.

cards.q: What triggers rosacea?
cards.a: Sun exposure, hot drinks, spicy foods, alcohol, temperature extremes.

cards.q: What is the treatment for rosacea?
cards.a: Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. Oral doxycycline for moderate-severe disease.

cards.q: What is perioral dermatitis?
cards.a: Erythematous papules around mouth/nose (spares vermilion border). Often due to topical steroid overuse.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of seborrheic dermatitis?
cards.a: Malassezia yeast overgrowth. Greasy scales on scalp (cradle cap in infants), nasolabial folds, eyebrows.

cards.q: What is the treatment for seborrheic dermatitis?
cards.a: Topical antifungals (ketoconazole), low-potency steroids, zinc pyrithione or selenium sulfide shampoo.

cards.q: What is the most common benign vascular tumor in infants?
cards.a: Infantile hemangioma (strawberry hemangioma). Grows rapidly then involutes.

cards.q: What is a port-wine stain associated with?
cards.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome when in trigeminal V1 distribution.

cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for port-wine stain?
cards.a: Pulsed-dye laser.

cards.q: What is Langerhans cell histiocytosis skin finding?
cards.a: Seborrheic-like eruption in scalp and intertriginous areas. Birbeck granules (tennis racket) on EM.

cards.q: What is the most common malignancy in children?
cards.a: Leukemia cutis can present with blueberry muffin lesions (extramedullary hematopoiesis).

cards.q: What is mycosis fungoides?
cards.a: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Patch → plaque → tumor stage. Pautrier microabscesses on histology.

cards.q: What is Sézary syndrome?
cards.a: Leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with erythroderma and circulating atypical lymphocytes (Sézary cells).

cards.q: What is Kaposi sarcoma associated with?
cards.a: HHV-8. Classic in elderly Mediterranean men, AIDS patients, and transplant recipients. Purple plaques/nodules.

cards.q: What is the treatment for limited Kaposi sarcoma?
cards.a: Local radiation or intralesional chemotherapy. Systemic for widespread disease.

cards.q: What is dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans?
cards.a: Locally aggressive spindle cell tumor. 'Storiform' pattern on histology. t(17;22) translocation.

cards.q: What is the most common site for Merkel cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Head and neck in elderly. Neuroendocrine origin, CK20 perinuclear dot-like staining.

cards.q: What virus is associated with Merkel cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Merkel cell polyomavirus.

cards.q: What is the most common paraneoplastic pemphigus association?
cards.a: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

cards.q: What is the difference between pemphigus foliaceus and vulgaris?
cards.a:
Foliaceus: superficial (subcorneal), no mucosal involvement, anti-desmoglein 1.
Vulgaris: suprabasal, mucosal involvement common, anti-desmoglein 3 ± 1.

cards.q: What is linear IgA bullous dermatosis associated with?
cards.a: Drug-induced (vancomycin most common). 'String of pearls' vesicles.

cards.q: What is the target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita?
cards.a: Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils). Subepidermal blisters, trauma-induced.

cards.q: What is porphyria cutanea tarda associated with?
cards.a: Hepatitis C, alcohol, estrogen, iron overload. Blisters on sun-exposed dorsal hands, hypertrichosis, milia.

cards.q: What enzyme is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria?
cards.a: Porphobilinogen deaminase. No skin findings (neurologic/visceral symptoms only).

cards.q: What is pseudoporphyria caused by?
cards.a: NSAIDs (especially naproxen), tetracyclines, diuretics. Skin findings like PCT but normal porphyrins.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of erythroderma in adults?
cards.a: Psoriasis or drug reaction (atopic dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma also common).

cards.q: What is the most common cause of urticaria?
cards.a: IgE-mediated (Type I) hypersensitivity. Acute: foods, drugs, infections. Chronic (>6 weeks): often idiopathic or autoimmune.

cards.q: What is angioedema without urticaria most commonly associated with?
cards.a: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency (hereditary or acquired) or ACE inhibitor use.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acute urticaria/angioedema with airway compromise?
cards.a: Epinephrine IM + antihistamines + corticosteroids.

cards.q: What is mastocytosis?
cards.a: Clonal proliferation of mast cells. Cutaneous: urticaria pigmentosa (Darier's sign — urticaria on stroking).

cards.q: What is the treatment for mild psoriasis?
cards.a: Topical corticosteroids + vitamin D analogs (calcipotriene).

cards.q: What systemic treatment is used for moderate-to-severe psoriasis?
cards.a: Methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, or biologics (TNF inhibitors, IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors).

cards.q: What is the first-line biologic for plaque psoriasis?
cards.a: IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors (secukinumab, guselkumab) or TNF inhibitors.

cards.q: What is the characteristic distribution of lichen planus?
cards.a: Flexor surfaces of wrists, ankles, oral mucosa (lacy white Wickham striae).

cards.q: What is the treatment for lichen planus?
cards.a: Topical or intralesional corticosteroids. Oral steroids or immunosuppressants for severe disease.

cards.q: What is erythema nodosum most commonly associated with?
cards.a: Streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, pregnancy, oral contraceptives.

cards.q: What is pyoderma gangrenosum classically associated with?
cards.a: Inflammatory bowel disease (UC), rheumatoid arthritis, hematologic malignancies.

cards.q: What is Sweet syndrome?
cards.a: Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis — tender erythematous plaques, fever, neutrophilia. Associated with malignancy or infection.

cards.q: What is the most common cutaneous manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus?
cards.a: Malar (butterfly) rash — spares nasolabial folds.

cards.q: What is discoid lupus?
cards.a: Chronic cutaneous lupus — erythematous plaques with scaling, follicular plugging, scarring alopecia.

cards.q: What autoantibody is most specific for SLE?
cards.a: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) and anti-dsDNA.

cards.q: What is the classic hand finding in dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Gottron papules (violaceous papules over knuckles) and mechanic’s hands.

cards.q: What malignancy is most strongly associated with dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Ovarian cancer (also breast, lung, GI).

cards.q: What is the most common skin finding in scleroderma?
cards.a: Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with CREST syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: What antibody is associated with diffuse scleroderma?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

cards.q: What is the most common drug reaction pattern?
cards.a: Morbilliform (exanthematous) eruption.

cards.q: What drugs are most commonly associated with SJS/TEN?
cards.a: Lamotrigine, carbamazepine, allopurinol, sulfonamides, NSAIDs.

cards.q: What is the management of SJS/TEN?
cards.a: Immediate discontinuation of offending drug + supportive care in burn unit. IVIG or cyclosporine in severe cases.

cards.q: What is the treatment for acne rosacea?
cards.a: Topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin. Oral doxycycline for papulopustular type.

cards.q: What is rhinophyma?
cards.a: Advanced rosacea with sebaceous hyperplasia and fibrosis of the nose.

cards.q: What is the most common pediatric vascular tumor?
cards.a: Infantile hemangioma.

cards.q: When do infantile hemangiomas typically involute?
cards.a: Most involute by age 5–7 years. Propranolol is first-line for problematic lesions.

cards.q: What is a salmon patch (stork bite)?
cards.a: Nevus simplex — most common vascular birthmark, fades with time.

cards.q: What is a port-wine stain?
cards.a: Nevus flammeus — does not fade, associated with Sturge-Weber when in V1 distribution.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of alopecia in children?
cards.a: Tinea capitis.

cards.q: What is traction alopecia?
cards.a: Hair loss due to chronic tension from tight hairstyles (braids, ponytails).

cards.q: What nail finding is associated with psoriasis?
cards.a: Nail pitting, oil-drop spots, onycholysis.

cards.q: What is onychomycosis most commonly caused by?
cards.a: Trichophyton rubrum.

cards.q: What is the treatment for onychomycosis?
cards.a: Oral terbinafine (first-line) or itraconazole.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of paronychia?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus or Candida.

cards.q: What is the most common skin cancer in transplant patients?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma (reversed ratio vs general population).

cards.q: What is the treatment for actinic keratosis?
cards.a: Cryotherapy, topical 5-FU, imiquimod, or photodynamic therapy.

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor for melanoma?
cards.a: Breslow thickness.

cards.q: What mutation is targeted in BRAF-mutant melanoma?
cards.a: BRAF V600E (dabrafenib + trametinib).

cards.q: What is the most common site of melanoma in dark-skinned individuals?
cards.a: Acral lentiginous melanoma (palms, soles, nail beds).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of mycosis fungoides?
cards.a: Chronic pruritic patches/plaques in non-sun-exposed areas progressing to tumors.

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor for melanoma survival?
cards.a: Breslow depth (tumor thickness).

cards.q: A patient presents with a pearly, slow-growing papule with telangiectasias on the upper lip. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

cards.q: A patient with a history of organ transplant presents with a non-healing, ulcerated nodule with a keratin plug on the lower lip. Biopsy shows keratin pearls. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for multiple actinic keratoses (AK)?
cards.a: Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or imiquimod. (Note: cryotherapy for isolated lesions).

cards.q: The sudden appearance of multiple seborrheic keratoses (Leser-Trélat sign) is associated with what underlying condition?
cards.a: Gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: A patient has sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces. What is the phenomenon where minor trauma causes new lesions?
cards.a: Koebner phenomenon (associated with Psoriasis).

cards.q: A healthy 20-year-old presents with a "herald patch" followed by a diffuse "Christmas tree" pattern scaling rash on the trunk. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Pityriasis rosea.

cards.q: A patient with Hepatitis C presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with fine white lines (Wickham striae) on the wrists. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Lichen planus.

cards.q: Targetoid lesions appearing abruptly on the extremities, often following a Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Erythema multiforme.

cards.q: A severe mucocutaneous reaction characterized by epidermal sloughing involving <10% of total body surface area (TBSA), often triggered by medications like allopurinol or antiepileptics. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS).

cards.q: A life-threatening mucocutaneous disease with extensive epidermal necrosis and sloughing involving >30% TBSA, with a positive Nikolsky sign. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).

cards.q: An elderly patient presents with intensely pruritic, tense subepidermal bullae. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Bullous pemphigoid (antibodies against hemidesmosomes).

cards.q: A middle-aged patient presents with painful oral erosions and flaccid cutaneous bullae that easily rupture (positive Nikolsky sign). Immunofluorescence shows a net-like intraepidermal IgG pattern. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Pemphigus vulgaris (antibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3).

cards.q: A patient with Celiac disease presents with intensely pruritic papules and vesicles on the elbows and knees. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Tx: Dapsone and gluten-free diet).

cards.q: A patient with Hepatitis C or hemochromatosis presents with painless blisters and skin fragility on the dorsum of the hands after sun exposure. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Porphyria cutanea tarda (deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of isotretinoin (a derivative of vitamin A, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>28</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) used for severe, nodulocystic acne vulgaris?
cards.a: Decreases sebum production and normalizes epidermal desquamation. (Note: Highly teratogenic, requires two forms of contraception).

cards.q: A patient presents with facial flushing, erythema, telangiectasias, and papulopustules on the nose and cheeks, worsened by alcohol and spicy foods. First-line topical treatment?
cards.a: Topical metronidazole or ivermectin (Diagnosis: Rosacea).

cards.q: A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in the axillae and groin. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Hidradenitis suppurativa.

cards.q: A child presents with perioral honey-colored crusted lesions. What is the most common causative organism and first-line topical treatment?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Strep; Topical mupirocin.

cards.q: A superficial bacterial skin infection causing a well-demarcated, raised, intensely erythematous plaque on the face or legs, most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Erysipelas.

cards.q: A deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue infection presenting with ill-defined borders, erythema, swelling, and tenderness. Most common organisms?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.

cards.q: A newborn presents with fever, generalized erythema, and large flaccid bullae that slough off with gentle pressure. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS, caused by exfoliative toxins).

cards.q: A patient with rapidly spreading erythema, extreme pain out of proportion to exam findings, and crepitus on palpation. Next best step in management?
cards.a: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement (Diagnosis: Necrotizing fasciitis).

cards.q: Annular, erythematous plaques with a central clearing and a scaly, active border. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows branching septate hyphae. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Tinea corporis.

cards.q: A teenager presents with hypopigmented macules on the upper back and chest that do not tan in the sun. KOH prep shows "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Tinea versicolor (caused by Malassezia furfur).

cards.q: A child with a scaly patch of alopecia and broken hairs on the scalp. What is the treatment of choice?
cards.a: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine (Topical antifungals are ineffective for Tinea capitis).

cards.q: An obese patient with diabetes presents with an erythematous, highly pruritic rash with satellite lesions in the inframammary folds. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Candida intertrigo.

cards.q: Intensely pruritic, thread-like burrows in the interdigital web spaces and flexor surfaces of wrists, with itching worse at night. Treatment of choice?
cards.a: Topical 5% permethrin cream applied from neck down, or oral ivermectin.

cards.q: A school-aged child with intense scalp pruritus. Exam shows tiny, white, oval structures firmly attached to hair shafts. First-line treatment?
cards.a: Topical 1% permethrin lotion (Diagnosis: Pediculosis capitis).

cards.q: Firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules. What is the causative agent and the condition to screen for in adults with extensive disease?
cards.a: Poxvirus (Molluscum contagiosum); Screen for HIV.

cards.q: A pregnant woman presents with solitary or multiple cauliflower-like lesions on the vulva. Diagnosis and causative agent?
cards.a: Condylomata acuminata; HPV types 6 and 11.

cards.q: A sexually active patient presents with a diffuse, non-pruritic maculopapular rash that involves the palms and soles, accompanied by generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Secondary syphilis.

cards.q: A patient hiking in the Northeast US develops an expanding, erythematous, target-like rash (Erythema migrans). What is the treatment of choice for pregnant women or children <8 years old?
cards.a: Amoxicillin (Standard tx: Doxycycline).

cards.q: A patient develops fever, headache, and a petechial rash that started on the wrists and ankles and spread centrally, after a tick bite in North Carolina. Treatment?
cards.a: Doxycycline (always first-line, even in children) for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever.

cards.q: An autoimmune condition characterized by the destruction of melanocytes, resulting in well-demarcated depigmented macules/patches, often associated with other autoimmune diseases. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Vitiligo.

cards.q: An infant presents with diffuse hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes. What enzyme is deficient?
cards.a: Tyrosinase (Oculocutaneous albinism, inability to synthesize melanin from tyrosine).

cards.q: Acquired hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas on the face, commonly seen in pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Melasma (chloasma).

cards.q: Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques found in intertriginous areas (e.g., neck, axillae). Most commonly associated with what metabolic condition?
cards.a: Insulin resistance (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus) or gastric adenocarcinoma if sudden onset.

cards.q: Painful, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules on the anterior shins. Most common associated condition in a young African American female?
cards.a: Sarcoidosis (Diagnosis: Erythema nodosum).

cards.q: A firm, hyperpigmented nodule on the lower extremity that dimples centrally when pinched (dimple sign). Diagnosis?
cards.a: Dermatofibroma (benign fibroblast proliferation).

cards.q: Hypertrophic scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, characterized by excessive deposition of Type I and Type III collagen. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Keloid.

cards.q: A rapidly growing, friable, red papule that bleeds easily with minor trauma, often appearing during pregnancy or after an injury. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma).

cards.q: The most common benign vascular tumor in adults, presenting as small, bright red, dome-shaped papules that increase in number with age. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Cherry angioma.

cards.q: A vascular tumor in an infant that grows rapidly during the first few weeks of life and spontaneously regresses by age 5-8 years. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Strawberry (infantile) hemangioma.

cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count <100 cells/mm<sup>3</sup> presents with friable red/purple cutaneous nodules. Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial bacilli. Diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella); Tx with Erythromycin.

cards.q: An HIV patient presents with violaceous plaques on the skin and hard palate. Biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate and slit-like vascular spaces. Causative agent?
cards.a: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) causing Kaposi sarcoma.

cards.q: Sudden onset of localized, non-scarring hair loss with "exclamation point" hairs at the periphery of the bald patch. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Alopecia areata (Autoimmune).

cards.q: What medication used for male pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia) acts as a 5α-reductase inhibitor, preventing conversion of testosterone to DHT?
cards.a: Finasteride.

cards.q: A patient who frequently uses public pools presents with macerated, scaling, and fissured skin between the toes. Treatment?
cards.a: Topical antifungals (e.g., terbinafine, clotrimazole) for Tinea pedis.

cards.q: A patient taking allopurinol develops fever, facial edema, diffuse morbilliform rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and elevated AST/ALT. Diagnosis?
cards.a: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms).

cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor for cutaneous melanoma without distant metastasis?
cards.a: Breslow depth (vertical thickness of the lesion measured in millimeters from the granular layer of the epidermis).

cards.q: Differentiate Pemphigus Vulgaris from Bullous Pemphigoid regarding autoantibodies, Nikolsky sign, and mucous membrane involvement.
cards.a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: IgG against desmoglein-1/3; Nikolsky (+); oral mucosal involvement common; flaccid blisters.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: IgG against hemidesmosomes (BP180/BP230); Nikolsky (-); mucosal involvement rare; tense blisters.

cards.q: What body surface area (BSA) cutoff differentiates Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) from Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)?
cards.a:
• SJS: <10% BSA detachment.
• SJS/TEN overlap: 10%–30% BSA detachment.
• TEN: >30% BSA detachment.

cards.q: What premalignant lesion presents as rough, scaly, sandpaper-like macules/papules on sun-exposed skin, and what is the first-line topical treatment for widespread disease?
cards.a: Actinic Keratosis (precursor to Squamous Cell Carcinoma). First-line topical treatment for widespread field cancerization is 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) cream or imiquimod.

cards.q: What is the characteristic clinical presentation and histologic finding of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)?
cards.a:
Clinical: Pearly, translucent papule/nodule with telangiectasias and rolled borders ± central ulceration.
Histology: Nests of basaloid epithelial cells with peripheral palisading nuclei.

cards.q: What is the stepwise escalating pharmacotherapy for Acne Vulgaris from mild to severe refractory nodulocystic disease?
cards.a:
1. Mild: Topical retinoids ± benzoyl peroxide.
2. Moderate: Add topical antibiotics (clindamycin/erythromycin) or oral tetracyclines (doxycycline/minocycline).
3. Severe/Nodulocystic: Oral isotretinoin (requires negative pregnancy tests and enrollment in iPLEDGE due to severe teratogenicity).

cards.q: What chronic inflammatory dermatosis presents with recurrent, painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in intertriginous areas (axillae, groin)? What biological agent is approved for moderate-to-severe disease?
cards.a: Hidradenitis Suppurativa (follicular occlusion disease). First-line biologic is an anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody (e.g., adalimumab).

cards.q: What is the diagnosis for silvery-white plaques on extensor surfaces displaying the Auspitz sign, and which cytokine pathways are key targets for modern systemic therapy?
cards.a: Psoriasis Vulgaris (Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal). Targeted biologics include anti-IL-17 (e.g., secukinumab), anti-IL-12/23 (e.g., ustekinumab), or anti-TNF-α inhibitors.

cards.q: What key genetic mutation (epidermal barrier protein) is strongly associated with Atopic Dermatitis, and what non-steroidal topical class is used for facial lesions?
cards.a: Inactivating mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene. Facial/intertriginous flare-ups are treated with topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) to avoid steroid-induced skin atrophy.

cards.q: What greasy, erythematous rash with yellow scales affecting the scalp and nasolabial folds is associated with Malassezia fungi, and which underlying neurological condition is classic for severe recalcitrant presentations?
cards.a: Seborrheic Dermatitis. Strongly associated with Parkinson disease (and HIV infection).

cards.q: A patient with chronic Hepatitis C presents with painless blisters, skin fragility, and hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed hands. What enzyme deficiency causes this condition, and what accumulates in the urine?
cards.a: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) due to deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). Urinalysis demonstrates elevated uroporphyrins (turns tea-colored or fluoresces coral red under Wood lamp).

cards.q: What chronic facial dermatosis presents with central facial erythema, telangiectasias, and pustules triggered by alcohol, heat, or spicy foods, and what topical antimicrobial is first-line?
cards.a: Rosacea (papulopustular variant). First-line topical treatments include metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin. (Note: lack of comedones distinguishes it from acne vulgaris).

cards.q: What auto-inflammatory skin disease presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques with fine white lines (Wickham striae), and which chronic viral infection should be screened for?
cards.a: Lichen Planus (the 5 Ps: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules/Plaques). Strong association with Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.

cards.q: An adult with chronic diarrhea presents with intensely pruritic, grouped papulovesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. What is the diagnosis, autoantibody target, and acute medical treatment?
cards.a: Dermatitis Herpetiformis associated with Celiac Disease (IgA anti-epidermal transglutaminase deposits at dermal papillae tips). Acute treatment is dapsone; long-term management requires a strict gluten-free diet.

cards.q: What condition presents as painful, erythematous, non-ulcerative nodular lesions on the anterior lower legs (shins), and what are 3 major high-yield underlying etiologies?
cards.a: Erythema Nodosum (panniculitis). High-yield causes include: Streptococcal pharyngitis, Sarcoidosis, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), Histoplasmosis, and Tuberculosis.

cards.q: A patient with Ulcerative Colitis develops a rapidly expanding, extremely painful skin ulcer with violaceous, undermined borders after minor skin trauma. What is the diagnosis and primary management?
cards.a: Pyoderma Gangrenosum (demonstrates pathergy). Management involves systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclosporine, infliximab). Do NOT perform surgical debridement as it worsens the ulcer.

cards.q: What skin manifestation presents as hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous zones (neck, axillae), and what are the two main clinical associations (benign vs malignant)?
cards.a:
Acanthosis Nigricans.
• Benign: Insulin resistance (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, PCOS, obesity).
• Malignant: Gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma (especially gastric adenocarcinoma).

cards.q: What is the Leser-Trélat sign and what underlying pathology does it indicate?
cards.a: The sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses within a short period. It serves as a paraneoplastic marker for underlying internal malignancy, most commonly gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: A patient started on allopurinol 4 weeks ago presents with fever, widespread maculopapular rash, facial edema, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count >1,500/μL). What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: DRESS Syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms). Caused by drugs like antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, or antibiotics (vancomycin). Visceral organ involvement (e.g., hepatitis, interstitial nephritis) is common.

cards.q: What skin infection presents with small, firm, umbilicated dome-shaped papules with a central curd-like core, and when seen extensively in an adult, warrants testing for which underlying condition?
cards.a: Molluscum Contagiosum (caused by Poxvirus). In adults with widespread or facial lesions, screening for HIV infection (immunocompromised state) is mandatory.

cards.q: What is the direction of DNA replication and transcription?
cards.a:
Both occur 5' → 3'.
DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase add nucleotides to the 3' end.

cards.q: Which DNA polymerase is the main replicative enzyme in eukaryotes?
cards.a:
DNA Pol δ (leading and lagging strands in nucleus).
DNA Pol α (primase activity), DNA Pol ε (leading strand).

cards.q: What is the function of telomerase?
cards.a:
RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that adds TTAGGG repeats to the 3' end of chromosomes.
Prevents shortening during replication. Overactive in most cancers.

cards.q: What is the difference between leading and lagging strand synthesis?
cards.a:
Leading: Continuous synthesis (5'→3').
Lagging: Discontinuous (Okazaki fragments). Requires DNA ligase to join fragments.

cards.q: What enzyme relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork?
cards.a:
Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase in prokaryotes).
Topoisomerase I makes single-strand breaks.

cards.q: What is the role of helicase in replication?
cards.a: Unwinds double-stranded DNA using ATP. Creates two replication forks.

cards.q: Single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) do what?
cards.a: Stabilize single-stranded DNA and prevent re-annealing or degradation.

cards.q: What is the eukaryotic equivalent of the prokaryotic sigma factor?
cards.a: Transcription factors (TFII family) — help RNA Pol II recognize promoter (TATA box).

cards.q: Name the three eukaryotic RNA polymerases and their products.
cards.a:
RNA Pol I: rRNA (except 5S).
RNA Pol II: mRNA, miRNA, snRNA.
RNA Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA.

cards.q: What is the TATA box and its location?
cards.a: Core promoter sequence ~25 bp upstream of transcription start site. Recognized by TBP (TATA-binding protein).

cards.q: What are the three stop codons?
cards.a: UAA, UAG, UGA (no tRNA binds; release factors bind instead).

cards.q: What is the start codon and what amino acid does it code for?
cards.a: AUG → Methionine (Met). Also serves as the initiation codon.

cards.q: What is the wobble hypothesis?
cards.a: The 3rd base of the codon can have non-standard base pairing with the tRNA anticodon, allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple codons.

cards.q: What is the function of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase?
cards.a: Charges tRNA with its correct amino acid (uses ATP). Has proofreading activity.

cards.q: Describe the three steps of translation initiation in eukaryotes.
cards.a:
1. Formation of 43S pre-initiation complex (40S + eIFs + Met-tRNA).
2. mRNA binding (cap-dependent via eIF4E).
3. Scanning to AUG → 60S joins (80S ribosome).

cards.q: What are the sites on the ribosome (A, P, E)?
cards.a:
A (aminoacyl) — incoming tRNA.
P (peptidyl) — holds growing chain.
E (exit) — departing tRNA.

cards.q: What is the difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomes?
cards.a:
Prokaryotes: 70S (30S + 50S).
Eukaryotes: 80S (40S + 60S).

cards.q: Name three major types of post-transcriptional mRNA processing in eukaryotes.
cards.a:
1. 5' capping (7-methylguanosine).
2. 3' polyadenylation (poly-A tail).
3. Splicing (intron removal).

cards.q: What is alternative splicing and its clinical importance?
cards.a: One gene → multiple protein isoforms. Dysregulation seen in cancers and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

cards.q: What are snRNPs and their role?
cards.a: Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins. Components of the spliceosome that remove introns.

cards.q: What is a frameshift mutation?
cards.a: Insertion or deletion of nucleotides not divisible by 3 → shifts reading frame. Usually leads to premature stop codon.

cards.q: Differentiate missense, nonsense, and silent mutations.
cards.a:
Missense: Changes amino acid.
Nonsense: Creates stop codon.
Silent: No change in amino acid (due to degeneracy).

cards.q: What is a transition vs transversion mutation?
cards.a:
Transition: Purine↔Purine or Pyrimidine↔Pyrimidine.
Transversion: Purine↔Pyrimidine.

cards.q: What DNA repair mechanism fixes UV-induced thymine dimers?
cards.a: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER). Defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum.

cards.q: What is the defect in Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC/Lynch syndrome)?
cards.a: Mismatch Repair (MMR) defect (MSH2, MLH1, etc.). Microsatellite instability.

cards.q: What repair pathway fixes double-strand breaks?
cards.a: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) (error-prone) or Homologous recombination (error-free, uses sister chromatid).

cards.q: What is the function of p53?
cards.a: “Guardian of the genome.” Activates DNA repair, cell cycle arrest (G1/S), or apoptosis if damage is severe.

cards.q: What is genomic imprinting?
cards.a: Gene expression depends on parent of origin (e.g., Prader-Willi vs Angelman syndrome — chromosome 15).

cards.q: What is anticipation in genetics?
cards.a: Increasing severity/earlier onset in successive generations. Seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g., Huntington, Myotonic dystrophy).

cards.q: Name three trinucleotide repeat disorders and their repeats.
cards.a:
1. Huntington (CAG).
2. Fragile X (CGG).
3. Myotonic dystrophy (CTG).

cards.q: What is the difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin?
cards.a:
Euchromatin: Loosely packed, transcriptionally active.
Heterochromatin: Tightly packed, inactive (e.g., Barr body).

cards.q: What is X-inactivation (lyonization)?
cards.a: Random inactivation of one X chromosome in females to achieve dosage compensation. Forms Barr body.

cards.q: What technique is used to detect specific DNA sequences?
cards.a: Southern blot (DNA), Northern blot (RNA), Western blot (protein).

cards.q: What is PCR? Key steps?
cards.a:
Polymerase Chain Reaction — amplifies DNA.
1. Denaturation (94°C).
2. Annealing (primers).
3. Extension (Taq polymerase).

cards.q: What is reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) used for?
cards.a: Detects and quantifies RNA (e.g., viral load, gene expression).

cards.q: What is the function of restriction endonucleases?
cards.a: Cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences. Used in cloning and RFLP analysis.

cards.q: What is a cDNA library vs genomic library?
cards.a:
cDNA: Made from mRNA (no introns, represents expressed genes).
Genomic: Entire genome with introns.

cards.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9?
cards.a: RNA-guided endonuclease for precise gene editing. Used in research and emerging gene therapy.

cards.q: What is the central dogma of molecular biology?
cards.a:
DNA → RNA → Protein.
Exceptions: Reverse transcription (RNA → DNA) in retroviruses.

cards.q: What are microRNAs (miRNAs) and their mechanism?
cards.a: Small non-coding RNAs that inhibit translation or cause mRNA degradation by binding 3' UTR.

cards.q: What is the difference between oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes?
cards.a:
Oncogenes: Gain-of-function (one mutated copy sufficient).
Tumor suppressors: Loss-of-function (both copies usually needed — Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis).

cards.q: Give examples of proto-oncogenes that become oncogenes.
cards.a: RAS (GTPase), MYC (transcription factor), HER2/neu (receptor tyrosine kinase), BCL-2 (anti-apoptotic).

cards.q: What is the Philadelphia chromosome?
cards.a: t(9;22) → BCR-ABL fusion gene (tyrosine kinase). Seen in CML and some ALL.

cards.q: What is imprinting defect in Prader-Willi syndrome?
cards.a: Deletion or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-13 (paternally imprinted genes silenced).

cards.q: What causes Angelman syndrome?
cards.a: Deletion or paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-13 (maternally expressed UBE3A gene lost).

cards.q: What is the most common mutation type causing cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: ΔF508 deletion (class II mutation) — misfolded CFTR protein degraded in ER.

cards.q: What is the function of the CFTR protein?
cards.a: ATP-gated chloride channel. Defective → thick mucus in lungs, pancreas, etc.

cards.q: What is the lac operon? Key components?
cards.a:
Inducible operon in E. coli.
Components: Promoter, Operator, lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase).
Repressed by lac repressor; induced by lactose/allolactose.

cards.q: What is catabolite repression in the lac operon?
cards.a: High glucose → low cAMP → inactive CAP (catabolite activator protein) → low transcription of lac operon even if lactose present.

cards.q: Differentiate inducible vs repressible operons with examples.
cards.a:
Inducible: Turned on by substrate (lac operon – lactose).
Repressible: Turned off by end product (trp operon – tryptophan).

cards.q: What are enhancers and silencers?
cards.a: Cis-acting regulatory sequences that increase (enhancers) or decrease (silencers) transcription. Can act over long distances; orientation-independent.

cards.q: What is the role of histone acetylation vs methylation?
cards.a:
Acetylation (by HATs): loosens chromatin → ↑ transcription (euchromatin).
Methylation: usually repressive (heterochromatin), but depends on site (H3K4 = active, H3K27 = repressive).

cards.q: What is DNA methylation? Clinical significance?
cards.a:
Addition of methyl groups to CpG islands by DNA methyltransferases → gene silencing.
Hypermethylation seen in tumor suppressor genes in cancer.

cards.q: What is genomic imprinting? Give examples.
cards.a:
Parent-of-origin specific gene silencing via methylation.
Prader-Willi (paternal deletion) vs Angelman (maternal deletion) on chr 15.

cards.q: What are CpG islands?
cards.a: Regions with high frequency of CpG dinucleotides, often in promoters. Unmethylated in active genes.

cards.q: Name key tumor suppressor genes and their functions.
cards.a:
Rb: G1/S checkpoint.
p53: DNA repair, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis.
APC: Wnt pathway (FAP).
BRCA1/2: DNA repair (homologous recombination).

cards.q: What is the two-hit hypothesis?
cards.a: Both alleles of a tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated for cancer to develop (Knudson). Applies to retinoblastoma, etc.

cards.q: What are proto-oncogenes? How do they become oncogenes?
cards.a: Normal genes that promote cell growth. Become oncogenes via mutation, amplification, or translocation (gain-of-function, dominant).

cards.q: Give examples of oncogene activation mechanisms.
cards.a:
1. Point mutation (RAS).
2. Gene amplification (HER2).
3. Translocation (BCR-ABL, c-MYC in Burkitt).

cards.q: What is microsatellite instability (MSI)?
cards.a: Defective mismatch repair → errors in microsatellite repeats. Seen in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).

cards.q: What is the Warburg effect?
cards.a: Cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis (even with O₂) for rapid ATP and biomass production.

cards.q: What are the functions of p53 in response to DNA damage?
cards.a: Activates DNA repair, arrests cell cycle at G1 (via p21), or triggers apoptosis (via BAX/PUMA) if damage is irreparable.

cards.q: What is Li-Fraumeni syndrome?
cards.a: Germline p53 mutation → high risk of multiple cancers (sarcomas, breast, brain, leukemia) at young age.

cards.q: What technique detects specific mRNA?
cards.a: Northern blot or RT-qPCR.

cards.q: What technique detects specific proteins?
cards.a: Western blot (immunoblotting).

cards.q: What is ELISA used for?
cards.a: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay — quantifies antigens or antibodies using enzyme-linked detection.

cards.q: What is FISH?
cards.a: Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization — detects chromosomal abnormalities (translocations, deletions, amplifications) using fluorescent probes.

cards.q: What is Sanger sequencing?
cards.a: Chain-termination method using dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs). Gold standard for targeted sequencing.

cards.q: What is next-generation sequencing (NGS)? Advantage?
cards.a: Massively parallel sequencing. Allows whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing rapidly and cheaply.

cards.q: What is a restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP)?
cards.a: Variation in DNA sequence that creates or abolishes restriction enzyme sites. Used in genetic linkage analysis.

cards.q: What vector is commonly used for cloning large DNA fragments?
cards.a: BAC (Bacterial Artificial Chromosome) or YAC for very large inserts.

cards.q: What is a plasmid? Key features for cloning?
cards.a: Small circular dsDNA in bacteria. Contains origin of replication, selectable marker (ampicillin resistance), multiple cloning site.

cards.q: What is recombinant DNA technology?
cards.a: Combining DNA from different sources using restriction enzymes, ligase, and vectors to produce proteins (e.g., insulin).

cards.q: What is cDNA? How is it made?
cards.a: Complementary DNA synthesized from mRNA using reverse transcriptase. Lacks introns.

cards.q: What is the difference between Southern, Northern, and Western blots?
cards.a:
Southern: DNA
Northern: RNA
Western: Protein

cards.q: What is RT-PCR used for clinically?
cards.a: Detecting RNA viruses (e.g., HIV, SARS-CoV-2), measuring gene expression.

cards.q: What does qPCR stand for and its use?
cards.a: Quantitative (real-time) PCR. Monitors amplification in real time for quantification.

cards.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9? Mechanism summary?
cards.a: Guide RNA directs Cas9 nuclease to cut specific DNA sequence. Allows gene knockout, knock-in, or editing.

cards.q: What are the main types of RNA?
cards.a: mRNA (messenger), rRNA (ribosomal), tRNA (transfer), miRNA, snRNA, lncRNA.

cards.q: What is RNA interference (RNAi)?
cards.a: siRNA or miRNA-mediated gene silencing via mRNA degradation or translational repression.

cards.q: What are chaperones? Example?
cards.a: Proteins that assist proper folding of other proteins. Heat shock proteins (Hsp70, Hsp60/chaperonins).

cards.q: What is the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway?
cards.a: Major pathway for degradation of intracellular proteins. Ubiquitin tags proteins for 26S proteasome.

cards.q: What diseases are associated with protein misfolding?
cards.a: Alzheimer (Aβ, tau), Parkinson (α-synuclein), prion diseases (PrP^Sc), cystic fibrosis (ΔF508 CFTR).

cards.q: What is heteroplasmy?
cards.a: Presence of both normal and mutant mtDNA in a cell. Explains variable phenotype in mitochondrial diseases.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of mitochondrial diseases?
cards.a: Maternal inheritance (sperm contribute negligible mitochondria).

cards.q: Give examples of mitochondrial diseases.
cards.a: MELAS, MERRF, Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), Kearns-Sayre syndrome.

cards.q: What is pharmacogenetics? Example with warfarin.
cards.a: Study of genetic variation affecting drug response. VKORC1 and CYP2C9 variants affect warfarin dosing.

cards.q: What is the function of topoisomerase inhibitors in chemotherapy?
cards.a: Prevent religation after strand breaks → DNA damage. Etoposide (Topo II), irinotecan (Topo I).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate?
cards.a: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase → blocks thymidine and purine synthesis → impairs DNA replication.

cards.q: What is the role of telomerase in cancer?
cards.a: Reactivation allows unlimited replication (immortalization) by maintaining telomere length.

cards.q: What is the Hayflick limit?
cards.a: Normal cells can divide only ~50 times before senescence due to telomere shortening.

cards.q: What are oncofetal antigens? Examples?
cards.a: Proteins expressed in fetal life and re-expressed in tumors. AFP (hepatocellular ca), CEA (colorectal).

cards.q: What is HER2/neu? Clinical importance?
cards.a: Receptor tyrosine kinase. Amplified/overexpressed in some breast cancers. Target of trastuzumab (Herceptin).

cards.q: What is imprinting control region (ICR)?
cards.a: Differentially methylated region that controls parent-specific gene expression in imprinted loci.

cards.q: What are cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)?
cards.a: Cyclins are regulatory proteins that activate CDKs. Different cyclin-CDK complexes drive specific phases of the cell cycle (e.g., Cyclin D-CDK4/6 for G1).

cards.q: What is the role of Rb in the cell cycle?
cards.a: Rb binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors in G1. Phosphorylation by Cyclin D/E-CDK releases E2F → S phase entry.

cards.q: What is the G1/S checkpoint primarily regulated by?
cards.a: p53 → p21 inhibits CDK2. Rb pathway.

cards.q: What is the function of p53 at the G1/S checkpoint?
cards.a: Detects DNA damage → induces p21 → inhibits CDK → cell cycle arrest for repair or apoptosis.

cards.q: Name the main phases of the cell cycle and key regulators.
cards.a: G1 (Cyclin D/E), S (Cyclin A), G2 (Cyclin A/B), M (Cyclin B-CDK1). Checkpoints at G1/S, G2/M, and spindle assembly.

cards.q: What is the spindle assembly checkpoint (M checkpoint)?
cards.a: Ensures all chromosomes are properly attached to mitotic spindle before anaphase. Involves MAD2, BubR1.

cards.q: What are the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis?
cards.a:
Intrinsic (mitochondrial): Bax/Bak, cytochrome c, Apaf-1, caspase-9.
Extrinsic: Death receptors (Fas/TNF), caspase-8.

cards.q: What is the role of Bcl-2 family proteins?
cards.a: Anti-apoptotic (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) vs pro-apoptotic (Bax, Bak, Bad). Regulate mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization.

cards.q: What is the function of caspases?
cards.a: Cysteine-aspartate proteases. Initiator (8,9) and executioner (3,6,7) caspases execute apoptosis.

cards.q: What is the Warburg effect in cancer cells?
cards.a: Preference for aerobic glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation, even in presence of oxygen. Provides biosynthetic intermediates.

cards.q: What are the hallmarks of cancer (molecular level summary)?
cards.a: Sustaining proliferative signaling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, enabling replicative immortality, inducing angiogenesis, activating invasion/metastasis.

cards.q: What is the molecular basis of retinoblastoma?
cards.a: Biallelic inactivation of Rb gene (two-hit hypothesis). Familial form has germline mutation.

cards.q: What is the APC gene and its pathway?
cards.a: Tumor suppressor in Wnt pathway. Mutation → β-catenin accumulation → transcription of growth genes (FAP, colorectal cancer).

cards.q: What is the function of BRCA1/BRCA2?
cards.a: DNA repair via homologous recombination. Mutations → breast, ovarian, prostate cancers.

cards.q: What is Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant mismatch repair gene defect (MLH1, MSH2, etc.) → microsatellite instability → colorectal, endometrial cancers.

cards.q: What is the Philadelphia chromosome translocation?
cards.a: t(9;22)(q34;q11) → BCR-ABL fusion → constitutively active tyrosine kinase (CML).

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of imatinib?
cards.a: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting BCR-ABL. First-line for CML.

cards.q: What post-translational modification is critical for Ras activation?
cards.a: Farnesylation (lipid modification) by farnesyltransferase. Target of some experimental cancer therapies.

cards.q: What is the role of MYC oncogene?
cards.a: Transcription factor that drives cell proliferation and metabolism. Amplified in many cancers (Burkitt lymphoma t(8;14)).

cards.q: What is the BCL-2 translocation in follicular lymphoma?
cards.a: t(14;18) → BCL-2 overexpression → inhibition of apoptosis.

cards.q: What are the major types of chromosomal translocations in cancer?
cards.a:
1. Promoter fusion (overexpression).
2. Fusion gene with new function (BCR-ABL).
3. Chimeric transcription factor.
